A.   Well, when everybody entered the gym, they put a blanket down and four young boys sat there.  They were between 10 and 14 years of age, I would say.  When I crossed into the free territory I immediately asked whether four kids had been released, and I was told that yes.  That means that if they hadn't released those four kids they would have killed to 80 years of age because people who were there had been brought in from Potocari.
Q.   Okay.  So what happened after you saw these kids were on the -- they were allowed to sit on a blanket.  What happened to everybody else as you were there?

A.   They would pick out prisoners to bring water for us, and they would bring water.  And then after a long period of time a delegation of officers or some other persons like that came, and one of them asked whether there was anybody there from the Zvornik municipality and nobody responded.  Then they ordered that four rows should get up.  Those were the elderly from Potocari.  And they told them to turn around, face the wall, and have their backs towards the door.  Then they called another four rows and then another four rows.  And when my turn came, when four of my rows got up, we faced in the other direction and our backs were turned towards the exit where there was Serbian soldiers and a woman. And then they brought a lot of cloth, and it went on until one of us prisoners said, "You must not kill these people." It was mostly young men standing at the door, 18 or younger, Serbian soldiers, and they all held their rifles in their hands like that.

And the one that uttered those words, he was maybe 25.  And then they said, "Well, who says so?"  And the man again repeated the same words.  And then they said, "Well, we'll see whether we must or we must not," and then they told them to get up.  He had black trousers on him and a shirt similar to mine.  They took him out of the gym.  We heard rifle shots and the man screamed, and then more shots and then silence. Then they took out a young man again, 20 to 25.  I don't know why they took him out.  Again we heard rifle shots and the man never re-appeared. They stopped the water from being brought in.  I guess they needed time to clear that away, and then they started putting blindfolds on us.  And we would go into this room that was L-shaped.  Before that people asked them, "Where are you taking these people?"  And they responded, "To Bijeljina, to a camp there."  Nobody put any questions after that.

Q.   Okay.  Let me stop you for just one minute.  In one of your statements within a year or so after the events, it appears from that -- in the statement that the people that were -- got up that said, "Don't kill any of us," that they were killed in the gym in front of you.  Is that correct, or is your recollection now that they were actually taken outside and that's when you heard shots?

A.   No, no.  I never said that he was killed in the gym.  He was taken out, and the other one was taken out as well.  Right there, I only saw them slap one man.  Why they slapped him, I don't know.  People addressed the soldiers.  They would say, "Soldiers."  And they would respond saying, "We are not soldiers.  We are Karadzic's Chetniks."  So nobody was killed there.  People were taken out in front of the school building.
Q.   And can you tell us, in this gym, how full was it with Muslims?
A.   Well, we had to sit with our knees against our chests, and there were between 500 and 1.000 people there.
Q.   So was there any empty space in this gym or was it pretty full up?
A.   There, when all of us were there in the gym, you couldn't throw a matchstick and have it fall on the floor, and that was before people started going out.
Q.   And how hot was it in that gym that you were there?
A.   It was so hot that people started complaining.  You could just hear a rumour, and then Serbian soldiers would fire on the wall to make them go quiet again.
Q.   And you mentioned that there was some elderly men from Potocari. So when you say "elderly," how old did you mean?
A.   Well, there was a man from my village, I knew him, he was 70. And these people were between 60- and 70-something.  I know that this one man from my village was 70.
Q.   And when you say from Potocari, what did you mean by that?

A.   Well, the people who had left with women and children as not fit for the army service, it was them, not just those who went to Orahovac. Everywhere, at every location, young and old alike were killed.
Q.   And how did you know that these men were from the group that went with the women and children to Potocari?  Did you know that at the time or is that something you learned later?

A.   No, no.  We knew immediately that those people had gone with women and children because they were so frail that they couldn't walk 5 kilometres in the whole day, let alone 100 kilometres from Srebrenica.
Q.   So can you give us any kind of a rough time estimate of when you actually first got to this school.  When your truck first pulled up to the school, do you know roughly what time of day it was?
A.   It was in the afternoon.  It was in the afternoon.  But I didn't have a watch on me, so I don't know what time it was.
Q.   And how long were you jammed in this gym until you were stood up and blindfolded and put in this L-shaped room?
A.   I don't know how long we spent there, but when I came out there was maybe one hour before it fell dark.  I don't know whether we were there for three hours, five hours.  I haven't got a clue.
Q.   Okay.  Tell us what happened in the L-shaped room and -- where you were taken.

A.   Well, they took two prisoners there and blindfolded them.  There was a woman standing there and two uniformed men.  The woman also wore uniform.  She gave a cup of water to every person after they had been blindfolded.  Why she did that, I don't know.  They made a kind of swing TAMtruck there.  When I boarded the truck there were two benches but they were not full.  I sat on the right-hand side.  When the truck became full and all the places on the benches were occupied, people were sitting down between the benches. I forgot to say that once they started taking people out, a soldier appeared with a red beret.  He went with every batch of people. I don't know whether there were two or three trucks, because once you have a blindfold you can't see anything. truck is so we can get TAMtruck in our mind. TAMtruck was used by farmers to transport produce and cattle.  It is good for small cattle.  It could perhaps accommodate two cows but not more, so mostly people from Bijeljina and Janja used these kind of trucks for the transportation of agriculture produce.
TAMtrucks as well with benches on the side?

A.   No, no.  The army never had this kind of trucks.  They had bigger TAMtrucks, but they confiscated these smaller ones from the farmers because they commandeered all kind of machinery from farmers.
Q.   Now, this door that you went out and were -- from a ramp into the truck, was this the same door you came in to the building or a different one?

A.   No, no, we entered through a different door and we went out through this door.  In 1999 I went to visit the scene, and that is when this door was -- was built and closed with concrete blocks because Zvornik municipality.
Q.   Who did you go there with in 1999?
A.   I went with this investigator named Ruez.
Q.   And that was an investigator from the ICTY, to your knowledge?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And when he took you to this school, were you able to recognise it?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Okay.  Now, once you were put in the back of this truck with your blindfold, what happened?

A.   The truck rode down an asphalt road for a short period of time. I felt that it went to the left.  After this short ride it stopped.  We were told to climb down, and that's what we did.  I looked in front of myself and I saw a dead man.  I have three children and immediately I thought about them, and I thought that I would have the same destiny like this man, that I'm not going to see my children ever again.  And I was -- I started praying to God and I started thinking in what way they are going to kill me. A burst of fire was heard coming from the left.  I fell down and my right arm was across the chest of another man.  When this burst of fire stopped, a man came, started walking among the people lying on the ground and shooting them in the head.  I have a little bruise here probably from the ground and the gravel that was on the road --
Q.   Okay.  Let me just interrupt you for the record.  I see you're pointing to some fingers on your right hand.
A.   Yes.
Q.   And you've told us you had a blindfold on.  How can you see anything with this blindfold, was it still on?
A.   No.  I didn't see this on my hand.  I only felt it.  But at that very moment, because I was looking down in front of myself, I saw this dead man.
Q.   So did you have the blindfold on when you looked down to see the dead man?
A.   Yes, yes.  I was just looking directly in front of me, because you couldn't see anything ahead.  That was a very sick -- thick cloth and it wasn't see-through.
Q.   And after the firing and you fell down, what happened?

A.   When everything stopped, when the shooting stopped, they started shouting, "Let's go and take their watches off."  I didn't have a watch and my left arm was beneath me, but then one of them said, "We're not going to do that," and they didn't.  In the meantime, as soon as a truck would arrive the same would be repeated.  You would hear a burst of fire and all this was going on until darkness fell.
Q.   Can you give us -- and -- just your rough estimate of how long this -- these executions were going on from the time you first got to this site?

A.   Well, it -- they definitely lasted until 11.00 in the evening because it lasted for quite some time after darkness fell.  Overall I don't know how long it started from the very -- how long it took from the very beginning.
Q.   Were there any lights around?

A.   There was an excavator there, and it was digging.  When I slowly removed my blindfold I saw this excavator opposite us.  When this was finished, they didn't have any more place and they all gathered around this machine, and this man who was in charge told them, "Let's go to this field where grass had been cut to kill all those people."  The man stopped the excavator and said, "If you leave, I'd like to go with you."
Q.   Did you ever hear any names mentioned by any of these men that were doing the shooting or were at the site?

A.   They mentioned the names Gojko, Vojo, that's how they were addressing one another, Risto.  This Gojko was my fellow worker from the company and we had known each other for 15 years.  Gojko thought that all the men were dead, and he said that he would like to be kissed by some of the men who were killed.  I recognised his voice when he said that.
Q.   Did you ever see his face while you were there?
A.   No, no.  It was dark.  It was night-time.  I couldn't see his face.
Q.   And how can you be sure it was this voice of this Gojko?

A.   Well, he had a very specific voice.  If you know someone for a long time you can recognise their voice everywhere, and as I said, we knew each other for 15 years.  And they also were addressing one another by name.

A.   Well, I said only those who were in mass graves had their limbs in different graves and maybe of -- it was necessary to dig in to three or four graves in order to put together one person and his body parts.
Q.   So have you been following the exhumations of these mass graves by the international community?
A.   No.  I only heard that the majority of these graves were dug out. They did find my brother, but not his complete body.
Q.   Okay.  I understand.

MR. McCLOSKEY: Q.   What else, if anything, did you hear Gojko say?
A.   Yes, he said, "Collect all your ammunition, let's go to this mowed field and let's shoot the people."  He seemed, he appeared, to be the person in charge.
Q.   And where were you when you heard him say this?
A.   Well, some 10 to 20 metres from him.

Q.   And you mentioned an excavator.  Can you describe to the Court what you mean by excavator, what kind of excavator -- or not the brand name, but there's lots of big digging equipment.  Can you tell us what it is you saw?
A.   Well, that is a construction machine used for digging trenches and canals.  It can also load cargo on but it has a small bucket, so it's different.  It's really a digger.
Q.   All right.  And did you see another kind of a machine there besides this excavator?

A.   Well, after this I saw a loader.  This loader came with the lights on because the excavator was turned in the opposite direction so the lights were only used -- the excavator lights were only used to actually throw some light on the area that is being excavated or dug up.
Q.   Now, what happened after this, after you saw this digging equipment?

A.   Well, when the digger, or rather, the loader arrived, it had the lights on and we were all lit up.  One of us was alive and he was on the other side, on the opposite side from where we were.  So he sort of stood up and ran into the woods.  They fired after him, and the driver of this digger turned the digger so that he could actually light up the area where the man fled into the woods.  And at that moment I moved and then he said, "Well, there's another man moving here."  Fortunately, they didn't hear him, and then I just lay -- I just took two long strides and I could feel some stones there.  And then I looked around.  When I saw that no one was going in my direction, I stood up.  And as I ran up this embankment, a stone-built embankment, I realised that it was really rail tracks there.  I ran up and I could hear a burst of fire being fired behind me.  I didn't see or hear the bullets actually hit the stones around me and I didn't feel being hit. I flew over the railway tracks, and then I just threw myself over the other side of the embankment.  I jumped up again on to my feet, and then I realised that there was a maise field not far off.  They were already very tall, the corn stalks.

I ran halfway, and then I thought they will start shooting because they will see the corn rustling.  And then I just threw myself on the ground, and then as I slithered through it, I realised that there was some stream or water somewhere, but I didn't see it.  The Serb soldiers went searching through the cornfield. They shot just randomly, I don't think -- and I didn't feel that anything hit me.  And then they turned back and went away. I could hear the shooting for a long time after that, and when everything was over, I got myself up from the cornfield.  There was a copse of trees not far from there, but I was very afraid as I left the cornfield into the open field, but there was no one there, fortunately, because had there been someone they would have caught me and killed me, I am sure.  And then I started moving but I didn't really know where I was going because I knew when they had brought us to the school, but from there onwards, I didn't know where I was. And then as I was walking along the paved road there was -- there were bodies there, but there were signs of life from one of these persons.  He was -- the sound that he was producing was inhuman.  It was almost like an animal squealing, but I couldn't really help him.

So I moved along and then I came across the railway tracks again, and then as I crossed them I realised that I was at the railway station in Orahovac. So I concluded that I was again heading in the direction of Zvornik.  So I re-traced my steps.  I went back and got on to the road again.  I didn't know where I was going.  I decided to go into the wood because I was afraid it would get light, because it was a summer night and they're not very long. I headed from there towards a home.  There was a light coming from there.  I didn't hear any sound, not even a dog barking, and then as I passed by a hut, I saw a person sleeping there with a rifle against the wall.  And then I went around that house, and again I had no idea where I was.  Soon after that it grew light.  I went through some villages that had been burnt down.  I know they were Bosniak villages because they had been burnt down.  I had no idea where I was going.  The sun was high up and I still had no idea where I was going.  But as I walked on, fortunately I was walking in the right direction, not in the opposite direction, and once I reached Krizevici where a store used to be, I knew -- I found my bearings, I knew where I was. So then I retraced my steps a bit.  I went backwards.  And then as I went up a slope, I saw that a mosque which used to be there had been destroyed.  And then I arrived in Seferovici.

I knew that because I had some relatives nearby, in a village nearby, and as I was there, there was a patrol that was walking there and they started shooting, but I managed to get through Seferovici, this village.  I walked across some grass. The houses were all burnt down.  And then as I crossed over that field, I realised that there was this village that I knew, that I was familiar with, because I had some relatives there. The grass was so high that I was wet almost up to my waist.  So then I decided to take a nap.  I lay down and slept for maybe an hour or two, I have no idea how long, but when I woke up I realised I hadn't eaten anything for a very long time because we were only given water, nothing else, since we had been detained.  Maybe I had a fruit or something but -- so then I went down to the village and I found a pear which was ripe.  There were some green buds or fruits on fruit trees, but I couldn't eat that.  There was only this one pear. So then I tried to find some clothes in the village -there was no one there because it had been burnt down - because I wanted a change of clothes because the shirt that I had on had a blood-stain because of the man who had leaned against me who had been shot.  So I wanted to make sure that I had clean clothes because had they found me like that, they would have known that I had escaped.

So I returned -- I started going back.  I headed back toward Baljkovica when it got dark and I found a house that remained almost intact.  It hadn't been completely burnt down.  The roof was -- had fallen in, but -- but the walls were still up.  And then when I arrived there there were three buses, Drinatrans buses that were going -- local buses that were transporting people back from -- towards Baljkovici.  The direction the buses were going was a Serb village --
THE INTERPRETER:  The interpreter did not hear the name of the village.

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] -- and then I decided to spend the night in that house.  And in the morning, when it got light, somebody threw something, flung a stone against the wall and said, "Get up."  So I got up and I just was expecting someone to barge the door --
MR. McCLOSKEY: Q.   Let me interrupt you for one second.  I'm sorry, you had mentioned a village just now but they weren't able to hear it.  Can you tell us what village you had just passed through?
A.   Well, I think it was Delici, that was the name of the village.  I know -- I was not from that village, but I know -- I have a general idea, and I think it's Delici.
Q.   Delici or Dulici?
A.   Delici.
Q.   Okay.  And now from this morning that someone threw a rock at you, how many more days did it take you to reach the Muslim territory?
A.   Well, had the road been clear it would have taken 15 to 20 minutes because I was already nearby, but the roads weren't clear.
Q.   So how long did it take you to manage to get away?

A.   Well, I actually took advantage of the situation then because the people who were going from Srebrenica had arrived at Baljkovica at that time, and had there not been a breakthrough at that time of the front line, those people would have ended the same way we had.  And then when they arrived there, the Serbs had withdrawn all their artillery from Baljkovica.  So I took advantage of that situation and sort of flew over to the other side.  I was so close.  There were some hundred metres or so where I could see the houses on the other side, but it was all a clearing and I was afraid that someone might notice me.

Q.   Okay.  So when you say the people from Srebrenica made a breakthrough through Baljkovica, are those people from Srebrenica, is that part of the column that you were speaking of earlier, the front of the column?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And were there -- was that where the weapons were?
A.   Well, most probably.  I don't know.  I wasn't with them.

Q.   All right.  And -- okay.  Now let me take you back briefly to something you mentioned.  You said you didn't get any food during this time, but let me ask you when you were at Sandici, the area next to this asphalt road where you surrendered, did you see the Serb forces providing anyone with any food?

A.   No.  There were people there, wounded people.  They were crying out, asking for them to be -- for their wounds to be dressed, but then they moved and went on to another house and they never returned.
Q.   Who were moved on to another house?
A.   Well, the wounded people were taken to a house there.  There were some houses there some 200 metres away from us.
Q.   And did you see any of the Muslims that were in that field with you near Sandici get treated with any kind of first aid or medical or receive any help of any kind?
A.   No, no.  They just offered a bottle of liquor and they offered a few people to have a swig and maybe a cigarette or two, but there was no food or any medical assistance provided.
Q.   Was there some water provided at Sandici?
A.   Yes, they did bring water for us.

A.   No.  For the entire period since we had been captured, no one had seen a crumb of food.  They did give us water, not that evening but on the next day, both in Bratunac and in Orahovac.

Q.   Okay.  So just to be clear, once you got to the school in Orahovac, before you were put in an execution line, did anyone give anybody any food in that gym or any medical attention of any sort that you saw?
A.   No, nobody.  They just put a bucket for people to relieve themselves and there was nothing else.  They did bring water, but there wasn't enough for everybody to fill themselves up.

A.   No.  They did not write down any of the prisoners.  I don't know about what happened in other locations.  This is why the Serbs are claiming that it wasn't that number of people who got killed.  They don't know exactly whom they killed and how many.  They could have killed people of any ethnicity.  They asked whether there were any Serbs among us, but there were none.

A.   No, never.
Q.   They took you away in the direction of Keraterm in a mini-bus, if I have understood you correctly?
A.   Yes, you have.
Q.   The man who drove you there didn't allow anyone to stop you, maltreat you, or abuse you; is that correct?

A.   Well, he had to stop because we reached a barricade and had to turn back.  But he didn't want anyone to get off the mini-bus, although they asked for at least two persons to get out of the mini-bus.  But the driver didn't want to let these two people out.  He said he'd return them later, but he had to go to Prijedor for an interrogation with them. Q.   You don't know who that person is, to this very day?
A.   No.  I couldn't know his name.  He was wearing civilian trousers and a sort of camouflage shirt.

A.   I didn't hear about any one person having organised this, but it's quite natural that it was the Serbian forces who were behind its organisation.
Q.   While you were in Keraterm, you were taken away for interrogation?
A.   Yes.

A.   No, I don't.

A.   Yes.  He was in civilian clothing, but as for being an inspector, well, I don't know.  Perhaps he just an ordinary citizen, a peasant.  I don't know.
Q.   The subject of his interrogation, what he interrogated you about and what you did there; is that correct?
A.   Yes.
Q.   He also asked you how it was possible for you to reach Prijedor in April 1992?
A.   No, he didn't ask me about that.
Q.   And, by the way, did you go there by bus; and how did you travel in April 1992?
A.   I haven't understood your question.

Q.   I'll try and rephrase it.  I'm interested in part of your trip when you travelled between Derventa, which was under the control of the , which was under the control of the Serbian forces at the time.  How did you travel between those two points?
A.   I said I travelled by bus.  But as for the route the bus took, whether it drove down the main road or byroads, I don't know.  But in any .
Q.   On that occasion, no one forced you to give any kind of statement.  What you said, you said of your own free will?
A.   Yes.  They asked me whether I had anything in my bag, what do you have in your bag, they asked for my ID, and that was it.
Q.   When you were interrogated by this civilian in Keraterm, did anyone beat you there or did anyone ask you to state something that did not correspond to the truth?
A.   No, not in the course of the interrogation.

A.   Yes.
Q.   During that period of time, were you able to see whether Keraterm was under military or civilian supervision?
A.   I think it was under military supervision because they were wearing camouflage uniforms.  But, in fact, I didn't know whether the police had perhaps changed their uniforms
Q.   Your conclusion is based on the type of uniforms that the guards were wearing; is that correct?
A.   I couldn't have concluded that on any other basis.

A.   I heard that he was a Serb.  As for his full name, I never found out what it was, and I never tried to find out what it was.
Q.   Did you at any point in time find out that he was sentenced to 31 years in prison in a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

A.   You mean if they left -- if they exited before the shooting started?

Q.   Good afternoon, Mr. Begic.  Could you introduce yourself with your full name and your age, please.
A.   Good afternoon.  My name is Rajif Begic.  I was born on 23rd September 1967.  So I'm 45.

A.   Yes.  They call me Raho.

A.   Yes.  I was born and grew up in the village of Plevci, Sanski Most municipality.

A.   Yes.  That's Sanski Most municipality.

A.   Yes.
Q.   And directing your attention to the lower right-hand portion of the map, do you see the area in which you lived?
A.   Yes.  Villages Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Begici, Kenjari.  That's the area where I lived, in the lower right corner.

MS. BIBLES: Q.   Could you describe for us in the time period before the conflict what the relationships were like between Muslims and Serbs in your area?

A.   Yes.  In the village of Kljevci and with other villages around Kljevci, interpersonal relations were very good.  We grew up in villages with a mixed population.  We went to school together.  We socialised among ethnic communities, and before the war there had been no incidents on a nationalist grounds.
Q.   What is the ethnicity of your godparents?
A.   They are Serbs.
Q.   And could you tell us who they are?
A.   Yes.  Vid Krlic and Andza Krlic.  Our neighbours from Begici village.
Q.   Did you have a close relationship with them up through 1992?

A.   You could say so.  We were close.  We shared some agricultural machinery.  We owned them jointly.  We were friends.  They were my godparents, my godmother -- my godmother cut my hair when I was born, and according to our customs, thus, she same my godmother.
Q.   I'd like to turn your attention to May of 1992.
MS. BIBLES:  And Your Honours, I am going to be limiting my questions in this regard in reliance on adjudicated facts 1141 to 1144.

A.   My neighbours from Begici village handed over some weapons.  I didn't have any.
Q.   Were you able to hear the radio broadcasts directing Muslims to surrender weapons?

A.   No.  There were no such actions.

A.   It was the 25th of May.

A.   It was a part of the 6th Krajina Brigade that was based in the primary school, the four-year school, in Kljevci.
Q.   Do you know who the commander of that unit was in -- in May of 1992?
A.   Yes.  The commander of that unit was Mile Mijatovic, and he once visited us at the hamlet.  He introduced himself, so we knew who commanded that unit.
Q.   Do you know approximately what date he came to your village?
A.   I can't tell you the exact date, but it was a couple of days before the 25th.  Perhaps the 23rd or the 21st.
Q.   Can you tell us how he introduced himself to you and your family?

A.   Yes.  One day, accompanied by a soldier, both of them armed, we -- they came to our house with the intention of meeting all the residents of that village.  He said where he hailed from, whose son he was, and we knew that, although he wasn't living in Kljevci by that time. We knew his father.  And that conversation over coffee was not long.  He told us a couple of things about the situation, and then he left.
Q.   Did he say what army he was a commander in?
A.   Yes.  He said he had a unit from the 6th Krajina Brigade that was based at the school, which we had not known, and he said he was in charge of that part of Kljevci.
Q.   Did he say if he was with the JNA or the VRS or what military organisation?
A.   He did not tell us exactly the name of his unit.  He just said it was the 6th Krajina Brigade.  I did not hear him mention the VRS or the JNA.
Q.   Do you know who the komandant for the 6th Krajina Brigade was in 1992?
A.   Yes.  The commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade was Branko Basara.
Q.   And how is it that you know that?

A.   Well, after doing my military service, I was, myself, part of the reserve force of the 6th Krajina Brigade.  We all knew that, as far as the reserve force is concerned, our area was covered by the 6th Krajina Brigade. Just before the events, a month or two before, Branko Basara attended a meeting in Tomina, where he met locals from the surrounding villages, where he introduced himself.  He was wearing a uniform.  And the issue came up of where to put up some units and where to deploy some tanks and howitzers in the area, so that's when I met him.
Q.   And I don't believe that I've asked you this yet, but what is your ethnicity?
A.   I'm a Muslim, a Bosniak.
Q.   At the end of May 1992, did you come to know a soldier whose last name was Palija?
A.   Yes.  I met a soldier by the name of Jadranko Palija.
Q.   What was your understanding as to where he came from?

A.   I did not know that soldier, Jadranko Palija before.  Once, driving my tractor by a Serb check-point, I was stopped by my Serb neighbours, and Jadranko Palija was among them. They talked to me briefly while he searched the tractor checking whether I had any weapons in there, and I heard someone address him as Jadranko.  At that time I did not know his last name, Palija.
Q.   And did you later come to understand where he had come from?

A.   Yes, I think it was already on the next day when my godmother Andza, passing by, stopped at our house for coffee and he said that a soldier was visiting her house by the name of Jadranko Palija and that perhaps he had a thing for her daughter.  So that's the first time I heard his last name.
Q.   Is that how you learned where he came from?
A.   Yes.  When she was talking about him, she stressed that he lived and he was assigned to be in that locality.
Q.   And by that locality, was that your area?
A.   Yes.  I mean that locality.  More precisely, that first check-point that was put up next to Begici village.  He was assigned to man that check-point.

JUDGE ORIE:  For the completeness of the record, I notice that on the one screen the numbering of the lines is slightly different from the other one, but I think it is clear it is the words before it says "at that time I did not know his last name, Palija." Please proceed.
MS. BIBLES:  Thank you. Q.   The -- can you describe for us what the soldier, Palija's attitude towards the Muslims in the area was?

A.   Well, I did not see that soldier again after those days.  That was my first meeting with him, and then the next time I saw him it was already 31st of May, so I don't know if he had had any contacts in the meantime with my neighbours.
Q.   During the time-period from the 25th of May to the 31st of May, can you describe what life was like for you and your family?

A.   Yes.  After this first incursion of soldiers into our hamlet, until the 31st, we lived in fear.  On the 25th, when they entered the hamlet, they mistreated and beat people.  And in the days that followed, fear reigned, and we were completely at a loss what to expect.
Q.   Where were you when your village was attacked on the 25th of May of 1992?

A.   On the 25th, when the troops were coming into our hamlet, I was outside my house with my brother.  When they came by, it was in fact a young man who was running ahead of them, saying, The army is coming.  My junior -- my younger brother, Munib Begic, and I ran to the river to hide there, not far from the house.
Q.   Were you able to see or hear what was going on with your village?
A.   We were not able to see, but we could hear everything.  Perhaps not every word, but we could clearly hear what was going on around our houses.
Q.   Can you describe just briefly what it was that you were able to hear from the river?

A.   Yes.  We could hear our old aunt trying to defend her old husband, Huso, who was 75.  And next to them we could hear small children crying.  We could hear soldiers shouting, Get into the garage.  We're going to kill you now.  There were many voices at the same time.
Q.   How long did the attack last?
A.   Not long.  Not longer than an hour.
Q.   I'm now directing your attention to the 31st of May of 1992.  I'd like you to think about the soldiers that entered your village on that date.  Were there soldiers that you did not know?
A.   On that day, the 31st of May, I recognised some of the soldiers whom I had known from before, from the town and school, but most of them were not familiar.
Q.   Can you describe for us whether you knew the soldier who ordered the separation of women and children from the men?
A.   No, I did not know that soldier.  All I could see was that he was in command of that unit that was in Begici on that day.
Q.   Was there any fighting or resistance from the Muslims in the community?
A.   No.
Q.   Can you describe what happened to the men in your community as the separations occurred?

A.   Yes.  When the locals from Dizdarevici and Donji Begici were brought to us, I lived in Gornji Begici, the men who were found in the basement of Ekrem Begic were lined up outside the house.  As we were coming to Gornji Begici, it was ordered already that women and children should go to one side, whereas the men should form a column to join the men who had already been lined up.
Q.   And did the men do as they were told?
A.   Yes.  Yes, we did as we were told.  We had to line up.
Q.   And can you describe how the column was organised, the column of men?

A.   After separating the women and children, and even one underaged boy managed to join the group of women and children with his mother, they lined us up in a column two by two and told us to go towards Vinogradi.
Q.   How many armed soldiers escorted your group of men away?
A.   Our column that was going towards Vrhpolje was escorted by many armed soldiers.
Q.   Do you know who the leader of that group of soldiers was?
A.   The one who was in charge of escorting the column was Jadranko Palija.
Q.   At that time did you know any of the other soldiers that he was commanding?
A.   Yes.  I recognised some of the young men who were from Sanski Most, from the town.
Q.   Could you describe for us if you knew where you were going?
A.   Yes.  While we were still standing in Begici, the officer who was in charge of those soldiers on that day said the soldiers would escort us river where buses were waiting for us.
Q.   Approximately how far did you -- would you go from Begici to the bridge?
A.   At least 1 kilometre.
Q.   Can you describe for us the ages in your group, the ages of the Muslim men?  Just roughly.  The youngest and the oldest.

A.   Yes.  The youngest in the group was called Enes Dizdarevic, and at the time he was between 15 and 16 years old.  Edin Begic, my youngest brother, had been put aside with his mother because he seemed younger but he was the same age.  The oldest one was Sacir Begic who was over 70 years old, and there was Miralem Celic [as interpreted], who was perhaps a year or two younger.
Q.   As your group walked towards the bridge, did you go by some other soldiers?
A.   Yes.  Not far from the Begici hamlet that we were moving away from, we came across a group of soldiers who were resting by the road that we were travelling down.
Q.   And how did they react to your group?

A.   Jadranko stopped our group there, and then these soldiers, about 30 of them, insulted us, cursed us.  Someone even said that we should be killed there on the spot.  But they did not beat us on that occasion.
Q.   And how long did you stay in that location?
A.   Not long.  A few minutes.
Q.   And which direction did you go from there?
A.   After that, Jadranko Palija ordered the column to move on in the same direction, towards Vinogradine about 100 metres away from that road.
Q.   Were you able to move at the pace that you wanted to -- to move, or you and the group?

A.   Yes.  We were ordered to maintain a steady pace, although we had to bring these old people along with us too.  Because at one point in time, Jadranko Palija said that if someone shooted at the column from the surrounding villages, they would all kill us.  And that is why it was necessary for us to move rapidly.  Some were not able to keep up and we therefore had to help them.
Q.   All right.  Who had the most trouble keeping up?

A.   Sacir Begic and Miralem Ceric found it most difficult.  Miralem, after about 100 metres, had pain and felt pain in the heart and his son tried to take care of him.  We had to carry Sacir Begic.  Irfan and myself grabbed him by the arms and helped him, while the other people in the column were able to move ahead on their own.
Q.   While you were moving towards the bridge in this column, could you describe for us what was happening in the area?

A.   Yes.  As we approached the Hrustovac [as interpreted] station where there were a number of houses, we noticed that all the houses were on fire.  You could see a weapon firing.  You could see soldiers sitting by the road.  Some were cursing.  Others drinking.  Some were stealing cars or items from cars.  It was ugly.  An ugly scene.
Q.   How many smaller bridges did you cross before getting to Vrhpolje bridge?

A.   Yes, as we were approaching Hrustovac station there was a small bridge over the Glibaja river, that we then had to cross a bridge over the Sanica river.  That was in Hrustovo station.  And then we headed onto this other bridge.
Q.   In that area that you've just described --
THE INTERPRETER:  Near Vrhpolje, interpreter's correction.  A bridge near Vrhpolje.
MS. BIBLES:  Thank you. Q.   After crossing that area, could you describe for us how Miralem Ceric was doing?

A.   Yes, at that point in time, when we arrived at Hrustovac station we could see that Miralem Ceric was out of breath, and he was breathing with difficulty and it would have been good for him to have a break.  He was breathing with difficulty and moving with difficulty, although his son Enes was helping him to -- to walk.
Q.   Can you tell the Judges what, if anything, Palija did as a result of his difficulties?

A.   Yes.  At one point in time when we were crossing the -- a bridge over the Sanica river, right by the bridge on the left-hand side there was a slaughter-house, an abandoned slaughter-house.  At that point in time, as we were passing by that slaughter-house, Jadranko took Miralem Ceric and his son Enes aside.  In fact, he took them into that old slaughter-house.  When the three of them entered the slaughter-house, I saw Jadranko Palija taking out his pistol and following them inside, in fact.  I then heard a shot, and I saw Jadranko Palija coming out of the slaughter-house and putting the pistol back into its holster.  He then joined the column which hadn't stopped advancing.
Q.   Did you ever see either of these two men again?
A.   No, I didn't.
Q.   Did Palija take anyone else from the column after that?
JUDGE FLUEGGE:  Before you move to that question.  May I ask you to clarify.  Sorry.  You said you heard a shot.  One shot or more shots?

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] As I said, at that point in time, all the houses in the vicinity of the bridge were on fire and the bricks were actually cracking.  I heard a shot which was a pistol shot.  I'm sure that I heard one shot.  I didn't hear any other shots.  Perhaps because of the noise being produced by the houses that were on fire and by the bricks that were cracking.  But I am certain that I heard one shot being fired.
JUDGE FLUEGGE:  Thank you for that.
MS. BIBLES: Q.   Did Palija take anyone else from your column after that?

A.   Yes.  The column continued towards the Vrhpolje bridge and then we had to get to the main road that was about 250 metres from that location.  And at the exit that leads to the main road, Jadranko took Ismet Kurbegovic out of the column.  He took him to the other side of the road and killed him.
Q.   Did he -- did Palija say anything to Ismet before he killed him?

A.   Yes.  Jadranko took him aside.  He pointed his gun at him, and he said, For the last time, I'm asking you, where is your sniper?  Ismet said he did not have a sniper rifle of any kind, and this man then shot him.
Q.   Did you actually see the shot?
A.   Yes, I did.
JUDGE MOLOTO:  Sorry, Madam Bibles.  The shot or the shooting?
MS. BIBLES:  I'm sorry.  I will rephrase that to the shooting. Q.   Did you see the shooting?
A.   He killed him with one shot from the gun.
Q.   Was this the same pistol that you saw him holster a few minutes before?
A.   Yes, it was the same one.
Q.   Did Palija come back to your group at that point?
A.   Yes.  This all happened quite quickly.  The column hadn't really moved very far, and you could see him walking -- walking by with the column.
Q.   And what happened to Ismet's body?
A.   His body remained lying by the road, by a stop sign.  His body remained lying there.
Q.   When you came within 10 metres of the Vrhpolje bridge, could you see who was on the bridge?

A.   Yes.  From a certain distance you could see that there were a lot of soldiers on the bridge.  It wasn't really possible to see them clearly until we had actually reached the bridge.  Having reached the bridge, I could recognise some of those soldiers.
Q.   Were there buses on the bridge when you could first see it?
A.   I didn't see any.
Q.   As you got very close to the bridge, did any vehicles come alongside your group?

A.   Yes.  At one point in time, just before we reached the bridge, a military van, a small military van, arrived from the direction of Kljuc. There was one driver in it.  Though the van was advancing at the same speed as the column, and then the driver in the van told Jadranko Palija to get in and sit down to his right.
Q.   Can you describe what happened after he got in the vehicle?

A.   After Jadranko Palija got into the van, the column continued advancing on the left-hand side, and at that point in time Irfan Begic and myself were still helping Sacir Begic to walk.  Elmedin Begic instinctively grabbed Sacir Begic to help him move, and then Jadranko Palija who was sitting in the van called out to Irfan Begic and told him to move in front of the van and to go to the other side, the side on which he was sitting.  When Irfan Begic crossed over to the other side of the road in front of the van, I had a look to the right, to my side, and I saw that Jadranko Palija didn't say anything, but when Irfan arrived by the window, he shot him from his pistol.
Q.   At that point, what were you thinking?
A.   Yes, we were terrified by what we had seen.  Appalled by it.  We had to go to the bridge.  We had to continue to the bridge.

Q.   As you -- after you lined up, what did they have you do next?
A.   After we had lined up, we were ordered to take our shoes off and our clothes.  Not all of our clothes, but most of them.  And that's what we did.
Q.   All right.  And could you describe for us, as you did that, what the soldiers were doing?

A.   Yes.  As soon as we started approaching the bridge, they started cursing and maltreating us.  And then when all the people had taken their clothes off, one or two soldiers searched the people who were lined up there.  They asked us whether we had any money on us or any weapons, and they asked us to display what we had, if we had anything, and then they started beating certain people, certain individuals, on the bridge.
Q.   When you finished -- which clothing did you take off?

A.   I took off my trousers, my shoes, some remained in their trousers.  Some didn't take their shoes off.  Well, in fact, everyone took their shoes off.  But, on the whole, there were a lot of clothes piled up on the bridge.  Some would remain wearing two T-shirts, two shirts.  They didn't order us to take everything off.
Q.   And what were you still wearing?

Q.   What were you thinking at that point in time?

A.   We were frightened.  We had been beaten up.  It was cold.  We were no longer thinking about buses arriving there.  We were just waiting to see what the fate of the group would be.  We'd been abandoned to our fate.
