JUDGE ROBINSON:  Private session?  Yes.  Public session, let's go into public session, then.
[Open session] THE REGISTRAR:  We are back in open session, Your Honours.
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
WITNESS:  WITNESS VG-014 [Witness answered through interpreter]
JUDGE ROBINSON:  You may sit.
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Thank you.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Mr. Groome?
MR. GROOME:  I note that the blinds are still down.  Your Honour, this witness is the subject of protective measures, and I'd ask the usher to please hand a pseudonym sheet to the witness.
Examination by Mr. Groome: Q.   Witness VG-014, the usher is now showing you a sheet.  I'd ask you to take a look at it and ask you is that your name on that sheet?
A.   Yes, it is.
Q.   Is that your date of birth on that sheet?
A.   Yes, it is.
Q.   Could I ask you to sign your name to that sheet?
A.   Yes.

Q.   The Chamber has ordered certain protective measures with respect to you and these are that we shall refer to you as VG-014 during the course of your testimony and the image of your face will be distorted so that you cannot be recognised.  If you look down on that sheet, there is a name of a person with the pseudonym of VG-032 next to the name.  Is that the name of a person who you are likely to refer to in the course of your testimony today?
A.   It is.
MR. GROOME:  Your Honour at this time I would tender the pseudonym sheet into evidence as a sealed exhibit.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Admitted.
THE REGISTRAR:  Your Honours the exhibit will become P1 under seal.
MR. GROOME: Q.   VG-014, in the spring of 1992, can you describe for us where in general terms you lived, not your house address, but the area in which you lived?
A.   In 1992, I lived at Bikavac, which is a neighbourhood distant , some 300 to 500 metres.  I lived there with my family, with my wife and my minor daughter.
Q.   How old was your daughter at the time?
A.   At that time, my daughter was three and a half years old.
Q.   Did there come a time in the spring of 1992 that you left with your family, you left your home in Visegrad?
A.   Yes.
Q.   What is your best memory of when you left your home?
A.   I believe that that was in March or April 1992, when I left and went to Gorazde.
Q.   Are you familiar with an event in which a large amount of water was released from the hydroelectric dam south of the town?
A.   Yes.
Q.   When did you leave in relation to that event?
A.   I left immediately after that event.  I left town immediately thereafter.
Q.   And why did you decide to leave Visegrad and go to Gorazde?
A.   Well, you know, the Uzice Corps was about to enter Visegrad, and we were afraid of it.  We were scared that it might commit some wrongdoings and for the sake of my own safety, I left the town.
Q.   Did there come a time when you returned to Visegrad?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And around when, approximately when was that?
A.   I think that it was at the end of April 1992.
Q.   And what made you decide to return to Visegrad?
A.   Well, I decided to do that because the then-authorities probably in negotiations with the then-authorities of Visegrad, decided to send us back because ostensibly, our security was guaranteed.
Q.   Was there any announcement made with respect to people's jobs and the necessity for them to return?
A.   Well, you see, there was no written notice to that effect, but it was said orally that whosoever failed to return to their jobs would be fired.
Q.   When you said orally, how did you learn about this statement that people would be fired if they did not return to their jobs?
A.   Well, quite a few of us had the work obligation, so one could hear such stories, a colleague would tell a colleague and that colleague another colleague and so.
Q.   How did you get back to Visegrad?
A.   This was organised, the return to Visegrad was organised, by buses.
Q.   And did you return with your wife and your child?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Did there come a point in time in your return to Visegrad where the bus was stopped?
A.   Yes.  At a number of check-points, in fact.
Q.   Can I ask you to focus on the first one?  Can you tell us where it was?

A.   The first check-point was at the settlement of Medzedza.  There we were stopped and we were ordered out of the bus and we were told to take out of the bus all our things, to open our bags, and to pour the content of the bags on the ground.
Q.   And where was this first check-point in relation to the town centre of Visegrad?
A.   The first check-point was -- one of them was at the old bridge and the other one was at Nezuci.
Q.   This first one I think you mentioned, I think you said Medzedza, how far out of the town was that?
A.   Around 11 kilometres, I think.
Q.   And you mentioned people making everyone get out of the bus.  Can you describe those people or do you know the organisation that they belonged to?
A.   Well, this was the JNA troops, with some Serb locals.  It was a mixture.
Q.   Now, you've made reference to several check-points.  Can you simply tell us how many check-points in total you encountered on your trip from Gorazde until the time you returned to your home?
A.   I believe that, if my memory serves me well, that I mentioned five check-points, namely Medzedza, Nezuci, the old bridge, and the one outside new hotel in Visegrad and the one at Bikavac.
Q.   Was your -- were you ever required to show your identification papers at any of these check-points?

A.   Yes, at every check-point, they asked us to produce our identity cards and they had some sorts of lists against which they checked our papers and in respect of me, they said, in respect of me personally, "This is not him.  He is not on this list."
Q.   And that happened at every check-point?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Drawing your attention specifically to the check-point in front of the new hotel, who manned or who staffed that particular check-point?

A.   At that check-point, outside the Novi hotel, the new hotel in Visegrad, there was standing a soldier by the name of Oliver Krsmanovic, who checked my papers very often.  He was in a camouflage uniform and wore a kokarde with a two-headed eagle, and of armaments he had a heckler gun.
Q.   Were there any JNA soldiers present at this particular check-point?
A.   Yes, they could be noticed there.
Q.   When you returned to your home, could I ask you to describe what you found there?
A.   When I returned to my home, I saw that the door had been broken, the house had been searched, not only my house but the entire settlement had been treated as it were in this way.
Q.   The particular settlement that you lived in, was it predominantly one ethnicity or another or was it mixed?
A.   It was mixed.  There were Serbs and there were Muslims living there.
Q.   Were the Serb homes that you saw, were they similarly damaged when you entered your neighbourhood?
A.   No.
Q.   So the damage was confined to the Muslim homes?
A.   Yes, it was.
Q.   Now, VG-014, did there come a time when you returned to your job?
A.   Yes.
Q.   If you are able to tell us the place where you worked without compromising your identity, I'd ask you to do so.
A.   I worked for a construction company, and my actual workplace was .
Q.   So it was essentially in the centre of the town?
A.   Well, not exactly in the very centre, but a bit farther away, the seat of the company was in the town proper; but my workplace where I worked was about 2 kilometres away from that spot.
Q.   When you were going to and from work, did you have to go through check-points?
A.   Yes, I had to.
Q.   And were the procedures that you've already described, were the procedures similar on these repeated occasions that you went through the check-points?  Did you hear the question?
A.   I didn't have the translation.

Q.   Let me repeat the question.  You've mentioned that you've -- you went through check-points to get to work.  Was the procedure that you've described for us already, was that same procedure followed when you went through the check-points to and from work?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Can you describe what the conditions were like at work when you returned there?
A.   The conditions were not good.  We worked under stress.  It wasn't safe to work, and you could even see soldiers passing by and things like that, so we were afraid.
Q.   You've said it was not safe to work.  Could I ask you to explain what you mean precisely by that?
A.   It wasn't safe because people would enter the company premises and they took people away.  They executed them.  We didn't feel safe. And we had to work.
Q.   And the people that were taken away from the workplace, were they of the same ethnicity?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And what was that?
A.   They were Muslim.
Q.   Was there any logic that you could decipher with respect to who was taken away and when?
A.   Well, the logic was probably because we were Muslims.  I don't see any other logic.
Q.   I mean in terms of seniority or the place or the role that someone had in the community.  Was there any logic to distinguish between the order in which Muslims were taken away?

A.   Look, first they took away people who did have some important positions and they probably did that so that they couldn't organise the people, and then when they finished that, then they moved to the people who were less educated.
Q.   Did there come a time when you decided or reached the conclusion that it was no longer safe for you to go to work?
A.   Yes.
Q.   How long was the period of time from when you returned to work and when you decided you could no longer go to work safely?
A.   I think that this was for a month or so.  That was about the length of the period.
Q.   What did you do when you stopped going to work?
A.   I was hiding close to the house in a small wood.
Q.   And were you hiding alone or with other people?  Please don't tell us the names of the people but just, if you were, how many people.
A.   Yes.  There were three of my neighbours there too.
Q.   How did you eat or change your clothes?
A.   Our wives had organised things in such a way that at favourable times, they would bring us food and clothing.
Q.   And did your wife remain in your home with your child?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Did your wife give you information about what was taking place in the town and in the Bikavac area?
A.   Yes.  She said that the White Eagles were going through the settlement or the neighbourhood and were taking people away.
Q.   Did there come a time when you did, in fact, simply return to your home, leave the woods and return to your home?
A.   Yes.  I think that this was after about 10 days of hiding.
Q.   And why did you stop hiding in the woods?
A.   We couldn't take the conditions of the hiding any longer, and I thought that because I wasn't any criminal or I hadn't done anything bad, I didn't think that anyone would take me away.
Q.   Did there come a time when you were forcibly taken from your home?
A.   Yes.
Q.   How many nights had you spent in your home between the time you returned to your home and the time that you were forcibly taken from your home?
A.   Only one night.
Q.   And that one night, where did you stay?
A.   In the attic of my house.
Q.   Can you please describe for us what happened the day you were forcibly taken from your home?

A.   Yes.  This was on the 7th of June 1992, in the evening, around 5.30 p.m. I was sitting at home and actually my wife saw through the kitchen that some soldiers were moving around through the neighbourhood and were searching the houses, and she suggested that I hide, but I refused to do that.  Somebody knocked on the door.  I said to a woman who to go and see who it is and to say that there was no one at home, but when she went outside, probably because she was afraid, she couldn't speak, and I heard someone say that he would enter the house to check.  And I was sitting there when Milan Lukic entered with a sniper in his hand, and he was -- his face was blackened and he had a Blue Beret on his head and he was wearing a blue uniform, and he had the kokarde and the double-headed eagle on the cap and he had the same insignia on his chest.
Q.   Let me ask a few questions here, just to ensure that the record is clear as to your testimony. How many people entered your home that day?
A.   Only Milan Lukic came inside the house that day, and one of his soldiers was outside.

Q.   You're using the name of the person or calling this person by name.  Did you know this person from before this day? . .  I'm talking about the person you're referring to, Milan Lukic.  Did you know him before this day?
A.   Yes.
MR. GROOME: Q.   What was the name of the school that you attended?
A.   We went to secondary school together.
Q.   Was he in the same year of school as you?
A.   I think that he was in the same year, but we weren't in the same class.
Q.   Do you know what programme of study he was taking?
A.   I think it was the metal processing trade.  I don't know if he was going to learn -- if he was learning to be a welder or something like that
Q.   And for what length of time were you in the same school as this person you're referring to as Milan Lukic?
A.   We were together for the first two years.
Q.   And did there come a --
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Give us the years, if you can.
MR. GROOME: Q.   Can you tell us the years that you were in school with Lukic?
A.   Well, just give me a moment.  In 1985, I completed school, the third level, maybe 1983, 1984, I think that's the year that that would be.
Q.   Did there come a time when he left school?
A.   Yes.  I think this was in the second year of high school sometime, or secondary school.
Q.   And did you know where he went?
A.   I heard that he went to Obrenovac, to be in the police.
Q.   Now, when you say you knew him in school, did you simply recognise that he was another boy in school with you or did you actually know his name at that time?
A.   Yes.  I knew him from seeing him around, when he was a boy, but I also knew him by name.

Q.   Did you know where, what area, he came from, where his family lived? . Q.   You've said that you were in different programmes of study.  Can you tell us under what circumstances in school you would see Milan Lukic?

A.   When the bell would ring for the break, all the students were outside in the yard or in the halls of the school, so -- in the corridors, so that's how we could see each other and spend time together.
Q.   Can you describe your impression of him as a boy in school with you?
A.   Yes.  He was a quiet boy.  He didn't have any kind of attitude in terms of other ethnic groups.  He was a nice boy.

Q.   Now, I want to take you back to the 7th of June, and you've made -- you testified that you saw him enter your house.  My question for you is:  How long did it take you to recognise the person that walked into your house?
A.   It didn't take long.  As soon as he came in, I recognised him.
Q.   You've testified that he had some black markings on his face. Did that give you concern that maybe it wasn't the person that you thought it was?
A.   No.  I didn't have any doubts about it.

Q.   I want you now to describe, as carefully as you can, what you remember about his appearance on that day.  You've begun to describe some of the things he was wearing, but I would ask you if you could now just enumerate for us everything you remember about how he appeared to you that day.

A.   When he entered my house, I already said that he was wearing a blue camouflage uniform.  He had a police insignia on his arm.  I don't remember which one but I do remember seeing it there.  He had a black face, and then he had the kokarde and the double-headed eagle on his cap, and he had white sneakers on his feet, and on one of his arms he had a band-aid on the vein in the crook of the arm.  He also had a mole on one side of his face, above the lip.
Q.   You mentioned white trainers.  Do you recall if he was wearing socks?
A.   He wasn't wearing socks, no.
Q.   You've mentioned a band-aid on his arm.  Could I ask you to indicate for us using your arm, your best memory of where you saw that?
A.   Yes.  [Indicates].  It was here, like this, on the vein.  It's usually the place where one would have their blood taken.
MR. GROOME:  Could the record reflect that the witness has pointed to the inside of his right forearm, just below the elbow.
Q.   Now, earlier you described the gun or weapon that he had.  Could I ask you to describe it with a little greater specificity now?
A.   It was a sniper with a silencer.  Well, the calibre I'm not able to say right now.  I'm a little bit forgetful, but I do know that it was a sniper with a silencer, in any case.
Q.   Was there anything unusual about his demeanour or the way he was acting that you recall?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Please describe.

A.   When he entered my house, the first thing he did was to ask what we had in the house.  Actually, he asked me my name, and I told him.  He asked what did I have in the house?  I told him to look, that I have the JNA reserve forces uniform.  He went around, searched the house, and told me to take the uniform and to go with him.  He acted as if he didn't know me.
Q.   What were the lighting conditions in your home at the time that Mr. Milan Lukic came into your home?
A.   Yeah.  It was daylight.  It was 5.30 p.m. in June.  So you can imagine what the light was.
Q.   Was there anything obstructing your view of Mr. Lukic?
A.   No.
Q.   Where were you precisely in your home when he first walked into your home?
A.   I was sitting on the couch behind the door.
Q.   And how far away was he from you when you first saw him?
A.   Well, if I were to stretch my arm out, I would have been able to touch him.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  You told us earlier that his face was blackened. Can you tell us with what was it blackened?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know.  It wasn't any kind of grease paint.  It could have been some kind of soot or something.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  How much of his face had that black soot on it?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Only the face, around the eyes, cheeks.  It wasn't thickly applied, this black-grey stuff.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  On those parts of his face that had this black stuff on it, could you see the underlying skin?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  What is it that made you recognise him, as you told the Prosecutor, immediately as he came in?  What was there about his appearance that made you recognise him so quickly?

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] The mask that was on his face wasn't something that would conceal his face so that you couldn't tell who it was.  It was very easy to recognise him, and as I said earlier, he also had a mole on his face, and I knew him anyway from before; and I'm the kind of person who if I see a person once or twice, I always am able to recall that face later.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  You say that he pretended that he didn't know you.  Did you say anything to him to indicate that you knew him?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] No.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Why was that?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I was afraid because if I let him know that I knew him, perhaps he would have killed me.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Yes, Mr. Groome?

MR. GROOME: Q.   Returning back to the -- your secondary school years, can you give us an approximation of either by how many times per week or how many times per month you would have seen Milan Lukic while you were at school?

A.   We had five or six classes a day, and if we multiply that by five days, let's say that there were at least five classes a day, that was at least 25 classes a week, and then there is a break after each one or in between the classes, which are 45 minutes long each.  So there is plenty of time to socialize and ...
Q.   So am I right in concluding that you -- your testimony is that you saw him during the breaks between the classes and you had approximately 25 classes per week?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And how many years were you in school at the same time that Milan Lukic was in school?
A.   I said earlier that it was two years.  I think at the end of the second year, I think, he left for Obrenovac.
Q.   I just want to return to something you testified a few moments ago.

JUDGE ROBINSON:  Mr. Groome, just a minute.  I'm sorry, I'd like to find out from the witness whether he had a speaking relationship with Milan Lukic while he was at school.  Was he somebody with whom you spoke normally, with whom you had conversations?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] No.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  He was not a friend of yours, then?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] No.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Mr. Groome, what about the period after school?
MR. GROOME:  I can inquire about that.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  You haven't come do that.
MR. GROOME:  I hadn't intended but I will --
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Go ahead, yes.
MR. GROOME: Q.   How many students in your year of school can you approximate, how many students altogether were in your year?
A.   Well, that takes a bit more calculation, but if I were to give a number, I would say 300 to 400 times in either school shift.

Q.   I think there may have been some mistranslation.  I'll ask my question again.  I'm asking you how many students altogether were in your year at school?  Not how many times you saw him over the course of the year but simply how many students altogether were in your year at school?

A.   Yes, yes.  This is what I meant when I said that in one school year, there were 300 to 400 students in both shifts, the first and the second shift, in school.  Yes, that's how I understood the question.
Q.   Okay.  You've testified that he left school, and I believe you said he left Visegrad.  Is that your evidence, that he left Visegrad when he left school?
A.   That's right.
Q.   And do you know where he went?
A.   I believe that he was in Obrenovac then.
Q.   From the time he left school until the 7th of June 1992, had you had any other occasions to see him?
A.   No.
Q.   Now, did there come a time when you were taken from your apartment or your home?
A.   Yes, there did.
Q.   Approximately how long were you with -- were you in your home -- or was Milan Lukic in your home before you were taken from it?
A.   After this hiding, I spent the night at my place.  This one night.  And then Lukic came and he took me out of the house, if that is what you meant.
Q.   The time period I'm asking you for is from the time that Milan Lukic entered your home until the time you were taken from your home, how long is that period of time?
A.   I believe that lasted for about ten minutes or so.
Q.   And where were you taken?
A.   When he ordered me to take my uniform, we set out towards the car, which was parked outside on the road and which was guarded by a soldier of his.
Q.   That soldier, did you recognise that soldier?
A.   No, no, I didn't know him.
Q.   What happened when you arrived at the car?

A.   Before we reached the car, itself, my wife and my daughter were standing in the doorway.  I asked Milan Lukic to allow me to go back and to kiss my daughter and wife, and he refused to let me go.  I disregarded his refusal and at my own initiative I went back and I kissed my wife and my daughter and then I went back towards the car.  When I got near the car, Lukic opened the boot of the Passat car which he was driving.  He put the uniform in the boot of the car, and he ordered us to sit in the rear, on the rear seat in the car.
Q.   Where was he when -- when the boot of the car was opened?
A.   He was right behind the car, behind the boot of the car, where it is normal for one to stand when one opens the boot of the car.
Q.   Where were you?
A.   I was at the corner of the car, as it were, by his side.
Q.   Can you approximate the distance between you and him at this time?
A.   Between half a metre and a metre.
Q.   And did you yourself put the uniform in the car or did he do that?
A.   I believe that I've said in my statement that it was he, it was him, who did that.
Q.   Can you describe the car for us?
A.   Yes.  It was a Passat.  It was the property of Behija Zukic, whom Burgundy colour, and that was that Passat vehicle.
Q.   Did you know -- did you know this car before -- or had you seen this car before this day?
A.   Yes.  While it was the property of Behija Zukic.
Q.   And did you know Behija Zukic?
A.   Yes, I did.
Q.   Was this car similar to other cars in town, or that you had seen in town?
A.   Well, at that time, I believe that it was the only one of its kind, the one owned by Behija Zukic, that is, that was such a Passat make car.
Q.   You said "we" were placed in the car.  When you say "we," who else are you referring to?

A.   Amir Kurtalic was also there, a friend of mine and of my family, because it wasn't safe there.  When we got out of my house, Lukic caught sight of Amir Kurtalic and then he told him, "You too come with me."  And he told him to -- Kurtalic said, "Let my take my identity card."  And Lukic told him, "You need no identity card.  I am your identity card."
Q.   The Passat car, can I ask to you tell us how many people can sit in the Passat car?
A.   In the back, three people can sit, one person can sit next to the driver, and with the driver it's five people all in all that can fit into it.
Q.   How many people can sit in the front of the car?
A.   The driver and the co-driver or the person sitting next to the driver, two people.
Q.   That would mean three people in the back of the car?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Where were you sitting in the car?
A.   Amir Kurtalic and I were sitting in the back seat.
Q.   And were you sitting behind the driver's seat or behind the other seat?
A.   I think that I was in the middle.
Q.   And where was Amir Kurtalic?
A.   I think that he was on my right side, if I remember correctly.
Q.   Did Milan Lukic get into the car?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Where was he sitting?
A.   He was actually driving the car.
Q.   Did anyone else get into the car?
A.   Yes.  His soldier who was standing -- who had been standing by the car.
Q.   Was there a space between the two front seats on the car?
A.   Yes.  There was a space around the gear shift lever where Lukic actually put his rifle, and he placed it so that the rifle barrel actually was pointing at my head.
Q.   Were you able to see -- were you able to see him while the car -- while you were driving in the car?
A.   Yes, I was able to see his back.
Q.   Where did the car go?

JUDGE ROBINSON:  Mr. Groome, before you move on to that point, I wanted to ask the witness -- Witness, you told us that this car was the property of Behija Zukic, that Lukic had killed her and he had taken her car.  How did you know that?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I have said in my statement that this is something that I did not personally see for myself but this is something that I heard from my fellow citizens.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  When did you hear that first?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I cannot recall with precision but I believe a day or two after the murder.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  When was that?  In relation to your incident, can you tell us when that murder took place?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I cannot specify the date, and the day; but I believe that it was some 10 days or so before my own incident.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Tell us what you heard.  Tell us exactly what you heard.

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] What I heard was this:  That Lukic had entered Behija's house, killed her and took her car.  He had probably also asked for or looked for money, but I'm not quite sure because I didn't actually inquire much about it.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Did you happen to hear other stories about Mr. Lukic?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes.  I heard other stories.  I also heard that he had liquidated the Smajic family in the centre of town, in the neighbourhood called Jondja.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Anything else?

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, I heard lots of things. There were two cases of fire, of arson.  This is not what I put in my statement, so these are not things that I'm exactly sure of but if you insist, it's not a problem.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  So that it is -- it would be correct to say that prior to your incident, you had heard many stories about Mr. Lukic's conduct, unlawful conduct?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes, also prior to my own case, and after my own case as well.
JUDGE ROBINSON:  All right.  Thank you.  Mr. Groome?

MR. GROOME: Q.   You've mentioned of these -- when Judge Robinson has asked you about some of the other accounts that you've heard, you've mentioned two fires.  Was that something that you heard before you -- your incident or after?
A.   These two fires occurred after my own incident.
Q.   Can you tell us with as much precision as you can how many different incidents you heard Milan Lukic was involved prior to the 7th of June?

A.   Well, I mentioned already this murder of Behija Zukic.  That is one.  And that I also stated in my statement.  I did not refer to the murder of the Smajic family in my statement but I also heard that story and that it had been committed by him, but if you can put me a more detailed question to a more specific question, I could perhaps give you an answer, but at this moment, I cannot recall any details myself.
Q.   Was your prior knowledge of hearing these stories the reason why you recognised the person who walked into your house on the 7th of June? Is that why you believed it was Milan Lukic?
A.   No.
Q.   Why did you believe it was Milan Lukic who walked into your house?
A.   Because I recognised him.
Q.   Now, you've mentioned the car leaving your neighbourhood or your -- the front of your house.  Where did it go?
A.   It went not far from my house and it took a turn into a side street, an adjacent street, where there was on the road a grey-coloured Yugo, and that's where he pulled up and stopped the car.
Q.   The grey-coloured Yugo, did you recognise that car?
A.   Yes.  It was my neighbour's car.
Q.   Can you tell us his name?
A.   I think that his name was Osman Dzafic.
Q.   Can you describe for us what you saw when the car, the Passat pulled up beside this grey Yugo?

A.   Yes.  Immediately after the -- after stopping the Passat, a soldier whom I knew, but I cannot remember his name, who came out from an adjacent house and was leading another five people towards the car, and I saw that as I was sitting in the car.  That was happening on the left side of the car.
Q.   Did you know the name of the five people that were being led towards the car?
A.   Yes, yes.  Meho and Ekrem Dzafic, father and son.  And then Hasan Mutapcic and Hasan Kustura and VG-032 were all there.
Q.   Were all of those men Muslims?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Can you -- how many of -- how many men were there that were not part of the group that was detained?
A.   Are you referring to the soldiers?  If you are referring to the soldiers, there were three of them.
Q.   Yes.  I was referring to the soldiers.  Were they all armed?
A.   Yes, they were.
Q.   In addition to the men that you saw there on the street, did you learn that there were other men being detained, other Muslim men being detained at that time?
A.   Yes.  Later, I learned that there had remained another six men in that same house.
Q.   How long did you remain at that location?
A.   Well, we stayed at that particular location only until we got into the car, and then we continued on our journey.
Q.   Did you leave that location still in the Passat?
A.   Yes.  I was still in the Passat in the same seat.
Q.   And was Amir Kurtalic still in the same seat in the Passat?
A.   Yes, he was.
Q.   Who drove the Passat at this stage?
A.   Milan Lukic did.
Q.   Who was in the front passenger seat of the Passat?
A.   The soldier of his.
Q.   Was there anyone else in the Passat aside from you, Amir Kurtalic and the two people in the front?
A.   Yes, from among the five men who had been taken to the spot, Hasan Mutapcic also sat in the Passat.
Q.   Was anyone placed in the grey Yugo?
A.   Yes.  The remaining four men, together with a soldier.
Q.   Where did the car go this time?
A.   This time, we set out in the direction of the Vilina Vlas Hotel.
Q.   Can you estimate for us how long in kilometres the distance is from where the car left to the Vilina Vlas?
A.   Well, looking from the centre of the city, the distance to Vilina Vlas was five kilometres, plus this portion up there, so it's 5.5 kilometres all in all.
Q.   Can you estimate for us how long it took you to drive from where you're mentioning now to the Vilina Vlas Hotel?
A.   Well, I cannot say with precision but perhaps 20 or 25 minutes.
Q.   During that 20 or 25 minutes, were you in a position to see Lukic?
A.   Yes, from the back, actually I could see his back.
Q.   Did it ever occur to you while you were driving that perhaps it was not Milan Lukic?
A.   No.
Q.   On the way to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, did Milan Lukic ever stop the car?

A.   Yes.  He did stop the car at a couple of places, when he had occasion to see a pedestrian, a man, he would stop the car and ask the man for his name, and when the man replied, he would tell him, "Oh, you are not a balija."
Q.   When you use the word "balija", is that a derogatory term used to describe Muslims?
A.   Yes, it is.
Q.   What happened when you arrived at Vilina Vlas Hotel?

A.   When we arrived in front of the Vilina Vlas Hotel, Lukic ordered us out of the car and to get into the hotel.  He ordered us to line up in front of the reception desk until he found the keys to the manager's office.
Q.   Prior to going into the hotel, was there a check-point that you passed through?
A.   Yes, there was a check-point at the Sase crossroads.
Q.   And what if anything happened at that check-point?

A.   Yes, something did happen.  Passing by that check-point, Lukic, Milan Lukic, stopped the car and he said probably or, in fact, he did say to the Serbs, his Serbs there, that he had hunted himself a number of balijas.
Q.   Returning now to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, did you see anyone else that you recognised in the hotel?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Who was that?

A.   At the hotel, I recognised Mitar Vasiljevic.  He had an olive-drab uniform, black, large black hat with a kokarde and a double-headed eagle and he also had a red ribbon on his shoulder.  He was armed.  I also recognised Momir Savic.  He was in a camouflage uniform, wore a large black hat with the same insignia, the two-headed eagle, and he also had a red ribbon on his shoulder.  Also, I recognised this Susnjar, I don't know what his name, first name, was or is but I did recognise him because before the war he used to work as a security guard in the hotel.
Q.   How many men -- you're referring to as soldiers.  How many men altogether are in the Vilina Vlas Hotel at this stage?
A.   Well, if you are referring to soldiers, there were three whom I recognised at the hotel, and then there were the three who had taken us to the hotel, so there were a total of six men.
Q.   And out of those six, you've testified that you recognised four of them from knowing them prior to this day; is that correct?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And as far as you know, the other two, you had never seen before the 7th of June?
A.   No.
Q.   You said you knew Mitar Vasiljevic.  How did you know Mitar Vasiljevic?

A.   Yes, I knew Mitar Vasiljevic well.  He worked as a catering worker at the Panos hotel, and I would be there often because they had Bingo there and one would go there for a drink or to have a snack, so that I had occasion to have -- I had quite a few drinks with this self-same Mitar Vasiljevic so I knew him quite well.
Q.   So you actually interacted with Mitar Vasiljevic on a social -- in social terms?
A.   Yes, indeed.  When I stayed at the Panos, that's the way it was. We would have a drink or two together.
Q.   Of the six people you're referring to as soldiers in the Vilina Vlas Hotel, how many of them had black paint or black markings on their face similar to Milan Lukic?
A.   Well, I mentioned or in fact I did not mention this.  The fact is that the soldier who came with Lukic to take me away, whom he called , he had two streaks, to black streaks, on his cheeks.
Q.   How about the other men?  Did they have any black markings on their face?
A.   No, they didn't.
Q.   Now, you said that Milan Lukic was looking for some keys.  Can you please remind us what type of keys he was looking for and was he successful in finding them?

A.   To the best of my recollection, I believe that he was -- he asked Mitar Vasiljevic to give him the keys to the manager's office.  He gave him some keys.  He tried to open that office.  He could not.  And he was angry, and he just threw the keys into the corridor and he ordered us to get back into the cars and sit in the same way as we were sitting before.
Q.   Were all of the men brought into the hotel?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And what part of the hotel were you all brought into?
A.   We were in the area in front of the reception.
Q.   Now, you've testified that Milan Lukic ordered you and the other men that were detained to get back into the cars.  Did you get back into the cars?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And approximately how long in total were you in the reception area of the hotel?
A.   I don't know exactly.  It seemed like an eternity, but we didn't really stay that long, maybe 15 or 20 minutes.
Q.   And what was the lighting conditions in the reception area?
A.   It was good, natural light, that entrance area was full of windows so there was no doubt about being able to see everyone clearly.
Q.   And during the 15 or 20 minutes you estimate you were in the reception area, was Milan Lukic in the reception area that entire time as well, or did he leave for some period?
A.   He was there in the corridor looking for the keys, and trying to open the manager's office.
Q.   At any time were you or any of the other men blindfolded or made to turn around and face the wall?

Q.   Was there anything obstructing your view while you were in the reception area of the hotel?
A.   No.
Q.   Which way were you facing while you were in the reception area?
A.   We were all focused on Lukic and the soldiers, whether he would find the keys, whether we would be locked into that room or not.  We were always looking at him.
Q.   Did there come a time when you did re-enter the cars?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Which car did you get into?
A.   I got into the same vehicle that I was brought to Vilina Vlas in, the Passat.
Q.   Did all of the people get into the same cars that they were in when they came to the Vilina Vlas?
A.   Yes.  Only when we were leaving Vilina Vlas, we were joined by Mitar Vasiljevic too.
Q.   And which car did he get into?
A.   This time, Mitar Vasiljevic sat together with Lukic in the Passat and the soldier who had driven the vehicle to Vilina Vlas moved into the Yugo vehicle.
Q.   Who drove the vehicle to -- who drove the Passat to the Vilina Vlas?
Lukic.

drove from Bikavac to Vilina Vlas, and the soldier who was with him was sitting in the co-driver's seat, in the passenger seat, next to him.
Q.   And that's the person who moved into the grey Yugo?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Where did the car go?
A.   When we came back to the cars, they again drove us in the direction of Visegrad.  We were returning by the same road, in the direction of Sase.
Q.   And did there come a time when the cars stopped?
A.   Yes.  They did stop, after we passed the intersection at Sase and were driving along the road towards Prelovo, some 500 metres after they stopped the cars.
Q.   Am I correct in saying that the road from Vilina -- that there is a road that goes from Visegrad to Prelovo that travels roughly along the ?
A.   Yes, yes, you are.
Q.   Am I right in saying that there is a road that travels from Vilina Vlas that intersects that road at a T junction?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And in this trip from Vilina Vlas that you're now describing for us, did the car arrive at that T junction?

A.   Yes.  Going along the road from Vilina Vlas towards the Sase intersection, in the conversation between Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic, actually Mitar Vasiljevic asked Lukic what are we going to do with them?  And he replied, Lukic replied to Vasiljevic, that they were going to exchange us for 300 soldiers who had fallen at Zepa and driving along like that we reached the Sase intersection and continued along the road in the direction of Prelovo. At one point, Milan Lukic asked Mitar Vasiljevic, since he spotted a house on the right-hand side above the road, if it was a Muslim house, and this other man confirmed that it was, and that's where they stopped the cars, and he left the car, his soldiers also came out of the car, and ordered us also to come out of the vehicles.  At that point in time, Milan Lukic said, I quote, "I don't want to hear a sound."  And .

As we walked in the direction of the River Drina, in a column, one behind the other, we passed through a field which was planted with potatoes at the time, and we walked for a while, and then suddenly Milan Lukic ordered us to stop, some ten metres before we actually reached the river, which is what we did.  And at that point in time, my village, my native village, was just across the river, so all my memories from early youth passed through my head at that time, and most of all -- I'm sorry.  I held the image -- I'm sorry, excuse me.

GROOME: Q.   VG-014, before we recommence my questioning, I want to say the break we just took was, it had nothing to do with you getting upset.  We recognise that this brings back traumatic memories and we certainly understand and hope that you don't feel embarrassed in any way.  Just before the break, you were telling us that Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, the other men, were bringing you and the other detained Muslim men down to the river bank.  Can I ask you to continue now from the point in time when you're approaching the river bank?

A.   Yes.  At the time when we were -- at the point in time when we approached the river bank, some ten metres in front, Milan Lukic ordered us to stop.  He asked which one of us was able to swim?  We were all silent except for VG-032.  He replied that he could swim.  He ordered us Drina bank and that no one should even attempt to escape because they would be killed.  We did so.  As we were getting close to the river bank, one behind the other in a line, I could see, and I also was able to sense that the end was coming.  I still had an image of my daughter and my wife in my head, but what could I do?  Nothing could be changed.  At that moment, Meho Dzafic, Mitar Vasiljevic's colleague, was heard.  He was begging Mitar Vasiljevic not to kill him because they were colleagues from work.

Mitar Vasiljevic pretended not to know him. Then one of the soldiers asked how they should fire.  Lukic said that they should fire individual shots.  I could hear them cocking their weapons.  For a moment everything went quiet.  And then after a brief period of time, a shot ensued.  After that first shot, I don't know if it was by instinct or how, I just fell down.  I wasn't actually hit.  I fell in a way that I actually turned by 180 degrees.  We were standing facing the water and Lukic and his soldiers were behind our back, some five or six metres behind.  When I fell in the water, I could hear the scream of one of my colleagues.  I didn't know who it was.  Then another shot was heard.  Everything went quiet, and the person from the bank fell on top of me and on top of VG-032.  I heard bodies jerking, and then everything went quiet for a moment.

After a certain period of time, somebody came up to the bank and said, "Well, there is one of them that's alive.  Why don't you go there?" I don't remember who said that, but there were two more shots close to my head, and there was a third shot which was a little bit farther away. And this was what happened there.  Even after those two shots, I was still not hit, and I was listening, I didn't want to be surprised by shots or anything, so I was listening to see if they would go away.  When I heard the doors of the vehicles closing, I slowly raised my head, I looked towards the bank, I could see there was nobody there, again I returned to the same position, and I had doubts that they had all left. I thought that somebody may have been left behind to see what would happen.

But actually nobody was there, again I raised my head and on my left-hand side, VG-032 also stood up.  I asked him if he was wounded and he said that he wasn't.  He asked me if I was wounded, and I also told him that I wasn't either.  And then I suggested that we should run from the place because before Lukic said that he had six more people to bring, and we were afraid that he would bring them to the same place, and so I and VG-032 stood up from the water.  Before us there was the body of Hasan Mutapcic.
Q.   If I could ask you some specific questions about your ordeal, you said that you were lined up along the river.  Were all the men -- which way were you facing?
A.   We were lined up along the bank, and we were facing the water, the river.
Q.   Do you remember who was to your left or where you were in this line of people?
A.   Yes.  Hasan Kustura was on my left-hand side and on my right-hand side, Hasan Mutapcic stood.
Q.   And do you know the position of the other men, the other four men?  Are you able to say?

A.   Yes.  I will go in the order that we reached the bank. Meho Dzafic was at the head of the column followed by his son Ekrem and then VG-032, followed by Hasan Mutapcic, VG-014, Hasan Kustura and Amir Kurtalic.
Q.   When you were describing what happened, you talked about a conversation that seemed to concern the way the guns would be used. Could you please tell us exactly what you recall hearing?
A.   One of the soldiers asked, "How should we fire?"  And Lukic said, "Individual shots."  Could you could hear the weapons being cocked and the preparations for firing.
Q.   Am I correct in saying that you had some military -- you have done some military service, mandatory military service, as part of the Yugoslav army?
Q.   And are you familiar with weapons generally that can be found in ?
A.   Yes.
Q.   You've already described the gun that Milan Lukic had.  Can you describe, if you recall, or identify, if you recall, the weapons that the other men had at the river?
A.   Yes.  I will start from Mitar Vasiljevic.  He had a semi-automatic rifle, and the other two soldiers had automatic weapons. Milan Lukic, of course, had a sniper.
Q.   And when you say semi-automatic weapons, were they -- I mean sorry, automatic weapons, were they pistols or rifles?
A.   No.  We are talking about rifles, semi-automatic rifle and automatic rifle.
Q.   So when you heard the conversation, "How should we fire," and Milan Lukic saying, "Individual shots," what did you interpret that to mean?

A.   Well, when he said, "Individual fire," I had a feeling then that he, Milan Lukic, and the rest of his soldiers were taking pleasure in killing because they had decided on individual fire, giving them time to aim at the person and kill them with relish, as we would say.
Q.   Would someone have to do something to an automatic weapon to make it fire single shot?

A.   Yes.  Automatic weapons have a kind of knob which you would have to put into position for individual fire or to return it to bursts of fire, so you could set it for individual or bursts of fire.  In semi-automatic weapons, you don't need to do that.  Semi-automatic weapons didn't have that knob or -- all you needed to do was to cock the weapon and there are ten bullets in a semi-automatic rifle, so you would fire the shots as long as you had the bullets to do that.
Q.   With respect to the automatic weapon, does it generate a sound when it is -- this knob that you described is moved from automatic mode to single-shot mode?
A.   Yes, yes, you could hear the click.
Q.   Did you hear the clicks that day?
A.   Yes.
Q.   When the gun -- when an automatic placed is semi- -- or in single shot mode, does that cause it to operate very similar to a semi-automatic weapon?

A.   When you have an automatic weapon on single-shot mode, it can fire one bullet, depending on the speed of firing, depending on the speed of the person actually firing.  That is the speed at which they can fire single shots.  When it's set on automatic mode, an automatic weapon can fire at least, according to what I know, it can fire a short burst of bullets.
Q.   So am I correct in concluding from your answer that in semi-automatic mode, the gun can be fired as rapidly as someone is able to pull the trigger?
A.   Precisely.
Q.   Now, drawing your attention to the point in time where you -- when you first hear a shot, can you describe again for us how -- what you do, what happens to you?

A.   When I heard the first shot, my body, whether instinctively, or I don't know how, I don't know what happened, anyhow I ended up in the water, I threw myself into the water; and I came to be in such a position that I turned relative to the initial standing position looking towards the river, namely when I fell into the water, I had turned by 180 degrees.  So my head was then facing the bank of the river when I was in the water.
Q.   And was your head in the water when you had reached this position?

A.   No.  My entire body was in the water and my head was -- it was partly in the water but not all of it, because this was a part of the bank that was -- where the water was not that deep, so I was submerged partly and partly above the surface of the water.
Q.   You mentioned that there was someone lying on top of you.  What part of your body was someone covering?

A.   The top part of my body -- actually Hasan Mutapcic was lying over the top part of my body, the bottom part of his body was over the top part of my body.  Check and the other part of his body covered VG-032.

Q.   You said at some point, when you thought it was safe, you -- you got up.  I'm sorry, if I could ask you a question before that, you mentioned hearing something, some reference made, to six other men.  When did you hear that statement?
A.   This was en route towards the river, because Lukic said that they had to hurry up because there were another six people that they had to get and that had to be executed.
Q.   And who did you believe those six people were?
A.   Well, I didn't see them, but I heard actually Hasan Mutapcic who was executed at that spot had told me that his son had remained at that house, and I don't know his name.
Q.   And is that the house in Bikavac?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Now, after you felt it was safe to get up, did you look around and look at the other men who were down at the river?  The other Muslim men.
A.   Yes.
Q.   Were you able to determine the extent of their injuries?

A.   I couldn't see their injuries because they were in water, but I could see their bodies.  Except for the injury on the body of Hasan Mutapcic who was lying on his back, on top of us; and he had been hit in the back of the head and had an injury there, and his lower jaw was dislocated, the right-hand side of it.  That I could see clearly.
Q.   The men that were in the water, can you describe your observations about them?

A.   Yes.  All of them lay there with their heads in the water.  They were lying on their stomachs, all the four bodies, that is, Ekrem, Meho Dzafic, Hasan Kustura and Amir Kurtalic.  While Hasan Mutapcic was lying on his back in contrast to the rest of them, with conspicuous wound that I -- with the wound that I have described.
Q.   Did you have any doubt that they were dead?
A.   No, I had no doubt, not for a second.
Q.   Did there come a time when you left the area?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Who did you leave with?
A.   When I looked around to see whether the situation was safe for me to leave the spot, VG-032 also got up, as I was looking around; and we left the spot together.

Q.   Now, the details of the path you took from the scene are not essential for the Chamber in adjudicating the facts of this event but can I ask to you tell us where did you go and how long did it take you to get there?
which is I believe some 2.5 kilometres distant from that spot.  There we waited for night and for an opportunity to cross the river.
Q.   And did you finally reach the other side of the river safely?
A.   Yes, we did.  We crossed the river using a tree stump.
Q.   And were you at some point able to get word to your wife that you had survived and that she should come and join you?
A.   Yes.  If I remember correctly, I believe that was three days after this.
