Q.   Thank you.  You said there were other men with you in that house. Do you know how many men there were?

A.   There was a room.  I couldn't say but there were people upstairs as well.  I was on the ground floor in that room.  I don't know how many people could be crammed into this room, 40, 50, maybe, I don't know how many were upstairs.  They brought two buses.  We boarded those two buses and we were taken to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.
Q.   [Previous translation continues] ... the house in Potocari?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Thank you.  Now, while you were in the house, did any Serb soldier ask you for your name?
A.   Nobody asked me.
Q.   In the house, did any Serb soldier interview you?
A.   As far as I'm concerned, I wasn't.  I haven't seen any other.  I just heard that person seeking money, German marks.
Q.   [Previous translation continues]  ... Why you were being detained?

A.   Nobody said anything.  They would just say that we are being separated, that we are going to be interrogated, and then we are going to be let go to reach Tuzla.  This is the only thing they used to tell us, nothing else.  They didn't interrogate us on any other matters.
Q.   And you were starting to tell us about how you were taken to the school in Bratunac.

A.   We were taken to this school in Bratunac.  At Bratunac we reached the service station.  Then we took a left turn and reached the Vuk Karadzic school.  When we were about to enter the school, we were forced to leave the bags with food in front of the school.  I thought, well, I'll take my food when we come back, but when they took us into the school, they never let us out so those bags were left outside.  That night, as far as I can remember, maybe one, maybe two nights we spent there, they would take people out and kill them outright, throughout the day, throughout the night, without respite.

They were working in shifts, a single shift could not cope with that.  It was a 24-hour process.  There were people killed, moaning, screaming, outside. One policeman entered the school when we arrived there.  A person was there, close to the door.  The policeman started kicking him, and while he was kicking that person, another Serb brought a hose, a rubber hose, to him, handed it over, and said, "Use this."  And he took the hose, hit him two or three times but found it wasn't very handy, and grabbed a rifle and started hitting that person.  He was bloodstained.  His face and shirt were bloodstained.

That policeman, I believe he was a policeman, he wore a blue uniform.  He had a white belt, and a pistol in a white holster.  And that beaten person, the beaten man, remained among us, but after one hour, they came back to the door and pointed him out and said, "You, get out with us."  Of course, he was hesitant, he knew his fate.  They screamed at him, "Get up."  And as -- he never came back.  We could hear moaning and screaming.  We stayed there.  Later, they said, as far as I can tell, one day and two nights.  And then we were told that we are going to proceed to Tuzla.
Q.   [Previous translation continues] ... questions about the Vuk Karadzic school.  You mentioned that there was a policeman there.  Do you know if it was a military or a civilian policeman?

A.   Well, now, could be a military policeman, judging by his holsters and belt, but judging by the uniform, he looked like a civilian.  So I couldn't tell.  I was not familiar with the uniforms.  White belt, I remember military police wearing white belts, but the uniform was blue, and blue as in the civilian police.
Q.   Did you also see Serb soldiers in or around the school?
A.   Yes.  They would walk around.  They would sometimes enter the room and take people out.
Q.   Do you know how many Serb soldiers there were?

A.   I wouldn't know.  There were many of them because they had a headquarters there.  Most probably there were many of them.  They sent people out to catch our people who were trying to go through the woods and they had a detachment of soldiers to take care of us.
Q.   Were they wearing uniforms?
A.   Yes.  They did.  Their soldiers, camouflage uniforms, they looked like soldiers.
Q.   And for the roughly two nights that you say you spent at that school, can you give an estimate of how many Muslim men were in the school?

A.   I can tell you, we were told you are going to Tuzla, we emerged from the school, boarded the buses.  We were not permitted to look outside because a soldier or two would be standing next to the driver.  They were making sure that we won't look outside so we were supposed to just look in the seat in front of us.  At one point, I managed to sneak a peek and saw seven buses, Bratunac-bound.

JUDGE AGIUS:  One moment, Ms. Soljan, sorry to interrupt you at this stage but I see that you are embarking on another phase in your examination-in-chief and I think there are still several matters that the witness testified about which are not exactly clear.  And I'm trying to take them one by one.  Perhaps you can ask him first.

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes, please ask me.  Maybe I've skipped something but these are details, minor details.  It's not as if I had a script in front of me and I was reading out off it.  I may forget certain things.

JUDGE AGIUS:  I fully understand, Mr. Hasic, and please be patient with us.  We are just trying to make sure that your presence here would be made use of to the best possible. Perhaps you can ask him first whether he ever served in the JNA, what he did, and how familiar he was with ranks, insignia, et cetera. Then we can proceed from there.
MS. SOLJAN:  Mr. President. Q.   Sir, did you ever serve in the Yugoslav National Army?
A.   Yes, I did.  In former Yugoslavia.
Q.   Do you remember when that was?
A.   1960, I came back home from national service.  During Tito's time, I served Tito.
Q.   And are you familiar with military insignia?
A.   Yes.  With the former ranks, but with the modern ones, they are being changed, I'm not very familiar with.  I was familiar with the former ranks in the JNA.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Yes.  Thank you. Could he describe the uniform of a military police in the army, in the JNA, during peace time, in other words?

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, in peacetime, they would wear the same uniform as the rest of the soldiers, they would have a white belt and a pistol in a white holster, and this is what distinguished them as military police.
JUDGE AGIUS:  But the colour of the uniform itself would it be the same colour as that of an ordinary soldier or not?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, yes, it was the same uniform.  I forgot certain things.  I left the army in 1960.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Was the colour of the ordinary uniform of the Yugoslav army, JNA soldiers, drab olive or what colour was it?  Was it a green olive?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes, it used to be, while I did my national service.

JUDGE AGIUS:  So you've told us basically that one -- in peacetime one would distinguish a military police from an ordinary military officer or soldier from the white belt and white pistol holster; is that correct?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.  This is how I understood that somebody was a military policeman.  Officers had special uniforms. They had either stripes on their sleeves or stars.
JUDGE AGIUS:  And would a military police officer have any insignia anywhere on his uniform that would also distinguish him as a member of the military police?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, I can't really remember anything else, any other insignia.
JUDGE AGIUS:  All right.
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] White belt and white holster, and since this was a long time ago, maybe something else was there, but I forgot because I did my national service and finished it in 1960.
JUDGE AGIUS:  No problem, Mr. Hasic.  Now, I'll take you to civilian police now.  What was a civilian policeman's uniform like in the former Yugoslavia?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] It was blue, civilian police was blue uniform.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Blue uniform.  And do you remember the colour of the belt?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I believe that the belt was an ordinary one.
JUDGE AGIUS:  And if they carried a holster and a pistol, the colour of the holster would also be ordinary leather?  Brown, black, white?  What colour?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Well, usually similar to the colour of uniform, maybe blue.

JUDGE AGIUS:  All right.  Now I take you back to one answer you gave to a question that was put to you earlier on, and perhaps you can now explain a little bit as we go along. Madam Soljan asked you -- you mentioned there was a policeman there.  Do you know if it was a military or a civilian policeman?  And you said, you answered, "Well, now, could be a military policeman" -- one moment let me read it first and then I will ask you the questions.  "Well, now, it could be a military policeman judging by his holster and belt but judging by his uniform he looked like a civilian so I couldn't tell.  I was not familiar with the uniforms, white belt, I remember military police wearing white belts but the uniform was blue and blue is as in the civilian police." So I will just ask you a simple question.  So do I understand you now to say that the person that you saw there in the Vuk Karadzic school had the uniform of a civilian policeman but the holster and belt of a military policeman?

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I don't know now.  I cannot get round to it myself, whether he was a military or a civilian policeman but he was a policeman, as long as he wore a gun and a white belt.  I remember that well.  I noticed it straight away.
JUDGE AGIUS:  What's a military police in your language?  What are the words, the Serbo-Croat words, for military police?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] "Vojni policajac" or "vojna policija," military policeman, or military police if there are more of them.
JUDGE AGIUS:  And did you see those words anywhere, either in their full form or in an abbreviated form, VS, on the uniform of that policeman?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I did not see that.  I wasn't looking for such.  I was quite frightened.  I really did not notice such things.

JUDGE AGIUS:  All right.  I thank you for that information.  Now I'm going to take you to another part of your testimony dealing with something completely different and perhaps you can then answer my question.  You are referring to the first night when you arrived in Bratunac, when they took you in and didn't let you take your food with you. And then you said, "That night, as far as I can remember, maybe one, maybe two nights we spent there, they would take people out and kill them outright, throughout the day, throughout the night, without respite. They were working in shifts, single shift could not cope with.  It was a 24-hour process.  There were people killed, moaning, screaming outside." So let's take it bit by bit.  How do you know that people were being killed?  Did you see anyone being killed?

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I didn't see with my own eyes, but I would hear them moaning and screaming, then I would hear a burst of gunfire and then these people were never taken back to my room or other rooms, most probably they were killing them but I didn't see them with my own eyes.  But it is a known fact this is 100 per cent sure.  They found some graves in Potocari.  They found two mass graves very recently, mass graves.

JUDGE AGIUS:  Mr. Hasic, please try to understand me that we need to know exactly what happened in Bratunac during those two nights.  The fact that they found graves in Potocari and elsewhere does not necessarily mean that those people were indeed killed in Vuk Karadzic school on those two nights when you were there.  So you need to be very precise in your testimony.  I'm going to hand you back to Ms. Soljan. I think this part needs to be elaborated.  We can't have testimony which just assumes and concludes that several people were killed and shifts -- in shifts and -- on a 24-hour basis, et cetera, because at that rate I would imagine that the whole population of Muslims in Vuk Karadzic school would have been exterminated according to the witness so you need to elaborate on this part.  Thank you.
MS. SOLJAN:  I understand, Your Honour.  Thank you.
Q.   Sir --

JUDGE AGIUS:  And I'm saying because there is no allegation that there was mass killing in Vuk Karadzic school.  There is an allegation of opportunistic killing in Karadzic and some other killings but not to the extent -- all right.

MS. SOLJAN:  Thank you, Your Honour. Q.   Mr. Hasic, I'm still asking you questions about your period of time in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.  Can you give an estimate of how many Muslim men were taken out of your room that were not returned to your room?

A.   I could tell you from my room, some six, seven people were taken out.  From other rooms how many people were taken out, I cannot say, really.  I wouldn't be in a position to say how big was the school and how many people were imprisoned there but screaming were constant, daytime, night-time.  We could hear bursts of machine-gun fire that would suddenly cut the screams.  Then sounds of screams would diminish and then stop.
Q.   Just from your room, how often were people coming -- how often were people taken out of your room?
A.   Perhaps after about an hour, a couple of hours.  It depends. Perhaps in an hour or a couple of hours or in three hours.  It depended.
Q.   And who took these men out of your room?
A.   The soldiers themselves, in camouflage uniforms, soldiers.  They did whatever they wanted.  There was nobody there to say, "Stop," to prevent that.
Q.   Did you ever see any of the men from your room later perhaps, in the buses?
A.   Of the Muslims?
Q.   Yes.

A.   No, no.  I never saw them again.  It was over.  Those people who were there, I didn't see them any more.  People that I knew, I didn't see any more.  I buried my brother last year.  They found him in Pilica.  He was identified.  That was a brother who was seven years older than myself. Another brother I buried this year, on the 11th of July.  He was five years older than me.  They were at that time almost 70, the older brother was almost 70, and I was almost 60.  I had passed the age of 55.  I was almost 60.
Q.   Thank you, sir.  I'll ask awe few more questions about the conditions in the Vuk Karadzic school.  While you were there, were you allowed to go to the toilet?

A.   It was allowed but with escort.  They would line up in the corridor, four or five of them, and then as people were passing by on their way to the toilet, as they walked by, they would be hit on the ribs with the rifle butt.  This would happen a couple of times, if people wanted to go out and then later people didn't want to go out any more. They were afraid, so they would just urinate where they were.  That's what they did.  They didn't want to go out any more.
Q.   Did you see this happen, sir?

A.   Yes, I did see that, of course. I saw them urinating where they were or to urinate in a bag.  The others would rush because they wanted to drink, meaning that there was a shortage of water as well.
Q.   So did the soldiers give you any water during those two days you were in the school?
A.   Yes.  They did.  Had they not given us water, more than half of the people would have perished.  They did give water but it was insufficient and they didn't give any food.
Q.   Sir, did anybody require medical treatment, of the men who were in that school?

A.   Probably they did require medical treatment, but why would anyone want it when they were probably be taken out and killed?  What use did they have then of -- to get medicines?  There were such people but what was the point of treating them and then killing them?  They didn't let anyone go.  Did they let anyone go?
Q.   Sir, the soldiers, the Serb soldiers did not give -- you did not see them give any medical aid or medical treatment to anybody during those two days?

A.   No, no, no, not at all.  If they felt sorry for people, they wouldn't have done that.  Why would they just give people medical treatment?  They didn't give any food.  They gave insufficient water.  The food that the people had was confiscated from them.  Why would they bother to provide medical treatment for these people?  They were not interested in that.  I was living in a village --

JUDGE AGIUS:  I'll try to help you finish your testimony as early as possible.  Try to answer the questions that are put to you with a yes or a no as required without going into further detail.  I mean, we all understand here.  You don't need to explain certain things to us, but certain questions have to be asked and they need to be answered.  If they can be answered with a yes or a no, please restrict yourself to a yes or a no, and you will be out of this place much earlier than you think.  Thank you.
MS. SOLJAN: Q.   Sir you said you were placed on buses after being taken out of the school in Bratunac.  Who all was placed on these buses?
A.   The Serb soldiers and drivers.
Q.   Are you saying they alone were on the buses or they were the ones who placed the Muslim people from the school into these buses?

A.   They put the Muslims in the buses to transport them further.  They said we were going to Tuzla.  They gave us some bread, couple of slices each.  That was all.  And then when we set off, we could see we were going in a different direction.  We were not going in the direction of Tuzla but in the direction of Zvornik, and then in Zvornik the buses crossed into Serbia, seven buses, so we went through Serbia.  And maybe somewhere near Loznica, they crossed back into Bosnia again, over a bridge.  At one point, when they were already close to Pilica, they stopped and they stopped for so long that one person lay down in the aisle, this Muslim, and these people started shouting, "lift him up" because then you cannot walk up and down the aisle and they left lifted him up and they were saying, he's dead.

They were just thinking that he lay down, just like that, but he actually died and they said, "Just take him out and lay him on the side of the road."  And that's what they did.  They laid him down on the side of the road and he remained there and then there was a person who asked if he could go out to urinate and the Serb soldier allowed him to go out and he went out and then he started to run, and the Serb soldiers cut him down with a burst of gunfire.  He knew that he would be caught like that, but he, I guess, preferred to be killed by a bullet than to be the subject of genocide, and this is what happened.
Q.   Did you see the man being killed?
A.   Yes.  I did see that.  How could I not have seen it when I was sitting in the bus?  I was sitting close to him.  I was sitting next to him.
Q.   Did you actually see him get killed?
A.   No.  I didn't see him.  He wasn't killed there.  He just died by himself.  He died of fear.  Perhaps he wasn't healthy.  Maybe he would have needed some assistance, but nothing of that happened.
THE INTERPRETER:  Could the counsel please wait for translation? Thank you.

Q.   You had mentioned that the -- a man had died and had been taken out of the bus.  A man who had helped take him out from the bus asked to be able to allowed to urinate.  He then tried to run away, started to run and was killed.
A.   Yes, yes
Q.   Did you see him be cut down with a burst of gunfire?
A.   I saw him.  He was in the woods and there were two bursts, the gunfire.  The first one did not get him but the second one cut him down and he fell.
Q.   Thank you, sir. Now, how long did you stay on these buses?

A.   We stayed there for about an hour, an hour and a half, and it was already getting dark.  I don't know what they were waiting for, and it was dark for about half an hour or so, and then we went to Pilica.  We were almost at Pilica, at the entrance to Pilica, and then when we entered we turned to the left to a school or a cultural hall, something like that, and then when it was already dark, we took the stairs to get in, and they forced us there to take all of our caps off, all of us had to take our caps off.  Us elderly men we all wore caps.  They were the French kind of caps, berets, we were all wearing berets, we took them off there and we entered the rooms and the same thing happened there.  They immediately started taking people out, beating them.  You could -- killing them.  You could hear screaming and moaning.  If somebody would get up and look through the window, if I did it or somebody else did it, there would be a burst of fire, gunfire.  They were killing outside.  You could hear screaming, shouting, moaning, from outside.  This went on like this.  And I think that if I can remember correctly, I was there for one night or two nights, possibly for two nights, I was there, and then at approximately on the 17th, people were already being taken out for execution.

JUDGE AGIUS:  I think he just touched on what I was going to refer to now.  If he could be precise as to the exact date when they arrived in Pilica, this particular spot in Pilica, if he remembers when they left Bratunac and when they arrived in Pilica, whether it was on the same day and in that case, what was the date?
MS. SOLJAN: Q.   Sir --
JUDGE AGIUS:  And when did the events that he is describing happen?
MS. SOLJAN:  Thank you, Your Honour. Q.   Mr. Hasic, do you remember the date you arrived to Pilica?
A.   I think it was the 15th.
Q.   Thank you.  And could you roughly tell how many Muslim men were in this building in Pilica?

A.   In the room where I was, the room was full.  You couldn't move around.  If a person stood up, they couldn't sit down later.  There was no space.  It was very tightly packed in the room where I was.  In any case, the room was full.  I didn't go into the other rooms and I don't know how many people there were.  You weren't allowed to go out.  You didn't dare. If you went out into the corridor, you were hit with the rifle butts.  You didn't even dare to go to the bathroom.  Many of them didn't dare go to the bathroom.  They urinated where they were.
Q.   Could you tell how big the room was you were being kept in?
A.   I don't know.  Perhaps three and a half metres by five, approximately.
Q.   Okay.  And could you roughly tell how old the Muslim men who were being kept in the room with you --

A.   There were some elderly people there too.  Up to the age of 80. That's for sure.  100 per cent.  There were also children of 15, 16 years of age.  They asked who was 15 or 16 and they said, "Come, line up here so that we can see you."  And there were about 12 children like that ranging from 15 to 16 and they said, "We need people or kids like this for Abdic, Abdic is looking for people like that and they took them out.  I don't know what they did with them.  This is what happened in that room.  As for the other rooms, how many of them there were, how many they could assemble, I don't know.  Perhaps it was 100, 120 of them that they assembled from the other rooms.  In any case, they were taken out and were never heard of again.
Q.   Sir, you mentioned that they asked who was 15 or 16 and said to come up and line up.  Who -- who were the "they"?  Who were the people who asked the question?
A.   Yes.  It was the Serb soldiers who were guarding us and keeping us there and doing whatever they wanted with us.
Q.   Could you tell how many Serb soldiers were around or in the Pilica building, who were guarding the Muslim men?

A.   I can say that approximately there were about 10 who were there, and there were another 10 at the place where they were killing, where the executions were going on, so the 10 there, the 10 were up there, then there were two or one always on the buses who were escorting and I noticed at the school that there was a deaf and dumb person, and one of our men asked if there was anything to eat, and this other guy said, "We don't have anything to give you."  And then after about half an hour or so he brought a loaf of bread and he was breaking off bite-sized pieces and giving them to the people and I think, if I can remember correctly, we spent about two nights there. The following day, after those two nights, it was said that those who wanted to go to Sarajevo and has the money can pay for the bus to go to Sarajevo, and one of them said, "I have 100 German marks and I'm going to pay for my friend, my colleague, my neighbour.  We can pay for five of us."  And that's how people left.  As long as they had the money, they could go, allegedly to Sarajevo.  After people ran out of money, then it was said, "You are going to Tuzla," so now it was possible to go even without money.  It was possible to get on the bus without money.  And then after that, they brought two sheets.

They were long ones.  And they said, "This has to be torn into strips" and we were going to be tied up and two men were tearing them, this sheet, up, and tying our hands behind our back.  And people were leaving, the buses were going quickly, and returning quickly.  I thought, well, I was going to get tied up as well. Very few people were left in that room and I placed my hands on my -- behind my back and that's how they tied me up.  We were going out, and as we were going out, going down the stairs, and when we reached the ground floor, there was a man who was dead there.  There was blood, a pool of blood all around him.  He was lying at the bottom of the stairs.  He was dead.  We went outside.  We were going towards the buses.  There were two buses there.
JUDGE AGIUS:  One moment.  Stop there, Mr. Hasic.  Mr. Lazarevic, I noticed you before.  Something wrong with the transcript, I imagine.

MR. LAZAREVIC:  Yes, Your Honour is right.  What I have noticed when the witness was giving his evidence regarding this event that he had with Serb soldier, it's on page 28 -- in a moment I will find, yes, well, basically what I heard the witness saying is that Serbian soldiers said, "We don't have enough food for ourselves and that's the reason why I cannot give you food."  And if Ms. Soljan can clarify this.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Yes, Mr. Hasic, you've heard what Mr. Lazarevic has just stated.  Is it correct that when the soldier --
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I heard that.  That was true.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Yes, okay.  Then we can proceed.
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] It's true that he said that.
JUDGE AGIUS:  All right.  Let's proceed, then, with the rest of the examination-in-chief, Ms. Soljan.
MS. SOLJAN:  Thank you, Mr. President.
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] So, when I came down from the first floor, and I said --

MS. SOLJAN: Q.   I'll just stop you and just take you back to a few more questions about what was happening in Pilica.  During the time that you were there, you mentioned that there was also mistreatment, there were killings going on.  Did you see any of those killings happen?

A.   I didn't see anything.  All I heard was moaning and the screaming outside.  This went on day and night, constantly.  It was incessant.  They were probably killing in shifts.  This is 100 per cent certain.

JUDGE AGIUS:  One moment, Ms. Soljan, because earlier on when he also said more or less the same thing, let me find it- apart from screaming and moaning which he has repeated now, he also mentioned, at least that's what we have in the transcript, bursts of fire, gunfire. What I would like to know is whether the screaming and the gunfire -- and the moaning that he heard was at the same time he was hearing the fire, the gunfire, or whether it was -- whether it was --

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] The screaming and the moaning was before, and then after the screaming, when you hear the burst of gunfire, then there is no more screaming.  It's finished.  It's quiet.  That means that they were get -- being killed.  If we were to look through the window or if we were a little bit noisier inside, then the burst of fire would be directed at us, so we didn't dare look out of the window.  And that's why we didn't see what was going on.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Thank you.
MS. SOLJAN: Q.   Sir, do you recall how many times these bursts of -- or the shooting happened?

A.   I don't know.  It happened many times.  I cannot describe it.  I didn't count it at the time, but I also heard several voices, moaning, at the same time, when four or five people were taken out at the same time, they were being dragged here and there.  I would hear four or five voices, sometimes, and then there would be a burst of gunfire cutting them down and then everything would be quiet and then after a certain interval, more people would be taken out.  This is how it happened.  And I saw this dead person there when we were leaving the school.  I saw the person, the body at the bottom of the stairs as we were going on -- as we were on our way to the buses.  One of the buses, I remember very well, was a Sedmo Julac Sabac bus.  It belonged to that company, the 7th July company from Sabac. I don't remember who the other bus belonged to.  I just remember this one.
Q.   How big were these buses?  How many men fit inside?

A.   Maybe about 50 or so.  We got to the buses.  There were about 10 soldiers escorting us to the buses and when we reached the buses I looked across a little bit.  I saw four officers standing in the shade.  These soldiers were swearing at us, telling us to move forward.  They would hit somebody occasionally with a rifle butt.  The others they didn't do anything.  They were just watching and perhaps saying a few words amongst themselves, and then we entered the buses.  When we got on to the buses, and we were tied up, we were told that we were going to Tuzla.

JUDGE AGIUS:  Ms. Soljan, we've come to a particular stage now in the -- covering the events in Pilica.  Until this particular time, when now he is together with others being taken out of the school, to the buses, and from the time he left Bratunac, apart from soldiers that he's been continually referring to, did he ever see military police or any other members of the armed forces or armed personnel?
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I didn't see military policemen.  I just saw the regular multi-coloured uniform that they were wearing.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Whether they were wearing any berets?
MS. SOLJAN: Q.   Sir, were they wearing any berets?
A.   We were wearing the French berets, black or blue ones.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Any of the soldiers wore any berets and whether you could see any ranks, insignia or any identification as regards ranks amongst the soldiers that you saw there.
THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I did not.
JUDGE AGIUS:  Go ahead.

THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] I was not looking out for insignia. I just noticed their variegated uniforms.  There were officers for sure there but I wasn't on the lookout for that. MS. SOLJAN: Q.   Sir, up to this point, since you left Bratunac, did any of the Serb military ask you for your name?

A.   They never asked me personally.  They would take out individuals, ask them questions.  Some of them returned.  Some of them never returned after being led away.  Maybe if they knew somebody personally they would ask them questions after taking them out of the room.
Q.   Thank you, sir.  Did any of the Serb soldiers register you with the ICRC at any time since you left Bratunac?
A.   Nobody registered me.  There were people who were registered but never came.  The wounded who would be registered but -- he would disappear there -- are no more.
Q.   Did you see people being registered anywhere from Bratunac to your arrival in Pilica?

A.   I did not see that.  I believe that they did the registration at the headquarters somewhere, where the Dutch government or defence was located.  They did some registration there.  I heard about that.  I never saw that.  I -- there are some of my neighbours who were registered but who never came back.
Q.   Thank you, sir.  You said that you were placed, that there were two buses in front of the Pilica building and that you were placed on one of these.  Were any of the Serb soldiers on these buses?

A.   There would be one or two soldiers.  There were escorts, they would sit next to the driver.  We would be sitting on the seats and were not supposed to look outside the window, just straight ahead of us.
Q.   Were these the same soldiers you had seen in the Pilica building before that?

A.   The same soldiers.  They would escort us to the bus, we would board the bus and then one or two would enter the bus with us and the rest would stay at the school building.  The point where we came to, there was a group of soldiers who would wait for the buses to off-load and then would execute people.
Q.   Sir, how long did you travel in those buses?

A.   It wasn't a short -- it was a short journey, two and a half kilometres approximately.  We climbed a hill.  We heard bursts of gunfire. When we reached the place where there was gunfire, the buses stopped and as soon as they stopped, the doors would open.  Serbian soldiers gathered round the buses.  Said -- and they were cursing our mothers and us, and Haris Silajdzic's mother as well.  They said, "They don't want you.  Get out of the bus."  And then death -- you could see death in their eyes. Until that point, you feel you never knew what was going, because they would say one thing, do another, and they started -- people started emerging from the buses and after the buses were half empty, they would stop people from disembarking. I was still on the bus and was looking at what was going on.  They took the people down a path in the field, there are dead people, bursts of gunfire would cut people down.  People fell dead to the ground.  When this was finished, they would come back.  I emerged from the bus.  There were cursing, "Fuck your mother and Alija and Haris."  "They don't want you."  "Get out of the bus." "Come here."  And you reckon there are still a couple of seconds of life left.  When everybody disembarked from the buses with their hands tied, including me, we formed a column and there were dead people in the column, there were dead people on the path, you could see them lying on the ground.  They didn't even reach the execution site.

They were killed in between.  One Serb soldier, he was walking in front of me, he said to me, there were some eight of them, walking next to the column, he told me, "Give me some German marks." I told him, "I don't have any."  And I was ready to be killed.  He kicked me in the stomach.  I doubled back and crouched, started screaming, screaming for help, and the Serb soldier who was walking behind me, he called to the first soldier, "Don't perpetrate genocide, be a soldier about it.  Take a rifle if you want to kill anybody."  I stood up, and started following the column, and the soldier who kicked me asked me, whether I want to convert to and register as Serbs to survive?  There are only two people in the column who opted for that, but to no avail.  Even those two who opted for this, one of our people from the column asked, "Give us water and then you may kill us."  You see how thirsty we were, hungry and thirsty.  But to no avail.  If somebody felt sorry for us, they wouldn't be leading us to be executed.
Q.   Sir --
A.   100 metres --
Q.   Was there anything particular about this location, any prominent buildings or other objects that stood out in this location, as you recall?

A.   Where we disembarked the buses, there was an apple tree.  I noticed a garden, and a house in some distance, maybe two.  I couldn't notice, I was too terrified.  And there was a ditch leading away from the homes, those houses, and there was a glen 100 metres down the path, this is where they executed people.  We were put in lines and people lay dead in lines.  We reached the people who had been murdered and we passed through the ranks of the dead, through the lines of the dead, and they would be expanding these lines starting from the top.  There was an incline where people were killed.  I was somewhere in midline.  When we reached that point, there was a command, "Turn around, turn your backs to us."  We did so.  And instead of fire, they commanded, "Lie down."  But before somebody issued such a command, they would open fire.  I fell immediately. The others fell down when fire was opened at them.  When the bursts of fire died down, one of them asked, "Are there any survivors?" "I survived," said one person, and the other one said, "I survived.  Kill me."  So they -- that person would go from one survivor to another and fired a single bullet to the head.  I thought about notifying them that I was alive.  I was contemplating if I could free my hands, then I would -- if I could not free my hands, then I would yell that I was alive and they would kill me but I reckoned if I could free my hands then I would be able to survive and escape, and there I lay.

A.   So there were seven columns of people that they brought here.  I was lying down.  Rounds of ammunition hit all around me.  Fortunately none of the bullets hit me.  They would excavate earth.  I was hit by soil, by stones, but lie down, one hit me in the elbow.  Nothing else.  Seven columns of people were then executed.  I noticed that they were dead. There were very few people remaining in my room.  Then they took a break to the house where the buses stopped.  They would sit down in the shade.  I tried to free my hands.  Fortunately, I managed to free my hands, and then assumed the same position because I knew that they would be patrolling, and half an hour later, a patrol of five soldiers came.  I could hear them speak.  I could hear their steps and I would take a peek every now and then.  And suddenly I heard, "one of them escaped," "another one escaped."  I would hear gun bursts and people would escape.  One remained there of the five.  Two of them came back after a while and said, "What happened?"  The one who left behind asked, "What happened?" And the answer was, "When one of them hid, and the other two are still looking for the other one.  So one was killed the other one was still being chased." Q.   Sir, you were just telling us about you lying on the ground after the execution.  Could you tell us how you were finally able to get away from the spot, the execution site?

A.   When they left the place to retreat to the shade, somebody close to me was whispering the second line, I turned around and whispered is there anybody alive?  Let's get away.  We were trying to ascertain the time before night-time.  It was some two hours before dusk.  I was trying to see whether there was a forest close by to hide in.  People were lying in lines.  I knew that they would be bringing earth-moving machinery. They wouldn't -- it was clear to me, they wouldn't try to bury those people manually.  So below the field, there was a ditch, the ditch that I mentioned close to the houses, close to the spot where the buses parked. There was some shrubbery, some 150 square metres of shrubbery and trees. I decided to head towards the scrub, the shrubbery.  I tried to free my hands to be able to move better.  When I freed my hands, I took a look.  Two people were crawling into the shrubs, shrubbery.  I jumped to my feet to crawl some distance.  I was afraid there would be a patrol coming back. I jumped to my feet.  I decided to risk it.  I trod on dead people, on soil.  I tried to avoid treading on dead people but I could not avoid it.  And I was listening for a cry, "Look at him, he's running away."

I knew that if I were -- was spotted, I would be dead.  I crouched and travelled some 20 metres until I reached the bushes.  Two other people were crawling and they ended in the same shrubbery.  The four of them, and I was the fifth one, we lied.  Everybody else was dead.  Among -- 1.000, 1.500 people that were killed there, in my estimate.  So we were concealed in the shrubbery.  There was a patrol.  They walked around the dead, making sure that nobody escaped.  We were close by in the shrubbery.  They did not check whether there were anybody -- any survivors in the shrubbery.

We lay low until dusk. When darkness fell, they left, and we emerged to the other side from the shrubs.  There were dead people in the field as well.  I did not know that before.  Those were the people who were taken away in the morning, who were presumably paying their way to Sarajevo.  They were killed there, probably.  There were five of us.  We crossed that field until we reached a forest.  There was some moonlight.  When we reached the forest, I couldn't see anything.  I was exhausted by that time, thirsty, hungry, terrified, and I was of an advanced age.  The others were younger, ranging from 16 to 25, judging by their appearance.  They went away.  I was left there alone.  I didn't know what to do, where to go.  My progress was very slow.
Q.   Sir --
A.   Some five minutes --
Q.   You mentioned these four other younger men who were with you.  Do you know who they were, where they were from?

A.   I asked one.  He said that he was from the Jagonje village.  I didn't ask him his name.  And I don't know it.  I asked them whether they reached their target but I couldn't find out.  They did not, because I asked whether anybody from that village managed to escape.  They told me no.  Maybe two years ago, I heard that they were captured, they were led away to Zvornik, and Zvornik is a notorious place. So I continued alone.  I reached an ambush because they -- around the place where they executed people, they would set up ambushes to catch those who managed to escape.

There was one who managed to escape.  I started to cross the road.  A soldier cried out, "Who is it?  Who is it?" I meant to escape but I reached a village with some civilians living so I could not enter the village.  I tried to hide where I was.  That patrol started threatening that they would be throwing a grenade.  Identify yourself, they yelled.  They knew I was somewhere in the dark.  I tried not to move.  They issued some military-style orders, "Left flank, right flank, turn left," they opened fire, rifle fire.  I was keeping very silent and some two hours passed in this manner.  They went away.  I crossed the road and entered the woods above the road.

I could not proceed towards the village because it was very steep.  So I traversed the woods throughout the night, over some hills.  It was very difficult to make progress.  I was exhausted.  And it was difficult to walk in the woods, through the thicket.  At the crack of dawn I reached a mountain and a meadow.  I managed to find some water, some unripe fruit, plums and apples, some wheat.  I ate some wheat grains, managed to eat something, fell asleep.  And this is how I managed to survive. After that night, I planned to cross a wood to enter a valley that day but I heard some noise, some trucks.

It was a truck or a tractor, so it meant I couldn't proceed in that direction because there was somebody there and could be the site of a mass grave.  So I hatched a plan to go in another direction.  I reached a tarmacked road.  I took that tarmacked road some 20, 30 metres to reach another wood, that was the second day. It was one and a half hours before sunset.  I reached the tarmacked road, and I took the road towards the woods, some 20 metres, but when I took a look there, the road, the tarmac, was bloodstained, half a metre wide, a flow of blood in the direction of the commotion or noise.  And as soon as I reached the woods where I was supposed to take a turn, a truck emerged right -- driving towards me.

As soon as I took a look at the truck, I saw it was filled with dead bodies up to the height of the driver's cabin. And somebody shouted from the truck, "Look, there is the one who escaped yesterday." And the truck stopped, and it took about 30 or 40 metres for the truck to stop.  The truck stopped, and since I heard what was said, I didn't dare go into the woods.  I just continued walking along the road. I reached a bridge.  The bridge is about ten metres wide and 15 metres long.  There is no water beneath it.  There is no woods there.  It's an irrigation ditch or something.

I crossed the bridge, I didn't turn around any more.  I walked for a while, and then I looked back.  It was going behind me.  It reached the bridge, and was standing there and looking at me.  I wasn't running or fleeing.  I was just walking straight down along the street, and he kept looking at me.  He thought I was a Serb, I guess, and at that point, the person turned back and started running back towards the truck.  I turned into the ditch so if that Serb was still looking at me I wanted him to see me, that I was not a Serb.  I wanted him to see me because he wanted to get me, to throw me on the truck and kill me and put me in the mass grave.  I wanted him to see that it was me.

Q.   So sir, you were telling us about how you were in a bus.  Where were you being taken to?

A.   We were brought to Karakaj and we were told to report to the command and we set off to do that and then someone else said, "Go back, go to the truck and you can go together with this guy."  It was a two tonne truck covered with tarpaulin.  I went to the truck and then I could see that inside there were some other people who had been caught in the woods. There were 27 of them all together.  And the two of us also, 29.  Then they shouted out that they should all be tied up.  And I did not -- I was not tied up.  I was given a water bottle and I was told that if anybody wanted to drink, I was supposed to give them water to drink.  So I wasn't tied up, and all the others were tied up.

We were under the tarpaulin. One of our people said, "It's a good thing that the Red Cross is here. They will be accompanying us."  So that's how we set off and we were being escorted by the Red Cross. And we were going through Bijeljina and we reached Batkovic where we were put in a camp.  We received pallets there where we would sleep. We were issued two blankets, one we could put on the pallet, the second one we used to cover ourselves.  If you had something to put under your head, very well; if not, that was it.  That day, we shaved, all of us shaved.  We had baths.  We had haircuts.  The Red Cross was there and they registered us that day.  This was the 26th of August, I remember very well, if you want to write that down.
Q.   And how long approximately were you at the camp?
A.   The 26th, not August.  It's July actually.  It was the 26th when I got there.
Q.   And how long were you there until?  What was your last date there?  Do you remember?

A.   The Red Cross was registering us.  The last day was actually the 24th of December, shortly before new years.  That was when the last exchange took place.  I spent a full five months in that camp.
Q.   And sir, where did you go once you were released from the camp?
A.   We were exchanged.  Serbs came from Tuzla and us Muslims were brought from Batkovic, so this was an exchange that took place on the 24th of December, shortly before the new year.
Q.   And where did you go from there, from the exchange point?
A.   I went to my family.  I had grandchildren, a daughter-in-law, a daughter, my wife.  I went to Gracanica.

Q.   Sir, if I may, I will just -- I'd like to take you back to the 13th of July.  You were mentioning that on that day, there were separations taking place.  Could you tell us about it in a little more detail?  Who was separating whom and how?

A.   There were two barricades, and they were letting through about 150 to 200 people who were supposed to go on the buses.  They were letting them through.  There was another barricade about 15 meters further along down the road and there were soldiers there who were immediately separating the men from the women and the children.  That day, I came out, it was Thursday, the 13th of July, and every day people were coming out. This didn't happen just on that day.  It went on every day for as long as this was going on.  People were leaving every day.  And the separation was also something that was ongoing.
Q.   And who was controlling these separations at both the barricades?
A.   Serb soldiers in multi-coloured uniforms.  They were conducting these separations.  That's what they were doing.

MS. SOLJAN: Q.   Sir, who was with you?  Was any of your family with you when you were making it through these barriers?

Q.   And sir, when you mentioned multi-coloured uniform, you are talking about camouflage uniform?

A.   That room, they crammed so many people, as I've said, maybe 150 to 200 people.  It was so crammed that if you stood up, there would be no place for you to sit down.  You could not move around, even move your legs.
Q.   You also mentioned that throughout the day, at the school, they were continually killing people; is that correct?

Q.   How many other rooms were there, if you know?

A.   No, I couldn't.  I was outside.

A.   Yes, those two nights.

A.   Yes.  I was separated from my family.  The second night I was together with my family outside.
Q.   So the second night, the night of the 12th to the 13th, you were with your family but you were not sleeping inside any of the factories?
A.   No.  On the 13th I left Potocari and went to Bratunac.  Finally I hope it's clear to you.

A.   Yes, go ahead, ask me.

Many were moaning that night, and the next day after that, on Thursday, Bratunac, Vuk Karadzic, where what food we had left was taken away from us so we would have nothing to eat. Q.   You're talking about Bratunac now?
A.   I'm talking about Bratunac and wherever you like.

A.   The second night.

A.   We were taken to the convoy because it was suggested to us by our Zagre.  I trusted him, and he -- he was actually the first bait that we swallowed and got caught.
Q.   And in terms of the bait do you think that he knew that it was not a convoy to remove you from the area and save you but in fact a convoy to take you to be executed?

A.   I'm convinced that he knew that our convoy was not a convoy of salvation, and those that had organised it had already judged us.  They only used the good neighbourly relations that we had before to deceive the people to get on the convoy, and unfortunately that's what we did.
Q.   What about the other local Serbs that you remembered their names, Dusan Maric?

A.   Those people today, as far as I know from some people who returned to Visegrad, live normally.  I must also say that Ljupko Tasic, upon the questions of some returnees what had happened to the people on the convoy, answered that he is not to blame for anything and that the decision to execute us was taken by Milan Lukic in the square when he turned up, and that's why it is important for me to know what the conversation was that they had in the square.  It was very brief, only a few sentences, and I believe that conversation relieves Milan Lukic of the responsibility of that convoy.
Q.   You believe that conversation relieves him of responsibility? What do you mean by that?

A.   Milan Lukic simply appeared and wanted to take his schoolmate out of the bus.  I think that during those months there was -- there wasn't probably anybody who could prevent Milan Lukic from doing something that he wanted to do, but Ljupko Tasic at that moment prevented him from taking Esad off the bus, and that -- it was impossible to achieve unless Milan Lukic promised to Ljupko Tasic something -- or, rather, the other way round.
Q.   Well, who is Ljupko Tasic and what was his profession?

A.   He was a neighbour of mine.  I must say that we were on good terms.  He was a haulier.  He had some machines, some baggers.  We've known each other since birth.  We never had any problems with each other.
Q.   But he had no problem taking you to be executed.
A.   Yes.
Q.   And it's easy to assume that all the people that either escorted you to the place of the execution all knew the fate of you and the fate of your brothers?

A.   All the events around the execution were experienced through something of a haze, a haze of disbelief.  I can only say that the guys who actually executed those people knew very well how to do that.
Q.   What about Rade and Sladjan Simic?

A.   They were also neighbours of mine.  Rade owned a pub at Bosanska Jagodina.  We had a meeting there on the 13th of June with Ljupko Tasic. I wanted to find out what kind of convoy that was, because sometime ago a similar convoy had been organised by Milan Lukic, and 17 or 19 people ended up in the vicinity of Bosanska Jagodina. I'm not an eyewitness.  I only heard accounts from other people and from the families of those that were executed, and among those 17 or 19 people there was also a relative of my wife.  He is the only one who was buried at the cemetery, and the remains of the others were found in a chasm some eight kilometers from Visegrad, but only about half of the bodies. I only went to Bosanska Jagodina to prevent the same thing from happening to us too. when you mentioned the fate of the 17 people on the earlier convoy, you made no mention of Milan Lukic being responsible.
A.   When did I make that statement?

Q.   Well, you simply made the statement that you wanted to make sure that the same fate didn't happen to your convoy that happened to the 17; but you did not indicate Milan Lukic's name, nor that you believed that he was responsible.  And I believe that's on page 2 of the statement in Serbian.

A.   That is possible.  At the moment I possibly didn't know that Milan Lukic was responsible for that convoy.  I still do not know, but based on the accounts of other people whose family members ended up there, it must have been Milan Lukic.  But there were bodies found there DNAanalyses were conducted, and the remains found were buried.  And it is beyond doubt that an execution was conducted.  But based on the conversations I had and from people who know Milan Lukic, at the all say that it is his responsibility. I knew about this event, and I went to Bosanska Jagodina to talk to our neighbours to avoid the same thing from happening -- that the same thing happens again.  And about this convoy of 17 or 19 people, I cannot say much because I'm not competent.

Q.   But you're convinced Tasic knew your fate from the meeting on the 13th.  Isn't that true?

A.   Please, these are assumptions.  I suppose so.  Actually, I'm quite clear that it was so.  I'm quite sure that it was so.  But I should like to say once again that Ljupko Tasic simply, when talking to the returnees claim that Milan Lukic had changed the overall concept of the convoy in the square.

Q.   And he also told the other escorts and drivers what to do?
A.   I don't know that.
Q.   They moved the buses at his direction?
A.   I don't know that either.

A.   If you are referring to the three or four seconds -- that three or four seconds that I had available to me, afraid as I was to actually take in the details that is really impossible.  I just looked at his face and then I bent my head again.  At that time one didn't just actually look at Milan Lukic.  It wasn't a done thing.
Q.   You didn't know who Milan Lukic was at the time.  Why would it matter?

A.   The man simply stood by my seat, and instinctively I looked up and I looked at his face, and then I gazed down again.  This was done instinctively on my part.  If he gone to the seat behind me I wouldn't have known it was Milan Lukic.  I would have known from other people telling me that but I wouldn't have seen him myself up to today, and today however is the second time that I see him.  The first time that I saw him he really was there.

Q.   And you can tell me that you can recognise a man who has aged 16 years after seeing him for three seconds and not knowing his name and not knowing who he was until afterwards, not mentioning his name until 1997?

A.   I just have to clarify something for you.  Those moments when someone is actually deciding your fate, life or death, your mind in such moments it registers everything.  In hindsight, looking back at all these years, in the reports that I saw in the media, I saw Milan Lukic many times in the media reports, on television and so on.  So this is not actually the second time that I see him.  This is the second time that I see him in person, in the flesh.  And believe you me, it is possible to take in one's face within the space of two or three seconds and have it etched in one's mind forever.  It is possible, but one has to experience it.  One has to experience some terrible ordeal in order for one's mind to react in that way.  I believe if we had a drink then I wouldn't have remembered his.
Q.   But do you think someone with all the responsibility and command power would be able to snap his fingers and have Mr. Kustura off the bus, no problem?

A.   That is the key, in fact.  If you want us to unlock this lock, please tell the -- relate to Their Honours just the dialogue that Milan Lukic had conducted with Ljupko Tasic.  It is just a couple of sentences.  Of course if Milan Lukic remembers that dialogue, then I think he should remember it.

MR. ALARID: Q.   Mr. 11, let's talk about the other people that participated in the execution at the end of your trip that day.  Do you recall the day of the week?

Q.   Well, I mean did you have any other activities that would tell you whether it was a weekday or a weekend?
A.   No.
Q.   Tell me the people that participated in the execution, either by escorting, driving, or shooting.
A.   I only know two people, Predrag Milisavljevic, who started the execution, and Boris Ceho, who was standing -- who was standing on the side close to us.
Q.   Isn't it true that Boris Ceho was a reserve policeman?
A.   It is true, and at the time he was wearing the uniform of a reserve police officer.  I also used to be a reserve police officer.
Q.   How many other people in that detail were wearing uniforms of policemen or reserve policemen?

A.   I think that only Boris Ceho was wearing such a uniform of a reserve police officer.  And apart from these two there were another nine people there, a total of 11 as far as I could tell at the moment and as far as I remember.  Eleven people were at the pit.  I know that the guy who when Predrag Milisavljevic started the execution at the pit had a flak jacket on him.  He was wearing a flak jacket.
Q.   Over his uniform?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And Predrag clearly told other people what to do?

A.   That's an interesting thing that nobody commanded anybody there. They gave the impression of a well-trained team who knew what they were doing.  I never heard a single command being said.  But it's a fact that Slavisa Vukojicic who, didn't know at the time, he's from Rogatica, only after my escape did other people tell me his name based on my description.  He seemed to be in charge, and I believe that he was wearing no arms, no weapons.
Q.   Now, isn't it true that as of your December 1992 statement you had learned that Baja Zukic had been killed?
A.   The name must be wrong.  Zukic.  Yes, that's the last name, but it is not Baja.
Q.   Okay.  I'm sorry.  What is her first name?
A.   We're talking about a woman.
Q.   Yes.
A.   There were no women at the pit.  There were men exclusively.
Q.   I'm sorry, you misunderstand me.  I'm talking about after your escape you later learned that Ms. Zukic had been killed somewhere else.
A.   I heard that the following convoy that left after ours -- on the other convoy there was a woman who was killed.  It's possible that it was Ms. Zukic, but I cannot confirm that.
Q.   So you never heard the name of Milan Lukic associated with Ms. Zukic?
A.   Behija Zukic, whether she was really killed on one of those convoys or in town, in her house.
Q.   So you don't know.
A.   If are talking about the person I mean Behija Zukic, she was killed in her house.
Q.   And you did not hear Milan Lukic associated with this?
A.   I did, that Milan Lukic was mentioned in connection with the killing of Behija Zukic if we're talking about the same person, I mean the one who had a house in Duce.
Q.   And you didn't mention Mr. Lukic in your December 1992 statement, so you later learned of this between 1992 and 1997?

A.   I think I knew that even before that time, but the statement I gave in two, I've already described the circumstances in which it was given.  I was still under the impression of my or deal, because this isn't anything I know first-hand.  I only heard accounts from other people.  I didn't see it.  I don't know for sure.  I heard lots of things.  We can talk for days about all the things I heard.
Q.   Well, would it be fair to say all the things you heard about Milan Lukic was sometime between your December statement of 1992 and 1997 because you never mention him till 1997?
A.   Well, believe me, I really cannot tell.
Q.   Well, you didn't know who Milan Lukic was in the square at Visegrad when you were on the bus; correct?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And the only word you got was that a name was mentioned that day that you didn't remember until 1997; correct?

A.   No.  I heard that name on the very same day on the bus.  I asked Mirsad Zukic, who the man was who got on the bus, and he told me.  I don't know if they were schoolmates, but Milan Lukic called Esad out by calling him a schoolmate.  So I knew that it was Milan Lukic on that very day.
Q.   And you knew on that very day that he did not have the power to take him off the bus?
A.   On the following day I found out that Milan Lukic did have a lot of power, unfortunately.
Q.   You found that out on the following day but never mentioned it even in 1997?
A.   Well, probably nobody ever asked me about it.
Q.   And you didn't mention it in your testimony of 2001?
A.   Well, probably even then nobody asked me about that.
Q.   But would it be fair to say that based on your overall understanding of the power structure in Visegrad, the Crisis Staff and Perisic had the control in town?
A.   Dear sir, if I may ask you one thing.  Is there one single protocol about the crimes --
JUDGE ROBINSON:  Just a minute.  Just a minute, please.  You are not to ask questions.  That is counsel's right.

A.   Yes.

A.   Yes.  That was all before the war started.  We were even on good terms.  We had more drinks than just a few together with Mitar -- or, rather, fortunately I never met Mitar Vasiljevic.

A.   Yes.

A.   Well, look here.  Visegrad is a very small town.  It is a beautiful town, at least it used to be up to the war, where everybody knew everybody.  It is inconceivable, for instance, for a -- for schoolmates to kill one another.  It was inconceivable.  And the same Milan. As for Mitar Vasiljevic, and actually in respect of everybody who is proved who have been or even not proved to have been something of the kind, well, I've lived through too many things in order not to remember the situations.
Q.   But would it be fair to say that a guy like Mitar Vasiljevic couldn't have killed the thousands that died or disappeared in the Visegrad area during that time?

MS. SARTORIO:  Your Honour, I object to the question.  I mean, first of all it calls for speculation.  I don't know if this witness -- there has been no foundation laid whether this witness would know that answer, and it really, quite frankly, isn't relevant.

A.   That's right.

A.   I had heard these stories about Milan Lukic even prior to joining the convoy, but I was not at all interested in that person.  I didn't even know who that man was.  It was totally immaterial to me.  It was unimportant who he was or what he did.  Simply what I knew from these stories was that his chief occupation during these months in 1992 was killing.  Nothing good.  Nothing, absolutely nothing good.  From all the things that I heard about -- in all the things that I heard about Milan Lukic there was nothing good.

A.   It was given in Mostre; right?  The conversation, rather, the statement that I gave to investigators in Mostre, if that is what you're .00 p.m., until 2200 hours.

A.   At the moment when I decided to leave the hospital, the state of chaos reigned among the health-care workers, as well as among the wounded who were hospitalised in large numbers.  The hospital did not have enough capacity.  People were lying all over the place, in the corridors, in the rooms, in the cellars.  We had not received any orders from the authorities of the hospital.  We didn't know what to do.  So the health-care workers were forced to make their own executive decisions as if -- as it were.  I stayed there until the moment I felt I was safe. However, at the moment when I realised that the moment was no longer safe, that the situation was no longer safe, when I heard shells and bullets falling on the hospital roof, then I decided to use my white coat that was bloodstained.  I actually decided to take it off and leave it behind, and I just took a first aid kit, and that's how I left the hospital.

Q.   Thank you.  In the Popovic transcript you said that you did take the coat, the first aid kit, and that without any documents you left the hospital, and you said that you were following all the other staff who worked there.  That's on page 3943 in the Popovic case. Could you please answer the following question:  Did everybody from the hospital left the hospital and left together with you where you went, or maybe you followed them, or did you follow anybody's orders? Did you have anybody's guidance?  Did you follow some insider information or any such thing?  Thank you.
A.   Most us were moving in the direction of Kazin Kutlici and further on, up to the front line, but fewer of us or fewer of them, rather, went in the direction of Potocari.
Q.   So you're saying that some went to Potocari and the others joined Tuzlaon foot.  Did I understand you properly?
A.   Yes, you did.

Q.   Thank you.  Did any of you have any markings or insignia showing that you were affiliated with the hospital, the region, any unit?  Any of us who had coats, did those coats show any markings of affiliation? Thank you.

A.   I have to go back a little.  You're mentioning white coats.  As I've already stated and I repeated today, I had taken my coat off.  God forbid for me to keep the coat on.  There was no need for us to wear white coats.  All the health-care workers that I could observe wore civilian clothes.

Q.   I will not go back to page 3943.  I leave it to the Prosecutor and the Court to look at that.  I'm just asking you whether you in the hospital had any markings on the coats.  Did you have your name tags or any IDs that would show to any interested parties that you were health-care workers?  Thank you.
A.   You mean while we worked at the hospital?  Most of us had nothing.  I believe that only general practitioners had name tags on their coats.
Q.   Thank you.  Did you have IDs or maybe Red Cross markings or any such thing?
A.   I didn't.
Q.   Thank you.  Did you have an ID while you were in Srebrenica at all?
A.   No.

Q.   So if the MPs stopped you, how would they know that you were a hospital employee without any documents?  How come that you were not afraid that they would take you to the front line, because the mobilisation was on.  How come you were not afraid?

A.   There were no controls.  There were no curfews.  Nobody ever stopped me during my stay in Srebrenica.  Nobody controlled me.  The hospital had my details and information.  Everybody knew I worked there. Nobody ever controlled me.

Q.   Since you graduated from the nursing school and the rest were doctors, did you know that Red Cross markings or markings of affiliation to a health-care institution should be worn if you wanted to have and enjoy privileges in the territory or when you were called for emergencies or when you wanted to prove your status in case you were imprisoned? According to Geneva Conventions, you would have been entitled to some privileges if you had sported such insignia or markings.  Do you know that?

A.   The MSF or the Red Cross was there, and I was in an MSF car.  I travelled to Suceska, to a school where we were supposed to inoculate children.  I didn't have any IDs.  The only thing that we had was markings on that car, the Red Cross markings which enabled us to travel there.

Q.   Thank you.  In transcript on page 3945 you spoke about -- on line 6 [as interpreted] and 21 and I quote: there was a valley, and in that valley there were ham operators who had managed to send the last report and ask for assistance because Srebrenica had already fallen in the Serb hands.  However, they received information to wait and that NATO Air Force would act and that people should not leave Srebrenica yet." Do you remember that you stated that on page 3945, lines 16 through 21 in the Popovic case?  Thank you.
A.   Yes, I do remember.

Q.   Could you please tell us who these ham radio operators were and whether they belonged to some radio -- amateur ham radio operators association, or whether they belonged to some military unit?  Thank you.

A.   They belonged to the amateur ham radio operators, and this enabled them in view of the blockade of Srebrenica to maintain contact with their loved ones who were in some other country or whatever.  I don't think they had any influence or any impact on the military.
Q.   Could you tell me, then, where they got the information from about NATO air-strikes and that they shouldn't leave Srebrenica yet? Thank you.

A.   Well, I actually caught up with a large group of people there, and that's where I also met the hospital director.  This was in Kutlici, and that's where all these amateur ham operators were, and they told us that we should wait a little longer, that the upper parts of the town were already under Serb control.  They had sent out that report, but as they said, we should wait a little longer, that there would be NATO air-strikes, and that this was on the final reckoning.  However, indeed a few minutes later we heard NATO aircraft overhead.  Some of them did drop a few bombs, at least that's what I heard, but then after a while they disappeared, which to us was a signal that we should wait no longer and that we should set off on our journey.

Q.   Thank you.  Could you tell us whether these amateur radio operators, as you said, provided information to the NATO Air Force, and how did they actually prevent this from getting actually intercepted by the Republika Srpska Army?  Thank you.

A.   Of course they had no contact with NATO, with the NATO Air Force. They didn't send such information to them.  I assume that they were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, maybe in Sarajevo, and maybe -- and I think that they, the authorities, actually sent them all this information.

Q.   Thank you.  On page 3945 of the Popovic transcript, in your testimony at line 25 you said that: "On the outskirts of Srebrenica," I quote, "I saw a large group of prominent people." And on page 3947, you said that there were, I quote: "People such as the hospital director, radio operators, people from the municipal authorities who were actually planning on the route to take and whether they should wait for NATO aircraft or just try to reach the free territory."
A.   Of course I remember that.

Q.   Well, as you see, then, the group that you were in also included all these people who would decide on who would leave, those people who decided on who would be actually selected to leave Srebrenica or not, and that these people were actually in the group with you and they were waiting for the outcome of NATO air-strikes; correct?
JUDGE FLUEGGE:  Mr. Thayer.
MR. THAYER:  Mr. President, again if we can have some citation to the record, because I'm not familiar with it, where there was testimony about selecting who would be able to leave Srebrenica.
JUDGE FLUEGGE:  Mr. Tolimir, can you help us with the correct quotation, with the reference in the transcript?

THE ACCUSED: [Interpretation] Thank you.  That's page 3945, line 25, of the Popovic transcript.  And the witness in his testimony then said the following that on the outskirts of Srebrenica, I quote: "I saw a large group of prominent men." And on page 3947, he said that there were there such people as, I quote: "The hospital director, ham radio operators, municipal authorities members who planned the route on which we were to proceed and whether we should wait for NATO air-strikes or continue on our way, uncertain way towards the free territory." And this witness confirmed that this is what he said during his Popovic testimony.  If there is any other matter that needs to be cleared, I'm prepared to repeat my question.  Thank you.
