MR. PRESIDENT: Please be seated. The Court is now in session. Today, the Chamber will hear testimony of a witness, 2-TCW-817, in relation to Phnom Kraol Security Centre. Mr. Em Hoy, please report the attendance of the parties and other individuals to today's proceedings.

THE GREFFIER: Mr. President, for today's proceedings, all parties to this case are present. Mr. Nuon Chea is present in the holding cell downstairs. He has waived his right to be present in the courtroom. The waiver has been delivered to the greffier. The witness who is to testify today -- that is, 2-TCW-817, confirms to his best knowledge, he has no relationship, by blood or by law, to any of the two accused -- that is, Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan, or to any of the civil parties admitted in this case. The witness took an oath before the Iron Club Statue this morning, and there is no reserve witness today.

MR. PRESIDENT: Thank you, Mr. Em Hoy. The Chamber now decides on the request by Nuon Chea. The Chamber has received a waiver from Nuon Chea, dated 11 March 2016, which states that due to his health -- that is, headache, back pain, he cannot sit or concentrate for long. And in order to effectively participate in future hearings, he requests to waive his right to be present at the 11 March 2016 hearing. Having seen the medical report of Nuon Chea by the duty doctor for the Accused at ECCC, dated 11 March 2016, which notes that Nuon Chea has back pain -- back pain and cannot sit for long and recommends that the Chamber shall grant him his request so that he can follow the proceedings remotely from the holding cell downstairs. Based on the above information and pursuant to Rule 81.5 of the ECCC Internal Rules, the Chamber grants Nuon Chea his request to follow today's proceedings remotely from the holding cell downstairs via an audio-visual means. The Chamber instructs the AV Unit personnel to link the proceedings to the room downstairs so that Nuon Chea can follow. That applies for the whole day. Court officer, please usher the witness into the courtroom.
(Short pause) (Witness enters the courtroom)
QUESTIONING BY THE PRESIDENT: Q. Good morning, Mr. Witness. What is your name?
MR. NETH SAVAT: A. Neth Savat.
Q. Thank you, Mr. Neth Savat. Are you known by any other names?
A. Tha. My native name is Net Tha.
Q. And what is your official name, for example, the name that appears on your identity card?
A. It is Neth Savat.
Q. And when were you born?
A. I was born in 1942.

Q. Thank you, Mr. Neth Savat. And please wait for the microphone to be operational before you speak. Otherwise, your voice does not go through the interpretation system. Although you speak in Khmer, it has to be simultaneously interpreted into the working languages of the ECCC -- that is, English and French. You need to have a slight pause before you answer the question so that you also have a chance to think of how to respond. And please limit your response to the question. And where were you born?
A. I was born in Peam Chi Miet village, Nang Khi Loek commune, Kaoh Nheaek district, Mondolkiri province.
Q. In the document, it is stated that you were born in Laos and you only moved to Cambodia when you were 11 years old. Is that correct?

A. Yes, I was born in Bak village, Nam Nao commune, Keng Kang district, Savannakhet province. And when I was 10 years old, I came to live in Peam Chi Miet village, Chi Miet commune, Kaoh Nheaek district, Mondolkiri province.
Q. And where is your present address?
A. I live in Peam Chi Miet village, Nang Khi Loek commune, Kaoh Nheaek district, Mondolkiri province.
Q. And what is your current occupation?
A. I worked in the farm and in the plantation, and I also raised livestock.
Q. What are the names of your parents?
A. My father is Net, and my mother is Tum.
Q. What is your wife's name, and how many children do you have?
A. My wife is Thuoy Chan, and we have five children.

Q. Thank you, Mr. Neth Savat. The greffier made an oral report that you are not related, by blood or by law, to any of the two accused -- that is, Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan, or to any civil parties admitted in this case. Is that correct?
A. I am not related to any -- to any of them -- that is, Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan.
Q. And have you taken an oath before your appearance -- that is, before the Iron Club Statue to the east of the Chamber?
A. Yes, I have.

Q. Mr. Neth Savat, the Chamber would like to inform you of your rights and obligations as a witness. Regarding your rights, as a witness in the proceedings before the Chamber, you may refuse to respond to any question or to make any comment which may incriminate you. And that is your right against self-incrimination. On your obligations, as a witness in the proceedings before the Chamber, you must respond to any questions by the Bench or relevant parties, except where your response or comment to those questions may incriminate you, as the Chamber has just informed you of your right as a witness. You must tell the truth that you have known, heard, seen, remembered, experienced or observed directly about an event or occurrence relevant to the questions that the Bench or parties pose to you.
And Mr. Net Tha, have you been interviewed by investigators of the Office of the Co-Investigating Judges? If so, how many times, when and where?
A. I was interviewed twice: one was in Chi Miet, and on the other occasion, it was in Ratanakiri province. This is the third time.
Q. Thank you. Before you appear before us, have you read, reviewed or had it read aloud -- that is, your written record of the interviews with the OCIJ investigators in order to refresh your memory?
A. Yes, I read some yesterday, and I can recall parts of the written records of my interviews.
Q. And to your best recollection, do the written records of your interview reflect your answers that you gave to the investigators?
A. Yes, it is consistent. I refer to the written record of my interview is consistent.

MR. PRESIDENT: Thank you. And pursuant to Rule 91bis of the ECCC Internal Rules, the Chamber hands the floor first to the Co-Prosecutors to put questions before other parties. And the combined time for the Co-Prosecutors and the Lead Co-Lawyers is two sessions. You may proceed.
QUESTIONING BY MR. LYSAK: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

Q. Good morning, Mr. Neth Savat. My name is Dale Lysak. I'll be asking you some questions this morning. I want to start, if I may, with just a few background questions about yourself and also the province that you're from, Mondolkiri. Can you tell us a little bit about Mondolkiri province, including back in the 1970s? Was Mondolkiri a highly-populated province in Cambodia?
MR. NETH SAVAT: A. There were quite a large population living in Mondolkiri, but I cannot tell you the details. I cannot tell you how many thousands of people were living in the province.

Q. Well, let me see if I can help you. We have a statement from a witness who worked in the Mondolkiri provincial information office. Your Honours, this is document E3/5178. He said, and I quote, that: "During the Khmer Rouge period, the province was home to 19,000 people -- 19,000 people." Does that refresh your memory? Does that number sound about right to you, Mr. Witness?
A. That is about right. The number was more than 10,000.
Q. You, yourself, have -- are an ethnic Lao. Were there many ethnic minorities who lived in Mondolkiri?
A. Yes, there were other ethnicities, namely, Phnong, Tumpoun, Kraol and a few others that lived in Mondolkiri province. There could be more, but I could not get all.

Q. Do you -- are you able to provide us with an approximation of what percentage of the population of Mondolkiri were ethnic minorities back in the seventies? Was it the majority of the population, less, most of the population? Can you give us some sense of how many of the people in Mondolkiri were ethnic minorities?
A. I can only give you an estimate. There was about six to seven per cent of ethnic minorities living in Mondolkiri province.

Q. Can you tell us back in the seventies, before the Khmer Rouge -- or back in the sixties, perhaps, before the Khmer Rouge were in power in Mondolkiri, what were the most common languages that were spoken there among the various ethnic minorities?
A. The Khmer language was generally used.
Q. Were there any other languages that most of the people spoke in addition to Khmer?

A. And the Phnong language. That is all in Mondolkiri province. So the Khmer language was the first language -- or the primary language, Phnong was the second major language, and then there were other people who spoke various other ethnic language, including Laotians, Kraol and Jarai language.
Q. And can you tell us, what year was it when the Khmer Rouge gained control of Mondolkiri province?
A. It was 1970.

Q. Turning to your background, sir, you state in your OCIJ interview, E3/7695, that you joined the Revolution in 1966 to 1967 and that you joined the Revolution with a person named Phan Khon, alias Chuon. Can you tell us who Phan Khon alias Chuon, was?
A. The name was Phan Khon, and I joined the Revolution around 1967 or '68.

Q. And can you clarify for me, was it Phan Khon who introduced you to the Revolution, or did the two of you join together at the same time? And if so, who was it that introduced you to the Revolution?
A. There were people who actually persuade -- persuaded us to join the revolutionary movement, and those were Kham Phoun and Ta Ham. And they were there in Peam Chi Miet village.
Q. And after joining the Revolution, did you ever become a member of the Party?
A. I became a Party's member in 1970. That was when I was inducted into the Communist Party.
Q. And who was it that inducted or introduced you to the Party in 1970?
A. It was Kham Phoun and Ham.

Q. Now, in your OCIJ interview, you also describe how, after you joined the Revolution, you worked as a messenger from 1968 to 1970. During that time, did you ever escort or guard any senior leaders of the Khmer Rouge who were travelling through Mondolkiri?

A. I was appointed as a messenger and also to escort guests from my location to other locations (inaudible) from Torng Pang mountain to Kaoh Kalem river. And I was no longer a messenger by 1970, and I was assigned to be a member of the economic section to go and purchase unhusked rice and to look after cattle. So I was tasked to purchase unhusked rice and corn. And later on, I was assigned to be part of the economic section of a hospital, and that's due to a number of people who were admitted to that hospital.

Q. Thank you. I'll ask you a few questions about each of these positions. Let me start with the period you were a messenger back in 1968 to 1970. Who were the Party leaders, Khmer Rouge leaders, who you escorted through Mondolkiri?
A. As I said, they were Kham Phoun and Ham.
Q. Were there Party leaders of the Khmer Rouge who weren't based in Mondolkiri, but were travelling through the province who you were assigned to guard or escort?
A. At the time, it depended on the locations. And later on, in '70, after the liberation, the location was in Kaoh Nheaek.

Q. Let me see if I can refresh your memory on this, Mr. Witness. In your OCIJ interview, E3/7695, reading from Khmer, ERN 00236715; English, 00239485 through 486; French, 00274815; this is what you said in your OCIJ statement -- quote: "In 1968, I worked as a messenger escorting senior cadres from Torng Pang to Kalem in Kaoh Nheaek district. I used to escort Khuon alias Thuch, who later became secretary of the North Zone. Other persons whom I used to escort included Pol Pot's wife, named Khieu Ponnary, Tiv Ol and Nuon Chea." Is that correct, Mr. Witness? Were there some occasions where you escorted Nuon Chea when he was travelling through Mondolkiri?

A. That is correct. I, at one time, accompanied him from Torng Pang to Kalem. And also Tiv Ol, from Da Eh (phonetic) to Kalem. Ta Thuch, Ta Khuon, they were travelling together, and I also accompanied the two later individuals, but my task was to accompany them from Tonle to Torng Pang. And when they crossed to the other side of the river, it was others who were responsible for accompanying them to other locations. My task was to accompany them from Kalem to Torng Pang.

Q. As I'm not familiar with the locations you're describing, were they travelling north in the direction to go towards Ratanakiri, or were they travelling in some other direction when you accompanied them?
A. It was in the north from Torng Pang, so usually I accompanied them back and forth from Torng Pang to Kalem. And sometimes I accompanied those individuals back to Torng Pang.
Q. And were there soldiers or militia who were assigned to assist you when you were accompanying Nuon Chea and Ta Thuch on these journeys?

A. When Ta Nuon Chea went to that location, there was some soldiers with him. Around 20 of them were with him. Those people were soldiers, and I was with them at the time. So it was not a large trip at the time.
Q. And how did you know that the persons you were accompanying were Nuon Chea and Ta Thuch?

A. I do not understand about that issue. It was other people who were responsible for accompanying them after Torng Pang. I was only accompanying them up to Torng Pang, and then other people were responsible for accompanying those people to other locations, as I said.

Q. I understand that. What I was asking you is how you knew who these people were. Did they introduce themselves to you or, when you were given this assignment, were you told who it was that you would be escorting?

A. When they saw me, in fact, those people  were with Ta Ham and Sophea. And at the time, they said those people were Nuon Chea and Tiv Ol, so I learned that from those people, they spoke about that issue to one another, so this is what I can recall. They did not tell me directly, but on some occasion, I overheard what they were speaking about those people.

Q. Thank you. Let me turn to the positions you held subsequent to being a messenger after 1970. You've told us that you first were assigned to an economics unit and then, later, in 1976, were assigned to work in a hospital. Let's start with the economics unit, or office, that you worked at. You indicate in your OCIJ statement -- well, first of all, who was the chairman of the economics office that you worked for after 1970?

A. The chief of the economics section was Ta Kham Phoun. He was also the sector committee. To the communists' people, he was known as the chief of the economics section, so I was only a member within that economics section responsible for buying rice. That happened in 1970 up to 1976.

Q. You also identify in your interview a person named Sonthan. Who was the person -- you indicate he was your immediate superior; that he was the chairman of a unit and you were the deputy. Can you tell us who Sonthan was and what unit he was responsible for?

A. He was chief or secretary of the ministry; Ta Sonthan, Ta Chuon and me at the time were working in the Ministry of Economics. They were not part of sector committee. These people were responsible for commerce and economy. I am referring to Sonthan, who was the chief of economy at the time.

Q. So do I understand correctly that Kham Phoun was on the sector committee, the person who's overall responsible for economics, and yourself, Chuon, and Sonthan, worked at the ministry or office that was under Kham Phoun? Do I understand correctly?

A. Yes, you are right. Kham Phoun was sector committee, had overall responsibility for economy. And I, together with Sonthan and Chuon, were within the office of economy directly responsible for trading.
Q. And was the office of economy the same as the commerce office, or was it a different office than the commerce office?
A. Kham Phoun was in a different office, and Ta Sonthan was working within a different office responsible for commerce. And I was responsible for economic affairs at Kaoh Nheaek number 9.
Q. There are references to the commerce office as the K-16 office. What I wanted to clarify, did you work at the K-16 office or were you at a different office than K-16?
A. I worked in Office K-21, currently number 9 of village Srae Sangkom. The name -- the designated number was K-21.
Q. Did you know an office called K-16 and, if so, where was it located and who was in charge of K-16?
A. Office K-16 was for Kham Phoun, the sector's committee responsible for economic -- economy.

Q. Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. The next position -- you've indicated that in 1976, you were assigned to work in the economics unit of a hospital. Was that the sector hospital and, if so, where was the sector hospital located?
A. That hospital was belonged to the sector, and the actual location of that hospital at the time is now in number 9, Srae Sangkom village.
Q. So this is the same -- the same village in Kaoh Nheaek, the same place where you had worked at the economics office, Office 21. Is that correct?
A. That is correct. The same location where I used to work within K-21. K-21 was before located in this area as well.
Q. And when you worked at the hospital, who were the chairman and the deputy responsible for the sector hospital?
A. Ta Ham had overall supervision over the hospital, and then Ta Phat, Neang (phonetic) Bou Lai, they were also responsible for that hospital.

Q. And later, we're going to talk about a period where you were detained at the -- an office called K-17. What I wanted to just ask you now is, how far -- were the sector hospital and Office 21 where you worked, were these close to K-17, the sector secretary's office?
How -- what was the distance between the hospital, the economics office and the K-17 office where the sector secretary was based?
A. Regarding the distance, it was perhaps one kilometre away from hospital to K-17 where Ta Ham was located.

Q. Before we turn to the events at K-17, one other background question I wanted to ask you about, Mr. Witness: Were you a relative of Northeast Zone secretary Ya, who's also known as Men San? Were you related to Ya?
A. He was my brother-in-law. He married my younger sister.
Q. What was the name of your younger sister who married Ya?
A. Her birth name was Neth Ma (phonetic). And currently, which is her new name, is Neth Voeun (phonetic).
Q. When did she marry Ya?
Q. During the Khmer Rouge regime, did you ever meet north-- Ya, the Northeast Zone secretary? Did you ever see him and, if so, can you describe to the Court when it was that you met Ya?

A. I met him in the forest, and then, later on, in Tuol Kork when I was hospitalized in the hospital in Phnom Penh. I met him also at -- in Tuol Kork area, and I also went to his residence. He was assigned to be responsible for the Northeast of -- within Kratie, and when I was released from the hospital, I also met him. And then I went back to Mondolkiri.
Q. What happened to Ya during the Khmer Rouge regime?
A. I did not witness that. I learned from others that he was tied up and killed. I do not know whether it's true, since I did not witness that.
Q. Who was it that told you he was tied up and killed?
A. I heard from others. I do not know whether it's true. I heard from others saying about that. It is all I could remember.
Q. Did your sister ever tell you what happened to her husband, Ya?

A. Regarding my sister, after the arrest of Ta Ya, she formulated a letter and sent it to me at Kaoh Nheaek. She said she wanted to go and live in Mondolkiri after that time. And I was afraid of others after seeing the letter, and I forwarded the letter to Ta Ham. He said nothing, and he ignored that letter and kept it aside. And I have never -- and from that time, I did not hear about my sister. I did not dare talk about that. I, in fact, at the time, wanted my sister to go live in Kaoh Nheaek. I felt -- I felt pity on her since I heard that her husband suffered a bad ordeal. However, she had two children, they were all boys.

Q. That's one -- that's something I just wanted to clarify. During the Khmer Rouge regime, was your sister ever arrested? And can you clarify for us whether your sister, who was married to Ya, survived the Khmer Rouge regime?

A. From the news that I received, when the Khmer Rouge arrived, they could not transport all of them, so they left them there. And I, at one time, thought that she may not live through the period since, from that time onward, I never received any news from her.

Q. Let me just read to you an excerpt from an interview you gave to DC-Cam, document E3/7696; Khmer, 00231537; English, 00384159; French, 00384264. I quote: "Once he was arrested (referring to Ya) his wife was still there and sent me a letter. Then I heard the arrest and smashing happened." Question: "Who were arrested?" Answer: "My younger sister, Ya's wife." End of quote. Do I understand correctly that your sister was not -- initially not arrested at the same time as Ya, but later on was arrested and disappeared? Do I understand correctly, Mr. Witness?
A. Yes, that is correct. It was -- it did not happen at the same time during her husband's arrest. She was later on arrested.
Q. And have you ever seen your sister again since she was arrested?

A. No, I did not see her again. I did not see her again from 1975. Never saw her. I never saw her. After the letter was sent to me, I did not see her again. I did not know at the time whether she died or was living? From the news, I did not have any hope that she was living. I also thought that her children did not live also at the time.

Q. I want to turn now to some questions about some events you describe in your statements. Were you arrested by the Khmer Rouge during 1977 and, if so, can you describe to the Court how it came about that you were arrested? Can you describe the events that took place leading up to and the day of your arrest?

A. I was arrested in 1977 in January. And then I was placed and detained for one month. My relatives, my children, my nieces and my nephews and children and I were all arrested and detained for one month. For one month. And then we all -- we were all released and assigned to work in worksites. We were there at the worksites for two years. And later on, we were freed by the Vietnamese in 1979. This is all that I could recall. And at that time, they said Kham Phoun and Sonthan had betrayed the regime. They were arrested before me. And it was said that they had link to the Vietnamese. That was the reason of the arrests. How could we have relation with the Vietnamese at the time since we did not see them in the location?

Q. In regards to the time or -- the month or time at which you were arrested, we've heard testimony in the first trial in Case 002 and from the last witness about an incident in Phnom Penh in which Sector 105 secretary Ham was supposedly killed by deputy secretary Kham Phoun. What I -- I don't want to ask you about those events. What I do want to know is: Were you arrested before or after the death of Ham and Kham Phoun? Was it before or after their deaths that you were arrested?

A. I believe there were conflicts between Ham and Kham Phoun. As for me, I was the -- one of the subordinates of Kham Phoun. However, I believe the same thing happened to those under the subordination of Ham, so there were two separate groups. One belonged to Ham and one belonged to Kham Phoun. And Ham came from Kaoh Moueleu. He also had his relatives living in that area.

Q. In your OCIJ statement, E37695 at Khmer, ERN 00236715; English, 00239486; French, 00274816; you state, quote: "Shortly before they arrested me, Laing or Ham and Kham Phoun shot each other dead in Phnom Penh." My question to you was: How long after the deaths of Ham and Kham Phoun -- how long after that was it when you were arrested? You say it was shortly after that, but how many days or weeks, to the best of your recollection?
A. It was not long. It was about one week after Ham and Kham Phoun killed each other in Phnom Penh. And after that, there was this policy of arresting us.

Q. You've indicated that there were other people who were arrested. How many other people, to the best of your recollection, were arrested around the same time, and who were the other people who were also arrested?

A. I cannot recall them all. As for my relatives who were arrested, I could recall some of their names. And all together, there were about 80 people who were arrested and detained at where I was detained. And that included both men, women and children. And only a small number of the detainees were Khmer, as the majority were ethnic minority people. So there were numerous people, and I could not tell them all. As for the cadres, there was Ta Chanda (phonetic), So Sokhot (phonetic) and Sin Huor (phonetic). The last two are still living. And I cannot recall other names.
Q. Were the people who were arrested all or mostly people who were relatives of Kham Phoun or people who worked in the economics offices that fell under Kham Phoun's responsibility?

A. There were only a small number of relatives of Kham Phoun, as the majority were those workers who worked under the supervision in the office of Kham Phoun. Not everyone was related to Kham Phoun, but they were workers or his subordinates.
Q. You've indicated already that you had worked under Kham Phoun in the economics office. Were you also related to Kham Phoun?
A. Yes, I am related to his wife. His wife was the aunt of my wife.
Q. What was the name of Kham Phoun's wife, and what did she do in Sector 105?

A. Lap. Lap was the name of Kham Phoun's wife. She was also known as Bopha. She also worked in that office. She led people to work in that office as part of the economics work -- that is, to work in the rice fields and to work in the plantation. She did not involve in any politics.
Q. And when you say she worked -- also worked at the office, are you talking about the K-16 office, Kham Phoun's office, or the Office 21, the economics office where you had worked?

A. She worked at the economic office -- that is, at K-16 because her husband was in charge of the sector's economics. Here I refer to Kham Phoun's wife. However, herself did not have any major role. She would lead workers to  the rice fields or the plantations.
Q. What happened to Kham Phoun's wife after his death? What happened to Lap, alias Bopha?

A. I did not know what happened to her because the arrest was about a week after Kham Phoun and Ham killed each other. And I believed she also was arrested along with her children and family members during that time.
Q. Did you ever see her again after you were released from your detention?

A. No, I never saw her again because after I was released from the detention, I was sent to a worksite. I was not allowed to travel to Kaoh Nheaek area, and we were instructed only to go and work in the northern direction at Srae Pok river. And I did not know what happened to her because she had also been arrested. And her children actually fled, and the children are now living in Kampong Cham. In fact, I correct myself. I refer to only an adopted daughter who is still living in Kampong Cham.
Q. What ethnicity was Kham Phoun?
A. Kham Phoun was Laotian and Tumpoun, so he was a mixed ethnicity of Laotian and Tumpoun.
Q. Were you working at the sector hospital at the time of your arrest and, if so, were there other people from the sector hospital who were arrested on the same day or around the same time as you?

A. That was a sector's hospital. However, I worked for the economic unit for that hospital. For the leadership level at the hospital, there were Bou Lay and Bour Ly, who were female, and they were arrested as well. And I cannot recall any other individuals. So to my understanding, there were three, Bou Lay, Bour Ly, who were in the leadership level, and myself; all three.
Q. What was Bou -- you say two women, Bou Lay and Bour Ly. The first woman, Bou Lay, what was her position at the hospital and who was she married to?
A. Bou Lay was the chief, and she was my superior. She married Ra, so Ra was her husband. And Ra was a nephew of Ta Kham Phoun.
Q. And how about the other woman, Bour Ly? What was her position at the hospital, and who was she married to?
A. Bour Ly was in charge of midwifery, and her full name is Bour Ly Thon (phonetic), and she married Svay. And in fact, she came from Ratanakiri and she was Tumpoun.
Q. The day you were arrested, how were you transported, where were you taken and how were you transported there? Let's start with that

A. They brought a vehicle to take us to K-17. And after we got off the vehicle into -- and got into the house, they instructed us to sit down and they tied us up. And they placed us to the corner of that house.

Q. Mr. Witness, we were talking about the day that you were taken to -- arrested and taken to K-17. You talked about being driven in a vehicle there. Were there other people who had been arrested in the same vehicle with you and, if so, who was in that vehicle with you?

MR. NETH SAVAT: A. After that time, people had been sent into that location. My wife, together with my children, as well as my younger siblings and others had been transported to that location, many of them, 60, 70 or 80 of them. I cannot recall all of them since it happened long time ago.

Q. I understand. I'm asking about the vehicle in which you were brought to K-17. You've identified another person from the hospital who was arrested, your chief or superior at the hospital, Bou Lay. Was she in the same vehicle as you or was she taken to K-17 by a different vehicle or means?
A. They were transported in the same vehicle on the same day as I was also on that vehicle. We were in the same vehicle.
Q. And how long was Bou Lay detained or - I'm sorry, Bou Lay. How long was Bou Lay detained with you at K-17, and what happened to her?

A. I met Bou Lay in the detention facility at the time. Bou Lay was detained there for half a month, and then this individual was transported out while I was still being detained within that centre. I do -- I did not know where Bou Lay was sent to afterwards.
Q. Did you ever see her again after that day that she was taken out from K-17?
A. No, I have never seen her since then.

Q. Now, between the time of the deaths of Ta Ham and Kham Phoun and the time you were arrested, did you see a document or a circular about the subject of arrests and, if so, can you describe for the Court the document you saw during that time period?
A. No documents at the time. I heard from others about that.

Q. In your OCIJ interview, you referred to a circular that you received which you read to some of that hospital economics unit. Can you describe that document to us? How did you receive it, when did you receive it, and what did the document say?

A. On this particular issue, after the incident of Ta Ham and Kham Phoun, there were others going to our location to make an announcement, particularly Chuon alias Phan Khon, used a small loudspeaker going into the detention centre. He, at the time, made the first announcement that, "Please do not feel afraid or terrified. We, in fact, detained all of you, but we encourage all of you not to feel terrified or scared." And at the time, the second announcement was also about the treason committed by Kham Phoun. And third, he also stated that he was there in the name of the sector committee. He made such an announcement about the treason of Kham Phoun, but he did not show us any relevant documents. A few days later on, my child wanted to go to relieve him/herself, and my child called "Uncle Chuon". And the security guard said, "Why do you call out the name of Chuon since Chuon was also the one who betrayed regime?" That's how we came to know that Chuon was also accused of being a traitor. That was several days after the announcement was made.

Q. Okay. You're describing something from your DC-Cam interview of an announcement that Chuon made on the day you arrived at K-17. I want to focus on the period just before you were arrested, and I'm going to read to you an excerpt from your OCIJ interview, E3/7695; Khmer, ERN 00236716; English, 00239487; French, 00274817. This was your testimony to OCIJ: Question: "Did you notice who gave the order for your arrest?" Answer: "Shortly before my arrest, I received a circular from the upper echelon, probably from the sector secretary. I don't remember who signed it. I read that circular to the personnel of the hospital economics unit. That circular talked about the three categories of the enemy. The enemy in the first category had to be smashed. The one in the second category had to be detained. The one in the third category had to be sent to the cooperative." End of quote. Do you remember this document, Mr. Witness, and can you tell us how it was that you received this circular or document?

A. That was the case before my arrest. I was given a letter -- a document, rather, telling the female and male combatants in Office 80. I do not recall the -- all the content. And then that document, it discussed the three types of enemies. The first type was to be smashed. The second was to be detained. And the third group was to be sent to cooperatives. That was the first point. And I was -- I also received a letter of invitation to a meeting. The meeting did -- was not held -- did not usually hold at K-17. And at the time, as I received a letter of invitation to attend a meeting at K-17, I felt a little bit shocked at the time, but I did not know what to do or where to go. And the vehicle came to take me, and it was that time that I was arrested. In fact, at first, I did not know about the principle or the plan, but later on, it was only after I was arrested that I started to realize that the idea of sending us letters to make an announcement was to get us arrested.

Q. The first category of enemies in this document, the people who were to be smashed, were these people identified by name or what did the document say about who were going to be considered in this first category of enemies who were going to be smashed? What did the document say about that, if you remember?
A. It -- the document said there were three types of enemies, and the document did not discuss who were to be considered within the first group, second group or third group.

Q. On the subject of documents on the categories of people to be arrested, I want to read to you, Mr. Witness, an excerpt from the OCIJ interview of Sao Sarun, who you know replaced Ta Ham as sector secretary. This is document E3/367, E3/367; Khmer, 00251440 through 41; English, 00278697; French, 00486013. Sarun, here, testifies about a meeting at which the secretary of Division 920 had received a list of the people to be arrested, and this is what he said. I quote: "Ta San from Division 920 came to the meeting with Ta Sophea and me. He personally spoke about that arrest, for example, the arrest of Net Tha. Ta San already held the list, and I could not refuse." End of quote. The first question, Mr. Witness: Who was Ta San? Did you know this person identified by Sarun as Ta San?

A. I am not sure about Ta San. It was said that Ta San was the commander of the division, but I did not see him. I used to work with Ta Sarun. He was -- he used to be the sector committee as well. Concerning disclosing the document or documents, it was the policy of the upper echelon to arrest the three categories of enemies, the document or documents that were given to me on one occasion. After the arrests, soldiers from the division were sent to guard the detainees.
Q. Do I understand correctly that it was division soldiers who were assigned to guard you at -- while you were detained at K-17? Do I understand correctly?

A. That is correct. Soldiers from the division, as I said. The soldiers from the sector, then the soldiers from the division were assigned to guard all of us during the time that we had to go to relieve ourselves day and night, so they came to guard us day and night. So those people were from the division.
Q. And were those soldiers armed?
A. Yes, they were armed. While we were being walked to bathe or to relieve, they had weapons with them. Eight, nine or ten of them were there to guard the prisoners.
Q. And can you describe for us the building in which you were detained at K-17?

A. The building,  on the ground floor,  it had a concrete or tile floor. And the wall was -- the walls were made from wooden planks. It was two-storey building. And the walls upstairs were also made from a wood plank. And the roof was made from corrugated iron. There -- and as I said, it was a two-storey building.
Q. Were there prisoners detained on both floors of the building and, if so, what floor were you detained on?

A. I was detained on the ground floor, and some were on the second floor. I heard the sound of urinating, and also the sound when those detainees were released perhaps to -- were released, perhaps, to relieve themselves. And I also heard sounds of releasing or unlocking the shackles. More people were detained on the ground floor, that was the second category group, and not many of the detainees were on the second floor. There were only a few of them; they were the first category group.
THE KHMER INTERPRETER: Rather, correction from the interpreter, not many detainees were on the second floor.

BY MR. LYSAK: Q. Now, you've indicated that you -- when you were detained on the ground floor, you were tied up. Can you describe how it was that you were tied up during the period you were detained at K-17?

MR. NETH SAVAT: A. Our hands were tied to -- behind our back, and our ankles were also tied up. We were tied to a table set  in a corner of the ground floor for them to have meetings. And we were tied up and put in row.
Q. Were you tied up like that the entire month that you were at K-17?
A. Yes, that is true. I was tied up for the entire time.

Q. You mentioned that you heard the shackles -- the sound of shackles being unlocked. Was there anyone on the ground floor who was shackled, or was it -- the sound that you heard, was that coming from the upper floor?
A. I heard the sound of the shackles on the second floor. The detainees were -- on the ground floor were tied up to the hammock string. They were not shackled.
Q. The -- you've described hearing the sounds of the shackles being unlocked coming from upstairs. Did you ever see the shackles that were used on the upper floor at K-17?

A. Yes. That -- those shackles were made out of wood, and it had the bar -- the wooden bar to be inserted into the rings. The detainee was -- were shackled to one of their ankle. The shackles, as I said, were made out of wood.
Q. When was it that you saw these shackles? Was it during the month that you were at K-17, or was it later on that you saw these shackles?
A. It was before that time. One month before that time.
Q. I'm not sure I understood. Are you saying you saw the shackles before you were detained at K-17, or during the month you were at K-17?
A. I had seen those shackles before. I had seen those shackles one month before my detention.
Q. And can you tell us, what was the occasion? How is it that you came to see these shackles one month before your detention?
A. Ta Ham took me upstairs because, at that time, people from -- actually, Ta San, the chief of the division, was detained there along with other people from the division.

Q. Just to clarify, you're saying that, previous to your detention, Ta Ham had taken you to the upper floor at K-17 once, and there were prisoners from Division 920 who were detained there? Did I understand correctly?
A. Yes. Because at that time, the event did not happen yet, and Ta Ham was still there. And when he took me upstairs, I saw them shackled.

Q. Now, you've indicated that during the month you were at K-17, there were -- the guards there were division soldiers. Was there a person who was in charge of the detention of the prisoners? Was there one person who was -- who had overall responsibility and, if so, who was that?
A. I did not know because, at that time, I was being detained and I did not know who was in charge of that K-17 office because I was not allowed to walk outside.
Q. Did you ever see Ta Sarun there during the month you were detained at K-17?
A. No, I did not.
Q. What about Ta Sophea, the sector military chief? Did you see him at K-17?
A. No. Only later when I was assigned to work at the worksite, I saw Ta Sophea, who came to the worksite one time. And I was sent there after I was released from detention.

Q. You talked about there being a small number of prisoners who were held on the upper floor. Did you know who -- during the month you were at K-17, who were the -- who were the prisoners who were held on the upper floor?
A. From what people said, there were Sonthan, Tha, Ra, Voeun (phonetic) and Kem Chan.
Q. Who was Kem Chan?
A. Kem Chan had his native name as Phoeuk.
Q. But what was his position in the sector?
A. Kem Chan was a district committee, and Ra was also part of the district committee. And Ra was the deputy. As for Tha, Tha and Sonthan were at the economic unit or commerce.
Q. Now, you previously talked about Sonthan as your boss at the economics office. Was he at -- detained at K-17 the entire time -- the entire month you were there, or was he taken away at some point?

A. He was detained on the upper floor, and his office was the commerce office. And in fact, he was overall in charge of the Ministry of Economics there. I -- while I was detained on the ground floor, Tha and Sonthan were detained on the upper floor. They were the first category group. Ra was the deputy secretary of Kaoh Nheaek district, Kem Chan was a district committee member, and in fact, there were four members who were part of the district committee.
Q. Were these prisoners on upper floor, were they there the entire month that you were at K-17, or were they taken away at some point?
A. From what I heard, they were taken out and transported by vehicle, but I cannot recall whether they had been taken away before I was released or whether it happened after my release.
Q. Did you ever see any of those people again? Did you ever see Sonthan, Tha, Ra, any of those people who were detained on the upper floor? Did you ever see them again?
A. No, I did not. And they disappeared since.
Q. After you arrived at K-17, Mr. Witness, were you interrogated?
A. No, I did not hear anything about torture. As for the interrogation, I could not say because they were detained on the upper floor while I was detained on the ground floor.

Q. I know you've indicated that your recollection of this isn't great. Let me read to you a short excerpt from your DC-Cam interview, E37696; Khmer, ERN 00231542; English, 00384164; French, 00384268; this is what you said in your DC-Cam interview: Question: Once you were detained there, did you see prisoners were taken to be interrogated?" Answer: "Yes, they all were interrogated. Even I was." End of quote. I understand you're saying that there -- you were not tortured, but were you questioned and can you tell us about what questions you were asked, who you were questioned by, if you remember?

A. I was questioned once. We all were questioned. I was taken out of the detention room and questioned, and I was asked who actually inducted me into the Party. And I said it was Ta Kham Phoun. And then I was asked whether I was sure. I said yes. And they did not ask me any more questions after that.
Q. You said you were taken out of the detention room. Where was it that you were taken to be questioned?
A. I was taken out of the detention house, and then I was questioned. They did not take me far from the detention house.
Q. And who was it that questioned you? Who was it that took you out of the detention house and questioned you?
A. I did not know them, but they were people from the division. And I cannot recall it well. The chief was Theu (phonetic). That's all I can recall.

Q. Okay. You've talked about -- earlier about Bou Lay, the woman who was your chief at the sector hospital, being taken out of K-17, possibly others who were on the first floor. Did you ever hear where these people were taken? Did you ever hear anything about executions of people who had been detained and where it was that people were taken to be executed?
A. I did not know about that. However, what I could say is that some detainees were taken and placed on a vehicle and drove away. And I did not know what happened to them later.

Q. I want to read another short excerpt from your DC-Cam interview, E3/7696; Khmer, 00231531; English, 00384152; French, 00384258. You said -- quote: "Some killings happened, but not at the prison. They did along the way to Kratie." And earlier in the interview, you talked about hearing that people on the upper floor had been transported to the west. Who is it that you heard -- who is it that told you that prisoners who were taken away were sent to the west to the -- in the direction of Kratie? Who is it that you heard that from?
A. I heard it from other people, but I personally did not see that. People whispered from one to another about this.

Q. All right. You've indicated that the day that you arrived at K-17, Phan Khon alias Chuon, came to K-17 and made an announcement and that you described how, a few days later, your son and you asked about him and received a response from the guards that indicated that he had now been considered as one of the traitors. Do you know what happened to Chuon after you were arrested and detained at K-17?

A. Chuon was not detained at K-17 office. Maybe Chuon was arrested in Kratie. And he was not arrested and detained at K-17 office at all. However, as I said earlier, he came into that building where I was detained and made an announcement regarding the traitor, Kham Phoun, and that we should not worry about that. For that reason, in order to put things in orderly manner, we had to be detained temporarily. After the announcement was made, he left. And maybe later on he was arrested somewhere near Kratie, but I was not sure about that.

Mr. Witness?

MR. NETH SAVAT: A. Yes. The name Chuon is on this list, too. And that is correct because this Chuon also came from Sector 105.

Q. And you've testified that you joined the Revolution with Chuon. To your knowledge, was he a person who was loyal to the Revolution? Do you have any information about -- about Chuon and whether there was any reason for him to be sent to S-21?

BY MR. LYSAK: Mr. President, let me -- as I want to end and leave some moments for the civil parties. Let me refer the witness to a statement he made in his OCIJ interview. This is E3/7695; Khmer, 00236713; English, 00239484; French, 00274814.

Q. This is what you told OCIJ. You said, "As I know it, he" -- you were referring here to Phan Khon alias Chuon -- "was not the person who assigned Kham Phai to work as a spy, or he, himself, did not work as a spy with Kham Phai because Chuon was a real revolutionary." End of quote. What did you mean when you told OCIJ that Chuon "was a real revolutionary"?

MR. NETH SAVAT: A. I was asked by the investigators whether Chuon was appointed by Kham Phai to -- or rather, to let him to join the Revolution. And I said Chuon was a separate person from Kham Phai. And on the question whether he was loyal to the Revolution or not, I cannot attest to that. And I do not know the reasons why he was sent to S-21 because I was in Kaoh Nheaek.

Q. My last question for you, Mr. Witness. On the same S-21 list, you were looking at number 128. The next person on that list, if you could look at number 129, is identified as Sitang alias Bor Ly (sic), a 27 year-old female, who was the deputy chief of midwife in Sector 105, and the wife of Svay. My question: You spoke earlier about one of the other people who was arrested around the same time as you from the sector hospital, a woman named Bour Ly; is this the same person who you previously identified as one of the persons who -- who were arrested in November 1977?

A. Bour Ly could have been arrested a day before my arrest, and after she was arrested, I did not see her. She was not detained in the same detention centre where I was. And then it was Bor Ly (sic). And here it states about her age as -- of 27 years old, so this is about -- probably about Bour Ly, or maybe Sitang was her birth name.

QUESTIONING BY MS. GUIRAUD: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to all of you. I will probably need more than the five minutes that  I can see on the clock.

Witness, good morning. I am Marie Guiraud. I represent the collective of the civil parties in this trial and I have a few follow-up questions to put to you. Q. You said, this morning, that in your province, the main language was Khmer, but that people also spoke Lao, Tumpoun, or  Jarai, so I wanted to know if you, yourself  can speak Lao?
MR. NETH SAVAT: A. Yes, I speak both, the Laotian and the Khmer languages; and when I speak to my family members, I speak Lao.
Q. Thank you. So was Lao authorized during the DK period? Did you have the possibility of expressing yourself in that language back then; do you remember that?

A. Yes, we spoke Lao. When we met people who spoke Lao, we spoke Lao and if I saw Khmer people, I would speak Khmer to them. There were other minority languages including Tumpoun, Phnong, etc., and the language was not prohibited; however, as I stated, Khmer was the main language at the time.
Q. So during the Khmer Rouge period, basically speaking, you never heard that it was forbidden to speak Lao or another minority language; did I understand you correctly?
A. Yes, we were not prohibited from speaking any minority languages. We could speak Lao, Kraol, Phnong, Jarai, Tumpoun, or any minority languages that you could.

Q. Thank you. You said earlier that your wife and your children were also arrested in 1977 and I wanted to know how many children you had back then and how old your children were when they were arrested in 1977.

A. My wife and children were arrested, as well, and there were seven of them all together. My -- and my eldest son was about 17   or years old and the second one was about 16, so the age was           18   starting from there going downward. At the time, we had seven children, but two passed away and now we have only five.
Q. And do you remember the age of the youngest child who was arrested that day?
A. My youngest child is over 30 years old this year. He was born in 1981 or '82.

Q. And in 1977, when your wife and your seven children were arrested and detained with you, what was the approximate age of the youngest of your children? Was this child just a baby or a young child or a teenager? Can you give -- give us an idea?

A. At the arrest -- during the arrest, five of my children were arrested and later on, I had two other children, so together I have seven children. During the time, I had five children, three sons and one daughter, and after that incident or after that time, I had two other children, one son and one daughter. The youngest  son was around two years old. He was born in December '75, and in 1977, I went through the ordeal, so he was  around two years old in 1977.

Q. Thank you. Do you remember the conditions under which your children, aged between 17 and 2 years old, were detained with you? And do you remember, for example, the sanitary conditions and the food that was given to them? Do you have any recollections about the detention conditions of your children?

A. Regarding the conditions of the detention and meal, we had meals within the detention centre. We were there in -- inside the building. We can -- we could not go anywhere we wanted,  and for hygiene, it was us adults who cleaned the detention centre. The food condition was not good. We had pumpkin soup. We had pumpkin, at the time, for the entire month and -- together with rice; no meat, no fish or meat. We were given a small bowl of meal with merely one piece of meat or two pieces of meat and we had pumpkins. The food condition was very bad -- was worst. And there was only one toilet for all of us, no hygiene, no sanitation, no water for us to bathe. At the beginning, we were allowed and walked to take a bath once a week. The water was not clean. It was a small dike or bathing place for all of us. We were walked to that bathing place.

At the beginning, the string was released -- was untied from our ankles, that's how we could walk there; and while we were at the bathing place, our hand -- one of our hands was released from the string, and after bathing, we wore our clothes and then our hands were tied up again, and we were walked to the building. When we entered the room, our ankles  were tied up. So it was lucky enough for me to survive. Thanks to my mom's milk, I could survive the regime. So the conditions were the worst. The same happened to children. We had rice together with pumpkin. Fish was everywhere; meat was everywhere, but we were deprived of such latitude. We were not given  meat and fish. We did not dare to say anything about the food conditions.

Your own children were aged between 2 years and 18 years; were there many children in that detention facility; particularly, many young children on the ground floor where you were detained?

A. Children, yes, they were there, but not many. Some were younger than my 2-year-old baby, not many of them were younger than my 2-year-old baby. I may have forgotten. Some may have been 1 year or 2 years old, about 4 to 10 of them.
Q. Do you recall whether any of those children fell sick and if yes, what can you tell us about that?

A. I was removed from that detention centre. I was taken away from K-17 by  vehicle and the vehicle was driven northward -- northwards. That included children, men and women; perhaps 20 to 30 of us were sent to worksites. It was a Chinese-made vehicle, Celica (phonetic).

A. No, during the journey, there were the leading cadres, but no security guards. A. Ta An Sy was there on the same vehicle. He was considered the leading cadre. He was on the same vehicle, at the time, and now, I have heard that he is already deceased. Q. Before the break, Witness, I put a question to you about the militia and I would like you to explain to us how the militia would operate in Tram Kak cooperative.
MR. NEANG OUCH: A. In Tram Kak District, there were militia in communes and in districts. These two types of militia is to protect the security for the commune and for the districts.
Q. Can you be a bit more specific regarding the different tasks that were accomplished by the commune militia and the district militia?
A. I mentioned already that commune and district militias were to provide security to respective communes and districts. That's all.
Q. What do you mean by "security"?
A. As for the term "security", for instance if there was any issue or if there was any incident, the militia was to be deployed to provide security.
Q. And were the militiamen armed?

A. During that time they were lightly armed. For instance in one commune there would be ten militiamen and they had only two or three rifles or weapons. So in the platoon, there was a platoon as well, and one platoon had 13 members. And in Noreay, near National Road Number 3, there was a unit and in other areas near the mountain and in that area there was also unit. As I said, they were not heavily armed.
Q. Thank you. And how were the militiamen recruited, how old were they?
A. Upon my arrival I could see that the structure was already organised. As for the age of militiamen, the age range was between 18 to 35 -- rather 30.
Q. Thank you. So the commune militia -- were the commune militiamen in charge of supervising the couples that had just got married?
A. No.

Q. Thank you. I would like you to react on a testimony we heard a little earlier on in this Trial on 17 February 2015 and a witness came, he was a Base Person, and he came to testify. And I would like to read out an excerpt from the transcript, . And this person stated at around 10.55 while he was questioned about the role of the secret agents and he said, "After the wedding the unit chief sent chlop spies to listen at night. In reality there were two chlop spies per house to listen to the couple." A little bit further on he says, "they wanted to know if the couple would consummate the wedding and if that was not the case, the couple was summoned and would be reprimanded. If a couple got along well and consummated the marriage, there was no problem. The couple could go work as normal." I wanted to know, Witness, when you were at Tram Kak, if you saw militiamen listen to couples below their houses after they had got married.
A. No.
Q. Thank you. More generally speaking, how would couples get married at Tram Kak during the period you were posted there? Can you tell us how couples would marry at Tram Kak?

A. Actually as for marriage, four couples would marry in one time and the four couples would get married and after that there was dinner party and first the male would be asked to make a resolution and after that it was the time for the female. After making resolutions, these speeches or wishes were expressed by the head of the commune and there were wishes from the commune chief for the newly-wed and after that there was dinner time. And there was no music performed, there were no achar in attendance. This marriage would last only -- the marriage ceremony would last only two hours.
Q. Thank you, Witness. Were the men and women free to choose their partners?
A. Yes, there were some. In some places the head of the commune or the head of the cooperative would decide the partner for those people.
Q. What would happen if the men and women would refuse marrying the person who was proposed by the commune chief?

A. I never encountered such refusal. After they were matched, they would get married and for some couples they made their own decision and as I said the head of the commune and cooperatives on some occasions would decide which couples to be matched and after marriage I could see the newlyweds got along well with each other.
Q. Thank you. Did the district have a role to play in the way the weddings were organised?

A. Actually there was -- I did not see any involvement of the district. However the request would be made by the commune head to the district that the commune head would like to arrange a marriage for certain couples and request was made by the commune chief to the district for consideration and after that the marriage would be held. And most of time I did not see any attendance from the district.

Q. Thank you. I would like you to react to the answers that were provided by the person we spoke about since this morning and this person whose name we cannot disclose and who was interviewed by the Co-Investigating Judges. This is PV, .2, and this lady, whom you knew back then and with whom you attended district meetings, indicated to the Investigating Judge during her interview and in her answer 111 in particular, I'm going the read the excerpt in English because there is no French translation, "The commune level listed the names of the couples to be married and sent the names to the sector level to decide how many couples were to be married each time." Witness, does this description correspond to what you experienced back then -- that is to say, the fact that the commune would send the names of the couples to the sector level and then the sector would decide who would marry whom.

BY MS. GUIRAUD: Q. I will try to sum up my question in French under the supervision of the Chamber and the Parties. Witness, do you agree with the witness whose testimony I have just cited and who said that the list of names of couples to be married were sent to the commune at the level of the sector, who decided how many couples were to be married on each occasion, was that the practice to the best of your recollection?

MR. NEANG OUCH: A. People who were supposed to get married were sent to the upper level for approval and sometimes the approval could be made at the commune or at the district level so the situation varied. It's a case by case basis.
Q. Thank you. Did it sometimes happen that the higher level would refuse giving the authorisation for such marriages to proceed and if yes, what happened in that case?

A. I would like to clarify this issue again. Some couples, involved with - or some men or some women who were supposed to get married were forces from the sector level and if that is case then there has to be an authorisation from the district up to the sector level. However for those to be grooms not at the sector level then the authorisation could be only be made only up to the district level -- that is, from the commune up to the district. And to my knowledge, I never saw any disagreement or disapproval by the sector level in this case.

Q. Thank you. I have one last question, Mr. President, if you would allow me. It's a very short question and it is a follow up to the last question in the same transcript of that witness's testimony particularly on this subject, answer 117. I will read three lines of the witness's entire answer in English in order that there may not be any difficulty. "Nothing like that happened at my site, they all had known one another because my site was not large, we arranged their marriage and the couples agreed but if the upper level did not approve, they could not marry." Can you express an opinion on this? And this would be my last question, particularly to the fact that if the higher level did not approve of the marriage, those persons could not be married.

A. I never came across such an issue and if it happened probably it is out of my recollection. We made a request to the upper level and most of the time, they approved and I never saw a case where they disapproved such a request.

MR. PRESIDENT: Judges of the Bench do you questions to be put to this witness if so, you can proceed. Judge Fenz, you have the floor.

QUESTIONING BY JUDGE FENZ: Q. I have couple of general follow up questions. First, Witness, can you remind us, did you ever in life meet Pol Pot, Nuon Chea or Khieu Samphan and if I say, meet, I also mean, see.

MR. NEANG OUCH: A. During the period from 1975 to 6th January 1979, I met Om Nuon Chea during a yearly study session and I met him once. As for Khieu Samphan or Pol Pot, I never met them during the three-year period.
Q. And this study session was when? The study session when you met Nuon Chea.
A. I cannot recall the date. However it happened around September or October.

Q. Thank you. My next question goes to your relation to Ta Mok. Now, I understand you won't be able to give me a number of times you've had contact with him but give me an idea. In the time between '75 and end of '78, how often did you have contact of any kind, private or professional, direct or per phone or message with Ta Mok? Is this once a year, once a month, once a week, something in between?

A. I met Ta Mok in 1975, after Kampuchea was liberated. I met him when Ta Mok set a plan to build a historical dam at Angkor Borei Lake, stretching from Kampong Pou along Canal 99 and it stretched for four kilometres, then it turned to the north. I met him at the time that we were at the work site and he came to inspect the dam work site and while I led the workers to build that dam. That was the time that I was an assistant to Kaoh Andaet district. And from then on I met him on various other occasions, sometimes I saw him from a distance or sometimes I met him briefly. And during the two months that the dam was built, I met him rather frequently there when he went to inspect the work site. And after that period, I did not meet him or see him frequently.

I again saw him when I was called by him from Kaoh Andaet to Takeo and that when he assigned me to work as an assistant to Tram Kak District. And after that he left Takeo and went to the Northwest Zone  -- that is, to Battambang province and that is the fact.
Q. So can you give us an idea how often you met him in 1976, if at all?
A. I did not meet him that often in 1976.
Q. Can you be a bit more precise? That often is very vague, again, once a week, once a month, once every two months or what else?
A. In 1976, Ta Mok was still at the Southwest Zone and I met him probably once a month or once every two months when he came to Takeo.
Q. Were these private or professional meetings?

A. I met him during study sessions or during meetings -- that is, when communes or chiefs of communes were called for meetings at the districts and he also called me to attend those meetings or sometimes he called me to attend study sessions.
Q. What about 1977?

A. I did not meet him that frequently in 1977, because after he removed me from Kaoh Andeat to be an assistant in Tram Kak district, I did not meet him that often and subsequently he left Takeo for Battambang province in the Northwest Zone.
Q. Were there any private meetings, family things, weddings, funerals?
A. No.
Q. And to finish this, 1978, how often did you meet him then, if at all?
A. I already stated that after he transferred me to work at Tram Kak district, he went to Battambang district and I did not meet him since.

Q. Now, I have a couple questions about the wider Ta Mok family involvement in politics in the DK period. The Prosecutor started this line of questioning yesterday but used a document which hasn't been admitted so I'll ask you open questions. The questions will go to who of the Ta Mok family had which position? In order to structure this a bit, how many siblings did Ta Mok have and what positions did they have?

A. Ta Mok only had daughters and there were five of them. As for the positions, only the eldest daughter held a position, her name was Khom. Initially -- that is, after the 1970 coup, Khom, was the Tram Kak District Chief.
Q. What did her husband do, provided she had one?

A. Meas Muth was Khom's husband. In 1970, after the coup, he was in charge of the Sector 13 army -- that is, for Takeo sector. The sector army's main duty was to fight against the Lon Nol forces at that time. Later on, I cannot recall the year, but it was circa 1973 or '74, he was promoted to the zone level and further, later on he was promoted to the centre and he was in charge of the Navy of Division 164.
Q. I understand you married the youngest daughter, so we know about you. What about the husbands of the other daughters? I think there are three left.
A. There are four more. The next daughter after Khom, named Ho, and her husband was a former soldier who died in the battle field during 1979.
Q. Next one?
A. For the next daughter, her husband was named Ren and to my recollection Ren died after 1979 though I cannot recall the exact year.
MR. PRESIDENT: Mr. Witness, can you tell the name again of that daughter.
MR. NEANG OUCH: A. Her name was Krou.
JUDGE FENZ: Q. And what did he do before he died?
A. He was a soldier, although I did not know which position or rank he held and he went to live in Anlong Veaeng area after 1979.
Q. I believe that leaves us with one daughter and her husband?
A. The next daughter Heanh and her husband was Boran and the husband also died after 1979, probably died around 1990s.
Q. What did he do between 1975 and '79?
A. He was in the logistic transportation unit between the border to the Southwest Zone in particular to Takeo province.
Q. Do you know of any other relatives of Ta Mok, cousins, etc., who were in senior positions, positions of authority?

A. As for his cousins or other relatives, I do not know many of them. Originally I am from Kandal province while he was from Takeo province and as I did not stay much longer in Takeo province I did not know much about his distant relatives. I mean I refer to his cousins or his other relatives.
Q. My last question, did you ever hear the words "Brother Number One or Two" in connection with Democratic Kampuchea?
A. I heard the word "Brother Number One".
Q. When did you hear it?
A. That was during the three year period -- that is, after the war ended.
Q. So you never heard it between '75 and beginning of '79?
A. I already stated I heard that word used after the war ended so I refer to the period of 1975 to 1979.
Q. Sorry my mistake. Who was Brother Number One?
A. Om Pol Pot or Uncle Pol Pot was Brother Number One.
Q. Are you aware of any other brothers with numbers and who they were?
A. That's all I heard about brother with number.
Q. Thank you.
A. In addition, I also heard Brother Number Two but I did not know whom it refers to.
MR. PRESIDENT: Judge Lavergne, you have the floor.
QUESTIONING BY JUDGE LAVERGNE: Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. Witness, I have a number of questions for you and it is likely to take more than the five minutes remaining this morning. Q. I would like to start by asking you to clarify something. In response to a question put to you by Judge Fenz, you said that you met Nuon Chea during a meeting that was held in September or in October. But in any case, in French, I did not hear the year in which that meeting was held. Can you tell us where and in what year that meeting took place?

MR. NEANG OUCH: A. The meetings were held in September or October. It was one of these two months although I am not 100 percent sure. It was held in the year 1977 in Borei Keila compound located to the north of Preah Puth pagoda in Phnom Penh.
Q. How often did you have the opportunity to go to Phnom Penh to meet leaders? How many times did you have the opportunity to go to Phnom Penh to meet leaders or for any other reasons?

A. I came to Phnom Penh once a year for a yearly study session and it happened in 1977 and then in 1978 and in addition when my knee was injured I came for the treatment at the Soviet hospital and I was hospitalised for three months at the time.
Q. Who could attend those training sessions and who conducted those training sessions, apart from Nuon Chea?

A. The provincial level would select people to attend the study sessions and I observed that there were people from the District levels and some assistants also from the district levels and they were sent to study -- that study session and for the study sessions that I attended the only trainer was Nuon Chea.

Q. So when you say that you met with Nuon Chea only once that is false because you said that you went to Phnom Penh several times and that on each occasion, the training was conducted by Nuon Chea or did I not properly understand your testimony?

A. I think you misunderstood my statement. I attended a study session once in 1977 when I met Nuon Chea and again I attended a study session in 1978 and that was a second occasion that I met Nuon Chea and besides that I came to the Soviet hospital for my treatment.
Q. What was the content of this training? What was being discussed during this training?

A. It is very difficult to recall the contents of the study sessions as the period has passed for more than 30 years. There were documents -- several documents provided for the study sessions and I cannot recall the details of the contents of those documents nor the titles of those documents. Usually at the conclusion of the study session, they would hold a criticism and self-criticism meeting to evaluate our study session and what we learned. And then we would hold a joint meeting and after that a group meeting for the criticism but let me repeat again, I cannot recall the contents of the documents provided during the study sessions.
Q. Was the aim of these meetings to define the political line of the CPK?
A. I already stated that it is very difficult for me to recall exactly what were taught or discussed during the study sessions as it has been for almost 40 years now.

Q. So you went to Phnom Penh several times. So I suppose that meeting Nuon Chea is something that did not leave you indifferent. So please make some efforts, please tell us what you heard during these meetings.
A. I will try to recall it but if I force myself not to recall it I cannot do it. I may need more time to recall the contents of the study sessions.
Q. Fine. Do you have any memory issues? Do you manage to remember things that happened recently or maybe longer ago?

A. I have problems with memory as my recollection is not that good. Usually for example when I worked in my farm I will write down what I need to do in my notebook. For example, at what time I have to water the vegetables. So just to summarise, I do have problem with my memory.
Q. So regarding these meetings with Nuon Chea, you have no idea of what was discussed during these meetings, not even in very broad terms you have no idea, absolutely no idea?

A. I can recall some -- that is, on the building of a class, peasant class and about the class struggle and to get rid of the capitalist class from within ourselves, for instance. These are some of the contents of the study sessions that I can recall.
Q. Did Nuon Chea ever speak to you about the enemies, the enemies of the CPK?

A. I do not have anything to hide, Your Honour, but I simply cannot recall it. Even for my daily work with my family, I have difficulty with it and I remember about class struggle and we had to get rid of this capitalist class because it happened to me personally so I had to train myself or to refresh myself to become one of the people in the peasant class.

Q. Thank you, Witness, for this clarification. So I must therefore understand that document E3/4093 is a document in which you recognise your signature as well as your handwriting. That is what you're telling us; correct?
A. Yes, that is correct. However, as I stated, I only followed the instructions laid down by Ta Ran.

Q. And in document E3/2585, you tell us that this is neither your handwriting neither your signature, so I would like to specify that document E3/2785, the relevant ERNs in Khmer are 00079115; English 00322193; and French 00753636. So, I understood well, with regard to document E3/2795, this is neither your handwriting nor your signature? Yes, do you confirm what I just said or?
A. Yes, that is correct. The handwriting is not mine and the signature is also not mine. That's why it is very difficult for me and that's why it confuse me.

Q. Okay, we will get back to those issues later but now, I would like to cover all of the documents that were presented yesterday. So, I would like you to see again document E3/2422 (sic). If you could -- if the court officer could please provide this document to the witness. I have it here at hand. I -- the ERNs are; in Khmer, 00079127; and in French, 00611732; and English, 00322210. And the document reads as follows: "First, correct - interrogate the despicable Hul Muoy who is a second lieutenant and ask him to disclose the branch he belongs to. So, Witness, can you tell us if you recognise your signature and if you recognise your handwriting?
A. The handwriting is not my handwriting. Also the signature is not mine.

Q. Well, fine. I'm also going to show you another document that was also presented to you yesterday. This is document E3/2453, Khmer, ERN 00270774; English, ERN 00388577; French, ERN 00611769.
