You may proceed.

MR CHUM SIRATH: Mr. President, before I begin talking about my siblings who were the victims at Tuol Sleng, I would seek the President's leave to talk about my work that I have done in Cambodia in summary in order to shed some light on my following statement. I started working in Cambodia in 1970 to 1974 as the General Director of the Post and Communications Ministry and from '74 to '75 I was appointed as a representative for the expertise organization of the UN in Geneva.

When Phnom Penh fell under the Khmer Rouge on the 17th April 1975, I was abroad.  Later on, I migrated to settle in France and I took a French citizenship.  So at the moment I have dual citizenship, Khmer and French, and I had been living in France since 1975 in a company producing IT equipment. Also during the period I had lived in China for six years as the general director of a company and later on I came to live in Cambodia in 1999 as the director of this company in charge of the Southeast Asia branch.  And that was in 2003. In that 2003 I quit that French company and I established my own IT company and I was the director of that company.  As I informed the President, my parents had eight children and we were very poor.  We did not have sufficient money but the only intention and hope of my parents was for us to be educated.  It's like climbing a stair to the upper level in society.

As my counsel had just said, all the facts related to case file 001, I had two younger brothers, Chum Sinaret, he was 28 years old in 1976, and Chum Narith, 33 years old in 1976.  And Kem Sovannary alias Dan, the wife of Chum Narith, whom I never met, and an infant -- they were all detained at S-21. With the President's leave I would talk about each one of them. Now I would like to talk about Chum Narith.  My family was very poor.  I received a scholarship to study in France in 1960 and I only returned to Cambodia in 1968.  At that time, when we went to study abroad there was no opportunity for us to visit home until at the end of the study.  And during that eight year period that I was abroad, Chum Narith was the breadwinner of the family. Chum Narith was a leading student, studying at Yuk Kunthor college and the Lycee Descartes only selected the leading students for their class and then later on they would be offered scholarship.  And Chum Narith received a scholarship to study at that Lycee Descartes and would have the opportunity to study further in France.

But I was in France at that time, and due to the poor living conditions of my family, Chum Narith gave up his scholarship to France and when he finished his school, he entered the National Pedagogical Institution and later on he became a primary teacher in 1965.  It was the same year as the accused left his teacher training institution. Chum Narith was one of the few people who left schooling and got a job in order to support my parents and siblings.  That is including Chum Sinavi to finish the high school and also became a primary teacher later on.  He also supported my youngest sibling, Chum Sinaret to finish high school and to enter the medical faculty.

In 1968, that's when she entered the medical faculty, I was still in France at that time and in fact, my father passed away in 1964 and, as I told you, during the study, the eight-year study, I was not able to come to attend the funeral of my father. So upon my return in '68, I was so happy to reunite with my siblings and mother, and three months later the political police -- or the special police which was known at the time or sometime it's referred to as the political police -- under the leadership of two state secretaries, Sosthene Fernandez for the National Police Force and Um Manarin for the Internal Security Affairs, and the special police were under their supervision. And Narit was arrested on the allegation that he was a Khmer Rouge; that was in 1968.  At that time, he was a teacher at the Balang School in Kampong Thom. And the other day, I listened to the testimony of Mam Nai and he said he used to be a teacher too at the Balang School.  So my brother was arrested at the Balang School and brought to the PS Prison.

My mother had a chronic disease.  She got half the disease.  She was shocked and traumatized, and I was requested by her to help my brother to get out of the prison. At that time when people were arrested, tortures were not avoided, and there were some rumours that some people were even dropped at the valleys -- the mountains area to die, and I had to ask for assistance from my friends.  And at that time, Mr. Vann Molyvann, the Minister of Education -- so I would ask him to help me to assist my brother. And I was just returning from France.  I believed that I could be convinced to grant such a visit to Mr. Molyvann but he did not allow me to meet him and he had several pretexts for not allowing me to do so.

After all, I found a person named Sam An  who was the policeman who interrogated the people who were detained at the PS and that person used to study at the primary school in Kampong Cham, and since Sam An helped administer the interrogation session, my brother did not receive any punishment or tortures. Later on, he was reintegrated into the school and transferred from Balang to Chum Chao, an area which is close to our current Court location. In 1968, I was terrified.  Professor Phung Ton was also arrested at that time.  Professor Keng Van Sak, Chao Sao, the head of the bank, were also arrested at that time. Preab In, who was regarded at the right-ist individual, was arrested and killed in the public, and his execution was photographed and also could be seen in the movie.  So everyone who also watched the movie could never forget the memory of seeing such footages.

And, at that time, people were classified into groups of Blue Khmer, Red Khmer and, later on, after the DK regime started, and they classified people into categories of the KGB, the CIA or the Vietnamese sympathizers, or otherwise they would be regarded as the older people, the new people, and these kinds of routines or norms were well embedded long ago back then. And when Narith was arrested, he was like a normal intellectual like other intellectuals who were left-ist because they were progressive because they were with the developing ideas. And in France, at that time, there was an event we called the May 1968 event.  I may call it a kind of situation when people were rather left-ist and Maoist in France.  And in Khmer, I think the situation was the same.  So intellectuals tend to be in favour of the left-ist.  Left-ist means they are against the war, the Vietnamese war.

And, number two, they opposed the social injustice.  They would like the restoration of social justice.  And as a professor, Narith paid great attention to the future of young people, those who were unemployed.  And he himself -- he was a very modest person because he focused on the education and the promotion of good education. And there were partisans.  People were left-ists and then people got their different parties and Narith could not avoid being part in one of the groups. However, at that time, there was an injustice arrest by the police, the judicial police, at that time.  This phenomenon made Narith, being more involved in the movement to oppose the regime, and Sihanouk called the movement the Khmer Rouge or the Red Khmer Movement.  And the movement, of course, had their triumph in 1975.  And as I already said earlier, after he left Sosthene prison, Narith worked at Chum Chao.

Now, I would like to talk about my brother, Chum Sinaret.  He was born in 1948.  When he was arrested in 1976, he was 28 years old. Sinaret studied at grade two at the medical faculty in Phnom Penh.  In 1970, the 18th of March event erupted when Prince Sihanouk was toppled down and the war erupted.  My wife, in Skun, who found out that insecurity was everywhere, so she travelled to live with me in Phnom Penh. Sinaret was the one who really be close to my mother.  She had the heart disease for 20 years before she passed away, and without Sinaret her life would be in even worse condition because he, after school, had to be close to her to give great assistance to her.

He was a man with a sense of humour.  He always made my mother happy during the very critical time.  Narith and Sinaret were like friends, although they were brothers.  They really got along well with one another.  One was good at telling jokes, the other was good at laughing at the jokes, so they were very good pair. And Narith was a very good support, the one who supplied or supported the family and my mother. We had a very happy family in the midst of the war-torn country. There were about 300,000 people at that time.  Later on the population increased to more than one million in the city.  Life became harder and -- the grenades were dropped in Phnom Penh on a daily basis, and gasoline became scarce and electricity blackout was everywhere and very often.  Now people complain of brownout or blackout but back then, you know, we did not have electricity for days.

And our family was reunited and we cared for one another and we could move places so that we could avoid being dropped the bombs at.  And each family member had different political views.  My brother was in favour of the republicans -- Narith -- and Sinaret was in favour of the FUNK movement supported by Sihanouk.  They were in favour of the liberals.  However, we were not the pure politicians, so we could compromise our differences and we prayed that the war was over so that we could resume our normal works, but our dream was faded because the war was intensified. In February 1973, after having been sick for 20 years, my mother could no longer make it through.  She died of suffocation and she died in the bathroom, and Narith tried to seek medical assistance to assist her.  However, it was not possible to save her life.

After February 1973 -- actually in 1973 there was a big event at the Pedagogical Institute next to the Independent Monument. There was a demonstration, riots, revolts, rebellions done by the teachers, who claimed pay rise.  And my brothers -- at that time the police of the republicans accused him as being the ringleader of the demonstration or demonstrators on the 17th of March. My mother actually died at the end of February but on the 17th of March there was a big plane.  Pich Limkhuon was the pilot for the military aeroplane to drop bombs at the state building where Marshall Lon Nol was housed.  And at that time chaotic situation was imminent and my brother was searched to be arrested, but then he tried to escape, to actually run to the maquis jungle.  And according to my research, he escaped to the jungle along with Professor Nuon Khoeun.

He was a very popular professor and they went along with Hu Nim. Hu Nim was in charge of information or propaganda at that time, and he worked with Hu Nim in the propaganda section in the maquis jungle, I may say, in the Liberated Zone. From March 1973, when he already had been in the jungle -- although I'm not quite sure but I believe that he could have contact with Chum Sinaret because at that time the communication was done in secret, but he could have communicated with his brother.  And by the end of 1973 my brother Chum Sarun died and I received a letter from Narith from the maquis jungle, who offered his condolences and grief for the death of my brother, although he could not attend the funeral.  But according to the substance of the letter, although it's hard to convey the message, but I could believe that it would not be easy living in that zone.

In 1974, Mr. President -- I would like to be brief and I'm afraid that if I talk longer then you will get bored anyway.  So in 1974 there was a tragedy with my brother Chum Sinaret, who fell in love with a beautiful woman in Kampong Cham.  At that time when they fell in love, of course, they only -- in French we call it l'amour platonique.  And then when the war started, then the communication or the roads was cut and they could not really meet each other again.

One day a rocket was dropped at Kampong Cham province and the woman was injured that she had to be amputated otherwise the situation, the condition would be worsened.  And Narith (sic), having learned that his sweetheart was injured in the bomb, he called her but at that time we could not put the blame on the doctors because there was not sufficient medicine, and I did not know whether there was some kind of medicine to support the operation when the sweetheart of him actually was being amputated.  Unfortunately she died during operation.

And later on I was appointed as the representative of Cambodia in Geneva, representing Cambodia -- the telecommunication of Cambodia -- and there was three organizations at that time. There was International Telecommunication, or in French, Union Internationale, and also the nuclear energy organization. When I went there, it was November 1974.  I believe that in three months Sinaret could be reunited with me because when I had settled down properly then my family too would be reunited along with Sinaret.  And I asked them to be prepared to have their passport renewed, but then on April 1975 everything changed.  My dream, hopes faded.

It is my lifelong regretfulness.  At that time, I was not brave or clever enough or I lacked conscience.  I lacked analysis to analyze the situation that Cambodia would be in a war torn phenomenon in the next few months, so why having calculated wrongfully about the situation, I am now regretful and it was a miscalculation or prediction. I would like now to share with the Chamber the result of my research.  On the 17th of April 1975, according to the research, Narith came to Phnom Penh with the Hu Nim group and worked at the propaganda ministry. On the 30th of April 1975, I believe that the Chamber knows that there was a tragedy, a great tragedy, at the location of the French embassy in Phnom Penh, both French and Cambodians, in particular the French.

And those Cambodians who got married to the French nationals and with their children, they took refuge at the embassy, the French embassy.  And the pressure from the ruling people at that time who were Khmer Rouge -- the French consulate Dirac, Jean Dirac -- I probably don't want to say that he expelled the people there, but he actually ordered those who were not French nationals to leave the vicinity of the French embassy.  If not, they would be starved to death or would not be given food. I think it is now in the hands of the historians to really analyze the situation and to judge the decision by Jean Dirac at that time and why he made such a decision.  And, of course, his decision could be rendered and passed down from the Foreign Affairs office in France.   I did not know whether the decision was ethical and that I believe the historians can now take this into account and judge it.

After these people were expelled from the French embassy, they were marching to Battambang province and it was a kind of great tragedy.  I don't want really to recall it, however, when I were marching to that location later on I reached the different locations. And when I was in France, I was told that I should not come back to Cambodia because people who educated in France were implicated as those people who were left-ist.  And in France, I was sent a letter from my brother, Sinaret, telling me that he could move about in Phnom Penh but his relatives were all evacuated and moved to different places. And I think perhaps at that time SiNarith and Narith could have met one another in happy moment, maybe less happy moment. On the 29th of October 1976, Narith was arrested along with Sinaret and Dan, Kem Sovannary, his wife actually.  And the reason for the arrest, as seen in the confession of Hu Nim -- Hu Nim himself wrote that.  With Mr. President's leave, I would like to just briefly read the portion.

Prum Sam Ar, Yit Kim Seng.  Yit Kim Seng was the brother-in-law of Hu Yun.  They created a group opposing the collectivization and Prum Sam Ar during the republican's regime, they did not want to say but allowed Chum Narith to say about this. Chum Narith was brave and he was accused that the democratic radio was biased and that Chum Narith violated the collectivization regime and he claimed that because of this kind of collectivization, and that's why medicine was not sufficient and that privatization was banned and that it was not good. In his confession, Hu Nim said that because Chum Narith said that then he requested Angkar to remove him.  So on the 29th of September, he was removed.

From the 21st of July 1976, Pol Pot gave a speech in relation to the five-year plan concerning the collectivization.  Three months later my brother was removed as suggested by Hu Nim, and Hu Nim himself, six months later after the plan was released and after my brother was arrested, on the 4th of April 1977, he was arrested.  He said he gave in, himself, to the Angkar, but actually he was arrested after all. Your Honours, you may ask, "How can we believe that this confession of the person, Hu Nim, in which Mr. Pon already had beaten him five times before he made such a confession?  Can we really believe in such a confession if it was extracted by torture?"

But I think it is believable because the arrest was made and it was well known to the public in relation to arrest because there was a meeting held at the propaganda office and that he was challenging the policy of Pol Pot, and the police of Son Sen and Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, must have known this very well.  So how could Hu Nim lie in that confession? So my conviction is that the confession is true.  And it is consistent also to the nature of Narith.  Narith was outspoken like I am because when he wanted to say anything he would say so. Mr. President, Your Honours, in relation to Chum Narith, in 1993 after searching for the truth I came to Cambodia after 19 years abroad.

I have tried to search for all the evidence but everything was not clear.  In October '93 I went to Tuol Sleng Prison and on the list of names under order number 39 the name Chum Narith alias Nak in the propaganda entered on 29 October '76 and died on the 1st of January '77.  That is after he had lived in the prisons for 65 days and that he was tortured, dehumanized. I don't understand the purpose of such act.  If the policy is to kill, then just kill.  Why there is a need to beat them up?  If one says beating up is to find the true confession as said by the accused and even the accused himself acknowledged the information or the confession from the forced torture and interrogation is not true, then what is the purpose of beating them up?  Why don't just kill them straight away?

On that same list I saw the name of my brother Chum Sinaret and -- as a medic and there was no date for the entry and for the exit and I did not know when he died.  There was also a name of Kem Sovannary alias Dan, the wife of Chum Narith and preceding that name the word "ah" was used.  It's like "contemptible" in English -- from the propaganda section. And even about the infant; I saw the paintings done by Mr. Vann Nath, Mr. President, as we all have seen the painting which depicts the dragging of an infant from the mother by the Khmer Rouge clique, by the prison guard.  And on the other side the mother was being whipped by another person. And I think that would similarly depict the fate of my nephew, or the baby could be dropped from the upper floor or smashed against a tree stump at Choeung Ek.

Mr. President, I am proud to be a Cambodian person and this Tribunal has given opportunity to the accused to express his feelings and the civil parties also to make their statements like Martine Lefeuvre, like Ouk Neary, Tiouloung, Sophea and Phung Sunthary Guth.  They have all described the long path for them to search for the truth and the fate of their beloved individuals. And each story is different.  However, all only had the same point; that is the despair, the despair and the feeling of not understanding of what happened and the sorrow and the pain which happened with us for more than 30 years. I have struggled constantly every day and night not to forget the suffering, the misery of my siblings because this is my obligation for the dead ones.  However, at the same time I have tried to forget, to forget that because I also have the obligation for the survivors who are living with me.  The feelings that I have on both sides have been continuing for 34 years.  I could not separate these two feelings, or which side should I choose and forget the other one?

Before this Chamber I strongly believe justice is being made and done.  Up to today I even have written a letter to Kaing Guek Eav requesting information regarding my brother but he said he did not know about that. And Mr. President, this Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, started with my younger brother at the teacher training institution and yesterday he acknowledged during the rebellion he was at Sisowat School with Chum Narith. And also this Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch met Chum Narith at the Liberation Zone in the maquis forest.  And for Chum Sinaret at Skun he was a professor there at Skun and Chum Sinaret was not his teacher as my parents lived in Skun. And because of his love for pure intellectuals who held esteemed the idealism and he made frequent visits to his home and he knew my brother clearly but on the day he entered S-21 he said he did not know anything as he was busy working with his documents.  He had no time to pay attention to him.

As Duch said yesterday if he were aware of Phung Ton that he would give him food.  Of course I would not believe this. And  I would like to talk about another matter.  This accused, Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, always states that he is only a subordinate and that he was not a major leader and that he did only based on what he was ordered to do. And I keep thinking, if he only followed orders, how come we all say he is one of the most responsible?  For example, he say chairman of a prison and the CPK only sent those people to his prison.  And according to the policies, the people will be killed at the prison.  Then why he's being in charge?  Because we all believe that he is the most responsible, at least in my case, that is regarding the deaths of -- my brother's death and his family.  And this is the core point, the essence or the gist of this Tribunal.

I would like to say that if the CPK policy was to kill them, then just follow the policy and there is no need to torture them.  Or if confessions need to be extracted, then just do so, but with torture then as he said, the confession could not be true.  And in David Chandler's testimony, according to the annotations made by Duch on those confessions, and that Duch could not sleep well during his tenure at the prison at S-21 or if he disliked what he did and that he could not eat at the end of the day. Now, it's not like that.  He enjoys doing what he did until when Vorn Vet entered in '78, he still did the same.

On the third point, this accused, Kaing Guek Eav alias Duch, compares himself to a fox in a poem by Alfred de Vigny entitled, The Death of the Wolf.  This poet was a 19th century famous person and he was a former soldier.  And, of course, the life of a soldier was mixed, both joy and sorrow.  So he wrote a lot of poems regarding the lives of soldiers and one of them was The Death of the Wolf.

And he talks about a group of hunters, together with like 10 or 20 dogs, to try to kill the wolf, and there were four wolves -- one male, one female and two younger wolves.  And when the wolves realized that they were being surrounded, they struggled their best to fight against the dogs.  And the male wolf tries his best in order to defend the female wolf and their young wolves.  And in the end he died.  The wolf died.

And according to the poem, the wolf died without making any noise.  And the morality of this poem was illustrated at the end of the poem, and Kaing Guek Eav alias Duch quoted that poem on the 31st of March 2009, if I am not mistaken, at around 4.30 p.m. toward the end of the proceedings on that day while he was being questioned by his counsel, François Roux. And this Kaing Guek Eav alias Duch recited that poem: "To pray or to think is equally cowardly. You must carry out your duty where fate has brought you.  And you shall suffer and die without a word."

So what does it translate into the Khmer language? I apologize.  I saw the President is talking to me.  In the Khmer language, it means the person was moaning, crying, begging, and that we have to try to work, just carry on working, according to our fate.  And that I take the position of a wolf and that I die without making any noise. And, as I said, the accused recited the poem at 4.30 when he was questioned by his counsel, François Roux, and after he finished reciting the poem, he left two or three minutes for him to be silent.

And during that time everything went dead.  We could even hear the sounds of a mosquito if there was one in the Chamber at the time.  And, later on, François Roux said that he no longer have any questions for this accused, Mr. President.  And during the three minute time, everything was so moody, so quiet, and probably people would have a feeling of sorrow for this accused. This is a clever technique as they were playing before this Chamber.  And maybe they could join as a team to play theatre in France.  And if the accused compared himself to the wolf in the poem, The Death of the Wolf, it's actually -- it's just like a pretext, or un imposteur in French.

And it is the opportunity to grab the good points as a brave person, a stoic in French, and that he talked about people who tried to work without thinking of the hardship, personal suffering, as those French soldiers who were sent to fight in the battlefield.  So I, personally, would take into account the points that the accused wants to say regarding the sacrifice, the selflessness -- or the stoic in French -- because what bravery was it?

For example, regarding the teacher, Doem Saroeun, that is his teacher, she entered S-21 and he knew.  He knew that she was tortured and that she was dehumanized or degraded.  He did not even raise his smallest finger to assist her.  What brave was that?

If people used to fight in combat together or used to be together, then people would help each other but he didn't even raise his small finger to assist.  And compare to Him Huy.  Him Huy helped Saom Met, if we all recall.  Sou Met had a younger sibling, Saom Huy, who was arrested and sent to S-21 and he said that Saom Met was another brother.  But Him Huy told that younger brother not to say it and to keep it quiet, and Sou Met was transferred by Him Huy to another location.

MS. CANIZARES: Thank you for giving me the floor, Mr. President.  I believe that in order to preserve the serenity and dignity of this hearing, would you please, Mr. President, remind the civil party testifying at this time to please refocus his presentation and to speak to us. We understand that he is speaking to us of his suffering and the suffering of his family but perhaps to try not to evoke the reactions of Mr. Kaing Guek Eav or of other persons, perhaps, who were also victims and who are not connected to his particular case either by blood or kinship.

Thank you.

MR CHUM SIRATH: Mr. President, your leadership of this Chamber by you is up to the international standard and I understand that.  The accused is not yet regarded as a convict if he is not found guilty by the Chamber, but we are the victims.  We cannot accept that when the accused within this Chamber says that the moaning, the crying or the begging are the coward acts.  Sixteen thousand people died at Tuol Sleng and of course they would have cried, begged, wept. Can we say they were cowards? So within this Chamber, when he talked about these acts, he is just an imposter.
MR. PRESIDENT: The defence counsel, you may proceed.

MS. CANIZARES: Yes, Mr. President.  Please forgive me for again interrupting the presentation of the civil party. I do not think that at any time on the bench of the defence we've noted that the accused had used the expression "coward".  Now, I'm certain that the civil party is entitled to say what they want and to share their suffering with us, and we are respectful of that, but we cannot make the accused say things that he has not said.  We cannot put words in his mouth which he did not use.

MR. PRESIDENT: Let me now focus on the purpose of our proceedings, the civil party.  The Chamber, as you noticed, has not tried to interrupt you and allows you to express the suffering.  This is done for all the civil parties.  But please try to refrain yourself and make your statement related to the facts, and it is your right to believe or to not believe the statement made by the accused. The proceedings before this Chamber has been ongoing for several months and in the end the Chamber would consider all those information and evidence and then we would issue a judgment which is fair and just and which is acceptable by all the parties to the proceedings, including the civil party and the defence party. We will consider every aspect of the proceedings and the relevant documents. As I have just reminded you, your time is running out, so please focus only on the relevant facts.  Please go on.

MR CHUM SIRATH: I will conclude now, but before my conclusion I would like to talk about the conversion of religion by Duch from Buddhism to Christian. In the Christianity there was Cain, the person who was the important actor in the religion, who killed another person, and Cain was monitored because the dead bodies -- the eyes of the dead people kept following the person until he could never feel peaceful anymore so he asked somebody to dig a pit and covered it with dirt. The French writer wrote a French poem in French; when the grave was closed over him the eye was in the grave and was watching Cain.

So when he was buried in the tomb his sibling's eyes could be seen follow him in the grave.  So the eyes could even follow the dead body. I would like to ask the accused now with the more than 12,000 (sic) people who perished during the regime all together they could be multiplied by two.  Then they represent the eyes of the people all together there are 32,000 eyes who actually -- that the eyes that follow the accused each time of everyday to seek his explanation. Now, he converted the religion.  In Christianity his sin is forgiven for such a reason but in Buddhism those who commit good receive good.  However, I believe that the 32,000 pairs of eyes that are now following the accused, how could the accused himself escape.  I don't believe he has any place to hide. Thank you.

That was 17 days before Narith went to the maquis forest as I described earlier. These two were very close to one another. This is Kem Sovannary, alias Dan.  I had never met her.  She was my younger sister-in-law. QUESTIONING BY CIVIL PARTY COUNSEL BY MS. STUDZINSKY: Q. I would like to ask my client, Mr. Chum Sirath, now one question and that is the following:  I would like to know and that you explain here in this courtroom what do you think and how do you cope with the excuses of the accused and what it means for you?

A. In the beginning when I heard the apology made by the accused, I was happy.  I thought at least amongst the leaders of the Democratic Kampuchea one was brave to acknowledge.  I want to believe it, to believe the apology by the accused but the longer I have participated in the proceedings the feeling of trying to believe dissipated.  I believe it is not genuine.  And why do I say that? On the 31st of March 2009 the accused made a famous statement and I quote what he said from the transcript as follows: "At present I am remorseful and I feel shameful as a person who bears the responsibility and the guilt for the Cambodian people as a whole." And then he continues.  I quote: "In order to comfort myself I prayed for forgiveness.  First I seek forgiveness from my parents, then my mentor and I pray for forgiveness from the Cambodian people on the 17 November annually.  That was my date of birth and I would make a small ceremony to pray."

In the statement made by the accused he prayed but he did not pray for the souls of those who died to rest in peace.  He prayed in order to make himself feel better, "And I tried to find a way to comfort myself.  That is, I pray on my birthday, 17 November." And on the 9th of July 2009, under the questioning by Mr. Kim Mengkhy, the civil party counsel for Chin Met, he asked the accused whether the accused is responsible emotionally for the suffering inflicted upon Chin Met.  And I will quote his speech from the transcript: "Mr. Counsel, regarding the case of Comrade Met, I am not responsible emotionally but I am fully responsible before the law.  And this is my response."

And regarding my brothers, the accused knew them very well.  He wrote me a letter in response and I was so glad to receive it but he said he did not see them, and if he even did see them he would not be able to assist them because they were ordered by Angkar. He said he didn't know anything about this. So that's why I said his expression is not genuine and if Mr. President and Your Honours think that my speech, my statement here, is biased towards the accused, I would like the Chamber to please look at the report of a psychological doctor dated the 8th of April 2008.  This psychological doctor named Sironi-Guilbaud, Françoise.

Therefore, on behalf of my late brothers, Chum Sinaret, Chum Narith, Kem Sovannary, alias Dan, and my nephew, I would like to declare before this Chamber that I will not be able to accept this ungenuine apology. I am here before this Chamber to ask for justice, and this justice cannot be separated from the truth.  I haven't received justice for over 34 years now.  Thank you, Mr. President.

It seemed in your statement that you were insisting a great deal on the elements of information that you were able to obtain thanks to your research concerning your brother Narith and his wife. However, with regard to your brother Sinaret, I was wondering whether you could supply us with information regarding whatever details you may have received concerning his arrest:  when, why, who arrested him?  Was that arrest linked to the arrest of your other brother, Narith? So what did you learn through your research in regard to this? Of course this is only if you were able to obtain this information, which is notoriously difficult to obtain.

A. Regarding my younger brother, Chum Sinaret, although I have tried my best to do his research. Quite simply, how can one summarily execute with no remorse, no scruples, another human being?

I, daughter of a victim, I request that the punishment be commensurate with the crimes committed, with the suffering inflicted, and commensurate with the number of lives that the accused has taken away.  On behalf of my father, I refuse to forgive because to grant forgiveness comes down to saying that finally no serious crime was committed.  To grant forgiveness boils down to admitting that the atrocities committed do not touch us so deeply.  To grant forgiveness would mean to feel pity, but how can anyone feel pity for a man who has taken away so many lives?  Did he have any pity for the women, the children and the men he caused to be assassinated? On behalf of my father, I refuse to express the slightest amount of pity.  On behalf of my father, I request that justice be handed down."

This is the end of the letter of my niece, Mr. President. I speak here on behalf of my sister-in-law, my niece and those relatives I have who are still living.  I claim no financial reparation, no material relief.  I would simply like to know what happened during the 97 days and throughout these 50 pages of confession.  That is the reason why I applied to be a civil party.

Indeed, my representations before this Court is of a different nature.  I seek moral redress.  One person alone, my wife, was aware of my suffering during these 10,950 nights when I would wake up on a regular basis in a start, shouting and crying, unable to express my suffering in any other manner. Mr. President, like any Cambodian, modesty is required.  Everyone internalizes feeling.  The effort that I made before you today is very great, but it is a necessary effort, and for me it is through this testimony that a certain form of reparation begins to be born.  I know today that the accused in the first place, but also the international community taken as a whole, are aware of the horror that I have experienced, just like the thousands of families of victims of S-21.

I visited S-21 for the first time in 1992.  Absolute horror.  I was frozen.  At one point in one of the cells I looked out: beautiful weather, blue sky, sparrows singing, wonderful vegetation, and we were in an island of barbarity in the middle of an ocean of softness. How was it possible that such a massacre could occur in such a place, far from the eyes, ignored by the entire world, the fate of innocent defenceless people abandoned to pitiless killers?

Since that time, that day, I cried for injustice.  Why did they do this?  Why is it that the international community had forgotten us?  Why is it that the international community did not believe from the outset the testimony that was coming out?  Why did they not exercise their duty to interfere? As a civil party, Mr. President, I wanted to know what had happened inside the walls of S 21.  This trial has shed some light for me and we now know the very detail of the modus operandi that was practised.  Before this I had an abstract vision of cells, of shackles, of instruments of torture, of posts.  I saw pictures, pages filled with confessions.

Now for every one of these things, by watching and following this trial, I wanted to try to experience what he experienced, to share in my own way his suffering, his anxiety.  I wanted to imagine the pain that one can feel when one is being beaten, when one's fingernails are being pulled, when one is submitted to electric shock, when you are being shackled at every moment of life in Cambodia.  When it's cold I think of my brother, this unfortunate person who had nothing to protect him from the cold. When I was in Cambodia, when I was being stung by mosquitoes I was thinking about my brother and all these unfortunate detainees who were attacked and who were stung and could not react, thinking of the detail of all that they had to undergo.  And I also think and thought of the rhythm of interrogation, of insults, illness, lack of sanitation, mental and physical degradation and the deterioration which is forced upon you, a task consisting in total dehumanization.

Mr. President, I thought that I had no more tears left in me.  I thought that I had no more tears but I realize I still have some. I continue to think about my brother, his 97 days of suffering. And he probably then also thought about his children and his wife, what would become of them; would they have enough to feed themselves; would they be harmed. Because when he was arrested he asked his younger sister to watch over his children, one of the last words he uttered then.  Perhaps he had already understood then that he would not be returning.

Before asking a few questions from the accused, two questions to be precise, I cannot but recount to you a brief episode that occurred when I returned for the first time to Cambodia in 1992. One evening at a friend's there was a young woman who had the ability to communicate with the spirits and I spoke to her about my brother and she entered into a relationship with him.  We Cambodians we believe in this sort of thing.  I don't know how to define it.  And the young woman told me this -- and she was communicating with my brother.  She said he is sad and terrorized.  He had suffered a great deal in the world of humans.

He had suffered great pain during his life on earth and he did not wish to reincarnate.  He said that he was very much afraid and his soul sought refuge in a pagoda and said that he had placed himself under the protection of a monk.  The young woman told me the name of the pagoda.  I was totally upset.  And what I heard that evening will always remain seared in my memory. The next day I went to the pagoda with my sister and we organized a ceremony.  Oddly, inside of the pagoda I was continuously looking up.  And I could see the ceiling, and wished to preceive the soul of my brother which was there.  And I tell myself that every time I enter a pagoda I will look at the ceiling, because perhaps it is the case that my brother is not the only one who sought refuge in a pagoda and refuses to reincarnate, and instead seeks the protection of Buddha.  Now my niece today is pregnant, and when the child is born, together we will go to the pagoda and present to him his grandchild.

MS. CHUM NEOU: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all I would like to thank the Chamber, the Trial Chamber of the ECCC.  I would like to start my statement as follows. In 1970 my family lived in the Prey Veng provincial town; we were rice farmers.  Also in 1970 after the 18th March event, that is after the coup d'etat to overthrow Sihanouk, I was still in the Prey Veng provincial town. Later on during the year there was fighting in the provincial town and after the second round of fighting my family moved from the towns to the liberated zone which is the native village of my mother, in Prey Ruessei village, Tuk Laak sub-district, Prey Veng province. In 1971 my family, my siblings and myself voluntarily agreed to join the revolution movement of the Khmer Rouge.  At that time I was given a position as a chairwoman of the village.  In 1972 I rose to be the Chairwoman of the Chea Khlang sub-district in and in 1973 Angkar assigned me to be a combatant of the Prey Veaeng sub-district.

There was only one platoon at that time to serve the battlefield to transport food supplies and ammunitions to the battlefield.  I was at a battlefront with the combatants although I did not engage in attack; I only supplied ammunition and food. Later on, in 1974, Angkar recruited me and assigned me to be a female combatant of the east zone.  During the time I became a female combatant of the east zone the fighting activities were not that active.  I received military training and strategic training at the Sa Py Roy school or S-200 School.  That school is a place where people were trained to be ready as soldiers or in Khmer, "sla pul". We were trained in military techniques for four months.  Then Phnom Penh fell.  That was 17th April 1975.  After the fall of Phnom Penh, that is 17th April '75, I cannot recall the exact period of months but two or three months later Angkar transferred me to Phnom Penh to the Logistics Unit of the General Staff of the centre and my assignment was to guard the ammunition warehouse.

I was part of the Unit S-80 which is located somewhere near the vicinity of Tuol Kok.  We were assigned to collect the war spoils, ammunitions.  Some ammunitions were imported through the Sihanoukville port or from Vietnam border through Kratie province and I was stationed in Phnom Penh to receive those ammunitions and to then place them properly in the warehouse.  During my time working in that ammunition warehouse some of the ammunition were placed in some concrete houses from the Antrak Tavey (phonetic) High School to the Tuol Kok TV tower and extending to the vicinity near Pochentong.  They were all houses to have the ammunition.

Later on Angkar organized my marriage within the same unit.  My husband was a combatant from the same unit.  However, before he was transferred to the S-80 unit he was at the Division 310 in Kampong Cham. Later on, on the 9th of August my husband was taken to S-21 and three days after his arrest I was arrested.  That was in the same month in 1977.  I quote the date from the documents that I obtained because I personally cannot recall the dates. And I would like to tell the Chamber and the President that before my husband and I left the S-80 unit from the general staff my husband was first taken to the vicinity near Wat Kansan or Kansan Pagoda near Chbar Ampeou.  I was still being hospitalized at that time due to my four-month pregnancy and I had morning sickness.  So my husband was sent first.

After I recovered, though not fully recovered but I gained some strength, and because I missed my husband so much, I sought permission to leave the hospital.  I was not allowed to return to S-80 unit.  I was instructed to stay there for the moment and then I was brought some clothes and I was taken.  I was told that I would be taken to see my husband and, indeed, yes, I was taken to see my husband near the Kansan Pagoda in Chbar Ampeou where we grew vegetables to supply to our unit. About a little bit more than one month later we were not mistreated or anything.  That place was probably the place where they tempered us. Later on my husband was arrested.

MS. CHUM NEOU: On the 9th of August '77 I farewell my husband and he was put onto a truck together with about 10 other people.  I packed his belongings.  And probably he knew something was going on but he told me that he would not run away. Three days later I was arrested. In the beginning I did not realize that my husband was taken to S-21.  I only learned of the word "tempering" at the time. When they arrested me another person was also arrested, Chay Bunkhoeun.  The person came from Svay Rieng and I'm not sure whether the person is still alive or not.  He also was at the logistics department of the general staff repairing weapons.  I was taken in a car although I could not recognize the particulars of the car or the model of the car.  I was taken to the psychiatric hospital in Prey Tnaot (phonetic).  I knew that hospital because before my arrest I used to collect ammunition from that hospital.

However, I did not know that that hospital was used as a tempering place for S-21.  In the late afternoon, around 3 p.m., I was walked from that office to Stueng Chrov, crossing a village next to a river.  While I was walking I recognized the Krapeuha Pagoda.  And when I reached Stueng Chrov I realized it was a tempering place because I knew a person Vat.  He was from a company of the logistics.  He was accused of being a CIA and he was sent to S-21 for tempering.  Upon recognizing him I learned that I now was sent for tempering. At that location at that time they did not work in the rice fields yet.  They grew other vegetables and there was another group raising poultry and ducks and other growing other types of vegetables.

I could not go and work with the rest of the group.  It's because I still had morning sickness as I was not fully recovered and I could not eat anything or I would vomit. And the second reason that I could not go to work with the rest of the group:  because one of my hands was handicapped and I could not hold the hoe.  And I was so skinny already, in addition to the morning sickness that I received.  Even when I drank water I still threw up.  I kept throwing out and I could not eat anything except a little rice with some grains of salt and nothing else besides that.

And I was lucky as I knew that person Vat, so Vat gave me some grains of salt to help me to eat with the rice. During the time that I was at Stueng Chrov I stayed there from my five-month pregnancy until the day I delivered my baby.  I have never talked about this experience.  Only today is the time that I speak out.  Even if I was near full term I was still ordered to cut firewood, to carry water, and I slipped at the riverbank and then I was bleeding and by seeing that they stopped using me to carry water.

There was a midwife, Thach, who was also in that location.  She was skilful and she looked after me.  She took care of me.  Those people who stayed there asked her whether I was able to survive and the midwife said yes, so the midwife looked after me until the day I delivered my baby. The person Chay Bunkhoeun, who also delivered a baby a month before me, helped giving me some assistance.  So we took turns to take care of each other during that period of time. I could not recall the exact date of my baby delivery and about a month or so after that I was sent to Prey Sar, or S-24, which is a branch of S-21.  I was transferred up and down, and when I walked to S-24 I had to walk across Stueng Praeak Kroes and Preaek Tnaot.  It was quite a long distance.  One of my hands was handicapped and I had to cradle my young baby as well.  I had to stop for so many times.  I had to walk.  There was no transportation.  I had to walk across the open field, the rice fields.

I could not recall how long I was at Prey Sar.  I could not do any transplanting of the seedlings yet at the time as I was weak and my hand was still hurt.  Later on I was either sent to Bakou or Stueng Chrov, as I could not recall correctly.  I was asked to do and worked in the rice fields.  In the beginning I could not do it, so I was assigned to look after the children. So during the time that I looked after the children I looked after about four to five children and, of course, naturally we paid more attention to our children.  It was difficult for me to look after those children.  And later on when I could work in the rice field, that is two or three months later, I was assigned to work in the rice field.  Although my hand was still a little numb, I could hold the seedlings.

I could still recall the moment when my baby could -- I could only breastfeed my baby one time per day, during the break at noon.  Later on the infant of my friend, Chay Bunkhoeun, became sick and that baby died.  On the night the baby died my friend, Chay Bunkhoeun, dare not tell anybody.  So she slept hugging the dead baby until the next morning.  Then she told the people in charge there that her baby died.  Actually the baby was a girl and my baby was a boy.

So in the morning when she told the people in charge, the baby was taken and buried near the banana forestation nearby.  Five or six days later my baby became sick.  During that time I told them my baby had a fever and she needed to look after.  I told the caretaker and I went off to work in the rice fields. In the evening when I returned I was told that my baby was sent to a hospital in Phnom Penh.  I was speechless as I was not allowed to go.  Two days later a car came and I was told that I would go to see my baby.  I was so happy because during the two days that my baby was not with me I had to get rid of the milk from my breasts, so I was happy when I was told that I would be taken to see my baby.

On the contrary, I went to see the baby and I breastfed her but only an hour later my baby died.  I believe it was an overlapping of a measles that he received. During the time that I was tempered at S-24, a branch of S-21, we had to follow the instructions, the orders that were given to us. After the death of my baby I requested permission to go back to work in a rice field because I did not know what else I could do at the hospital where my baby died.  At that time, my baby was about seven or eight months old as I delivered the baby in January, and the transplanting season was somewhere around August.

Upon my return, the Unit K-14 was only for the married people, so those people who also had children were put into that unit. Upon my return, there was an announcement that I was a CIA so nobody dared to talk to me.  I tried to ask my friends what's going on; nobody said anything.  I tried to tempered my feeling to give into them.  I pretend to be a person like a crazy person and not to show my discontent with their behaviour and just try to go along with the group. In 1978, it was the year that the flood was huge.  It was historical.  The dam at Bakou was broken and the rice fields was overflowed.

I would like to make a proposal.  I would like that the Chamber gives information to the witness at the beginning that if they need time to cope with their emotions when they are moved, that they get this time, that they can be sure to have this time before they continue with their testimony; and as well to offer them, in the case that they continue, that they can ask to recover and have a short break.

And, as well, to offer them again that they can contact, even during their testimony if they feel it is necessary, with TPO, which is the psychological support organization, to recover and to come back. And the same for other events like, for example, discussion of any legal issues or whatever is not directly a part of our interrogation because, if not, we are feeling very much under pressure and I think this is only my perspective, seeking a clarification from the Chamber so that we know this time is for interrogation time.

These are my observations and I would appreciate if the Chamber could make this clarification that would facilitate our standing here in Court and, of course, the questioning of the civil party today and other civil parties and witnesses. And I also would like to inform the Chamber that the civil party today is somehow very strong but is, at some points of his story, very weak and will be moved very much by his emotions and, of course, willing to testify here before this Court and very happy to do this. However, we have also taken into account the other objections and other times interfere during the time when the civil parties are putting questions to the witness or the accused.

So the time is calculated based on the time when the civil parties are putting the questions, so the Judges are monitoring and observing the proceedings, and we will see if there is any time used other than the times used by the civil parties during the given time.  Then the Chamber would like to give extra time to them.  So we would be flexible accordingly. The starting time of the session can be flexible also, depending on something that happens practically in the Court, and yesterday we had some problems because the witness was very emotional while he was being asked by the prosecutor, and the prosecutors have not used all the times given to them, and for the civil parties we have observed that they have not used up all the times allocated to them.

The calculation of the times for the civil parties are appropriate.  It doesn't mean that the calculation is based on a few questions the civil parties would put to the witness or to the accused, but it's based on the proportion. Regarding the survivors of the regime, we note that they have been very emotional and yesterday, after having examined how we could control the witness when he or she is very emotional and we also checked to see whether there are doctors or psychiatrists on standby, then the Court would seek their assistance to help that witness before we proceeded further.

However, after a few moments, we observed that the witness could recompose himself and that he was under control to respond to further questions. To sum up, the Trial Chamber is very deliberate when it comes to the calculation of times allocated to parties, however, the times for objections have not been included in the allocated times to the parties.  So the parties could still exercise their full rights to use the full time allocated to them, except the objections or any matter that arises during such proceedings. The Court officer, you are now instructed to bring the survivor, Mr. Bou Meng, into the courtroom.
