QUESTIONING BY THE BENCH BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. What is your name, Uncle?
A. My name is Bou Meng.

MR. PRESIDENT: You can sit down, no problem, because we will take the full day to hear your testimony, so you are allowed to be seated. Before you respond to any questions, could you please wait until you see the red light on the mic.  If you speak when the light is not on, your message would not be interpreted and the international colleagues in the proceedings and the public gallery would not hear what you are saying. And, number three, according to the note of the Greffier, you seem to have a hearing problem.  So the Chamber would like to inform you that when you listen to any question and that you understand the question, you should be quiet and wait until the red light on.  Then you can respond.  If you are not able to understand the questions, then you can make a request to the party who puts such question to rephrase or to ask you again before you can respond.
BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. How old are you?
A. I'm 68 years old this year.
Q. Where do you live now?
A. I live in Kampong Kong Commune, Kaoh Thum district, Kandal province.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Since I have been detained at Tuol Sleng, I had hearing problems.  My eyesights are not good and I am physically weak.
Q. Could you please be reminded that you should wait until you see the red light before you can respond, otherwise your message would not be communicated.  Please wait, Uncle.
Are you married?
A. I have another wife.
Q. What is her name?
A. She is 48 years.
(Microphones not activated)
A. My ex-wife was Ma Yoeun, alias Thy.  She died during the Pol Pot regime.

Q.  You have filed a civil party application to join as a civil party.  Now, before the Chamber, what is actually the purpose of your application?  Would you like to seek reparation on your behalf or you would like your lawyers to act on your behalf?
A. I would like to allow my civil party lawyers to act on my behalf regarding these reparations.
Q. After having decided to join as a civil party, what is your involvement in the facts regarding the accused in this case?
A. Mr. President, I'm not really sure whether I understand your question.  Could you please make it in a more simplified Khmer language?

Q. The Chamber would like to ask you that you have already joined as a civil party, but we would like to know of your involvement into any particular fact; for example, the fact of S-21 or the fact of S-24, Prey Sar. And, number two, have you been the direct of victim of the fact or you are here on behalf of your loved ones who were victims of S-21 or S-24, or you were here as the victim of both facts?

A. Mr. President, I am here to be on behalf of myself who is the victim of the regime because I had been beaten severely and my wife disappeared, and I don't know where she has gone or how she would have been tortured.
Q. Before the 17th of April 1975, where did you live and what was your occupation back then?
A. I went into the maquis jungle to liberate the territory and to save King Norodom Sihanouk.
Q. Could you please tell the Court about your experience and what you have come across during the Khmer Rouge regime after the 17th of April 1975 until the 7th of January 1979?

A. After the 17th April 1975, I was ordered by Angkar to work in the technical school in Ruessei Keo.  I did the drawing and the sketches for the workshop participants.  It was at the technical school in Ruessei Keo.

Q. You can just continue to describe your accounts from the time that you were at the Ruessei Keo Technical School until you were free from the Tuol Sleng on the 7th of January 1979.  If you can, describe all those accounts. If you can not, then the Chamber would put some questions to you based on the certain periods of the events.

A. Mr. President, during the times that I served at the Ruessei Keo Technical School, I had worked for about one year; I cannot recall exactly.  My apology if I cannot recall the exact date due to the serious torture that I received.  So my memory is not in great shape.

In 1976, Angkar arrested my superior, Hak, from the Ruessei Keo Technical School.  Two or three months later, the Southwest Group came to take control of that school.  I was then transferred to Ta Lei Co-operative in Dangkao Commune, Dangkao district, Dangkao province.  It was the co-operative with the education site. At that time, I was forced by Angkar to dig canals from Ta Lei village to the Prey Sar prison.  I was forced to build dams, to dig canals actively, so I was so severely physically used to provide the labour to Angkar.  It was to the limit of my physical stance to do that labour. Later on, Angkar ordered me to the group of adult people to make ploughs and some other wooden tools, rakes, and the chief of the group was Pak.  We called him Brother Pak.  It was still at the Ta Lei Co-operative. And later on, I was assigned to plant vegetables, and while I was working the soil at the vegetable beds, I grew cabbage, and over there we use human fertilizer.  It was called fertilizer number one.

And one day, there was a group of people in black clothes.  I think they were driving a Jeep, if I can recall correctly.  At that time, I was planting eggplants.  I was told by that group that Angkar required me and my wife to prepare my belonging in order to teach the children at the school of fine arts. By hearing that, I thought that would be right because it's my expertise.  So I was happy, very happy, and I thought that I would now work in my right profession.  However, unfortunately, at that time when I was in the car with my wife in that Jeep, I was taken to a location near Kirirom location and I thought that was not the way to the school of fine arts.

I felt uneased and I felt a bit scared and I felt I was dizzy. For about a half-an-hour later, we reached a location which was unknown to me at the time and the chief stopped there.  And we entered a house which was near by the Tuol Sleng prison or the S-21 Office.  There was a house opposite that office. They had two rows of chairs and we were asked to get off the car and we went to sit on the chairs.  Then there was a person who ordered me to put my hands behind my back, so my wife and I put our hands behind our backs and they cuffed our hands.

Then my wife started crying and said, "What do I do wrong?  We both are orphans."  I was so pitiful of my wife.  At that time, they used a piece of black cloth to blindfold both of us, my wife and I.  Then we were walked into the S-21 Security Office or Tuol Sleng prison.  Then I realized that was a prison.  From then onward, I was asked to enter a room and I was photographed. After they photographed my wife, then they photographed me, and that was the only photograph of my wife that I have had with me until today because I lost all the photos from the 7th of January 1979.  And with me I only have a photo of my wife that I would like to show to the judges.

After we were photographed, we were walked to Building C and from that time onward, I separated from my wife.  I did not know which building she was taken to. So I was placed in the common room on the upper floor.  I think about five months or one year later, I received torture.  First, I was threatened that they would peel my skin.  I didn't know what it means by that, but a person who slept next to me told me that it means that you will be beaten during the interrogation and I felt so horrified in my mind.  I was so shocked.  I thought, what mistake did I make?  I tried my best to serve Angkar.  And in the end, I became and fell into such a situation so I kept thinking.
While I was in the prison, all the clothes were stripped off except my underwear.  So I slept directly on the floor for several months.

Then they started to interrogate me and beat me up.  It was -- the interrogation location was in a house outside the compound. It was behind the Building A.  They cut me and they asked me to lie down on the floor with my face facing down and they had a bunch of sticks and they dropped it on the floor and it made noise.  And I was asked to choose which stick I preferred.  And I responded, "Whichever stick I choose, it is still a stick that you will use to beat me up so it is up to you, Brother, to decide which one you want to use." Mam Nai stood up and grabbed a stick and started to beat me up. After he felt exhausted, then another person came to take turn to beat me up.  So that Mam Nai was Mam Nai alias Chan.  He got his skin condition with a spotty skins and quite a red in his face. He asked me to count the lashes and when I counted up to 10 lashes, he said, "How come you count to 10 lashes?  I only beat you for one lash."

I was -- I felt so painful at the time.  There were wounds -- many wounds on my back and the blood was on the floor flowing from my back.  Whips were also used to torture me.  I was so shocked and painful.

Every time they beat me up, they asked me questions; when did I join the CIA and, "Who introduced you into the CIA network and what was their name?"  And I responded that I did not know.  So the first beating, I responded I did not know.  The second time of the beating, the third times; I gave the same response.  Even if my back had wound, they beat on that wound.  It was so painful and I could not think of any mistake that I made.  I did not know what CIA or KGB network was; then how could I respond?  So they just kept beating me up.  I had a lot of scars on my back as evidence from that torture.

In my mind, I thought of my mother; that if I could live, I would pray.  Probably it's because of my mother that gave me birth. And I would -- and I thought that if I could lived to give my story to the Chamber and now, finally, I am before the ECCC and that the ECCC would  find justice for me.  And I feel so happy even if 100 percent of justice cannot be provided by the Chamber, 50 or 60 percent of justice to me is fine because I determined from the prison where I was detained that I had not committed any mistake or offence and that I prayed just to be survived.

Q. Uncle Meng, please try to recompose yourself so that you would have the opportunity to tell your story. As you have stated, you have been waiting for this opportunity to tell your accounts, your experience and the sufferings that you received from those unjust acts; from the torture committed by the Khmer Rouge, as well as the ill treatment on your wife.  So please try to be strong, recompose yourself so that you are in a better position to recount what they did on you so that the public and the Chamber who are participating in this proceeding or the Cambodian people as a whole as well as the international community to hear, to understand the acts committed by the Khmer Rouge clique on you and that they would express the pityness on you as you received those ill treatment from them.  So do not let your emotion overwhelm you.  So try to grab the opportunity to tell your accounts to the Chamber as well as to the public. Uncle Meng, do you understand what I said?
A. Yes, Mr. President; I understand.

Q. Please try to recompose and be strong.  Today is the opportunity for you to reveal, to describe your sufferings to the Chamber so that the Chamber can understand.  If your emotion overwhelms you, then it's unlikely that we have another time to hear your account because the Chamber has scheduled other witnesses to provide the testimonies and they had gone through similar experiences, either at S-21 or Prey Sar -- although some of them are not the direct victims but they're relatives or family members, wives, husbands, parents -- received the unjust acts over there.

So, in summary, please continue to recount the experience and the sufferings that you received from those unjust acts during the time that you were detained until the day you were free from that prison, thanks to the National United Front for Salvation armies on the 7 January '79.  Do you understand what I said?

A. Yes, I can continue, Mr. President. Let me go back a little bit because I forgot to talk about the food ration in the common room.  In that common room, there were about 30 or 40 of us and at one corner I saw foreigners with light complexions and they were detained there as well, and they received the same food ration; that is, very thin gruel.  There was no rice grain in there, just one (inaudible) or one there, and I was so skinny I had no strength.  Even if I had a stick, I would not be able to use it to attack them.

When Him Huy took me to the upper floor, he rode on my neck, on my shoulder, and I stumbled on the stairs and my knee was hurt and there was a wound on my knee.  So when I think of those events, I felt so painful. Each day when they took me for interrogation they took me twice, from 7 to 12 in the morning, and in the afternoon from 2 to or              6 p.m.  The interrogators who beat me up, I could recognize their            7   faces because when they talked to each other, I recognized their names. They were Brother Mam Nai, Comrade Hor, Comrade Huy, Comrade Tith and Peng, so there were five of them altogether.  My apology that I went back to describe this account because I forgot.

Q. As I told you, please try to re-compose yourself.  This is the day that you have been waiting for for so long.  I know you are very emotional now and probably you will miss certain events that you would want to recount.  Of course, the sufferings you and your wife received were indescribable and right now the Chamber would like to ask you some questions.
When there was a vehicle going to pick you up from the Ta Lei Co-operative in Dangkao district to the School of Fine Arts, were you tied or cuffed, and what about your wife?

A. Mr. President, Your Honours, at that time I saw a vehicle but there were no cuffs in there.  We were asked to pack our clothes, so I had some clothes so I put them in my backpack and they were all taken away at Tuol Sleng.

Q. When they took you to Tuol Sleng, did they take you to Tuol Sleng straight away or were you taken to another place first? For example, like the place that you described where there were two rows of chairs.  Was it within the compound of the Tuol Sleng prison?

A. It was outside the Tuol Sleng prison.  It was opposite the Tuol Sleng prison.  There was a house and there were two rows of chairs, and in the middle there was a long table.  So we were asked to enter that house and they ordered us to put our hands behind us and then they cuffed our hands, both of us.
Q. When they ordered you to put your hands behind your back and then later you were cuffed, did they tell you the reasons for the arrest of your wife and yourself?  Did they tell you the reasons?

A. Mr. President, at that time they did not tell us any reasons or any mistakes we made, and I and my wife asked them what mistake did we do and we told them that we were orphans and what mistakes we did?  And they replied, "You, the contemptible, you don't have to ask.  Angkar has many eyes, like pineapples, and Angkar only arrests those who make mistakes or offence."  And I was still wondering what mistakes I did, and my wife wondered the same. At that time. I was in the adult group in the co-operative to make ploughs and rakes, and my wife worked in the rice fields and I could not think of any mistake that my wife and I made.  Until today, I could not think of the mistakes that I made at the time.
Q. The people who ordered you to put your hands behind your backs and then they cuffed you and your wife, were they the same people who went to pick you up from Ta Lei Co-operative?

A. Mr. President, they were different people.  They were not those who took me, who brought me from the co-operative.  They were there waiting for us in that room.  So once we entered the house we were asked to sit, in a nice gesture, and later on what happened I already described to you. So I broke into my tears because I did not know what offence I committed.  If I stay home and did nothing, maybe I made a mistake, but I did not do that and I cannot think of the mistake I committed.  Whatever I was asked by Angkar, I just did.
Q. Can you recall the day that you were arrested and taken to Tuol Sleng prison or can you recall the year?

A. Mr. President, I can remember the year.  It was 1977 when I was entered into the S-21 Office.  I am a bit weak on the month because at that time there was no calendar to see, so it's only just based on the thinking or estimation.  I think it could be in May or June in 1977.

The reason why I thought it was in May or June because after they tortured me and they were fed-up with torturing me, there was a teenager about 16 or 17 years old made an announcement.  He said, "In this room, who can do the painting?"  So I raised my hand.  I said, yes, I can do the painting. And that person ordered another person to unshackle me and they then put a chain on one of my feet.  I was then walked from the upper floor of that C Building to the ground floor in order to meet Mr. Duch.  The reason I recognized him because when I was painting the portrait of Pol Pot, he was sitting nearby me, watching me, sitting on a chair with his legs crossed.  I did a lot of portraits, not only just for Pol Pot, I also did a portrait for Mao Zhedong.

Q. The Chamber asked you to describe about the situation but you have not been able to detail what we asked you, so I would like you to please listen to the question of the Chamber step-by-step until the 7th of January 1979. I think would you please wait until the question is referred to a particular section that you can respond otherwise you would not be able to recall the consequential event.  So could you please be waiting for the question from the Chamber before you could respond to them?
When you were arrested and sent to S-21, were you sent in at night or in the daytime?
A. It was at about 9 or 10, I can't remember it well, and when I reached Tuol Sleng there was no clock that I could check the time, but it was during the daytime not at night.
Q. When you were handcuffed all together with your wife and walked into Tuol Sleng compound, were you both blindfolded?
A. We were blindfolded before we were walked into Tuol Sleng compound.
Q. You stated earlier that when you entered the location you were taken photograph.  Before the photos were taken, did they ask you for your biography or was it done later after the photography?

A. I don't remember all.  Please accept my apologies. I think the document from Tuol Sleng still survives and the person who kept the record was Ti (phonetic), and I was shocked and confused because I did not know why I was arrested and I did not know how I responded to them.  I did not know whether my biography would have been sent to them earlier, prior to my arrest.  I'm not sure.
Q. You said your wife and yourself were blindfolded.  Were you still being blindfolded while being taken photograph or were the blindfolds removed?
A. When we were at the photo workshop then our blindfolds were removed, and we were seated and I was taken photograph and followed by my wife.
Q. What about the handcuffs?  Were you removed from the handcuffs while being photographed?

A. I don't recall having been removed from the handcuffs.  I'm not sure; I forget it.  Maybe the handcuffs were removed or maybe they were not.  But so far as I remember after our photographs were taken, then we were blindfolded again before we were walked to Building C.
Q. You said you were stripped to your underwear.  When was that, before you were sent to Building C or only after you got to Building C that your clothes were stripped off?

A. I think maybe my clothes were stripped off downstairs before we were walked upstairs or maybe only when we reached upstairs that our clothes were stripped off.  I seem to forget.  But as I remember, it is sure that after we were taken photographs then we were re-blindfolded and I did not know where my wife would be walked to.
Q. When you reached the building, it was the common building for all prisoners or it was a separate prison cell for detaining you alone?

A. Mr. President, at that time I was put in a common large room in which about 20 to 30 detainees were placed.  They all looked like hell because their hairs grew long, even they were male but their hairs grew so long.  I felt dizzy when I entered the room and I was so confused.

Q. When you were being handcuffed, were you handcuffed and attached to the bar, the metal bar with the other detainees, or you were handcuffed and then isolated?  Could you please tell us about the condition of the shackles?

A. We were put into the common rooms and in each metal bar resembled the shackles.  There were a lot of detainees attached to the shackles by our ankles, maybe five to 10 people for each long shackles and we were put to sleep head to head with other detainees, so my head was put against the east wall.
Q. At that time could you sit up when your both legs were shackled to the long bar like that?

A. I could sit up but we had to ask permission from the guards before we could relieve ourselves, although we were given an ammunitions box for such purpose and we were given a plastic jug for our urination.
Q. Who collect the wastes or were they left with the detainees all day?

A. At that time the people who worked there in the common cell, the person whose age was about 15 years old, would go up and collect the waste because the detainees would only be put to lie down in the cell and could not be moved.

Q. You mentioned about the food ration, the thin gruel with very few rice grains and sometimes you would be offered a watery soup with water grass.  The question is how food was provided to you? Were you fed with a plate, a spoon or what was it like when food was delivered to you, and how often did you get the meals?

A. When it was time to eat it was at 12 or 11.30; let's say between 11.30 to 1.  That's for lunch.  In the afternoon, late afternoon, the food was served at 5 p.m. or 6 p.m. and when the food was carried to the place then they would leave it there, and if people made noise then they would be beaten with the stick that they used to carry the food to the detainees.  I felt very pity for them and for myself because we were treated like animals.  We whispered to one another, I mean to the neighbours, but we could not make loud noise.
Q. Did the detainees have to share -- have to distribute the porridge or the gruel, or were they distributed by the guards?

A. We were given the gruel on a plate by the guards, and after we finished the meal then the plates and spoon would be collected because they were afraid that those items could be used for the detainee to commit suicide, because every night people would come to search for any metal items or sharp items.  I did not know why they came to search for those items.
Q. When you were thirsty what would you do?
A. We had to ask for permission; for example, "Brother, I am thirsty.  Could you please give me some water?"
Q. So it means in the common cell there were the prison guards who stationed there regularly.  Is that correct?
Please wait until you see the red light before you respond.
A. When I needed some water I would ask them for the water and they would give it to me.
THE INTERPRETER: The President's mic is not on.

BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Now, you have not answered the questions about the guards who would be regularly stationed at the cell, and you said that when you would like to relieve yourself or you were thirsty you would ask the guard.  My question was:  were there regular prison guards at that location, and how many guards were there in your room?

A. I think guards would be seen walking on the corridor, several of them, because we were locked inside and we could see them walking on the corridor, passing the windows.  And when we needed to relieve ourselves then we would call them.  But they gave us the boxes for relieving ourselves, although we were not removed our shackles.  But I seem to be forgotten when it comes to how we could ask them when we would like to relieve ourselves, but I am sure that we were shackled at all times.

Q. I think we learned from you that there were the plastic jug and ammunition box placed for the detainees to relieve themselves, but when you were thirsty how could you do it, because there were no water jars left with water for detainees, so you had to shout to the guards?  I mean, if you shouted it means that the guards would be outside but if they were inside, the detainees would not need to shout to alert them. However, during the time when you had a bath -- because you were detained quite a long time from mid-1977 to 1979 and you were detained the longest there among the others, so when it comes to having a bath, what was it like?

A. When we had a bath we would take off our shorts and then remove it from our legs, one leg at a time, and then we had to be naked and then the water would be sprayed from outside through a water hose, and some would get soaked, some would miss the water. And then we would use the clothes to dry the water.  It was so miserable because we would -- had been treated like the cattle while we were sprayed the water on. When we asked for water, of course we had to ask them for permission.  Otherwise we would never be given such water to drink.
Q. You said you took off your shorts to dry the water.  What was the purpose of doing so?
A. We only used them to dry the floor so that we could -- when the floor dried then we could lie down, because the water floods the floors and we had to dry it to make sure that it's dry.
Q. So the purpose of removing your shorts was to dry the floor so that you could sleep on it.  Is that correct?
A. That is correct, Mr. President.
Q. How often were you sprayed the water on like this?

A. Once every week or maybe once every fortnight.  I don't remember; you know, it has been 30 years or more already, but I know that every time we had a bath, everyone had to be naked.  It was like hell. Everyone would look the same and sometimes they mocked at us. They said that you guys look small physically but your thing was not that small.  I'm sorry to say that, but we would laugh by mocking on some other things, private things.
Q. When you were detained, besides being removed from the shackles to be interrogated, were you released to do exercises, for example, every now and then or were you never allowed to do that?
A. I don't remember it.  I think we were never allowed to do exercise in the room or maybe we were allowed to do so.  I am not sure because it has been so long already.
Q. When you were taken to be interrogated, how was the process carried out?

A. Every time I was taken to be interrogated, they would handcuff me and walked to the compound of the prison to Building A.  I think the previous trace of the building vanished over time and I think I could never take any visitors to the same original location as it already altered.
Q. When you were removed from shackles, then you would be handcuffed before you would be walked to be interrogated.  Can you please tell us how this process would be carried out?
A. I was walked to the interrogation room into the house.  We walked to upstairs.

Q. No, I'm talking about the time when you were in the room and were shackled, and then you were shackled and attached to other people, other detainees.  And before you were taken to the interrogation room, would you be removed from the shackles and then walked outside of your room before you would be re-shackled again and walked to the interrogation room?
A. They removed the shackles from the long bar.  The shackles were removed then they cuffed -- they put the cuffs on me again and then they walked to the outside area of the room, or the prison.
Q. Were you blindfolded when you were being walked away?
A. Of course, I was blindfolded while I was being walked away.
Q. Could you please tell us about the moment when you were put into the room for interrogation?  How were you treated by the guards?

A. They treated us -- they used derogatory language to me and they shackled me by my ankles -- the long bar of shackles which was about half a metre -- and then they locked the chain and then they closed all the windows and doors.  No, I think the windows would be left open because there were metal bars.  I could see Building A or B clearly. After I was shackled and they removed the handcuffs and removed the blindfold, and then they started to beat me to answer when I entered CIA and KGB.  I told them that I did not know anything about it and I could not answer anything about CIA and KGB. I kept repeating my response and they kept beating me and, of course, if we did not respond or answer to satisfy their request, then we would be beaten severely.

Q. During the time when you were interrogated, you would be shackled and then you would be asked to sit on the floor while your handcuffs would be removed along with the blindfold before you would be interrogated.  In case you did not respond to what they wanted to get the confession from you, then you would be beaten with a stick.  Do I understand you correctly?

A. They removed the blindfold and handcuffs.  They put me to lie face down and then they started to beat me until they had enough, and then they kept asking me when I entered CIA and KGB and who introduced me into the agents.  And I did not know how to respond to them because the person who worked honestly and worked the best to serve Angkar and never been involved in such organization, how could I respond to them that I introduced anyone into the CIA, even myself.  I did not know what CIA was.

Q. You said you were shackled and put face down.  I find it difficult to understand because if you talk about the shackle, then you could sit up.  And how could you be put face down and then if you were shackled before that, you could not sit up because it was a wooden kind of shackles.  Then you put your legs -- or your legs were put into the shackle then you would not be able to lie face down on the floor. Or were you put to lie face down on the floor and tortured before they removed the shackles, and then -- or what?  Could you please clarify it to me or to the Court?

A. It was not a wooden shackle, Mr. President.  It was a metal bar, long bar, designed to only put on one individual detainee. After having that long metal bar attached to my legs and my ankles, then they locked both ends and then they put me to lie face down in order for the interrogator to be able to beat me on my back and I could put my face down.
Q. Were you taken to be interrogated immediately when you were sent during the first night at S-21 or were you kept a few days; only later that they would take you to be interrogated?

A. Mr. President, I was detained for quite a long time.  I think it was until May or June 1977 so I had been detained for four or five months before I was interrogated and tortured.  And as I stated earlier, then a guy came and asking for anyone who could paint.
Q. Can you try to recall the S-21 staff who took you for interrogation and torture?  How many times were you taken and what about the types of torture?

A. Mr. President, when -- for every times they interrogated and tortured me, they did not use or change the method.  First, they used a rattan stick or a whip to beat me up.  They beat me up with the stick or the whip for the two sessions.  So from 7 until 12 or 1 p.m. in the morning, then I was allowed to eat and in the afternoon, they only stopped after 6 or 7 p.m. when I was taken back to the room.  After they beat me up, they did not take me to the common room.  They took me to the individual cell.  So every time after the interrogation and the torture, I was taken to the ground floor -- to the individual cell.  And for the mealtime, then we were fed with a bowl of food.

Q. So in summary, you were detained in two different rooms. First, you were in the common room and about five months later, when they started to interrogate and torture you by using the stick, then you were detained in an individual cell.  Is that correct?
A. Mr. President, that is correct.
Q. Was your torture in a different method; for example, by electrocution?

A. Yes, Mr. President. One day after they beat me down -- they beat me up, they walked me to Building D and there was a power outlet on the wall and then they used an electrical wire to electrocute me.  I felt unconscious and later on they used the water to pour on my face and I became unconscious again.  I did not know the voltage of that electricity, but once they started it, I felt unconscious immediately.  That was done in Building D.

Q. I already asked you and you said that you did not know if you committed any offence so when you were detained in the prison, was there any decision by a trial committee to punish or sentence you -- for example, in a form of a trial in a similar form of this Chamber -- during your detention there?

A. Mr. President, no, there was no judgment; no order from anybody.  We were just detained.  And one day after they exhausted by beating me up, then they walked me back into the room and while at the path walking to our Building D -- there was no concrete path there at the time  -- and at that juncture, I was beaten up again.  And another person came and said, "Don't beat him up today because Brother instructed so.  Keep him alive." Because there were a lot of wounds on my back, I felt so painful, but because they beat me up so I had to lie down on my back. However, Him Huy used a stick to push under my back and a lot of gravels went inside the wound on my back so because it was so painful, then I had to turn myself again for them to beat me up on the back.
Q. When did they decide to use you as a painter?

A. One day, I was taken from that individual cell to the upper floor for treatment.  Actually, there was no medicine at all. There was a bowl of saltwater and they just poured that saltwater on my back and it was so, so painful because of my open wounds and the salt.  You could see when you used the salt on the frog, you could see the effects and you could imagine how painful it was when they pour the water -- the saltwater on my back.  And indeed, finally the wounds recovered from the saltwater. Sometimes, I was given a rabbit pellet tablet.  It was so miserable.
Q. And now to the scars from the beating; do you still have the scars or are they completely gone?

A. The wounds recovered, but the scars are everywhere on my back, on my shoulders.  They were the scars from being whipped or beaten.  Sometimes, there were five of them beating me up at the same time.
Q. Can we see the scars on your back?

MS. STUDZINSKY: Mr. President, I would like to make break now before Mr. Bou Meng shows his scars and to decide if this is appropriate -- an appropriate measure now and maybe it is time for an adjournment, and that would be great if he could get it. Thank you.

MR. PRESIDENT: Please be seated.  The Chamber is now back in session. We would like to inform the parties and the public that the Chamber now cancels its attempts to show the scars on the survivor's back and all parties are also reminded not to proceed with the request to show the scars on the survivor's back. Do you have any further requests or observations?

MS. STUDZINSKY: Thank you, Mr. President.  We would suggest to proceed in closed session and then Mr. Bou Meng could show the scars to the Chamber and the parties.  That is something that could be a possibility to do.

MR. PRESIDENT: The Chamber already decided to cancel its attempts to show the scars, even if in an in camera hearing.  In case of necessity, it can be shown by photos.  So the photos can be shown of the scars on his back.  Bou Meng, you think you can have those photos for the Chamber?
MR. BOU MENG: Mr. President, I do not have any photos of the marks.  I only have the marks on my body.
MR. PRESIDENT: The Chamber would like to request to take photos of your -- of the scars or your marks that can be displayed on the screen.  Do you agree to this proposal?
MR. BOU MENG: Yes, I agree.
MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Next, so you were chosen to be a painter.  When were you chosen?

A. Mr. President, towards the later '77, because in early 1978 I already painted a canvas.  One day I heard the noise from the loudspeaker, I think they celebrated something at the Olympic Stadium, and we were given a lot of food.  We ate to our fill and the guards gave us the food.  And I even have the noodles, Chinese noodles to eat. And Nath said I had to jump, to jump up so that the food will go down lower through my stomach and I can eat more to fill to my stomach.  And I told him, "Once you are full, you are full.  You only have one stomach to fill in."

I think I started painting the portrait in late '77 or early '78 because there were four portraits and each portrait, when Duch asked me, "How long did it take to make that portrait?  And the portrait must look the same as the photo," and I told him -- I requested to have three months to make that portrait because the canvas was huge.  It was 1.5 metres wide and three metres high. I would like to seek your permission to show the portrait of Pol Pot that I painted.  I survived because I could paint the exact portrait of Pol Pot, so I was spared until to the 7th January, '79. This is my response, Your Honour.
Q. During the time that you were released to work by doing the painting, where did you paint and who else worked with you in that location?

A. Mr. President, yes, I myself, Bou Meng; Vann Nath too; Im Chan, the wood sculptor and the wax moulder, another wax moulder; so that's all.  And we worked in Building E.  Building E is the building in the middle of the compound.  I think that is used as the reception area for the guests who come to visit the museum.
Q. What about the food ration after you were chosen to work as a painter?  Was the food ration the same as those given to the prisoners?

A. Mr. President, the food ration was better than previously, so it was from the thin gruel to rice and we had sufficient soup. So the prison guard carried the soup to deliver it to us and we shared among ourselves.
Q. During the time you were selected to work as a painter, where were you allowed to sleep at night?

A. After I painted and when it was time to sleep, it was at the generator's room.  It was behind Building E.  At that time there was a generator there, so when the electricity was cut off, then they started the generator and we slept in that generator's room.
Q. Were you cuffed or shackled in that room or were you locked from outside?

A. I was allowed to sleep in that room but I was not cuffed or shackled, so there was seven of us -- Oeng Bech, Vann Nath, Im Chan, Pha Tha Chan, Ruy Makong.  There were seven of us -- and Chum Mey.  I requested to see the photo: Pha Tha Chan, Bou Meng, Vann Nath, Im Chan, Ruy Makong and Chum Mey.  And now only Chum Mey, Vann Nath and Bou Meng are alive.  The other four died.
MS. STUDZINSKY: Thank you, Mr. President.  I would like to suggest to the Court officials to show the photo on the screen.  Thank you.
MR. PRESIDENT: I don't think it is yet your time.  It is now my question and I have the discretion.
BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. During the times you were asked to do the painting, did you meet the accused, Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch?

A. Mr. President, Your Honours, at that time Mr. Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, sat next to me watching me painting the portrait of Brother Number One, Pol Pot, and he ordered me, "You should adjust the throat.  It's not a tumour, it's just fat."  So as can be seen from this photo which was taken of the portraits that I painted, so you could see that the throat was slimmer.
Q. Did he come to visit you often to see you painting?  And if he came, during the day or nighttime?

A. He came often during the daytime and he wore shorts and a short-sleeved shirt.  So he came in, he sat with his one leg across and watching me drawing, for example, another portrait of the head of Ho Chi Minh on the body of a dog.  It was like a cartoon which they -- it was like a sketch of the sea with a flat, windy situation, et cetera and et cetera.
Q. Did you notice his character and behaviour during the time that he watched you making the painting or the portrait?

A. Mr. President, he did not really beat me up, however, one day I didn't know what I did wrong.  He asked me and Im Chan to beat each other up.  So we were given a piece of black plastic tube to hit, to beat each other, and he sat there watching us beating each other up.  After a while he ordered us to stop. But if I could make a very lifelike portrait, he would look at it carefully and I think I lost some of the portraits.

Q. The question is, did you observe his facial expression or his behaviour; that is the behaviour of the accused, Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, during the time that he went to watch you painting? Was he a person full of joy or full of sorrow?  Did you notice that?

A. Mr. President, his facial expression was normal.  If he needed to laugh, he laughed.  Sometimes he smiled.  I could see him through his face but I could not judge his feeling or emotion, and that's the word I was asked especially by a journalist, and I always tell them, "I know his face but I don't know his feeling". He was close to me, observing me painting.  Sometimes he gave me cigarettes to smoke.
Q. Did he ever beat you up personally?
A. No, but he ordered me to beat up with Im Chan.  I was not happy with that.  He did not treat me like a human being. Q. Did you ever see him going from one building to the next

Q. Did you ever see him going from one building to the next within the compound of the prison; for example, from Building A to B to C, or did he only enter the compound and only come to the place where you worked?

A. Mr. President, I did not see him walking along each building because when he entered his main focus was on the portrait of Brother Number One, Pol Pot.  I only saw him coming to my workshop.  I did not see him going anywhere else.
Q. So besides him, besides you yourself, did you see him torturing or beating up other prisoners?

A. Mr. President, let me go back a little bit. One day there was a Vietnamese citizen.  He boasted that he could make a wax mould and then he was ordered to show his skill.  So he was tested and Duch saw that he could not do it.  Then he ordered the interrogators to kick him like kick a ball because, from what I understood, he was angry that that person lied to him.  And I did not know what happened to that Vietnamese person. Probably he was taken out.

Q. Did he himself order the guards or his subordinates to torture that person?  And if he did order, can you recall his exact words; that is, the words that Duch used to order his subordinates to torture that Vietnamese person?

A. Mr. President, I forget some parts.  I am not sure.  I think probably he signalled his guards to beat that Vietnamese person. And the Vietnamese person was taken away from the workshop where I worked.  So there were woodcrafters; there was a painter and another artist.  We worked in the same workshop.

Q. You saw the guards beating up that person who boasted about his skill.  Was the beating taking place within the workshop vicinity in Building E or was he taken out and beaten up outsides that area?

A. Mr. President, at that time the three or four of them kicked that Vietnamese person and beat him up and walked him away.  I did not hear his order.  So when those guards beat the Vietnamese person up, Duch had already left.
Q. So during the time you were asked to work as a painter, how many portraits did you paint and whose portraits were they?

A. There were four portraits of Pol Pot.  However, there was another portrait in 1981.  There was a German group to make a film on that portrait, so I showed the portrait to the person and then I used paint to make a cross sign on that person to express my hatred of that person, and that was filmed by the German group.
Q. You said that you painted various other paintings or portraits; for example, a painting of a dog with the Ho Hi Minh head on it.  But for Pol Pot portraits you only made four portraits?
A. That is correct, Mr. President.
Q. So besides the portraits of Brother Number One, Pol Pot, did you make any other painting or portrait?
A. Mr., President, yes, I painted Hua Guofeng, Mao Zhedong in large canvas as well, so the canvas was as big as the canvas for Pol Pot's portrait.

Q. When you did your painting or portrait, did you do it individually or together with Vann Nath?  That is, Vann Nath was painting his own painting or portrait and you yourself had a separate painting or portrait?

A. Mr. President, at that time he did not have a skill of painting black and white portraits so I mixed the black and white painting by myself with one litre of gasoline to burn it and the smoke would go into that painting and then I mixed it.  And Vann Nath did not have this skill.
Q. So it means that your painting was separate from him because one was colour and one was black and white.  Is that correct?
A. Yes, that is correct.
Q. You talked about the portrait of Pol Pot.  This is one of the portraits of other people that you painted.  Is that correct?
A. Yes, Mr. President, that is correct.
MR. PRESIDENT: Court officer, can you take a photo of the portrait of Pol Pot to be projected on the monitor, on the slide?

BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Is this the portrait of Pol Pot that you painted by yourself during the time that you were detained there and then when you were asked to make a drawing or portrait of the leader of the Democratic Kampuchea?
A. Yes, Mr. President, this is the portrait.
Q. You stated just then that because of your skill of making the portrait that you survived until today.  Can you explain further the reason of this portrait that led to the survival?

A. Mr. President, the reason, from my understanding, is that my painting is a resemblance of the photo, so I started painting portraits 1, 2, 3 and 4 and another one.  While I was painting, then the time came when the Vietnamese and the National United Front for Salvation army entered Phnom Penh and we fled. They gathered us to move from the compound in one long straight line without stepping anywhere off the line or we would be shot.
MR. PRESIDENT: The Court official, can you remove the sketch?

BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. There are still some other documents in which you stated that you were sent to Prey Sar and then you stayed at Prey Sar for a while before you were returned to S-21.  What happened back then? Is it true that you were sent there?

A. I think it is not true because I stayed in Tuol Sleng prison, but when we were evacuated it would be true that I was walking and reached Prey Sar somewhere near Boeung Choueng Ek for about five minutes, and then we later on were ordered to move to Prey Sar prison.  I think after about 10 to 20 minutes then we would be ordered to move further during the nighttime.

Q. So you went to Prey Sar during the evacuation process when the United Front of the National Army actually liberated Phnom Penh, and you went along with the other people, so you were forced to move out with other people.  Is it correct?  I think you were leaving on the 7th of January 1979; is that correct?
A. Mr. President, it's correct, we left at night in the late evening at about 6 to 7 p.m.
INTERPRETER: The witness's mic is not activated.
MR. BOU MENG: We dragged our legs -- our feet.
BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Please wait until you see the red light.

The question is where were you up to -- I mean, you were at Prey Sar and then you moved forward to other locations.  So could you please tell us about the date during the process you were marching or you were getting out of town that time?

A. We left Prey Sar prison at night and we walked to National Road Number 4, and at dawn we saw the presence of the United Front army, and the guards who guarded us all the way while we were on our journey then left us.  And I could proceed with Pha Tha Chan and I did not know where the other people went to because Vann Nath also left us, except I and Pha Tha Chan who would be left alone, and we walked until Amleang and stayed at Prey Chrov co-operative. I did not ask for the food from the co-operative because we would be afraid that we would be killed, because if he got in trouble then I would too be in big trouble.
Q. When did you return?

A. When Nath came to Phnomn Penh ahead of me and along with Oeng Bech and Comrade Kong, and I walked with other people until I reached Pursat province.  And Vietnamese troops would be seen in several jungles. And at Svay Dangkao we could also see Vietnamese militaries and I was recruited as the soldier during that time.  I worked as the typist at that moment at the provincial office with Ros Sreng, Kang Heang, who at that time were the governors.

Q. Can we talk about your wife, because we have heard your good accounts of your story, because in your complaint you state about the inhuman acts against you and your wife.  So now could you please tell us a little bit about your wife when you were both sent and taken to S-21 while your photos were taken, biographies were taken and while you were blindfolded and put into the detention room?  Have you ever heard anything about your wife?

A. After we were blindfolded and sent to the upper upstairs I have never known or seen my wife.  But at one moment when I was painting the portrait of Pol Pot, Him Huy was outside of the window and told me that, "Your wife was working in the rice field," and then I told myself -- I thought that probably she would be kept there to be killed, but I did not tell anybody because I only were thinking alone.  Because I was also a farmer and Duch once said that people could be used as fertilizer for rice field or rice farming and that's why I had to be very careful and I had to work so hard to concentrate on my work and it took me three months to finish one portrait.
Q. Have you ever learned anything about the fate of your wife or what happened to her?

A. I don't know what happened to her, whether she would be tortured.  We were parted since we were taken into that common room.  Until now we have never seen each other and I never know what happened to her.
Q. Do you think that she would be killed at S-21, or what else?

A. Your question reminds me the question that I would like to ask to Mr. Kaing Guek Eav, I want to know whether he asked his subordinates to smash my wife at S-21 or at Choeung Ek so that I could collect the ashes or remains so that I can make her soul rest in peace.

Q. You have not answered to my question, but you would like to refer the question to the accused; is that correct?  You said you have obtained a photo of your wife named Yoeun alias Phy; have you brought it along with you and when was the photo taken?
A. I have the photo with me.  If you would wish me to present, then I could present it to you.

Q. When was the photo taken?  Was it taken during the time when you were sent into S-21 or Tuol Sleng prison compound at that moment when you were taken all together or was it just another photo you took with her?
A. This photo was taken during the time we were sent into S-21 because her photo was taken first, followed by me.  You can see her ID on the photo.
MR. PRESIDENT: The Greffier, could you please make sure that the photo could be projected on the monitors?
BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Is your wife, Yoeun alias Thy, what is her family name and how old was she at that time?
A. Her name was Ma Yoeun alias Thy.
Q. When she was taken photograph -- I mean, when you were sent into S-21 office; how old was she?
A. She was about 25 years old because I was about 30 years old; maybe 36 or 37 years old.  I am nine years older than her.
MR. PRESIDENT: The court official, could you please remove the photo from the monitors?

BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Now, the story of yourself and your family have been heard, we would like to put further questions concerning the time when you were detained and then later on, you were chosen to be the painter; the position you hold until 7 January 1979. During that time, had you seen or been aware of any activities of the guards at S-21 towards the other detainees?  Through your observation and recollection, could you please tell the Court about those events?

A. During the time when I worked as a painter in Building E painting a portrait of Pol Pot, I could see through the window the sending of Vietnamese soldiers and the Khmer Rouge soldiers who were sent en masse into the compound.  I did not actually witness the torture, but I heard the screams; people crying for help all around the compound.  I did not see the tortures directly, but I did hear people crying for help.
Q. When you were detained in the common room, did you see dead body of other detainees in the room and if you saw them, did you see them often?

A. Mr. President, I saw a dead body who was lying head to head with me.  He was with dark complexion, a small person.  He was taller than me.  He was about the same age as me.  If he would live, now he would be 67, 68.  A young guard stamped on his chest and he coughed with blood and he was lying dead there inside the common room.  At night, he would be taken to be buried in the compound not far from that.
Q. So how long was it -- I mean, the interval between the time when the person died and the time when he was buried?

A. I noticed that he was dead in the daytime and then late at night -- I can't remember when, but it was at night that the person disappeared and would be buried.  I don't know where he would be buried or discarded because I was still shackled and I didn't know more about something outside.

Q. You were detained and shackled for a long period of time before you were let out to be a painter.  And have you noticed the people who were sent in and shackled along with you in the same room would be taken out and disappeared or had they returned or have you noticed that?

A. I'm talking before the God, the Buddha.  I'm talking the truth.  People would be put into the trucks and carried away and they never returned.  And after being interrogated, I would be kept downstairs and I did not know much about the fate of those people, but when I was in the common room, people who would be taken away would never come back so they just disappeared.
Q. What about the other situation, for example, when a detainee was so weak that he would be carried to the truck or to the other location?  Had you seen such scenes?

A. I did witness the very thin person who were tied to his legs and arms, and a stick would be put to -- and then carried by two people.  He was carried like a pig, like people would be carrying a pig, and he was passing the place where I was painting, and the guard banged the door shut in order not to let me see them carrying that very sick and thin detainee.  I did not know where he was up to.
Q. Were they carrying the dead body or a person who's still alive?
A. He was not yet dead.  He was still breathing and then he would be carried onto the truck waiting outside the prison.  We could hear the sound of the truck coming in and out all day long.

Q. I think you should have known about this, about the trucks that came and take people away all night.  Can you tell us whether the trucks only came during the night or during the daytime, or detainees would be taken by the trucks at any time from S-21?  I mean, those people who would be taken away and would never return.

A. I was in the common cell or common room.  After being interrogated, I was put in the cell and I could hear the sound of the trucks.  I never saw the trucks; just heard the sound, the noise.  I did not know or see the detainees.  I only saw him once when I was painting the portrait of Pol Pot while they were carrying him, passing me.

Q. So was it at night or during the daytime?  I'm asking this because after hearing testimony we have received two different kinds of information, especially concerning the transportation of detainees to Choeung Ek, because the information we obtained so far is that detainees would only be sent during the night. Another thing is that I don't know whether you're confused among two of you.  One witness who testified said that during the time he was detained at the location from the morning until 12 p.m. he would not be able to sleep because he wait until 12 p.m. passed so that he knew that no people would be carried away to be killed after that.  So that's why I would like you to clarify whether prisoners would be taken at night or in the daytime, especially regarding the person who was very sick and would be carried away by two people with a stick.  Was it done during the day or at night?
A. At that time I did not see at night, of course, but I saw it during the daytime.  It was about 9 or 10 a.m.; I think more or less at about nine, between 9 and 10 a.m.
Q. Normally when the trucks came, were the trucks driven to Building E or just they were parked right in front of the entrance; close to Building B or C, for example?

A. Mr. President, regarding the trucks that transported the detainees, the truck parked outside under the gate -- I mean near that gate.  The truck did not come into the compound of the prison.  They parked outside.
Q. Did you notice other activities of the staff at S-21 towards other detainees?

A. When I was painting at Tuol Sleng, I saw female detainees. Some pregnant detainees would be walked away while being kicked by the guards -- female guards.  And they asked them to walk faster and they walked past Building B and then -- I mean from south to north, from Building A to B.  I did not know where they would be detained, but they passed us while we were painting the portraits.
Q. The last question.  When you left with Uncle Nath and other survivors from S-21 on the 7th of January 1979, did you notice that in the buildings of S-21 there were some prisoners left?
A. Mr. President, I think it is more about freedom of the prisoners.  Prisoners were deprived of their liberty and we would not be allowed to move, so people -- I think there was quiet inside.

Q. My question is this.  I mean the last day, the last day when you left S-21, because there were dead bodies on the beds.  There were 14 of them.  Some witnesses would say that there were only 10; the accused said that there were only four people; and now the survivors, including you yourself, have noticed that there would be some kind of noise and could see people were still left inside the building during the time when you were leaving the premises. The question is whether you could receive any information or see that detainees still were there on the 17th (sic) of January 1979, the moment before you were leaving S-21.  So just tell us whether you saw people still there at the premises when you were leaving.

A. Mr. President, the last day on the 7th of January I left S-21 at about 9 a.m.  We heard the gunshots and we were ordered to leave immediately.  At that moment I did not see or hear any noise, and I was so panicked that I did not pay attention to who would remain, because they pointed the guns at us and they warned us not to even turn back.  We had to really walk forward otherwise we would get killed or shot.  So I did not see any one I guess.
BY MR. PRESIDENT: Thank you very much, Uncle, for your responses.

So the Chamber will now take adjournment, and we resume at 1.30 p.m. The court official, please make sure that Uncle Bou Meng is offered the food, and please bring him back to the courtroom by one thirty. The security guards, please take the accused to the detention facility and bring him in by one thirty. The court is adjourned for lunch.
