BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Uncle Meng, when the interrogators stopped torturing you because you agreed to confess and it was a false confession, was it based on the purpose in order to satisfy the interrogators, or you survived because of your skill as a painter?

A. Mr. President, regarding the torture inflicted upon me -- after they still couldn't extract the confession from me because I gave the same response every day, and because I did not know who was the leader or who introduced me into the CIA or KGB, they kept beating me up every day. And because they could not get my confession, they took me to the building which is now where you can purchase the ticket to visit the museum.  I was asked to sit there and they wrote a false confession and ordered me to sign.  I can not recall the content of that confession, it's been so many years now, and also because of the serious torture inflicted upon me my memory was not good. And at that time, if my memory was like I am now, I would not be able to paint the portrait and I would not survive because during that time if they thought somebody lied, especially lying to Angkar, then that one would be dead.

Q. During the time that they decided to use you as a painter to paint the portraits of the leaders, including Brother Number 1, Pol Pot, and other leaders including the Chinese leader as you stated, what happened during the times that you did the painting? For instance, were you detained again as a prisoner?
A. Mr. President, no.  During the times that I did the painting I worked every day regularly so it took me a long time to complete the four portraits.  That was after I had been tortured.

Q. Until now, can you try to remember or recall, besides the serious torture inflicted upon you with the present scars on your back until today, was the situation of receiving torture physically or emotionally, did it happen elsewhere?
A. Mr. President, if you talk about my memory, I am very forgetful now.  My memory is not as good as when I was young. For example, if I leave something somewhere, sometimes I forget where I left it.
MR. PRESIDENT Judges of the Bench, do you have any questions to be put to Uncle Bou Meng? Judge Cartwright, you take the floor.
JUDGE CARTWRIGHT: Thank you, Mr. President.

BY JUDGE CARTWRIGHT: Q. Mr. Bou Meng, you were at S-21 for a very long time and you have described your suffering and your experiences there; thank you for that.  But I have just one or two small questions to ask you. I want to know something about other prisoners whom you might have seen at S-21.  You have talked about the people who were in the same room shackled as you were.  You have spoken of seeing some pregnant women being kicked by female guards and told to walk more quickly. Did you see any foreigners at S-21, other than the large number of Vietnamese soldiers that you have described?

A. Your Honour, the inmates in the common room where I was detained, there were some foreigners.  I was not sure of their nationality, whether they were European, American or Australian. They were detained in the same common room as I was detained, and they had the same food ration as I received.
Q. Were you aware of any foreigners other than westerners or Vietnamese, such as Thais, people from Thailand?

A. Your Honour, I did not see any Thai citizens.  I only saw Vietnamese people and some foreigners.  They were tall, they had bright eyes, and sort of bronze hair.  Besides that I did not see any other nationality, including Thai.
Q. In addition to the Vietnamese soldiers, whom you saw, did you see any ordinary Vietnamese people; that is people who were not soldiers?

A. Your Honour, yes, I saw civilian people.  They were not soldiers.  And I saw these one civilian, as I said earlier, he said he knew he was a real artist, but when Duch ordered him to test, to make the mould and he couldn't do it, and, of course, at that time Angkar was not happy -- was not happy of anybody lying to Angkar.  And I don't have anything else to say regarding this question.
Q. The people whom you think might have been westerners, and the ordinary Vietnamese people whom you saw, were they all treated the same way as you were?

A. Your Honour, for the prisoners the treatment was not the same. For example, I, myself, I received very serious torture, so only I, myself, knew clearly about what happened to me, and I cannot say about what happened to other inmates.
Q. Did you see many children at S-21?

A. Your Honour, for children at S-21, I did not see any of them walking around or detained there.  I only saw those children in the photos, but I did not see them personally during the time of my detention.  This is my frank and honest response.
Q. Did you ever hear the sounds of children around S-21?

A. Your Honour, for the sound of children, I did not hear.  I only heard the screaming, asking for help of the adult people while I was in the common room.  And while I was in the individual room, individual cell, I also heard the screaming, but the screaming of the adult, not the children.
JUDGE CARTWRIGHT: Thank you very much, Mr. Bou Meng.
Mr. President, I have no further questions.
MR. PRESIDENT: Judges of the Bench, do you have any questions? Judge Lavergne, you take the floor.

BY JUDGE LAVERGNE: Q. Good afternoon, Mr. Bou Meng. I also have a few questions to ask you, to try to clarify what you already explained in detail to the Chamber earlier on today. I think I understood through what you said this morning, and through what I have read in your testimony, that your life was essentially impacted by many sacrifices, and by a life of obedience.  And you said this morning that you answered Prince Sihanouk's call in 1970 to free Cambodia, to liberate Cambodia. Is that so?

A. At that time, I heard the appeal of the Prince Sihanouk on the radio broadcast.  I was not sure which broadcast was it.  He appealed for his children to go to the maquis forest to struggle, so I decided to enter the maquis forest in 1971 with another friend from K25 office. So we went to the maquis forest to make some sketches and drawing of Marx and Lenin.  I was the one who drew the pictures of Marx and Lenin.  And those sketches were stencilled and distributed to various units in order to understand the supreme leaders of the Communists -- of the Communist country.  There were five of them all together: Karl Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zhedong.  So I even drew the sketches of these people on the cloth.

Q. So you worked there for the -- at the services of the Communist Party of Kampuchea's propaganda.  You were very respectful of what you were requested to do.  And then between the end of your activity with the propaganda services and your job at the Orussei Technical School, did you do anything else between; was there another episode in your career?
A. Your Honour, let me correct that.  It was called the Russei Keo Technical School, not Orussei Technical School.
Q. Did you go directly from the propaganda services to the Russei Keo Technical School or did you do anything in between?

A. In between that time -- in order to make it easier to understand, let me go back. First, I worked for the Ministry of Commerce, of State Commerce,  and Koy Thuon was the Prime Minister at the time.  I was requested to draw placards for a boat.  It was called Marinal Transport.  And I made some other placards and signs and boards for those boats and vehicles while I was there.
Q. Well, back then did you trust the CPK entirely?  Were you somebody who was very much obedient, who would follow what you were being told to do?

A. Your Honour, that was my specialty, the skills that I had.  I knew that the evacuation of people from Phnom Penh disappointed me because I struggled, I was so sick with malaria, and in the end I received such a suffering which is indescribable.  I felt so regretful for such inhumane acts of leadership which did not satisfy my willing -- my understanding.  I physically served them but emotionally I did not, although I wore black shirt, but my mind was not black.  I did what I was instructed, based on my skill. This is my response, Your Honour.
Q. Was there a specific moment where you might have entirely lost trust in the CPK?  Was there any moment when you said to yourself that what you might have believed in did not correspond to reality?
A. I don't really understand your question.  Can you rephrase your question again and please try to be simplified and make it short?
Q. Well, can we say that when you were working for the Russei Keo School and when you worked previously for the propaganda services, that you trusted the CPK and Angkar?

A. Your Honour, I carry out the task based on the assignment from my superior, including drawing the sketches of the machines or for the new parts of the machines.  Everything was done based on the instructions from the chairman of that technical school. This is my response, Your Honour.

Q. You explained that your superiors at the technical school had been arrested and that you yourself had been sent to be re-educated.  At that moment, was your trust in the CPK -- was it -- did it change or did you still have full trust in the CPK?

A. At that time, Your Honour, I lost my trust because my performance in carrying out the assignment was excellent, I did what I was asked, but I could not understand why I was transferred to be re-educated at the Ta Lei Co-operative.  I was disappointed and this is my frank response to you.  I no longer had my trust.

Q. But, however, despite the difficult conditions in which you were, you continued obeying and you continued following the orders that were given to you.  Is that why it was particularly difficult for you to understand why you had been arrested by security cadres of the CPK?

A. Your Honour, at that time, I myself and some other people totalling about 10, were transferred from the Russei Keo Technical School to Ta Lei Co-operative and I did not know the reason for the transfer. However, before the transfer we were instructed to make our biography, as I can recall, so I made my biography to the Angkar and about one or two months later I was transferred to the Ta Lei Co-operative amongst about 10 other people, including my wife. So we were tempered to do hard labour at the Ta Lei Co-operative. I did not know the reason for the transfer, Your Honour.
Q. Back then, had you heard of the security centres?  Were you aware, for example, of the existence of S-21 or of other security centres?

A. Your Honour, regarding the security offices or the prisons, I did not hear anything at all during the time, however, people kept disappearing.  Some probably were sent for re-education or sent for training here and there. I had heard a lot about transferring of people or relocation of people starting from 1976, and I was wondering how come, while people were still working good and they were transferred elsewhere?  Or whether they had any plan of transforming in the agriculture production?  I only had doubt in my mind, however, I just kept doing what I was given or instructed. So I typed some documents that I was asked to do and I drew sketches for the students to study.  I could not understand their thinking.  They were in a higher class and I thought I belonged to the lower class with limited technical capability.

Q. Can we say that you were not at all aware of having committed any kind of offence that you absolutely were not aware having betrayed the CPK, that you had absolutely no awareness of being part of a group of traitors?

A. When I came I knew that there was a Minister of Propaganda, Mr. Ho Nim, who called me to draw a portrait of the embarkment structure.  And at that time the current king was teaching students how to perform the ballet dancing and then he told me to help draw a portrait of his father.  And he called his father the normal, ordinary person's language and I was surprised but I did not ask further questions. Probably they saw the picture, the photo that the king asked me to draw; that's why they arrested me, or not.  I'm not quite sure.

Q. This morning, you also talked, at length, about the ill-treatment that was inflicted upon you.  You also talked about the physiological consequences thereof.  You also said to us that you still had scars.  I seem to have understood that these tortures led to other consequences, such as problems with your hearing.  Do you have other physiological conditions or difficulties that you may ascribe to being the consequences of that ill-treatment?

A. I was slapped and I was beaten on the head; all kinds of tortures had been inflicted on me.  So in short, I believe that because I was severely tortured, that I look older than my age and I lose all the teeth, and I can observe that Brother Chum Mey still have his teeth.  And also I have had problems with hearing and I think this is probably the consequence of the torture.  And I look much older than I am and if you compare to the age, I think I should have not been that old if I was not tortured.
Q. From what you can remember, do you have the feeling that the people interrogating you were enjoying themselves by making you suffer or seeing you suffer?

A. During the time when I was being interrogated some people ate the jackfruit and they threw the remaining -- the peel of the jackfruit onto my head and I could feel like then I was perceived as enemy and prisoner.  I could not do anything but to let them do whatever they wish and they did not show any mercy towards me as a human being.  And whenever I recall it, I cannot hold back my tears.  I was so disappointed that I had devoted myself for the work and after all I end up being tortured.  I wished I were killed by the malaria in the jungle, but I think my life was valuable that I could survive longer to be tortured again. That's all, Your Honour.

Q. When you were a painter at the workshop, do you now remember having been taken out of the workshop in relation to an incident? You were taken away from the workshop for about two weeks; do you remember that?  Do you remember then coming back to the workshop, having to say you were sorry, seek forgiveness?  Do you remember having been kicked?  Do you remember this episode or something like this, or do you not remember something like this happening to you?

A. I think, through my recollection, this incident might not have happened.  I knew that one of my neighbours in my next room was taken away -- no, the guy who worked next to my school -- the technical school of Russei Keo.  A couple were taken or arrested. I don't know whether two of them or one of them was arrested but they both disappeared.  Then it came my turn who were transferred to Ta Lei Co-operative and that's what I have seen and known and I think my memory is not that good.  Maybe I have not fully recollected all the episodes, and accept my apologies for not being able to recall everything.  That's all.

Q. Mr. Bou Meng, sorry, I was referring to the period when you were working in the workshop at S-21.  You were at the workshop in S-21.  During that period when you were working at S-21 workshop, where you were working with Vann Nath and other artists; during that period, was there an episode the result of which was that you had to go and say sorry; that you had to go and apologize?
A. I don't know whether the apologies were made to my colleagues or to the guards.  I'm not quite sure I understand the question.

Q. Were you forced to apologize to your colleagues in the workshop at S-21 or to other people?  Were you, one day, shackled or tied up and led to go and offer apologies to either your colleagues or somebody else in the workshop?

A. I cannot recall or maybe I forgot, because I never offered my apologies to anyone, even to my colleagues.  It is based on my recollection but of course I would have forgotten.  As the Khmer proverb says, "The elephants with four legs would have collapsed sometime and the wise person would forget anyway."

Q. Thank you, Mr. Bou Meng, for these responses.  I have one very last question for you. This morning you told us that the accused had talked about fertilizer, saying that humans could be fertilizer in the paddy fields.  Could you explain to us the meaning of this term, please?

A.  The statement is based on the accused Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch.  He said that if I could not resemble the portrait of Pol Pot then I would be used as the human fertilizer. And I didn't understand whether I would be used to produce fertilizer or would I be used as the fertilizer myself for the rice field.  That's what he asked me and I found it difficult to respond to him also at that moment.
Q. Thank you very much, Mr. Bou Meng.
JUDGE LAVERGNE: I have no further questions, Mr. President.
MR. PRESIDENT: Next we would like to give the opportunity to the prosecutors to put questions to Uncle Bou Meng, the survivor of S-21. The floor is yours.
MR. SENG BUNKHEANG: Thank you, Mr. President.
QUESTIONING BY THE CO-PROSECUTORS BY MR. SENG BUNKHEANG: Q. Good afternoon, Uncle Bou Meng. I have a few questions to be put to you.  Regarding the food ration, was it enough?

A. The food ration, during the time when I was detained, was inadequate.  But when people were looking for someone who could paint and when I came out to work as the painter with Vann Nath, with Kong, with Pha Tha Chan and Bech, the food was adequate. But it was inadequate when I was still in the prison. And there would be other documents to support my arguments about this condition.  You may refer to it.  Thank you.
Q. Thank you. When you were being detained at S-21 in the common room and in the individual cell, you said that the food ration was inadequate.  How could you fulfil your hunger?

A. There was no substitute.  I was so hungry.  When I saw the lizard crawling on the ceiling I would wish that it dropped down so that I could grab it and eat to fulfil my hunger.  I told myself that I did not know what kind of bad deeds I committed previously that I would be treated like this without enough food, without enough water, and I was questioning myself and I was asking myself what kind of mistakes I had committed that I would end up being here. And I was thinking of karma and I did not even recall any mistakes.  But then Angkar would say that Angkar had multiple eyes like the pineapple so they never made any wrong arrests.
Q. Thank you. Have you ever seen or known that at S-21 the practice of blood drawing took place -- I mean blood drawing from detainees?

A. I have no idea of that practice because when it comes to tortures, as I told you, for me I know it for sure,I was being tortured, how I was being tortured.  But for the other people, whether their blood were being drawn or were they inflicted other kinds of tortures, it was far beyond my knowledge because it was their own business.  That's all.
THE INTERPRETER: The Co-Prosecutor's mic is not activated.

BY MR. SENG BUNKHEANG: Q. You said you were tortured and you were beaten until you were bleeding and that one day you were sent to be poured with salt water.  Who actually poured such water, salty water, on you?

A. When I was called to be treated upstairs when I was detained, I was called so that my wound would be treated on the second floor.  That person was a medic who would come to distribute medicines to sick detainees and they would give us some kind of rabbit pellet medications.  I could not even swallow that kind of medication and they would beat me and scolded me for not being able to just swallow such a small piece of rabbit pellet medication.
Q. Thank you. When they were searching for a painter at that time you were being taken to see Duch.  When you saw him were you happy or were you terrified?

A. At that time I was so happy because I would be able to eat enough food and I told myself that it would be the moment that I could be relieved from those kind of hell.  And then I was determined that I would do my best to devote myself to work with the painting, but I was at the beginning tested.  And I would like to go back a little bit how I was tested. Because they wanted to know whether I was really a painter, they gave me a paper and a pencil so that I could draw.  I think that person was smart.  Mr. Kaing Guek Eav is very smart.  His education is much higher than me, so far as I know, and I know for sure that he is smart and intelligent because he was the first-class student in mathematics.  So for me, I am just a very little and ordinary person.  I only know how to draw; that's all.
Q. Thank you.  During the time when you were asked to paint portraits did you see any senior leaders of the Democratic Kampuchea regime pay a visit to S-21?

A. I used to see them but I don't remember their names.  I saw a well-built and tall guy, taller than him.  A few people paid a visit to the workshop.  They went there briefly and then they left when I was still painting the portrait of Pol Pot.
THE INTERPRETER: The Co-Prosecutor's mic is not activated.

BY MR. SENG BUNKHEANG: Q. You said you have seen the Vietnamese soldiers were being walked into the compound and you saw it through the window.  How did you identify them as the Vietnamese soldiers?  Were they brought in with uniforms, or what?

A. I could tell that they were Vietnamese soldiers because their hats were very identical and their uniforms were different from the black uniform worn by the Khmer Rouge soldiers, because the Vietnamese soldiers would wear other like a green kind of uniform.
Q. Thank you. Now I would like to move back a little bit to the time, the episode when the accused would like to test your painting ability.  How could he test you?

A. As I already mentioned, I would like now to add further for full details I may have not fully told the Court yet.  He gave me a piece of paper to just make a few sketches and I -- when I was in the jungle I used to drawing pictures, and at the technical school I was used to drawing and then he noticed that I could be a good painter and he asked me what kind of equipment or tools that I would need to make sure I could paint on a big portrait; on a big board, for example, and he would go and find those tools for me.

So he asked his subordinates to look for the tools.  At that time in Phnom Penh it would not be difficult to find those materials because many things were left, including the big sheet of paper. The roll of those paper could be easily taken, and then I took a long piece of paper about one metre and a half long and one metre wide so that I could really paint the portrait of Pol Pot on it. I did not see Pol Pot or his picture before.  I was given a small photo of him and then the photo was put in a photo frame, and then there was a label underneath.  It tells us about the photo shop in China.
Q. Thank you.  Could you please tell us more about when you were being sent to S 21?  Have you ever thought that at that moment your life would be ended although you have not made any mistakes?

A. I did not think about this because for a frank, honest person like me I did not know that I would be taken there to be killed, because I thought that when I could be used to work then I knew that I could survive longer because I was very obedient to their orders, assignments.  I could do whatever they wished me to do and I could paint the four portraits as requested and ordered. And the last portrait was missing already and I am sorry that that painting is lost because the international community had been asking for such a portrait but it is gone already, and we have a lot of people from other countries who paid a visit to Tuol Sleng and they asked me about that.
Q. Thank you very much.
MR. SENG BUNKHEANG: Mr. President, I have no further questions.  I hope my colleague would like to make some further questions.
MR. PRESIDENT: The floor is yours, the Co-Prosecutor.

MR. PETIT: Thank you, Mr. President.  I don't have any further questions for the witness but with your permission I'd like to thank him for his testimony today on behalf of the Co-Prosecutors.  Thank you.

MR. PRESIDENT: Next we would like to give the floor to the civil party lawyers and, according to the observation we obtained yesterday, the civil party lawyers whose clients are to be testifying today would get the most time.  I don't know whether they still maintain the position or would they want to change?  Then they could tell the Chamber to know also.
MS. STUDZINSKY: Thank you, Mr. President. We would like to continue with the same procedure the whole time this week and next week, as long as we are here as civil parties. Thank you.
MR. PRESIDENT: Now you take the floor.
MR. KONG PISEY: Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the opportunity to put questions to the survivor of the regime, Your Honours.

QUESTIONING BY CIVIL PARTY COUNSEL BY MR. KONG PISEY: Q. Good afternoon, Uncle Bou Meng.  My first question is the follow-up question concerning the earlobes, your earlobes.  You said that you received tortures onto the earlobes -- no, the ears as a whole, and you said you had a hearing problem. I would like to ask whether now you can listen to people and your ears are okay, or you need a hearing aid to assist you with the hearing?

A. The Court officials have helped me and taken me to the hospital specializing in hearing and then they offered me a hearing aid.  I now can hear better.  If I use my bare ears to listen to people talking I would not be able to listen or to understand their conversation unless I paid very close attention, or move very close to them.  So if I could put number one to 10, I could hear about 30 percent.  I mean three out of 10 because of my impairment.  And I think my eyesight were not good.  My teeth, also, are not good.

Of course, when people get old, this kind of thing will get old as well, but you know, like, Chum Mey is still young, and I am older than my age because I had been tortured, otherwise I would be ok now.  And my ears would have not been that bad.  So here -- I can sit here, I cannot even listen to you if you talked over there.
Q.   Thank you.  My next question. I want to know about your suffering.  How long had you endured this suffering or you still feel the suffering at the present time?
A. Are you talking about the suffering, the physical suffering, in addition to the emotional suffering?
Q. Thank you.  I meant regarding your earache.  So you suffered when they tortured you.  Are your ears in a better condition now?
A. They are fully recovered, however, I have had hard hearing. So that's why I need the hearing aid so that I could hear properly.  Without the hearing aid, I could hardly hear anything. That's all.

Q. Thank you.  Regarding the electrocution, as you stated that they used the wall power outlet to electrocute you.  You said you were electrocuted near your genitals.  How far was the spot where it was electrocuted?
A. It was to the inner side of my thigh.  So once I was electrocuted, I fell unconscious immediately, and when I gained my consciousness, the water was everywhere on my face.
Q. Thank you.  Did they place the wire on your pants or on your flesh directly?

A.  It was placed on my shorts, however, there was a machine that I think it controlled the voltage, and that machine hooked into the power outlet from the wall.  So I think they could increase the voltage from that machine. But you could easily understand that if the voltage was not strong enough, then I would not fall unconscious.  That's it.
Q. Thank you.  You already informed the Chamber that once you were electrocuted, you fell unconscious straight away.  And for how long did you become unconscious?
A. If you are unconscious, it's like you were sleeping.  You would not know how long you fell unconscious.
Q. On another matter, did you go and make consultation with the psychological support?

A. Previously, I have had consultation with a psychological support.  I was assisted with some tablets so that I would not have insomnia, and I take two types of tablets on a daily basis. But when I come to the Court and speak in this current condition, I can't not even eat my lunch today because I was overwhelmed and I did not feel like eating anything.

Q. Thank you.  Now, on the matter of interrogation, you stated to the Chamber that there were five interrogators: Hor, Chan, Tith, Peng and Kuy, but you haven't clearly verified that for each interrogation, were the five present and beating you up or were you interrogated and tortured by only one interrogator at a time?

A.   They were there during the interrogation, but only one person beat me at a time and then they took turns.  First Chan beat me up.  He asked me to count the number of lashes.  When I counted up to 10 I told him, and he said, "It's not yet 10, I only hit you once".  And I can remember his word.  I remember his words, I remember his face. I can always remember his face, the person who mistreated me.  I remember both, those who did good thing and who did bad things to me.
Q. Thank you.  The question is, on one day during the interrogation, were the five interrogators beat you up on that same day or only they came on another day?

A. That group of interrogators, the five of them, they took turns to beat me up until all the five became exhausted or when the time was up.  For example, from 7 a.m. until about 11 or 12, then they rested.  I saw all of them.
Q. So from what I can understand, you confirmed that in -- for each date, the five of them present at the same time.  Is that true?
A. That is correct.

Q. My next question.  You stated to the Chamber that when they water-hosed you in the common room, so all the inmates had to take off their clothes, and later on they had to dry the floor with their shorts. The question is, did the guards order the prisoners to take off their shorts or the prisoners took off their shorts by themselves?

A. I am not sure on this point.  My memory is not clear.  I can remember that all of us, 30 or 40 of us, were all naked, and I even remember one phrase.  The person was about 15 or 16 years old.  He said, "You, you have a small build but with big genital".  That's what he said.  "And this guy, you're big, but your penis is tiny".  That's what he said.  So they just make a joke out of us being naked.  And I still can remember what was said, but I can not say for sure whether we took off the pants by ourselves or they ordered us to take the pants off.  I'm not sure because probably they ordered us to take the pants off so they can joke about our genitals.
Q. Thank you. So for every time you were water-hosed, were all of you had to be naked?

A. Yes, we all had to be naked.  I looked around.  Nobody had underwear or pants on them.  People were like animals from hell, all naked.  Because they treated us as enemies, as traitors, they water-hosed us from outside so the water was everywhere in the common room.  So then we tried to dry the floor with our pants until the floor was completely dry.  Then we could lie down on the floor again.

And we all of us had skin rashes and a lot of skin lice.  It was so itchy everywhere.  I think it was Nhem En (phonetic) who wanted to find a cure, a treatment for skin rash and itch, and after that it was better.  Let me say, only the guards who could able to find that traditional medicines to help us with the itches and the skin rash.
Q. So when you were water-hosed, were you provided any soap?

A. No, there was no soap or nothing to scrub our body.  We were washed like pigs were washed.  Because I used to raise pigs, when I washed my pigs, then I water-hosed my pigs and I used my hands to clean my pigs.  But I was even lower than my pigs or my dog because no soap was used, no scarf was used to change or dry my body.
Q. Thank you. Regarding the common room, did you ever see the prisoners who were taken out and when they returned, did you see any wound or marks on their bodies?

A. It seems that I did not see such incidents.  I was not sure. Because maybe they were in the same way like I was there, it means after the interrogation and the torture, they would be taken to the individual cells so that those in the common room would not know that we were being tortured.

It was common when we still had full strengths, but once we became weak they would start to peel our skin.  That expression means they would start to interrogate and torture us.

However, when we left Tuol Sleng, we stayed in a house until it was dusk, then we continued our journey toward the direction of Chamkar Duong.  I still cannot recall the number of the guards. A. From my recollection, although I must admit I am forgetful, it was common for the vehicle coming in and going out. A. While I was sleeping in Building C on the third floor in the common room, at night I heard the screaming.  I think probably the screaming was a result of the person being interrogated and tortured. To me it seems the screaming was echoing and coming from everywhere at the surrounding vicinity of Tuol Sleng prison, probably because during that time those houses around Tuol Sleng were used as the interrogation houses. But now all those houses are gone, even the house where I was interrogated behind Building A outside the compound also disappears now.  I could not recognize it any more.  That's all.
MS. TY SRINNA: I have no more questions for you and thank you for answering the questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

I saw them for only a short period of time and then they disappeared.  They were there for probably two weeks being detained on that floor of Building C. A. A. I did not see any guards who were 15 or under, unless I was mistaken.  Usually they were 15 or above.  That was through my observation at the time.  That's all.

Q. Thank you.  And I have two personal questions for you now. Do you feel bad about having signed the confession that you had to sign because of duress, whereas you knew that this confession, the content of it, was false?

A. Ms. Lawyer, at that time my emotion was mixed.  I was fearful, worried; I could not describe the emotion.  So I just did what I was ordered to do because there was absolutely no reason for them to suspect me to be a CIA or KGB agent, and I was tortured enough. Some prisoners, when they were tortured and interrogated, they confessed and finally they were taken and smashed, but for me I was different.  Of course physically I signed the confession but inside my heart I of course did not approve the confession.

Q. I'm sure nobody would challenge that, sir. Another question.  Within the workshop amongst the sculptors, painters, artists would you amongst yourselves talk at all about the tortures that you had been subjected to and the confessions that you were forced to sign?  Did you talk about these things amongst yourselves within the workshop?

A. Ms. Lawyer, I never talked about that.  The reason is because I was scared.  Usually there were two or three prison guards who were there constantly and the door was locked both inside and outside, so if we whispered or chit-chatted on this thing then it's so risky.
Q. One last question.  Today how do you feel about the fact that you are a survivor?

A. Ms. Lawyer, I am so delighted that now my chest seems to be lighter.  All my statements to the Judges and to the lawyers and the rest, I felt much better now and I believed through peace and justice would be done for those 1.8 or two million people who lost their lives during that regime, and I myself too, I was a victim and the scope of suffering was incalculable.  I was almost killed.  My back was wounded severely and still I could carry out my profession, painting the portraits to satisfy the chief of the prison.

But it was shameful that I could not save the life of my wife. I'm not sure if it was my mistake or not and I really want to ask the accused where was my wife killed.  If I know where it is then I would go there in order to pray for her soul, and that I am now being testified before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Court of Cambodia, only the spirit of the earth would know where the soul has gone to or where the dead bodies were buried.  So only the spirits of the wind, of the water, of the earth would know. And for those who killed the people, they could tell the truth or they could lie, but only the spirits of the earth, the wind and the water know where my wife died, so that I could pray for her soul.  That is all.
MS. JACQUIN: Thank you, Mr. Bou Meng.

Mr. President, on behalf of all the civil party groups, we have a request to put to you.  We would like to ask for 10 extra minutes.  There are seven lawyers present here representing 90 victims.  All of these victims are important.  If we are to share out this time it would amount to one half-minute per victim, but we have legitimate questions to put. Sir, you have been showing tolerance in interpreting the time allowance and we are grateful for this.  However, we have all sorts of time management problems.  If you could assure us that we have could have, if need be, an extra 10 minutes, this would make it possible for us to work amongst ourselves more harmoniously. Thank you.
MS. CANIZARES: Mr. President, if extra time were to be granted to the representatives of the civil parties would it be possible to have extra time, if necessary, for the defence to ask questions?

MR. PRESIDENT: In order not to complicate the matter regarding the request by both sides and the civil party lawyers use the time as allocated by the Chamber, however, the Chamber will not allow extra time and the time has run out already. Now I would give the opportunity to the survivor, Bou Meng.
Uncle Bou Meng, do you have any questions that you would like to ask the accused at the moment?

MR. BOU MENG: Mr. President, I would like to ask him where did he smash my wife; whether it was at Tuol Sleng or Choeung Ek or at another location. Did you have the authority to relocate her or to smash her?  It has been so many years already.  I went to her native village in Tboung Khmum district in Kampong Cham province.   I went to ask her elder sibling whether my wife has ever returned to the village and the response was no.  So I presumed that she was killed while she was detained. And my question is just to tell me, just to tell me where she was killed or smashed.  Then I would go to that location and just to get the soil from that location to pray for her soul because there was not her document at the S-21 Office.  I used to have some documents as well, but some of the documents I have I have lost or are missing.  And I want the matter to be done legally.
MR. PRESIDENT: Can you verify that your wife, who was detained at S-21 with you, her name was Ma Yoeun alias Thy.  Is that correct?
MR. BOU MENG: That is correct, Mr. President.

MR. PRESIDENT: Mr. Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, the first question is, do you know Ma Yoeun alias Thy?  If you know her, could you answer to his question that when you were the chairman of S-21 and that his wife was taken away to be executed, where was she killed?  In Phnom Penh or at Choeung Ek?

THE ACCUSED: Mr. President, thank you, Mr. President for giving me the opportunity to respond to the question. Mr. Meng, especially for you I have been moved.  We have lived together and you were healthy and I was shocked to see you on the 28th of February 2008 before the Co-Investigating Judges.  I would like to respond to your desire, but it was beyond my capacity because this work done by my subordinates, but I would like to presume that your wife might have been killed at Boeng Choeung Ek. Meanwhile, to be sure, I would like to ask you to please ask Comrade Huy who may be able to tell you further detail about the fate of your wife.  Please accept my highest assurance of my regards and respects towards the soul of your wife.  That's all.

MR. PRESIDENT: The accused, please control your emotion and re-compose because the moment is important that it takes time to listen to the testimony of the survivors who have survived the regime and to recall the past.

So, Uncle Bou Meng, I hope you have already been told by the accused about the fate of your wife because his conclusion is that she could have been killed at Boeng Choeung Ek, especially when it comes to the time when she was sent in during the year of 1977.

At the beginning, the killing would take place only at the premises of Tuol Sleng compound and later on, after 1977 to '78, then the execution sites had been shifted to Choeung Ek.  So it could be possible that the fate of your wife would be ended there at Choeung Ek or she would be killed there. And to get further information, it is rather difficult because the people who perished amounted to more than 12,000, and those more than 12,000 were registered and there were still numbers of detainees who are still unaccounted for.  At the beginning, we know that there would have been 12,300 or something detainees, but after inspecting the list and compared with other lists, then we could see more numbers, different numbers of the people killed during that time.  But I think the actual number of people who would have been killed would be even higher if all documents could be supported.

Next, the accused, besides your response to Uncle Bou Meng, one of the survivors who asked you about the fate of his wife, the Chamber would like to also know whether the accused would like to make any comments or observations, testimony, concerning the remarks or testimony of Uncle Bou Meng.  So you are now given the opportunity to do so if you would wish.

THE ACCUSED: Mr. President, first, I would like to confirm to Mr. Bou Meng and the other victims.  He keep asking what kind of mistakes he had committed; what kind of mistake his wife committed that led to their arrest.

Frankly, during that time, I already -- I think yesterday I told Brother Mey already -- anyone who opposed them would be singled out as the CIA, the KGB, or the expansionist, so on and so forth. So I would like just to repeat it and to be more precise. I would like to state that the Cultural Revolution of China would be seen as the reference.  Although Pol Pot did not follow exactly that kind of philosophy, he used his own improvised theory, so he would implicate anyone as an enemy. And I told Brother Mey already about the CIA.  He asked me whether CIA or KGB agents have already been smashed and I told him that anyone who opposes the Pol Pot were those who have defeated the Pol Pot regime.

And, after all, the fascist political politics ended on January 1979, so the reason why people were implicated or opponents, this lead to the destruction of the whole regime, and I would like to emphasize again that this crime is so severe, although it was committed by the upper echelon.  But members of the Party were part of the process all across the country, because more than one million people were executed, and emotionally I am responsible for all the crimes, although they were committed by the senior people.

I am responsible in the eyes of the law, and I now would like to be tried by the ECCC alone, and I don't want my subordinates to be on trial too.  And I have already dedicated -- I have already prayed for the souls of the dead people to rest in peace.  I'm not talking here to evade the responsibility of my crimes but I want to reveal my frankness.  That's all.

MR. PRESIDENT: Next we would like to give the floor to the defence counsel to have the opportunity to put questions to Uncle Bou Meng, one of the survivors of S-21. The floor is yours, if you would wish to do so.
MR. KAR SAVUTH: Thank you, Mr. President.  Your Honours, my questions here are first I would like Mr. Bou Meng to clarify on some points because I have been ambivalent regarding those points.

Because this morning, before we adjourned for lunch, you said that there were full -- everyone was quiet and people could not even whisper to one another.  So I think your testimony in the morning seems to be contradictory to your testimony in the afternoon.  Could you please repeat or confirm your both testimonies?

A. I said it was very quiet because the doors were all shut when I left, evacuated.  I did not have a chance to look inside the rooms because I were at -- I was walked away at gunpoint and I was not brave enough to even look back to see how many people would be in the room.  That's why I said it was quiet. And I think regarding the screams, the cries, I knew that my ears were too good to listen to those noises because I was also a very good artist.  Having heard the sound, I could even draft or sketch a kind of portrait, so I think I was not mistaken to hear those screams during the time when I was detained.

Q. Thank you.  Could you please emphasize again: you said that before the morning break, you said that the building was full of people.  And you said that the building was full of detainees but it was so quiet because people could not even whisper into the ears of the neighbours.  But how could you say that you heard the screams, the cries that people cried for help?  I don't want you to tell us about the time when you were about to leave S-21.

A. I would like to state that when I was inside the detention centre, around the compound there were a lot of interrogating houses.  And inside the room, of course, you could not hear anyone scream or cry because we would be punished.  But I'm talking about the people who would be taken away to be interrogated inside those houses, and we could hear from the houses.  I'm not here to talk and to implicate anyone.  I'm talking here, right before the iron genie, and if I talked something, exaggerating anything, then I would be run over by a bus.

Q. Thank you.  I would like you to only confirm.  Number two, I would like your confirmation also.  You said the subordinates of Duch, who treated the Vietnamese prisoner who did not keep his promise that he was a sculptor, and that you said Duch ordered his subordinate to kick or to torture him but later on you said that Duch was not there when his subordinates tortured him.  So could you please tell us whether Duch was there when the torture took place?

A. Mr. Lawyer, I said, my memory is not good.  And I said clearly that it is because I have had been severely tortured, and I don't want to evade any responses but if I made any mistake in my testimony it is resulted from the very poor memory of mine; resulted, of course, from such torture.  So I think my memory is now about to 20 percent good, compared to the 100 percent I           10   could have had previously.

BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Uncle Meng, could you please control your emotion?  I know that you have been bombarded with questions, and you have been answering to those questions for almost the whole day already. We would like you to please recompose yourself.

And the question is implied as, have you heard that Duch ordered his subordinates to beat the Vietnamese detainee?  And some said that he was the Khmer Krom national who pretended to be a good sculptor.  So the question is whether Duch did order such torture or punishment to be inflicted on that person, or Duch subordinates initiated such ideas of punishment spontaneously, because there was a torture inflicted on that person; so whether it was ordered or not ordered by Duch.  Could you please verify?

A. I did not see or hear it.  That's why I cannot presume that he ordered his subordinates to do that.  Or maybe his subordinates just did that by themselves.  I can say that without any order from their subordinates I don't even think that their subordinates could inflict any kind of tortures on them - on anyone.  So I could see that, after their work, they covered -- you know, like, when they treated their staff, they would cover the blankets all over their body and walk them away because they were afraid to let us know.  I don't know, but I think it is just my presumption.

Q. I think you probably be confused.  You are the survivor of that regime and that it is, of course, in your testimony reflecting your emotion and your story and how you have suffered and, also, you have told us about your wife's story. But now we have another matter that we would like to ask about your testimony concerning the accused because a witness is not supposed to give a kind of presumption because it is not really appropriate.  Because in the name of the witness, if the question is put to you whether you say that you saw it or you didn't see it, you should just say "yes" or "no" and please try to avoid giving your presumption or your -- some kind of conclusion because the term "conclusion" is not aimed to be coming from the witness.
A. At that time, I'm not sure so I would like to say that I don't know, but I saw the person was being kicked and beat up.  I don't know who ordered them to do so.  That's all.
MR. PRESIDENT: Could the lawyer put further questions?

BY MR. KAR SAVUTH: Q. Thank you, Mr. Bou Meng. The third question.  When you were arrested all together with your wife from the cooperative to be put at wooden shed right in front of the prison, were you shackled by your ankles?

A. At that time, they treated me better because they used the very cold method because there were no cuffs, no chain, no shackles.  They mislead me. They lied to me because they did not actually take me to the Fine Arts School.  It was the fine arts school of Tuol Sleng prison, so they cheated on me.  I could just easily be convinced to climb onto the truck and then be taken away and then they did not take me to the Fine Arts School. Instead, we were taken to the prison.

Q. Thank you.  The reason I asked you that question to confirm your statement because your statement before the Co-Prosecutor on the 29 of August 2006 in ERN-00145528, you said you were handcuffed and shackles; both your wife and you.  And this morning, you said that only your hands were cuffed and that your legs were free from being shackled. And as you said, you are old and you had been tortured; your memory deteriorating.  I think everyone can forget except the God who is able to remember everything.  Human being will be forgetful anyway.  Thank you. Question number four.  Your statement before the Co-Prosecutors -- and you said later, "I learned that I was taken -- prisoners were taken to be executed at Choeung Ek, days and nights".  Do you maintain that your statement is still confirmed?
A. Mr. Lawyer, I did say that there were trucks which brought people in and out, but I did not say that they would be taken away to be killed.  I didn't say that.
MR. HONG KIMSUON: Could you please repeat the ERN number?
MR. KAR SAVUTH: ERN 00145533, the fourth line from down up. BY MR. KAR SAVUTH:

Q. "And later on, I learned that they were carried or taken to be executed at Choeung Ek and the truck would take them days and nights." That's why I am asking whether you maintain your statement or would you like to change it because some witnesses said that they only saw the prisoner being carried away by trucks at night, not during the daytimes.  Thank you.

A. When I was detained in Building C, I heard the sound of the trucks during the nights and days.  I don't know whatever other people would testify, but this is what I have heard because there were trucks coming in and going out.  I don't know where people would be taken to, but I have heard the noises.  I did not see the trucks. I think the trucks would have been parked right in front of the entrance to the east or maybe to the west; let me recall it. I had been working at the premises for some time.  I still cannot remember whether Tuol Sleng entrance would be to the east or to the west, but I think the trucks would be parking somewhere near the entrance when I was walked into the premises during the first time when we were approaching the location and, again, I did not -- or I don't know whether people would be taken away to be executed.
Q. Thank you.  Question number five. When leaving S-21, did you go with Vann Nath and Chum Mey or did you go with other people?  Could you please recall the people?

A. We left with the survivors who were either sculptor, painter, artist. I paint a black and white portrait while Nath paints coloured, and we have other artists who also left at that time -- Pha Tha Chan, Oeng Bech -- so altogether about more than 10 people who would be leaving the location but many of whom have died already, including Grandfather Thuon. So I, of course, left with several other people and when we reached the area near Ang Snuol we departed, were separated because we heard the sound of the trucks of the United Front army and then there were exchanges of fire between the soldiers, and then we were scattered and I walked across National Road Number 4.

Q. Thank you.  I just want to know when you left, you left along with Chum Mey and Vann Nath. And my next question is I just want the confirmation.  This morning you said when you fled S-21, one time you said it was at 6 p.m. and the other time you said at 9 a.m.  And when Ty Srinna asked you, you said you went at about 6 or 7 p.m.  So can you tell me exactly what time you left S-21?

A. Mr. Defence Counsel, I left Tuol Sleng prison at 9 o'clock. We left the painting workshop and we were ordered to walk straight in one line.  We were so fearful, so we walked in one line and when we reached a house we stopped and stayed there for quite a while.  I cannot recall the location.  Maybe it's the Beehive radio station.

Q. I just want to know the time.  So you say now it's at 9 o'clock in the morning. And my seventh question, which is the last question; when you were painting the portrait did you ever see Khieu Samphan coming to visit?

A. Mr. Defence Counsel, I never saw Khieu Samphan come in.  All those senior peoples, I never saw them.  Even Pol Pot, I only saw his photo; I never saw him in person.  Sometimes people ask whether I saw Pol Pot personally because I painted his portrait. In fact I never saw him in person.  I also had my portrait painted for a Chinese shop in Shanghai.
Q. Thank you.  So when you painted the portrait at the technical school did Khieu Samphan ever go there?

A. Mr. Defence Counsel, I can recall when you ask me that question because I worked there.  At that time I was preparing the numbers of the pages and Mr. Khieu Samphan asked me, "Do you have a telephone?" and then I told him and I pointed -- oh, the telephone was at the corner, because I didn't know that he was Khieu Samphan.  But when he left, my work colleague told me that, "That was Khieu Samphan," and I felt rather surprised.  So now I can recall.
Q. Thank you.
MR. KAR SAVUTH: I have no questions, Mr. President.
MR. PRESIDENT: The international defence counsel, if you have questions for Bou Meng the floor is yours.
MS. CANIZARES: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

Judge Lavergne brought up earlier on the fact that when you were working in the CPK propaganda service, which was at the Russei Keo, you were somebody who was very obedient.  And if I've understood correctly, you indicated that you followed along physically but not emotionally.  Could you please develop this assertion, this idea?

A. Ms. Defence Counsel, the work that was assigned to me by Hak to draw sketches of the machines, of the half a machine or of the new spare parts, or the sketches of vehicle machines, all types of machinery, I drew all those sketches to include in the book for the students to study at that time. My recollection in making that document for those technical school participants, that was what I did.  Of course I obeyed the order from the upper echelon and my superior, Hak, assigned me to make or compile those documents.  That is all my answer.

Q. Could you please tell us why emotionally you said that you didn't follow along?  I understood that you were just obeying to an order, so therefore of course you were obeying physically, we could say, but why do you state that you did not obey emotionally?

A. On this matter let me tell you, Ms. Defence Counsel, physically I followed the assignment and, as my skill was in drawing sketches, I just did it.  But in my mind I did not have 100 percent confidence and trust in the leadership, and the reason?  Because I saw people being evacuated from the city, and the city became like a ghost city.  And this is my response to you.
Q. This will be my last question.  So why, therefore, did you continue obeying physically?

A. Ms. Defence Counsel, regarding my assignment as a painter or a sketch drawer, I had to do it.  I had to carry out my task and even if I completed and carried out my task 100 percent, I was still being transferred. So I was transferred to the Ta Lei Co-operative and that act made me lost my trust in that regime.
Q. Given the answer, would you please give me the leave for another question?  Therefore, could I understand that it was because you were afraid that you continued obeying physically?
A. I don't really understand your question.  Can you ask the question again?

Q. You are telling us that if you did not follow the orders 100 percent that were given to you that you could be transferred.  So therefore can I conclude from this answer that it was fear that made you follow 100 percent the orders that were given to you?
A. In fact, that was the case.

MR. PRESIDENT: The hearing of the testimony of the survivor, Bou Meng, that has been for the whole day has now come to an end.
