QUESTIONING BY DEFENCE COUNSEL BY MR. KAR SAVUTH: Q. Mr. Prak Khan, can you please confirm for us to be sure, because before the Co-Prosecutor under document 00145597 on page 14, down from the below page to the upper page -- you said yesterday that you left S-21 on the 7th of January 1979 at about 9 to 10 a.m.  So you made different statement before the Co-Prosecutor.  So which statement do you think is correct?
A. The statement, as you said, that I left on the 5th of January was not correct because I left on the 7th of January 1979.

Q. Thank you.  So you stated clear that the statement that you said you left on the 5th of January 1979, before the Co-Prosecutor, is not correct.  But here we got your thumbprint on that piece of document.  You stated that you left S-21 on the 5th of January 1979 on that document.  So the reason I ask you to confirm is because I want to know whether you stand by the recent statement or by the previous statement given to the Co-Prosecutors. Question number two.  Do you know two medics, Lorn and Khim?
A. I don't know their names but please tell me in which unit these people would have worked in?
Q. The question is that whether you know these two medics, Lorn and Khim at S-21.
A. I don't know them.
Q. Thank you.  Have you known Lorn, the chief of the medics -- female medic?
A. I only know Try, who was the chief of the medics at S-21.  I don't know other people who were also medics.

Q. You stated that at night you were put to guard outside and you saw Pon, Bou and other interrogators interrogating a female detainee, and that you saw Dek Bou carried out tortures against that detainee.  Is that correct?
A. Yes, that is.
Q. Thanks.  You said that you did not see Duch, the accused, use torture against that detainee.  Is that correct?
A. That's correct.
Q. You also indicated that since you worked at S-21 you never saw the accused torture any detainee.  Is that correct?
A. That is correct.

Q. Thank you.  So your statement with ERN 00146599 D19/8, in that statement it is contradictory to what you state here in the Court.  So do you stand by your current statement in the Court or you stand by the statement you made in that document?  To be clear, you said that you saw the accused use torture against any detainee, but here you said you have never seen the accused torture any detainee.  So which statement you stand by?  Do you stand by the statement before this Court now or the previous one?
A. I saw him taking part in the process but I am not sure whether he tortured the detainee, but I will stand by the current statement in this hearing instead.
Q. Thank you.  At S-21 do you know Him Huy, and how well do you know him?
A. I know him very well.
Q. Thank you.  You said you know Him Huy very well.  So after you left S-21 on the 7th of January 1979 did Him Huy leave the S-21 along with you?
A. When I left S-21 at that time I did not see him.  I only met him at Prey Sar, the rice fields.
Q. Thank you.
MR. KAR SAVUTH: Thank you, Mr. President.  I have no further questions now, and I would like my colleague to put some further questions to the witness.
MR. PRESIDENT: Mr. François Roux, you take the floor.
MR. ROUX: Thank you, Mr. President.

BY MR. ROUX: Q. Good afternoon, Mr. Prak Khan.  We met during the re-enactment and during the confrontation at Tuol Sleng.  And therefore I am Mr. Roux.  But before I release you from this lengthy hearing I do have a few questions to put to you and I would like to thank you in advance for answering these and for helping us to ascertain the truth. The Co-Prosecutor this morning asked you why you had revealed many things in the press and in films over the past years and you answered that you wanted to say the truth.  So my first question: you said yesterday that you knew that Nam Mon had come to testify before the ECCC before you.  How did you get to know this?
A. I learned of this through watching her testimony on TV.
Q. Thank you.  So you saw Nam Mon testify on television.  Is that so?
A. That is correct.
Q. And you also saw the other witnesses testifying on television?
A. Yes, I did.

Q. Thank you.  I would like now to ask for a few clarifications concerning your biography.  And you explained to the Chamber that after April 1975 and before you went to S-21 you said that you had worked at Prey Sar in the 703rd Division in the rice field. Is that so?
A. That is so.
Q. Who was your boss back then at Prey Sar?  Who was your chief?
A. At Prey Sar there was the head of the unit of 101 and there was the person named Konn (phonetic) or something, but I don't remember their names quite well.
Q. Was Him Huy with you back then at the rice field?

A. Him Huy was not with me back then.  He was in the Platoon 143 and I worked at the platoon -- at the different platoon, so we were in a different group.  We only known one another when we worked at S-21.

Q. Again I would like to have a few clarifications regarding your biography.  You told the Chamber that at a certain moment you had been injured, you received a bullet injury, and that you had been hospitalized for several months, first in the medical unit of S-21 and then in the hospital.  Is that so?

A. During the time when I had worked at the interrogation unit I had my wounds that I sustained previously reopened and I think these made me sick and then I was sent to Monivong Hospital and then to Preah Khmet Mealea Hospital and finally to the Soviet Cambodia Friendship Hospital.

Q. Thank you for this clarification.  So this is when you were an interrogator.  So according to you, when did this incident happen?  In which period in your life and at what moment were you brought to the hospital; do you remember?

A. So far as I remember, it was 1978 when I was hospitalized and I had been in the hospital for a long time, I can't remember, and I was off duty until I recovered.  So it was almost late 1978 that I recovered.

Q. Thank you.  Well, indeed you have stepped a bit ahead of what I wanted to ask because I wanted to ask you a few clarifications. So you said "a long time".  Can you be more specific?  Did this mean many months?  Can you be a little bit more specific about this please?
A. Could you please repeat your question?

Q. I would like you to be more specific regarding this period in your life.  For how many months were you invalidated?  For how many months -- first of all, how many months did you stay in the medical unit and then in the hospital?  How long did this last in 1978?  Was this for six months, eight months?  Can you tell me something, if you can recall?

A. I don't remember how many months, but it was quite a long time, and I can remember that I could hardly walk and then we were on the move already that we were leaving S-21.  So when I was on the move I was not well recovered yet.

Q. Thank you.  Mr. Prak Khan, I now would like to put a few questions to you based on a document that is included in the case file and that is known to be as the manual of the interrogator. So the prosecutors do not know who was the interrogator in question, so we do not know either, but apparently everyone agrees it was one of your colleagues who took notes during the training sessions organized either by Duch or by Hor.

And for the necessities of the written record, I would like to say that this document that had been misnamed originally as "Torture Manual" was then renamed following a check on the translation.  It is called "The Statistic List of the S-21 Special Branch".  It is document ERN in Khmer 00007445 to 713. So just a few questions regarding what seems to be the notes that were taken by one of your interrogator colleagues, and I am only asking you therefore to tell me if indeed these notes mean anything to you, if they remind you of anything and if you believe that this is what was indeed being said during these training sessions.

In the French version on  I can read the following: "Angkar orders us to interrogate intensively.  We have followed this order properly but we give more value to torture than to politics and this is contrary to the order according to which we must use politics." A little further on, under the heading "Improvement Objectives", three points are listed.  The first: "Use politics as a basis. 2. Follow the comparative answers in a detailed way before resorting to  torture. 3. Strictly follow Angkar's discipline during the interrogation." And we can find the same thing, therefore I will put to you a general question on this topic.  So we find the same thing a few pages further on  in French, paragraph 3, "Point of View and Stance on the Interrogation Methods", and it is indicated the following:

"First of all, the measures for each one of us during the interrogations must be of two kinds: a) political pressure:  we must exert political pressure in a sustained way and at all moments; b) the usage of torture is a complementary measure. "And second of all, it is indicated experiments from the past that were conducted by our interrogator comrades were generally focused on torture.  That is to say that they gave more weight to torture than to propaganda.  And this is an erroneous, mistaken experiment and we must understand this in a determinate way." This is what I have to say concerning this point regarding the interrogations.  Does this remind you, therefore, what you were hearing during the training sessions?
A. I did hear the content which was instructed by Brother Duch during the training.  I did hear that theory, yes.

Q. Thank you.  Now, regarding another topic and again in the same document, on  of the French version, point number 4, "Viewpoints and Stance Regarding the Enemies' Confessions".  In point 2 the following is written down. "Allow them to speak and to write.  They should not be interrupted.  Correct them immediately based on our own attention…" I would like to say it again, well: "…based on our own attention or let's say where we want to bring them to in the questioning, except for the points that the Party suggests, and that we ask requests from them because the Party understands the situation very well. But if we insist on the names and on the activities, the prisoners are going to invent things to suit our objectives.  But in so doing we are going to lose the revolutionary forces.  They are going to make the revolutionary situation muddled.  They are going to make the content of the confessions vague and pointless. In reality, this makes the entire influence of the Special Branch disappear."

And again, regarding this point on .3 regarding the method to compile documents, point B, and of course we are referring to the prisoners again: "The best thing is that they write on their own and in their own words, their own sentences, their own thoughts, while avoiding dictating to them what they should write." And again, regarding this topic, , point 6, the title in French which does not seem to me to be a perfect translation, well, the title is "How to Make the Party Welcoming Regarding the Enemy's Confessions": "(a)  what's the most important is that we must not designate the names, not make them speak or not force them to speak according to our intention." So my question is with regard to these methods.  Does this remind you of anything that you heard in the training?  You do not force enemies, or I prefer the term prisoner -- you do not force the prisoners towards the intentions of the interrogators.  You let them speak. Does this remind you of anything?

A. That point was taught to us because if we forced the prisoners to respond or to write to the extreme, which did not involve the activities, it would be of no use.  So we had to explain to them how to write properly to make them -- to make the text clearly understandable, and that was the continuous instructions by Duch.

Q. Lastly, on another point, referring to  of the French, at point 5, viewpoint and position with regard to the spirit of revolutionary vigilance and maintaining secrecy, point 2 of the paragraph says: "This period of secrecy is the driving force of the Special Branch.  Without secrecy the Special Branch has no further meaning." If I understand correctly, the Special Branch was in fact S-21. And on the following page -- I'm referring to  at paragraph 7, which is recapitulation, the following is indicated: "Interrogation work is to summarize confessions.  We summarize them by analyzing and extracting confessions.  This is detailed work on all aspects, balanced work which is carefully analyzed, carefully thought out and allowing for no gaps.  This is done in the most absolute secrecy." Do you confirm that you received this training?  Do you confirm that the training -- that during the training you were told that you were to work in absolute secrecy?
A. I used to study that.  I was instructed to perform the task and to make it secret and not to share amongst the work colleagues or to pass on from one to another.  So it was secretive.
Q. And did secrecy extend, to your knowledge, to anyone who worked in S-21 regardless of the unit in which they worked?

A. All of us had to maintain secrecy.  At that time we were told to plant a kapok tree, which means we had to be mindful of only our own business and not to interfere with other people's tasks or we would be reported.  We were only responsible for the works assigned to us.

Q. Thank you.  Mr. Prak Khan, I must tell you that this is what concerns me in your testimony.  As the accused told you in speaking in general this morning, he has no quarrel with you, but on several occasions you mention matters about which it is difficult to understand how you came to gain any knowledge.  Now I'm putting questions to you which require some clarification. On several occasions you have granted interviews in the press and on films.  You have expressed yourself.  But this is a courtroom where you are today, and what you say outside is not the same as what you say here in this courtroom.  In a courtroom we need concrete facts.

I'd like to come back to the drawing of blood, and let's be clear on this.  Duch has acknowledged that this occurred since the investigation.  More specifically, since the question was put to him in February 2008 in your presence, there is no problem with that.  My problem is that I still fail to understand how you could have witnessed what you are telling us, and my questions will arise from this.

My first question is this:  you said that it was Try who told you that the blood was intended for the hospitals that you named. How can you explain to the Chamber that Try, who was not a member of your group, was able to tell you such a secret?  Can you enlighten us on that?

A. Regarding the drawing of blood, as I have stated, I saw it happen on two or three occasions, and in each occasion the number of the people were between 10 to 30.  And I did not say up to 1,000 people like Duch said this morning.  I said on the few occasions -- on each occasion there was only a group of 10 to 30 people.  And I did not say it happened on a monthly basis.  So this is my verification on this matter.

And what the medic Try told me, after I asked him where was the blood taken to, and he told me that it was taken to the hospital. And from what I understood, we would have the Khmer Soviet Hospital, the Monivong and the Khmet Mealea Hospital.  And it is my conclusion that the blood was sent to those hospitals. But regarding the witness of blood drawing, I did see it on a few occasions.

Q. We shall return to the fact that you were a witness.  For the time being please answer my question.  How can you explain the fact that Try spoke to you and provided you with this information whereas you were all bound by secrecy, and forgive me, you were not a boss, you were an interrogator?  How can you explain to the Chamber that Try told you, in particular, such a secret?

A. We all had our principle of secrecy, but at that time Try resided just next to where I stayed and sometimes at night after the prisoners were returned -- it was not so strict at the time because at that time the internal purge did not occur yet and we could contact, and only at a later stage when the situation was intense that we did not contact each other.
Q. So would you say that this happened at the beginning when you arrived in S-21?  Is that what we are to understand from it?

A. It was not at the very beginning but I cannot say the exact period as it happened 30 years ago.  What I can only confirm, that I personally witnessed the drawing of blood of the prisoners, and I did not tell a lie.

Q. We are going to talk about that.  On two or three occasions you've said that you were witness to the drawing of blood and you say that it was because you were along the path that passed nearby. So, witness, how did you witness this scene?  Through the door, through the window?  How?
A. I actually walked into the location where the blood was drawn as I wanted to see how it happened.
Q. And you were an interrogator at the time or were you still a guard on the outside?

A. At the time that I saw it I was not a guard.  It was at night-time when I returned the prisoners back to the cells.  It was around 11 p.m., so after -- upon returning, I went into that location to have a look.
Q. So you're telling the Chamber that an interrogator had the right to enter the medical unit to take a look around.  Is that what you're saying?

A. This is not what I said.  Because I used to go in that location, I used to go in to ask for the medicine when I was not well, so it was normal to go into that location.  And when it happened that the blood was drawn, so I just stood there and looked.
Q. But that was just the once.  You said two or three times a while ago.  Does it mean that you went there two or three times at 11 p.m. to fetch medicine?

A. I personally went inside to witness it.  That was on one occasion.  But on the other occasions I stood from the street where I could see, and I saw the prisoners' blood was drawn.  And on the occasion that I went to see it I stood there and I saw they put the syringe, the needle into both arms and draw the blood of the prisoner.

Q. And you told the Chamber that on one occasion you saw a prisoner from whom five bags of blood were drawn.  How long does it take to fill one of those bags, Mr. Prak Khan?  Just for one sachet, how long would it take?
A. When I stood and watched it, it took about an hour to fill a pouch.  However, the blood was drawn from both arms and legs.

Q. This means that if there are five sachets, that's two hours. If it is one hour per packet and if you have four, one on each limb, then you have four for one hour and a further hour for the fifth one.  Let's say it's an hour.  So you're telling the Chamber today, "At S-21 I stayed one evening for one hour watching this happening."  Is that what you're telling the Chamber today?

A. I want to clarify on this matter.  I stood about an hour or so to watch it, and four pouches of blood was drawn from the prisoner at that time, during that hour, and I did not stay until it was finished.  So it is my conclusion that four or five pouches of blood were drawn from one prisoner, because I think that was all because all the prisoners were skinny and they lacked food.

Q. The Co-Prosecutor asked you this morning whether you saw the forms for the drawing of blood which were shown in the S-21 film, but my question is a lot more precise. During that scene, that is when you were an interrogator -- that means at the time -- did you see the forms recording the drawing of blood?

A. The blood voucher, I did not see them at that time.  I only saw it during the filming, and on the vouchers the medics were instructed to draw blood from the prisoner, and I saw the vouchers at the time of the filming.

Q. Thank you for the clarification.  And in the film in fact you do say, "We buried the bodies after the blood was drawn from them."  These are your words in the film we saw this morning: "We buried the bodies."  So question:  before this Chamber are you saying that you took part in the burial of bodies from whom blood -- the burial of people from whom blood had been drawn; yes or no?

A. I would like to clarify that the burial of the dead bodies, I did not participate in the burial but after the small house was dismantled, the house opposite the house where I interrogated the prisoners, I saw the fresh mark of the ground where the bodies were buried, so I made the conclusion that the medics buried the bodies there.

Q. Mr. Prak Khan, do you understand better when I said to you earlier that what is said in a film or an interview is not the same thing as what justice is expecting from you?  Justice is expecting concrete facts from you.  So you are telling us today that contrary to what you stated in the film, you did not partake in the burial of these people.  Is this what you are telling us today; you personally did not participate in the burial of these people?
A. I never ever said I took part in burial of the dead bodies of the people whose blood were drawn.

Q. Well then, we will verify whether it's an issue of translation but, however, it was indicated this morning that in the film you say "we buried the bodies" but we will check this.  And in any case, I am taking down your answer.
Mr. President, I am finished.  Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Prak Khan, as well.

MR. PRESIDENT: The testimony of witness Prak Khan has been heard and we thank you very much, Mr. Prak Khan, for spending so much of your time giving the testimony before the Trial Chamber.  The Chamber notes that you have had a lot of difficulties in giving the testimony and responding to several questions put to you from the parties to the proceeding and from the Judges and that the facts which happened several years ago were not easy to be recalled and that human memory seems to be fading when we age. So we thank you so much for your great effort to respond to almost all the questions put to you.  Since it comes to an end already we can release you to go to your residence now. The Court Officer is now instructed to coordinate with the WESU unit to make sure that Mr. Prak Khan can be accompanied or taken back to his home. We next are going to listen or to hear the testimony of Kok Sros, another witness, and after you have taken him, Prak Khan, out, then please bring in Kok Sros.
(Witness exits courtroom)

MR. ROUX: Mr. President, two questions regarding the proceedings. The defence would like to consider the document that we spoke about titled "Statistics List from the Special Branch" but we'd like this document as having been discussed during the proceedings. And the other point, the defence would like that a number be given to the document to which Prak Khan provided his own annotations.  He would have to sign this document and that a number be attributed to this document and that a copy be given to each one of the parties so that we do not lose trace of this document. Thank you, Mr. President.
(Witness enters courtroom)
QUESTIONING BY THE BENCH BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. The witness, what is your name?
A. Kok Sros.
Q. Do you use any other names other than Kok Sros?
A. No, I don't.
Q. How old are you now?
A. I'm 59 years old.
Q. What is your occupation currently?
A. I am a farmer.

Q. According to the report of the Greffier, it is clear that you have no blood relation to any parties in the proceedings and you have taken an oath before you were brought into this courtroom. Is that correct?
A. That is correct.

Q. As a witness before the Trial Chamber of the ECCC you are now informed and reminded of your rights and duties as a witness. Mr. Kok Sros, as a witness you can reject to respond to any particular questions which you believe that can self-incriminate you.  So this is the right to self-incrimination.  This means that if you are afraid that your testimony could self-incriminate you then you can exercise your rights not to respond to those questions, and that as a witness you are to respond or recollect the accounts in which you have witnessed, you heard and you have known.  So you are not to respond to any questions based on your conclusions or presumptions. So do you understand these matters?
A. Yes, I do.

Q. Mr. Kok Sros, can you please briefly tell the Court about your place of work and occupation between 1970 to 1975, until the 17th of April 1975?  Tell us where you lived and what kind of occupation you had.  Please be brief.

A. In late 1973 until 1975 -- by the end of 1973 I joined the revolution in the local villages and later on in the local villages, and later on I studied the political sessions and in 1975 I fought and approached -- in the battles and approached Phnom Penh.
Q. After the 17th of April 1975 until the 7 January 1979, what did you do and where?
A. In 1975 I worked in Platoon 138 under Division 12 and in late 1975 I was posted at S-21.  At the beginning I worked at the Ta Khmau prison, or psychiatric hospital.
Q. Could you please tell us more until the 1979 -- I mean the liberation day?
A. After living in Ta Khmau for some time then we were moved to work at S-21 as a guard -- inside the compound guard.
Q. When did you leave S-21?

A. After quite a while I was sent to work in the rice field before I was transferred back, and before the 7th of January 1979 I was once again put to work in the rice field again until the day when the liberation day came.
Q. You said during the times when you were the soldier in Battalion 138 of Division 12 and that division was taking part in the fight to topple down Lon Nol in 1975.  Is that correct?
A. That's correct.
Q. After the 17th of April 1975 you stationed at Ta Khmau and you were assigned to guard at the psychiatric hospital which turned the prison.  Is that correct?
A. That is correct.
Q. You worked at that prison in the compound of psychiatric hospital in Ta Khmau.  In which year did you work there?  Give us the approximate -- just approximate figure of that date.
A. It was in late 1975, early 1976.
Q. What was your function or role to play in that location at that Ta Khmau prison back then?
A. I were put to guard detainees.
Q. When you were assigned the task to guard the detainees, did you notice that there were a lot of detainees, or how many were they?
A. There were about 200 detainees.
Q. When you saw them, what kind of detainees were they?  Were they former soldiers of the former regime or they were the officers from the old regime?
A. There were only soldiers and cadres.
Q. The people who were arrested and detained at that psychiatric hospital were only revolutionary cadres and soldiers.  Is that correct?
A. Yes, that is.
Q. What made you think that they were the soldiers and the cadres of the revolution?
A. Because I saw them working in the leadership position.
Q. Who was the director of that prison, the prison at Ta Khmau, and who was second in command?
A. I only know that there was Brother Hor and I don't know the other people who were second in command.
Q. Do you know his full name, and what was the relationship between Hor and Division 12, as you said you worked in Platoon 138 under Division 12?
A. I don't know, Mr. President.
Q. What was Hor doing before he became the chairman of the prison in Ta Khmau?
A. I don't know either.
Q. Were there any other guards who were assigned to guard the compound back then and, if there were, how many were they?
A. There were about 100 people.
Q. Were they mainly soldiers or civilians?
A. They were recruited from the soldiers.
Q. They were recruited from the soldiers but when they were put to work at that location were they wearing uniforms and armed, or were they like normal workers?
A. They wore uniform and armed.
Q. To your best recollection, when were you transferred to work at S-21 and in which location was S-21 located back then?
A. I don't remember the date but the location of S-21 was at the current Tuol Sleng prison location.
Q. So when upper echelon transferred your workplace from Ta Khmau prison to Phnom Penh you were posted at the location of S-21, which is now known as the Tuol Sleng prison.  Is it correct?
A. That is correct.

QUESTIONING BY THE BENCH BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Mr. Witness, is your name Chuun Phal?

Mr. Chuun Phal, when did you join the military movement?
A. I joined the revolution movement in 1975.
Q. In what month, if you can recall?
A. I cannot recall the month.
Q. Did you join after the 17 April 1975 or before that?
A. I joined in 1975 after that date.
Q. When you first joined, where did you join and what duty was assigned to you?
A. When I first joined the movement I joined it through the village.
Q. What was the name of the village and in what subdistrict, district or province?
A. It was in Chaong Maong subdistrict, Tuek Phos district, Kampong Chhnang province.
Q. After you joined the movement in that village where were you sent to work?
A. I was sent to stay at Sala Lekh Pram.
Q. You were sent to stay at Sala Lekh Pram and what duty were you assigned to and how long?
A. I only stayed there at that location at the time.
Q. How long did you stay at Sala Lekh Pram before you were sent to another location?
A. I stayed there for about one week.
Q. And where were you sent next?
A. I was sent to Boeng Tumpun.
Q. You were sent to Boeng Tumpun, and when was that and what duty was assigned to you at that location?
A. I cannot catch your question.  Can you repeat?
Q. When you were sent to the location at Boeng Tumpun, when were you sent to that location, if you can recall?  And when you arrived at Boeng Tumpun what duty was assigned to you?
A. I was sent to Boeng Tumpun first to rest at that location.
Q. After you stayed and rested at that location for a while, where were you sent to work?
A. After about one month or a fortnight, as I cannot recall it correctly, I was sent to Ta Khmau.
Q. What duty was assigned to you when you were sent to Ta Khmau?
A. Upon arrival at Ta Khmau I studied the strategic training, the military lessons and so on.
Q. So you were sent there to study and train at a school.  It's a military training school, isn't it?
A. Yes, it is.
Q. You were trained at that military technical school.  How long did you study there?
A. I studied military techniques in Ta Khmau for quite some time but I cannot recall the exact period.
Q. After you studied at the military training school in Ta Khmau where were you sent?
A. After I completed my military training at that school I was sent to Prey Sar.
Q. You were sent to Prey Sar.  What duty was assigned to you at that location?
A. I was sent to Prey Sar in order to work in the rice fields, to dig canals.

Q. Can you recall when you were sent from Kampong Chhnang to Phnom Penh and to study military training, and later on you were sent to work in the rice fields and dig canals in Prey Sar, how old were you at that time?
A. When I was sent to Prey Sar I was about 15 years old.
Q. After you had worked at Prey Sar where were you sent next?
A. After I left Prey Sar I was sent to Tuol Sleng.
Q. You used the term Tuol Sleng.  Where was the location of Tuol Sleng and what was that location for?
A. The location where I was sent to was a location where I was assigned to guard duty.
Q. You talked about Tuol Sleng.  If you can recall, where was Tuol Sleng?  In what province or in what city?
A. I did not know the province or the city of that location.
Q. Was it called Tuol Sleng at that time or was it known by another name, the place where you worked after you were sent from Prey Sar?
A. It was called S-21 but it was also known as Tuol Sleng.
Q. You said when you arrived at Tuol Sleng you were assigned guard duty.  What did you guard?
A. I guarded the prisoners.
Q. You worked as a prisoner guard.  Did you stand guard inside or outside?
A. I stood guard inside.
Q. When you stood guard inside what work was assigned to you in your role?
A. I guarded the prisoners when they were brought from somewhere.
Q. You stood guard inside.  What does it mean?  Was it inside a detention room or was it inside a compound where the buildings were used to detain people?
A. I guarded inside a building.
Q. Can you recall at that location how many detention buildings and which building did you stand guard those prisoners?
A. I stood guard at building number 2.
Q. Can you recall if building number 2, was it east-west or north-south building?
A. It was an east-west building.
Q. How many buildings were there in that compound, if you can recall?  That is at the Tuol Sleng prison, as you said.
A. There were four buildings.
Q. Can you count those buildings and the exact locations of those buildings?
A. I do not know the exact locations of those buildings.  I cannot recall.
Q. At that time you worked inside the S-21 compound.  Which entrance did you use to go into the compound?
A. When I worked at that location I actually cannot recall which entrance I used to enter the compound.  I cannot recall it.
Q. You just said building number 2 where you worked, and what about building number 1?  To which side of building number 2 building number 1 was located?
A. I suppose the building 1 and building 2 were next to each other.

Q. So that is after building 1 that is building number 2.  Is that correct?  And it cannot be after building 1 there was a building 1.  There had to be a building 2 if it's in that order. Is that correct? What about building number 3 and number 4?  To which side of building number 2 were they located?

A. I cannot say about the direction, like south or north directions.  I knew there were two buildings to one side and the other two were to the side, but I cannot recall exactly whether they were to the south, to the east or to the west.
Q. So you meant two buildings were parallel in each other and the other two were to the sides.  Is this correct?

A. One was to the side and another one to the other side, and the other two were lined up in a row but I cannot say whether they were to the north or to the south direction because now I seem to get confused.  I can only recall, yes, there were those buildings.
Q. You were assigned to guard building number 2.  From your recollection, is this correct?
A. At building number 2, yes.
Q. You stood guard; what does it mean?
A. I watch out for the prisoners in the location that I was assigned to.
Q. Was the building on the ground or were there many floors on that building?
A. The building had three storeys.
Q. Was the building built of wood or concrete?
A. It was built of concrete.
Q. You were assigned to guard at that building number 2.  In which particular room or which floor were you assigned to guard?
A. It was not regular.  Sometime I was assigned to guard the upper floor, or sometimes on the ground floor, or sometime on the middle floor according to the assignment by the group chief.
Q. In guarding the prisoners, in one day how many shift did you take and at what time; and how many guards were guarding at the same time in your shift?
A. One team was assigned to guard in each shift.  There were about 12 persons in each team.
Q. What about the working hours in the shift?
A. The group chief ordered us to guard the prisoners and do not allow them to escape or to commit any suicide or to hang themselves.

Q. At what time did you guard?  For example, in the 24 hour of a day, were your team assigned to guard at daytime or at night time or was your team rotated, and how many shifts did your team take per day and how long was each shift?
A. In each shift, if we started from 6 o'clock or 6.30, then the shift would end at 12 o'clock.
Q. So those who guarded during the daytime, were they supposed to also guard at night?
A. The shifts were at 12 midday, and at 4 p.m. there was another shift -- or maybe 5 p.m.  I were on duty sometime in the day, sometime at nights.
Q. When you were on duty to guard the building, were you assigned to guard within the rooms where detainees were detained or were you just patrolling on the corridor?

A. I did not go into the room to be close to any detainee because the cells or the room were -- the detainees were placed in the room and then we were asked to walk from -- on the corridor to lay the eyes on those detainees.
Q. So were you guarding at the location where detainees were placed in the individual cells or were you also on duty at the common cells?
A. There were individual cells -- small and big cells -- where detainees were put together.
Q. So when you were on duty to stood guard at the individual cells, could you please tell the Court how you perform your task?

A. Normally, we would walk from one cell to another because in the cells there were windows, windows through which we can see the detainees and we were supposed to only check the lock, whether the lock were properly locked and that detainees could not escape.
Q. At night, how could you see any detainee?  Was there any light or were you given any kind of torches?
A. At night, there was light because there was electricity the whole night.
Q. So could you then see the detainees and the locks through -- I mean under those -- I mean the light?
A. So far as I remember, the light was lit enough for us to inspect or to check the lock and detainees.
Q. When you were assigned to guard in the common room, could you please tell us how you discharged your duty?
A. In the common room where detainees were detained inside, I was only patrolling outside on the corridor.
Q. Had you ever seen any detainees who died while being detained?
A. During my shifts I had never seen any detainee die.
Q. Having watched the detainees while you were on duty, what was your impression in relation to the physical condition of those detainees?

A. I saw detainees who were very thin because they were not given sufficient food.  I was not in charge of providing food to them, of course; there were people who were assigned to distribute these meals to them.  I was only in charge of checking and patrolling the location.

Q. Those detainees who were detained inside individual cells and the common cells, were they shackled or were they allowed to move about freely inside their room?  Could you please tell the Court about this?  Or were there only locks?  I mean detainees were only locked from the outside and that they could move about freely inside?

A. The detainees in those rooms, whether in a common room or individual cells, so far as I remember for the male prisoners, they were shackled and one -- because they were shackled all together in one line.  For example, a long metal bar would be attached to seven detainees in a group.  And for female detainees I think they were not shackled but they were locked from outside.
Q. Could detainees stand up?
A. Could you please repeat your question?  I could not catch it.
Q. You said male detainees were shackled, even in the individual cell every one of the detainees would also be detained.  The question was whether they could stand if they would wish to do so.

A. They could stand up if they wanted because the shackles were big enough for detainees to stand up, but I think the detainee needed to use some kind of wooden board or a kind of piece of wood to make sure that they can hold the shackles so that the person could stand up.  Otherwise it would not be possible.
Q. Had you ever seen any detainee standing up?
A. Could you please repeat your question, Mr. President?
Q. During the time while you were on duty did you ever see anyone standing up?
A. Detainees could not stand up unless they asked for a permission to do so from the guards.  Without such permission they would not be allowed to do so.
Q. What about the clothing of the detainees?  Can you please tell the Court to the best of your recollection in relation to their clothing?

A. Detainees did not wear proper clothes like we did.  They were given ragged clothes and some had some long pants, some only got shorts, some got the very torn clothes.  And some were given some clothes to exchange but some could only wear their ragged ones.
Q. Did detainees wear shorts or trousers and shirts, blouses, or were they topless?

A. Some had shorts and shirts.  Some only had shorts and it depends on the chief of the group who made them wear anything they preferred because they said that the upper echelon would want them to wear that kind of clothes other than the other kind of clothes.
Q. You said that detainees were very thin, and can you tell us about the food ration?  How many times a day were detainees given meals and what kind of meals were given?

A. The food ration was in the form of gruel, so detainee would be given a bowl of gruel -- small or big; depends.  When I worked there as a guard I was in charge of guarding the location and when it comes to the food distribution there were people who were specifically assigned to offer the meals to detainees. That's why I can see that meals were given differently to different detainees.
Q. Did you ever see detainees being washed?  And how could they have such a wash while they were being detained, shackled and locked from the outside?

A. Detainees received a wash. For example, if it was scheduled to wash the detainees on any particular day, then normally all detainees would be washed all together at once.  We were not receiving any orders from the upper echelon to allow detainees to go free to wash themselves.  They would be given a water hose and then they could take turns passing this water hose to one another to wash themselves.
Q. What about the people who were detained in the common room, how could they wash themselves?

A. In those common rooms we did not go inside, and when we received orders from the upper echelon -- I don't know to what extent upper echelon was with the authority because here I refer to the chief of the team who asked us to wash the detainees.  If the chief did not make any instruction or give any instruction to us to allow the detainees to be washed, then detainees could not be washed. In the common room, the water hose would be used and that water would be sprayed on them, and that they were asked to stand up, and after they're done then we could remove the water hose.
Q. What did they do after having such a wash?
A. For the male detainees, they had a wash while being naked.
Q. What about the clothes they had worn before they were being washed?

A. During the wash, since they did not have other clothes to change, then since the guards were male and the detainees were male, according to the order and instruction from the upper echelon, detainees were asked to remove their clothes and they had the wash, and later on they could put on their clothes.
Q. How did they remove or take off their clothes because they were shackled?  Can you please tell the Court of such experience or observation?

A. The shorts were taken off from the detainees and for the thin shorts it was not difficult to be removed.  We could take it off through the shackles.  And some trousers which were rather heavy could not be removed entirely from the body of the detainee, so part of the sleeves of the trouser would be still attached to the shackles.  But then they could still had a wash and, since guards were not allowed by the upper echelon to go near to the detainees because they were afraid that detainees would counterattack or react, then we only watched from the outside while they were having a wash.
Q. Did you ever see foreigners being detained in such rooms?  For example, the westerners, the white-complexioned detainees with blond hair, hairy chest, for example?

A. I saw some foreigners but they were being brought and detained in the room, and for some time -- on some occasions during my guard duty, I saw them, but it was not long because during such duty, after one or two days the foreigners I saw would be taken away because they would be detained for very few days before they would be relocated.

Q. Were detainees treated the same?  For example, were the foreigners treated the same as the Cambodian detainees?  Were they shackled and locked in individual cells or were they placed in the common room among the other detainees like normal, ordinary detainees?
A. Foreign detainees were detained in a separate room, not mixed with the Cambodian detainees.
Q. Did you ever see Vietnamese prisoners of war who were detained at that location?
A. Yes, I did.  I saw them.
Q. Did you see them in the building you guarded?
A. Could you please repeat your question, Mr. President?
Q. Were the Vietnamese prisoners of war detained in the building you were assigned to stand guard?  Is that correct?
A. Those detainees were detained at the place where I guarded, but they were detained very briefly.  Probably two or three days they would be relocated to different location; I don't know.
Q. Did you see many of them being detained in that location?

A. I did not see a lot of them.  I sometimes -- you know, like for a certain period of time then I could see them, a few of them, being sent in.  And then time passed by and later on I could see a few more.
Q. Did you ever see female detainees?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. Were there a lot of female detainees in that location?  Were they put in the same common room or were they put differently in a separate room?
A. For female detainees, they could be detained in a common room. But the upper echelon instructed us, for example, when confessions or documents were needed from them, then they could be separated.
Q. Did you ever see children?  Did you ever see children who came along with their mothers to the detention location?

A. There were not very young children at my location.  I saw the mothers and sometimes I saw one or two children came along with them but I did not see children who would come along with the parents every time because sometimes parents came alone without children.
Q. Did you observe where these children would be taken to after their mothers were detained?
A. Sometimes after a few days the children could stay with their mothers and later on they were separated from the common room to a different location that I never knew where it would be.

Q. When the interrogators came to remove the detainees to be interrogated, who was in charge of removing the shackles from the detainees before they were escorted by the interrogators to the interrogating rooms?

A. The people who came to bring the detainees to be interrogated were not interrogators themselves.  When they came, for example, they would contact the chief of the group and that then they would ask the guards to take the detainees to be interrogated to them.

Q. After they were interrogated and that they would be sent back to their cells how could they be treated?  Were they then reshackled and handcuffed or were they only delivered to the guards, the interior guards, who then put them back into the cells or rooms?

A. After detainees were interrogated they were sent to the chief of the group who later on managed how these detainees would be relocated or would be put again into the rooms or cells.  As a guard I was only in charge of checking or patrolling the location.
Q. What was your observation in relation to the physical condition of any detainees who had just been interrogated and walked back to their cells?

A. The prisoners who had been taken for interrogation, upon their return some of them were beaten; some were not.  That was my observation at the time.  Sometimes at the location where I stood guard, in two or three days time a prisoner would be take to be interrogated and later on, after the interrogation was complete, was put in another location.
Q. Why did you think that the prisoners who were interrogated and then who were returned, some were beaten and some were not?  Why do you think that?
A. It is my understanding that some prisoners who were difficult, probably they would be beaten in order to extract the information from them.  This is just my assumption.

Q. You said that some prisoners were not beaten and some you thought were beaten during the interrogation.  Did you see the marks, for example, on the bodies of those prisoners, or the bruise or blood?  That's why you said they were beaten?

A. I saw the beating marks and wounds, that's all, and some of them did not have all these marks or wounds upon their return.  I think it was up to Angkar or the upper echelon to either torture or not torture those prisoners.  But in fact, yes, I did see those prisoners who were tortured.

A. I do not know for sure.  Only the group chief and above would know.  I only knew that the prisoners were taken out and in some cases they were brought back.

A. I do not know.

A. I don't remember who was actually the Chairman of S-21.  I did not know his name.
Q. According to your recollection, who was the top person, the most superior person at that location?
A. I only know the people at the lower level, including Peng and Hor, the persons whom I saw.
Q. During the time when you worked at S-21 did you ever have to guard outside?
A. Occasionally I would be assigned to guard outside but it was very rare.  Maybe once a month I would be assigned to guard outside or sometimes it would be once after a fortnight.
Q. To which direction were you on guard at the outside of the location and what did you do?
A. I sometimes guarded at the back or rear gate or the front gate.  I don't know which gate would be the front and which one would be the rear gate because there were two at that time.
Q. You said you guarded at the entrance and exit of the location of the S-21.  You saw incoming and outgoing prisoners.  Did you see incoming or outgoing prisoners?

A. I saw people being -- sending out and in.  Sometimes I saw them, sometimes I didn't.  I only saw them during the time when I saw them.  I mean basically when I was on duty it was not necessary that I would see them because they would not be taken out during that time.
Q. When detainees were being sent into S-21 how were they brought in?  Were they taken in by trucks, or can you please tell the Court a little bit about this?
A. Sometimes I saw them being sent in by trucks and then they would be walked to the buildings.  I did not know how they would be treated after that because I was working on the ground.
Q. How were detainees taken out?

A. I sometimes did farming and sometimes I planted vegetables.

A. I was assigned to work there once; on one occasion only.

A. The pit was about 3 by 2 metres.
Q. Did you see the bodies fill the pit?
A. The bodies were lying significantly in the pit, enough to be buried; not too many.

A. I did not actually inspect the dead bodies.  I was only focusing on burying them and it was already late in the afternoon.  I had to rush to bury them and I failed to pay more attention to the condition of the bodies.

That's how I learned about the deaths of those prisoners.
Q. So the guards, after when they walked and met each other they could talk to each other?  There was no rule or discipline for them not to talk to each other?
A. When we walked and came face to face, yes, we could talk to each other.  There was no restriction for us to just talk to each other.
Q. Can you provide further clarification on one point; that is, at S-21 did you ever see any female medic and were there any child medics?
A. I knew that I did not see any female medics and regarding the child medics I saw them dispensing medicine, yes.
Q. When you stood guard outside near the entrance; that is, near the medical house, did you ever see medics withdraw blood from the prisoners?
A. I stood guard outside and I could not see what work was done by the medics inside the office.
Q. At S-21 when you were working there you were assigned to guard the prisoners and not allow them to escape.  At that time were you satisfied with your work?
A. At that time in my mind I thought whether I was happy or not with my work.  There was no other alternative for me because in that regime there was only one option.

Q. Can you then clarify on another point; that is whether you were happy or not you could not find anywhere else to go or to escape from that place?  If you were to escape from that place you think you would be able to do it?
A. I would not be able to run away from it and that is the truth.
Q. So it means anybody who was not happy with that regime could not run away.  Is that true?
A. Nobody could run away.
MR. KAR SAVUTH: Thank you, Mr. President.  I would like my international counsel to continue questioning.
MR. PRESIDENT: International defence counsel, you may proceed.
MS. CANIZARES: Thank you very much.
BY MS. CANIZARES: Q. Could you please remind us for how long you were a guard at S-21?
A. I did not record the exact dates or times or hours that I worked as a guard at S-21.  I did not have anything to record my time there.
Q. Not even an approximate manner let's say in terms of months or in terms of years? I am wondering if Mr. Chuun Phal understood the question that I was asking him or if he heard it.
A. Can you please repeat your question?  I cannot understand it.

Q. You answered my first question telling me that you did not count how long you were a guard at S-21; you had no means of knowing how long this was.  But can't you at least in an approximate way give me an idea in terms of months or years and tell me how long you worked at S-21 -- in those terms?
A. As I have said, I would not be able to make any estimation.

Q. So we'll say a certain amount of time. During the confrontation that took place on the 28th of February 2008 before the Co-Investigating Judges, you stated that you did not know the charged person.  However, this morning you confirmed before the Chamber this assertion while specifying that you had neither seen him nor ever met him.  So therefore, I can conclude from this that you did not speak with him either. Can I also conclude from this that in fact Duch never came or, in any case as far as you can know, never came to the building or the buildings in which you were working?
A. That is correct.
Q. Thank you.
MS. CANIZARES: I have no further questions to put to the witness.  Thank you, Mr. President.
MR. PRESIDENT: Next, the Chamber would like to give the opportunity to the accused to make his observations regarding this witness' testimony. If you wish to do so, you can proceed.

THE ACCUSED: Mr. President, first I would like to clearly state that I acknowledge this person, Mr. Phal, as a member of S-21 staff. And the reason is he was once amongst the youths that I requested from Kampong Chhnang.  His district was from Kampong Tralach and he was younger than 16 years old.  He was within the selected criteria of my request and his class origin was a poor peasant background.  Therefore, his education was very low as evidenced in the Chamber today.  Probably he could read a few words, that's all.

And he fits the criteria for my request from the best.  And his age of 15 or 16 would also fall within the criteria of my selection.  I did not want to select any person who was already trained or educated by anybody.  So I needed to select those who I could train psychologically and politically. I think the Chamber also understands the stands and the psychology of Comrade Phal that he did not want to have anything or to possess anything or to know anything.  Even my face as his superior, he did not even want to see my face or to hear my voice.  And that view impressed me that he was staff of S-21. And when he said he's chief group, Sae, ordered him to dig pits at Choeung Ek, I was certain that he was a staff member. Sae was my first messenger recruited from the Special Forces as I requested to the (inaudible) and the digging pits at Choeung Ek was carried out by the Special Force. So I do not deny, and I acknowledge this person was a staff at S-21.

Despite this, there is a confusion in his statement; for instance, he said that the vehicles for the S-21 plates, also there were these plates at the political training school, and this is a confusion.  And Prek Ho actually did not have any land there.

Maybe these are small things that he could not recall properly. This morning I received a biography of Comrade Phal and I would like to state that I need time to consider this biography; that is also including the format of that biography-making.  From my recollection, after 17 April 1975 until the end of '75, the CPK ordered people to inspect the biographies of cadres and the components of the 703 Division entering S-21, Nat ordered You Penkry to monitor all those cadres.  And those people from M-13 I did not allow them to do it because I vouch for them before the Party.

Separately for those from Kampong Chhnang if the biographies were made before they arrived at S-21, for instance if they were made in '77 that would be different informant. So I would reserve the time to examine these particular biographies, why it was made in 1977. So that was the process of biography making under the CPK and I was a cadre of the Party and I was familiar with the process. Annually I had to made my revolutionary biography and my revolutionary view.  The Party wanted to check if anybody concealed any points from their biography. So actually the biography was made annually during the training. The view on the revolution was also done annually.  And I myself I did not believe that biography had to be that long for this Comrade Phal.  That's why I reserve the time to examine it. Despite this, I still acknowledge he's a member of the S-21 staff. This is my response, Your Honour.

MR. PRESIDENT: Mr. Chuun Phal, the Chamber would like to acknowledge your presence here and for your testimony before this Chamber as summonsed by the Chamber.  The Chamber also acknowledges the challenges and difficulties that you faced, namely you had to respond to several questions raised by both the Chamber and the parties to the proceedings. In addition to these several questions in a very limited allocated for your testimony, the facts that existed were more than 30 years ago.  Therefore, the recollection in general by anybody is limited.  The longer the fact exists, the less precise the recollection of that fact.  However, the Chamber noticed that you have tried to respond to the questions based on your limited knowledge and your recollection. You are now excused from the Chamber, so you can return to your residence.
(Witness exits courtroom)

Court officer, can you provide necessary arrangements for safe return of this witness to his residence by working in co-operation with the WESU unit?  And also, the Court officer, you're instructed to bring in another witness, namely Saom Met, into the courtroom.
(Witness enters courtroom)
QUESTIONING BY THE BENCH BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Mr. Witness, is your name Saom Met?
A. Yes, sir, my name is Saom Met.
Q. Are you known by any other names?
A. No.
Q. How old are you?
A. Fifty one years old.
Q. What is your current occupation?
A. I am a farmer.
Q. According to the report of the Greffier this morning it states that you have no relationship with any of the parties to the proceedings.  Is this correct?
A. Yes.
Q. Have you taken an oath before entering the Chamber?
A. Yes, I did.

Q. I am now going to give you instructions on the rights and obligations of a witness to provide testimony before this Chamber as follows. Mr. Saom Met, as a witness you can decide not to respond to any questions or any declarations that you think might self-incriminate.  This is your right of self-incrimination, which means if the response or the statement you believe would lead to self-incrimination.  Also, Mr. Saom Met, as a witness you are obliged to tell the Chamber only the truth that you have known, have heard, have seen personally and directly when you respond to the questions, and your responses should not be the assumptions that you make. Mr. Saom Met, where did you live and what were you doing between 1970 until the 7 January 1979?

A. In 1970 I was living with my parents and in 1972 I left my mother to study at the Preaek Sdei pagoda as a student of the monks there.  I only studied for one year at the pagoda and I quit schooling at that year one.  Then I returned to live with my mother, to work in the rice fields. In early 1973 Angkar assigned me to work at the Prey Sdei subdistrict.  In the end of 1973 Angkar assigned me to work as a militia at the district, and in 1974 I still worked as a soldier and Angkar assigned me to fight the Lon Nol soldiers along the Mekong River.

In 1975, when Phnom Penh was completely liberated, I stayed in Phnom Penh for only a fortnight and Angkar assigned me as a messenger through the battalion and regiments.  I was recruited amongst the other 50 messengers to study at the technical training school in Ta Khmau.  That also included the 703 Division.  The total number increased to more than 200. We studied political training and military techniques for about eight months.  I finished that study in 1976 and I was assigned by Angkar, and Angkar assigned those people at the messenger unit to guard the General Staff prison near Monivong. It was called Dam Pheng prison.  The chairman was Nat at the time and I did not know who was the deputy.  However, during the time that I worked there I saw Brother Duch, Hor, Chan and Pon who were there at the time.  Regarding Duch and Chan and Pon, they were on and off so I did not know the actual location where they stayed.  And this is my clear recollection of the event at the time.

In 1977-'78, Angkar assigned the messenger unit to guard the prisoners at S-21, or Tuol Sleng prison.  Therefore, some members of the messenger unit, who were literate, were assigned to work in the interrogation unit.  For those who were illiterate, they were assigned to guard the prisoners.  I did not guard inside the buildings inside the compound, I was assigned to guard the houses outside and they were the special prisons of S-21.  The supervisor there was Huy and Sry, who were the chairmen of platoon and company.  That is all.
Q. When did you leave S-21 Office, if you can recall?
A. In late 1978, Angkar transferred me to Prey Sar and about a month later Vietnamese entered.  That is all.
MR. PRESIDENT: Judges of the Bench, do you have any questions to be put to this witness? Judge Ya Sokhan, you go ahead.
JUDGE YA SOKHAN: Thank you, Mr. President.
BY JUDGE YA SOKHAN: Q. When you worked as a guard at Dam Pheng prison, what duties were you assigned?
A. At that location, I was still pretty young and I was assigned to guard the prisoners.  That is all.
Q. Where were those prisoners detained?
A. They were detained in the house, the one-storey house actually.
Q. Were they shackled?
A. Normally, detainees were all shackled in each room.
Q. Were they shackled and also handcuffed?
A. They were not handcuffed.
Q. Did you see any female detainees and children at Dam Pheng prison?
A. I don't remember whether there were female or children detainees because it was at the initial stage where the people the same age as mine were at the beginning detained.
Q. Were they the soldiers of the Lon Nol regime or former officials or the revolutionary combatants?
A. I don't know.  I saw the detainees and that's all.
Q. Did you ever see any detainees being transported in, and how often did you see that?
A. I don't know because when I came to that location I saw the detainees had already been there.
Q. Did you ever see detainees being transported from the PJ prison out?
A. I saw detainees being walked to be interrogated, but I have no idea where they would be interrogated.
Q. Who told you that they were being interrogated?
A. Sry, who was my chief, saw the interrogators and that detainees would be taken to them to be interrogated.
Q. Were they transported on a truck to be interrogated or were they walked?
A. While their hands were put behind and cuffed and blindfolded, they were being walked to the location where they would be interrogated.
Q. Had you ever seen anyone being trucked back or walked back?
A. Of course, after the interrogations they were returned.
Q. When they came back, upon arriving did you notice any scars or bruises on the back of any detainee?
A. It was not at the location where I guarded.  It was the location where other guards stood guard.  That's why I could not tell.
Q. Did you know what role Duch was holding at that time at Dam Pheng prison?
A. I don't know.  I only saw him paying regular visits to that location.
Q. Do you know how Duch was being promoted?  Was he promoted at the PJ prison or was he promoted at S-21 location?
A. I don't know, but when I came to S-21 I saw him at S-21 already, and I did not know whether he had been the chairperson of S-21 back then already because I had no good communication with him.
Q. At the Dam Pheng prison you said you had work.  How long had you been working there?
A. I worked there for less than a year and I don't remember the exact duration.
Q. Do you remember when Dam Pheng prison was relocated to S-21 prison?
A. As I already indicated earlier on, from 1977 to 1978.  I don't remember the exact date but it was during that period of time.
Q. Are you sure that the location was relocated to S-21 in 1977? Who told you about this?
A. The people in the same messengers unit told me about this. They told me that we would be relocating in 1977 or 1978 and that's what I learned about being relocated.
Q. Did you remember the messenger who told you about the relocation?

A. I don't remember his name because at that time Sry and Huy, who knew or expected the relocation, would share this information with us and I did not know until we reached the new location that I realized it was S-21 Office, which is now known as Tuol Sleng.
Q. Where were all the detainees at Dam Pheng prison transferred to?
A. I don't know.
Q. Do you know who were in the committee of S-21?
A. If we talk from the very beginning and up to the chief of the team level, there were Duch, Hor, Chan, Pon, Huy, Sry and other people.  This is only according to my observation.
Q. When you said about Huy, were you referring to Him Huy or Nun Huy?
A. I am talking about Him Huy.
Q. What was the role of Duch at S-21, to the best of your recollection?
A. I don't know, but I saw him at the location.  He could have been the person in charge of S-21.
Q. What about Hor?  What did he do?
A. Hor was like Duch.  He was supervising the prison.
Q. Did you know Nun Huy?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. What was his role at S-21?
A. He was in charge of S-24; Prey Sar.
Q. How many units were there at S-21?  Do you know that?
A. At S-21, I don't think I remember the details but there were the interrogators unit, the defence section, the teams to take detainees elsewhere, but I don't remember the details.
Q. Who were in charge of interrogators?
A. I don't know.  I did not work in that section and we were not allowed to make any contact.
Q. In which unit did you belong to when you were located to S-21 along with the location of the new office?
A. I was put to be in the guard unit who were guarding the special prisons of S-21.
Q. Can you tell us in which group you belonged to and who was the chief of the group and how many people were in the group?
A. There were only two groups and the chief of the group was Huy, Sry and Brother Chamroeun and I don't remember others.
Q. How many people were there in your group?
A. There were more than 20 people in the group who would take turn to guard the detainees.
Q. Among the more than 20 people in your group, do you still recognize any of them or remember some of their names?
A. I remember Huy, Sry, Chamroeun, Trie. These are the people I have remembered quite well.
Q. Where did your group stay at night?
A. It was inside the wall of the prison compound and close to the place where the detainees were placed.  It's just another house next door.
Q. How many common kitchens were there for S-21 and where were they located?
A. So far as I know, there was only one kitchen, which was located next to the fire department.
Q. During each meal, were all guards coming together to have their meal or did they have separate meals?
A. At that time we did not have meals in a big group all together, only when we took our shift.  Then people could take the break to have meals.
Q. How many people would be eating all together at one time?
A. At any one given time there were about 20 people who would be eating together, maybe 15 or less, and I don't know what happened to the other teams in relation to having meals.
Q. Are you sure that S-21 got only one kitchen, and how could you obtain this information or was it just based on your own observation?
A. Certainly I went to that location personally.
Q. Did the guards who were guarding outside have to eat at a different kitchen or eat in the same place as what you did?
A. They ate together with us.  I don't know whether they ate elsewhere.
Q. What was the food ration like for staff?
A. We had sometimes three meals, sometimes two, porridge or gruel in the morning and rice in the afternoon and evening.
Q. Was the food enough or insufficient?
A. It depends.  Sometimes we had only a bowl of rice and sometimes we had less.
Q. How many people did the common kitchen accommodate at any one given time?
A. The kitchen could accommodate approximately 50 people.
Q. Did you ever see the accused ever had a meal in that kitchen?
A. No, I didn't.
Q. Do you remember how many buildings S-21 contained?
A. Earlier on I did not pay a visit to that location.  I only went to that place later on and I could see there were four buildings.
Q. Where were these special prisons located?
A. The special prisons were located to the south of the building on the road, the east-west road, and they were in the compound of the first wall.
Q. Were the special prisons made of wood or concrete?

A. They were in the form of wooden houses, concrete apartments, and sometimes there were three storeys.  Sometimes there were two storeys only and probably it is difficult to recognize it if I would see them again.
Q. So how many houses were used for the purpose of special prisons?
A. So far as I remember, there were four houses:  one wooden house, one three-storey building and one villa, and there were rooms inside the villa.
Q. How many rooms were there in each of the houses?
A. I don't remember.  The three-storey building contains two rooms in each storey and one storey had even three rooms while one storey had only one room.  So that's all I remember.
Q. Can you give us the estimation of the size of each room?  How big was it?
A. The room was about three metres.
Q. At that time were detainees placed in each room of the houses you mentioned?
A. It depends.  Sometimes the detainees would fill all the rooms. Sometimes there were fewer detainees than the rooms.
Q. What were the special prisons aimed for?
A. They were aimed to detain senior cadres, the cadres of the sector or the zone or the regiment commander or brigade commander.  It is based on my observation.
Q. What kind of information do you think you can use to support your arguments that they were senior cadres who were detained at those special prisons?

A. I believe that those senior cadres could not be detained all together in a common room.  They would be put in a separate room, one detainee in each room, and one guard would be assigned to only one individual detainee.  So this is based on my observation that I believe that they were senior cadres.
Q. If you looked at the detainees at these prisons, were they healthy when they were brought in at first?

A. Upon arrival, the detainees were healthy and I could see that there were people with medium height or tall or short, and with fair complexion or with less-fair complexion, but I was not allowed to even ask a question to the detainees.
