JUDGE THOU MONY: Thank you, the President.
BY JUDGE THOU MONY: Q. Mr. Norng Chanphal, can you confirm that when you saw a woman you claimed was your mother standing near the window, how many times did you see her?
A. When I was separated from her to the rear workshop I saw her once only from the place where I was to her on the second floor next to the window.
Q. How long was it -- I mean, from the day that you saw your mother last to the date when the woman called you to leave S-21?

A. I saw my mother before she called me to leave prison and I never saw my mother again.  And regarding the woman who called me to leave the prison, she did call me only when the situation in the prison was calm, and then the gates were open and then she would call me out.
Q. Can you tell us how many days or months between this interval -- I mean, from the date the woman -- you saw your mother and the date when the woman called you?
A. I don't remember because I was too young.  I cannot tell you whether it was soon or longer.

Q. Another question:  when you said there were Vietnamese soldiers and some Khmer people who took you from S-21 and brought you to the hospital, were you taken to the hospital the same day when you were taken from the prison?
A. Two soldiers came and cooked a meal for us and the next morning, or maybe the day after, there were more soldiers wandering around the compound and many would be visiting the prison compound.
Q. Please tell us, when you were taken to the hospital was it the same day when you were being taken from the prison?
A. Of course we were taken to the hospital right away from the prison because the kid, the young kid, was in severe condition and did not have enough food.
Q. When you stayed at the hospital how long were you there before being discharged?

A. I don't remember the date.  We went there and stayed in the hospital and I saw some wounded soldiers and civilians and the Vietnamese, and the soldiers withdrew from the hospital to be stationed at Dangkao area, and I also followed them.
Q. How long did you stay with the Vietnamese soldiers; how many months or days?

A. I don't remember the date or the duration but I did not stay long with the Vietnamese soldiers because they would be moving from one place to another.  And Grandfather Keo Chenda asked that I be taken to live with a woman who has two children and then he would put me to study at Wat Koh School.

A. I don't remember a lot and I don't know whether she was a cook.  I did not ask her any questions so I did not know her name.
Q. When you were at the kitchen did you meet two children who claimed to be the children of Cheng On, maybe the children the same age as yours?
A. I think I did not see any other children other than the five of us.  And an elderly woman was looking after five of us and I did not remember seeing other children around.

A. Of course.  I still remember and I hope I can really point to the location.

BY MR. TAN SENARONG: Q. Please look at the aerial overview of the Tuol Sleng compound. To the left, the Building A and then we have the Building B.  And another building, it was Building C, and then D.  And the building in the middle is Building E. Can you show us or indicate which building you were taken to, along with your brother and your mother, when you were first arrived?  To the east that is the entrance, the main entrance, which is the current entrance at the moment.  So that was the gate of the Tuol Sleng Museum at present. So when you first arrived, which building were you taken into?

A. I can remember that after I stepped out of the vehicle, I was taken into a building with a white wall and tiled floor, and there was a photographer and other people whom I cannot recall, and later that we turned to the right of the office. So from this map, we were taken to Building C.  Then we went upstairs, we turned left to the first floor and to the second floor, and we entered the second room on the second floor.
Q. The location where you ate and stayed, as you described to the Chamber, which building was it behind?

A. When I was there near the workshop, it was to behind Building C a little bit to the west.  It was close to the pig pen and I could see the doors of Building C, and when I looked towards Building B, behind that I saw the workshop with a lot of old people working in it.  So it was behind Building B where the workshop those old people worked in.
Q. Thank you for your description.  I have no further questions.
MR. TAN SENARONG: Thank you, Mr. President.  I will now give the floor to my international colleague.
MR. PRESIDENT: The International Co-Prosecutor, you take the floor.
MR. SMITH: Thank you, Mr. President.

BY MR. SMITH: Q. Good afternoon, Mr. Norng Chanphal. Just continuing on with my colleagues questions.  You stated that the workshop that you stayed in was behind Building C to the west.  Was there a gate to S-21 that was close to the workshop, to the outside?
A. After that building there was a fence.  It's a barbed wire fence and there were a lot of barbed wires, and after that fence then there was the workshop.
Q. And after the workshop to the outer fence of S-21 on the west side, was there a gate to get out?
A. Could you please ask me the question again?
Q. You said that the workshop was behind Building C.  To the west of the workshop, further away from Building C, was there a gate to get out of the compound of S-21?
A. Yes.  To the back, from what I could see, it was a big field and there were trees, tamarind trees and mango trees, but I was not sure if there was a gate or not.
Q. And in answer to Judge Lavergne's question, you said that you think you left from the gate at the east of S-21.  Is it possible that you left to the west of S-21 when you left with the Vietnamese?

A. Regarding the west gate, I cannot recall, but there was of course a gate to the east of the prison and there were two gates; one at the front and one at the back.  And when I boarded the truck with the Vietnamese and the Cambodian soldiers, there were a lot of people looking at me and I did not know whether the truck turned left or right when we were taken to the maternity hospital.
Q. Thank you. Can you be sure whether you left S-21 from the front gate or the back gate, or are you uncertain?

A. I am quite certain that we left through the front gate, because we were carried by those soldiers and we were put into the truck.  The only thing I cannot recall, whether the truck turned left or right.

Q. Thank you. Mr. Norng Chanphal, you were asked by the Trial Chamber whether you had any evidence to show that your father was in fact arrested and taken to S-21. I would like to show you a document.  It's E5/12/1.  ERN Number in the Khmer is 00289900, in the French 00291146, and in the English 00289887.
MR. SMITH: Mr. President, with your permission can we show the Khmer document on the screen please?
MR. PRESIDENT: The AV unit, can you show the document 00289900 on the screen?

BY MR. SMITH: Q. Mr. Norng Chanphal, this is a prison biography -- prisoner biography from S-21.  Can you look at the name of the person and can you look at the other details in relation to the person, and can you tell the Court whether that's a person that you know?

A. When I was young I did not study how to read letters but now I can read and I am sure that this is the biography of my father. There was my father's name and the names of my mother, father and the actual village commune and district, and it was also the location where I was born.  So this is the biography of my father with the correct name of my father.  And the address where he lived was the place where they saw timbers for building the railroad.  There was a sawmill there and they cut a lot of timbers in the Treng Trayeang village.
MR. SMITH: Thank you, Your Honours.  Just for the record, that's a prisoner biography from S-21.
Thank you, Mr. Chanphal, for coming to Court today.
I have no further questions, Your Honour.

MR. PRESIDENT: Next I would like to give the floor to the defence counsel, and defence counsel, if you have any questions -- my apologies, the floor is now given to the civil party lawyers.  If you have, then you can take the floor. So which group will go first; Group 1?

MR. WERNER: Good afternoon, Your Honour. We would ask leave from the Chamber.  We understand that this witness is not a civil party technically but a witness. Nevertheless, we have an arrangement on this side of the room and I'm grateful to my colleagues who agreed to have our group asking questions for half an hour.  So I would request your leave to go with that arrangement.
MR. PRESIDENT: So if you are ready, whoever has to take the question first, you can do it.  The whole civil party groups have 40 minutes.
MR. WERNER: Thank you, Mr. President.

QUESTIONING BY CIVIL PARTY COUNSEL BY MR. WERNER: Q. Good afternoon, Mr. Norng Chanphal. Let me tell you first, on behalf of my group, that we really are grateful for you to have come today and we do understand that it's not easy, and I will try to be as short as I can with my questions.  I just would like to clarify a few matters. First of all, Mr. Chanphal, you explained to us that after your father was arrested you stayed with your mother and your little brother, and then you told us that your mother basically was waiting for your father. Can you tell us if your mother inquired -- did she try to inquire about the whereabouts of your father during the time she was waiting for him?

A. During that time only I who asked for my father.  I always asked my mother when my father would come.  And my mother was very concerned that we were all waiting for the return of my father.  And my mother did not ask anybody else; she only asked those whom she knows close about my father.  And I kept asking her all the time about when my father would return.
Q. And do you know why she didn't ask anybody else at that time?
A. I did not know.  My mother was concerned or worried but I didn't know why she worried, but to me it seems she dare not ask any other people besides those close people that she knew.

Q. And then you told us -- and I just want to clarify that -- when you arrived with your mother at Tuol Sleng and you were asked about what happened to your mother, who was sick at the time, as you said, and you said -- and I quote you -- you said that, "They pushed her" -- this is your mother -- "They pushed her back and forth and she was terrified." Let me ask you this:  was your mother hit at the time you and she arrived at Tuol Sleng and the photograph was being taken?

A. I can remember that event when I got off the vehicle.  At Treng Trayeang village the people respected my parents, but when we entered Tuol Sleng she was threatened and pushed here and there, and she was photographed with a camera, and she was pushed and shouted at her to stand straight.  And at that time she was sick, she also had swollen legs, and she was pushed around.  When she almost fell down the person pulled her by the hair to stand up.  When I think of that event it seems so new, so vivid in my mind.  They slapped her and she was kicked and she fell down on the floor.  Before she could stand and make a correct posture to be photographed she was kicked.
Q. So do you feel that I can carry on with my questions -- I do not have too many questions -- or would you like for me to request the Chamber for you to take some minutes?
A. I can continue.

Q. Well, you explained to this Chamber that after you were separated from your mother you were at the rear of the workshop with a woman who was looking after the children, and then later you explained very, very clearly how many children there were once this woman had left -- at the end when the woman had left -- but it was not clear to me, during the time you were at Tuol Sleng with that woman in the rear of that workshop, how many children were there with that woman; if you can remember?
A. I can recall that there were no other children besides the five of us and that a woman was looking after us at the time. That is my recollection of the event.

Q. And, sir, just to clarify because you spoke about a woman who was looking after the children in that place, and then you spoke as well about a woman who left at the end and asked you to come with you but you didn't come.  Are we talking about the same woman?

A. Yes, the woman who looked after me was the one who asked me to go out with her, but I was afraid that my mother would be looking after me so I refused to go and I was still waiting for my mother at the rear of the workshop.
Q. And when the woman left -- and I understand that you didn't go with her -- did she leave with anyone, with any children?
A. I cannot recall.  I think I only saw her alone and then I ran back inside the prison and I did not look back.  So I didn't know, when she left, whether she left alone or with any other people.

Q. Now, I just want to clarify a few things you told the Judges. Judge Lavergne asked you if you heard anything and you told him that you heard sound.  Which kind of sound did you hear, if you can remember?  Which kind of sound was it?

A. The sound that I heard, from my recollection, it was a scream. I heard it once in a while but I was not sure whether the screaming was from the pain or not, and it was rather weak.  When I heard the scream I looked to the direction of the building where my mother was there but I did not see my mother and I only heard the screaming and I was not sure which building the screaming came from.  I think it came from the third building.

Q. And so just to clarify because of the interpretation, I just want to be completely clear, is it the position that you heard that sound more than once from time to time?  So you heard that sound several times; is that correct?

A. That is correct.  Because when I sat behind the pig pen and the workshop occasionally I heard the sound once or twice and every time I heard the sound I looked into the direction of the window where my mother was standing.
Q. And at the time you were at the rear of the workshop, looked after by that woman, did you see any prisoners?
A. I did not see any other prisoners.

Q. And then, answering a question, you said that later a worker who was a blacksmith told you that he, the blacksmith, had seen you during -- in S-21, in Tuol Sleng.  Do you remember the name of that blacksmith who told you that?

A. From what I can recall, he told me he was a shackle maker, so after the Liberation Day he told me that he made shackles at the workshop and that he saw me too during the time.  At that time I saw him from a distance but I did not go close to the workshop where he worked.  I saw some -- oh, about four old people working in the workshop.  And that person, Ta Kung, I only met him after the Liberation Day and I think he worked at the Tuol Sleng Museum after the liberation as a gardener.
Q. Just to be completely clear, is Ta Kung the shackle maker?  Is that correct?

A. Yes, Ta Kung told me when I was in the workshop -- when I was in the workshop before the Liberation Day, from a distance I saw him working in a workshop, type of blacksmith, and only after the Liberation Day when I went to visit Tuol Sleng he recognized me and he asked me and talked to me, and he had pity on me at the time and he gave me some money, and then I returned back to the orphanage.

Q. Now, so you spoke about a pile of clothes and you said that you hid in the pile of clothes, and as well in some furniture, if I understood you correctly.  Do you know anything about this pile of clothes?  Do you have any information about these clothes or not?
A. From what I can recall, they were like old clothes that were no longer used and I did not know whom the clothes belonged to.
Q. And later on were you told anything about that, if at all?

A. When I was at the orphanage for one or two years, and when I made a visit to Ta Kung, I have heard that those clothes belonged to the prisoners.  I didn't know at the time.  I didn't know who the prisoners were and I was told that, "Those prisoners were those brought to Tuol Sleng, including your mother and father." So those clothes belonged to the prisoners.

Q. Now, I just have really two or three more questions and then I will be finished. I just have a question.  You explained that you went around when the place was quiet at the end, because you are looking for your mother, and then you said that you went inside one room and you said that you saw someone lying in a bed. If you can remember, did you see any wound or anything else when you looked at that person lying in the bed?

A. I can recall that after that woman called me I refused to go, and when the situation was quiet I ran along the corridor of the first building and I saw like a male person lying on the bed.  I was not sure whether he was dead or not but I saw some flies. From the video I saw on CNN it was a dead body there on the bed. So after I saw that person I ran back to go back behind the workshop.
Q. And how did you feel at the time you were looking around and entering this room, if you can say?

A. I was so scared.  I was thinking that if when I ran there maybe the person who was lying on the bed would sit up and call me not to run everywhere.  So I was afraid and I ran back to the workshop and I stayed there at the workshop until the day the Vietnamese took me outside.

Q. My last question, sir. Just to clarify -- you explained that one of the kids died, one of the kids who were with you died, and you said that the ants were running into his mouth and his ears.  Now, taking into account the context of what you said this morning, I don't have the exact words, my understanding was that that kid died out of hunger.  Is that correct?

A. It's correct, because when they came with their mothers they were still carried by their mothers but he was left without any proper food and that kid did not or was not able to eat the gruel yet and he was left crying until he could not cry any longer. And then the ants would run into his ears and I did not know yet that the little boy died.  Only when the Vietnamese troops came that I learned from them that the kid died already.
Q. I am very grateful for your answer and your time.
MR. WERNER: I have not further questions, Your Honours.
MR. PRESIDENT: Ms. Lawyer, you take the floor.
MS. JACQUIN: Thank you, Your Honour.

BY MS. JACQUIN: Q. Good afternoon, Mr. Norng Chanphal, and thank you for being here.  I would like to put a few questions to you to clarify certain issues that you have already referred to. First of all, when you arrived in S-21, your mother was photographed.  Were you and your brother also photographed?

A. After my mother was photographed, we were not photographed. When my mother was slapped and pushed until she collapsed, I was terrified but my little boy did not know anything about this because he was still young and were playing around.

Q. The first night that you spent there you spent with your brother and mother in one room on the second floor of Building C. Were you and your mother and brother alone in that room, or were there other people with you in that room, men and/or women?
A. The room was empty, only filled with my mother, I and little brother along with the other two women.  So we were all alone in that empty room.
Q, When you saw your mother at the window from where you were behind the building, did you see her alone at the window or did you see other women with her at the window?
A. I saw only my mother alone.  I did not see the other women.

Q. I think you have tried your very best to see your mother again.  When you were looking in the direction of that building, as you were often looking in that direction, did you ever see other people at that window?
A. I looked in the direction of the window where my mother once stood, but it was the last time I saw her and I never saw her again.
Q. Did you ever see other people at that window?  Or did you never see anybody at that window?

A. The other windows were not open except the window at which my mother once stood.  And I tried to look in the direction where she once stood later on, although it was remained open, but I could not see her again.
Q. So you were by then nine years old.  You were the eldest of the five children who were there in Tuol Sleng?
A. Yes, I was the eldest one.
Q. In the daytime were you playing?  Did you have somebody taking care of you, doing things with you?  Or were you supposed to work?

A. At the rear of the building I was not supposed to walk places and I was looked after by a woman who would tell us not to go anywhere.  And I could see that the woman would have been scared of the guards too. And after I seen my mother being pushed and beaten, I felt that I myself had to mind my business too because I would be treated the same, because I noticed already that my mother would be badly treated already.

Q. And to return to that very difficult moment at the time of the liberation, when you returned into the building to look for your mother, you said that you saw corpses.  In the first building where you looked for your mother did you see people alive, dead or nobody at all?

A. After the woman who waved to me and asked me to leave, I did not go and it was quiet and I was searching for my mother and I left from the east gate to Building A and I saw people lying down on the bed.  I don't know whether the person dies or not, but he seemed to be motionless and some flies could be seen flying around.  And I did not see other.
Q. Lastly, you said that out of the five children, four left with you to Tuol Sleng, two were adopted in Germany, and then there's you.  And where did the fourth child go?

A. When we were put into the orphanage and the other were too young, they would be taken to another orphanage for baby near Calmette Hospital.  And the teacher registered them as my sister and when there was a ceremony we were allowed to meet one another and I asked those women where those sisters are gone, then they told me that the German already adopted them.  And I tried to ask for them, but I think they were too young when we were separated that I probably could not recognize her when we meet again.  And my other brother still survives and work as the driver.
MS. JACQUIN: Thank you, Mr. Norng Chanphal.
MR. KIM MENGKHY: Mr. President, I only have very few questions to be put to Mr. Norng Chanphal.
BY MR. KIM MENGKHY: Q. You said after you had been arrested and sent to Tuol Sleng were you -- were there any scars left on your body until now?
A. We were not beaten.  We had some rashes, skin rashes, and wounds because of malnutrition so we looked pale, and we were bitten by mosquitoes days and night.  And that's all.
Q. I would like to seek your clarification also. When you said you ate the mouldy gruel, how much of the gruel you consumed that -- what was it like?

A. I cannot remember.  I was so hungry that I tasted the gruel, although it tasted sour, because it turned mouldy.  And my brother and other children could not eat the gruel.  And later on we were cooked the rice and a duck was prepared for our meal. And that's all I can remember.
Q. Another question: did you have water to drink after eating the meal?
A. We made use of the water left in the broken jar -- the rain. And we saw some water taps but there was no running water.  So, in conclusion, we drank water from a leftover in the broken jar.
MR. PRESIDENT: The lawyer, you take the floor.
MR. HONG KIMSUON: Thank you, Mr. President.  I have only two questions.  Maybe a little one more, Mr. President, Your Honours.

BY MR. HONG KIMSUON: Q. Good afternoon Mr. Norng Chanphal. My first question is: during the first day when your mother, you, and your little brother were arrested by the Khmer Rouge and put on the jeep and taken to Tuol Sleng, the first day you entered that location were you given food during the first full day at the premises?

A. I don't seem to remember having been given food or anything. Because I was terrified by the way my mother was being treated while we arrived there -- you know, when they grabbed her hair and beat her.  So I did not remember about having got any food.

Q. Thank you. The lawyer asked you already about the Vietnamese troops who went to see you and that you had eaten the mouldy gruel. The next question is, when the Vietnamese troops came to rescue you at that workshop, back then were you given adequate food?

A. I could remember that I was always hungry, and I did not know whether we ate adequate food because I kept being hungry, and my little boy kept crying for food, and only if he asked that the food would be given.
Q. Thank you. Could you please think back a little bit, whether you ever went to ask for crushed rice from the kitchen?
A. I don't think I remember it.  I think I had been terrified ever after having seen my mother being beaten.

Q. The last question: you told the court clearly already that when the Vietnamese troops or the Cambodian troops came to carry you and took you to the hospital and you stayed with the Vietnamese soldiers.  The question is, when you stayed with them, were you ever taken to be photographed somewhere?

A. When I lived with the Vietnamese troops I did not go anywhere, because the Vietnamese troops would relocate several times.  And then only when Grandfather Keo Chenda learned that some orphans were being with the Vietnamese troops that he asked that we were taken to him. And when we were taken photograph we were at the orphanage already and we had good clothes and we were put to school already.
Q. Now you are not a civil party, but my question is, you -- when you applied to join as a civil party, what would be the reparation you claimed for?

A. I think because I had other commitments with my job, after I got cashed, the salary, then I watched the TV regarding the civil party application which would be closed soon.  Then I rushed to file that application, but later on I learned that it was too late, that I could only become witness rather than civil party.
Q. At that time, what would you like?
A. I would like justice for my mother, that's all -- for my parents.
MR. HONG KIMSUON: Thank you, Mr. President.  I have no further questions.

MS. TY SRINNA: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we have five minutes remaining.  However, I personally don't have any questions to be put to Norng Chanphal, but I have a request to the President.  With your leave, I may put that request to the Chamber?

MS. TY SRINNA: We would like to request that -- from the President to ask the accused to clarify the statement by Norng Chanphal when he said that he saw the corpse on the bed. So I just would like to know whether these corpses would have been one prisoner, the last prisoner among the nine left.

BY MR. PRESIDENT: Q. Mr. Norng Chanphal, you said you saw a corpse while you were looking for your mother and that the corpse was lying in Building A.  Do you remember saying that?  Can you confirm? The question is, is the corpse that attached to the chain to the bed was lying on the ground floor or on the second floor?

A. Mr. President, when I was looking for my mother and while I was crying for her, I did not hear any sound back but I saw a figure, maybe a male or female, I don't know, with a lot of flies, but he didn't look swollen.

Q. We did not want to know that anyway, but we want to know whether the corpse lied on the ground floor or the second floor because you said something already, but it is not yet clear because you told us that you were running and that you did not step on the stairs into any building.  You only could see the corpse while you were running. So the question is, did you see the corpse in Building A, in ground floor or second floor?

A. I still remember when I was running; I was running on the ground floor.  Here we can call it E-1.  Then I saw the room with the door open and a man was lying.  He was about the same age as my father, and I think that person may have not died yet although I could see flies circling around on the first floor.

MR. PRESIDENT: Please be seated.  The Chamber is now back in session. The Chamber will now give the floor to the accused to make his observations regarding the testimony of Mr. Norng Chanphal.  If possible, the accused can also respond to the request made by the civil party lawyer. There is no need for you to reveal or to acknowledge your responsibility of the crimes. We just want your observation on his testimony today.  If the accused has the observation you can take the floor.

THE ACCUSED: Mr. President, I would like to make some clarifications based on the hearing of the testimony of Mr. Norng Chanphal. Initially I would like to acknowledge that this testimony reflects the suffering, the separation of Mr. Norng Chanphal. Initially, before I saw the document of Norng Chan biography, I thought this crime was outside of S-21 and maybe Mr. Norng Chan suffered under another security office, but when I read the biography of Mr. Norng Chan with DSL0529, then I acknowledge Mr. Norng Chan died there.  And as the mother of Norng Chanphal -- I do not have any document.

So let me put the matter into two separate aspects.  First, if there is such a biography of the mother of Norng Chanphal it would prove that Mum Yaul and his sibling also died there, because at S-21 no child was spared.  However, if we cannot find such document I could conclude that Mum Yaul, the mother of Norng Chanphal, would die elsewhere.  And this person survived because of the Vietnamese soldiers and the Heng Samrin soldiers collected him and raised him up.

So these are my observations on the two separate matters.  If we can find the S-21 document on the biography of his mother, then I would accept a complete testimony of Mr. Norng Chanphal, with respect.  I do not deny it or object to any of it. I would like to now respond to the question raised by Ms. Lawyer. I would like to say that the YO-8 people, there were only four of them, not nine.  I think I saw that photo of a man lying on the bed.  I think it was in 2006 or 2007 before I came to this Court. I met a Japanese TV crew or an Italian TV crew and I was shown the photo of a person lying on the bed; it was in the big room. So whatever was said by Norng Chanphal and that the person was dead or not, I think probably the photo reflected what was seen by Mr. Norng Chanphal.  This is just my observation. And this is my response to the Chamber, Mr. President.
(Deliberation between Judges)
MR. PRESIDENT: Judge Cartwright, you take the floor.

JUDGE CARTWRIGHT: Thank you, Mr. President. The statement made by the accused has left me unsure of whether he agrees that this witness Norng Chanphal was a detainee, a child detainee at S-21 or not.  Could defence counsel advise, if necessary after consulting with the accused, whether he acknowledges this or not? Thank you.

MR. KAR SAVUTH: Thank you, Mr. President. I would seek your leave to inform you that I have discussed with my client, and my client does not recognize that Mr. Norng Chanphal who survived during the last few days in Tuol Sleng. The fact that he does not recognize this, because the measures and the regulations from Angkar were so strict that nobody would dare to object to it or that person would be dead, especially the order for the 2nd and the 3rd of January 1979. Nuon Chea himself ordered all the children, all the male and female prisoners' heads to be smashed, all of them have to be smashed, and there was no-one left at S-21 except the four people who shot the foreign journalists whose confessions were not yet extracted, and they were the only four people left.  And the accused confirms with me that nobody dared to object the order from the upper echelon. This is our response, Mr. President.  Thank you.
MR. PRESIDENT: Judge Lavergne, you take the floor.

JUDGE LAVERGNE: Again, to try to make -- to get clear about this.  The defence is saying that Mr. Norng Chanphal could not have been somebody who had survived S-21.  But is the defence also telling us that he is somebody who was never detained at S-21?  Is it these both -- are they denying both things? But, however, the accused was saying earlier on that he does not object to the content of Norng Chanphal's statement, so I'm a bit confused here.

MR. KAR SAVUTH: Your Honour, in the matter of Mr. Norng Chanphal, and as defence counsel, I still do not understand how or whether he actually lived in Tuol Sleng. And I would like Your Honour to consider: he said his mother entered S-21 and she was slapped, she was pushed around, and she was grabbed by her hair a couple of times, the photos were taken from the front, from the sides, and he was horrified.  And after 1979, he went to Tuol Sleng to look for the photo of his mother and he could not find it.  So those people who entered S-21, they were all photographed and the photographs were all there, and how come the photograph of his mother was not there? And on the second matter, the number of the people who killed -- 12,380 people who were killed there -- none of the named has the name of the mother of Mr. Norng Chanphal.  How can we believe that? This is our response, and thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.
MR. PRESIDENT: Judge Lavergne, you take the floor.
JUDGE LAVERGNE: Does the accused -- could the accused tell us what he wanted to tell us when he did not -- when he said that he did not object to Mr. Norng Chanphal's statement?

THE ACCUSED: Your Honour, I do not object to the content of the testimony of Mr. Norng Chanphal.  That he was actually a person who suffered and who separated from his father and his mother.  I do not object to that.  And before I saw this piece of document, I thought his father would have died somewhere else, at another security office, however, with this document I acknowledge that his father suffered and died in Tuol Sleng in the hand of the people at Tuol Sleng. But regarding his mother and Mr. Norng Chanphal himself, where did they suffer? I'm certain on this matter.  Therefore, if there is a piece of such document, then it is evident that if his mother was sent to S-21 then he, himself, would come along.  Or, if there is another form of similar document in the form -- for Chum Mey for S-24 to send to the rice field.  So I would acknowledge any piece of S-21 documents confirming the identification his mother.
MR. PRESIDENT: Judge Lavergne, you take the floor.

JUDGE LAVERGNE: So if I have understood correctly, what you said -- you are saying, therefore, that it is possible that, according to you, that the witness is -- that what the witness is relating does not concern -- does not relate to S-21, but to another security centre.  Is that what you are telling us?

THE ACCUSED: That's correct.  Probably his mother had suffered at other security office, or maybe his mother was sent to S-24. So we would like the Office of Co-Prosecutors to help trace down the documents.

BY MR. MOSES: Q.   Witness CBR, how did you hear about the death of President Habyarimana?

Q.   And do you remember the date you found out about the death of President Habyarimana?
A.   Yes, it was on the 7th of April, 1994.
Q.   Who was Ndugutse?
A.   He was a teacher, *************.
Q.   And what did he tell you?
A.   He was leading us during the attacks.
Q.   What did he tell you about the death of the president?

A.   He told me that the head of state had died, and that we had to avenge that death.  He told us that the head of state had been killed by the Inyenzi, and he told us that the Inyenzis were the Tutsis, in fact.
Q.   And in terms of avenging of the death of the president, did he give you any instructions on that day, the 7th of April?
A.   Yes, he gave us instructions.  He was clear in saying that we had to attack ************************, rather, who was called Ndakubana.

A.   Yes.

A.   Yes, I went there.
Q.   And why did you go there?

A.   During that period there was an IPJ called Kayishema who came into our cellule in a vehicle.  He spoke on a megaphone asking us to come to the rescue of the parish.  That is why I went to the parish.
Q.   Do you remember the date that you saw Kayishema in the vehicle?
A.   Yes, I remember the date.  The first time it was on the 14th of April .
Q.   Do you remember what day of the week that was?
A.   Yes, I remember.  It was a Thursday.
Q.   Did you recognise the vehicle that Kayishema was travelling in?
A.   Yes, the vehicle belonged to a businessman called Rinamasirabo, it was commandeered from Rinamasirabo.  Rinamasirabo, in fact, was a Tutsi.
Q.   All right, and briefly, can you describe what the vehicle looked like?
A.   It was a white Toyota.
Q.   Thank you.  Now prior to Kayishema coming around on the 14th of April, had you been given any earlier indication that there may be a decision to attack the Tutsi at -- attack the parish, sorry?

Q.   What did he tell you?

A.   On the 7th he told us to go and attack Gregoire Ndakubana and to kill the members of his family and that we should do so to avenge the death of the president who had died.  So, we went to Ndakubana’s house on the night of the 7th.  We killed two people there, and we wounded others.  In the morning the authorities from the commune came to bury the dead, because we left them on-site.  Those who had been wounded were brought to the hospital by Rinamasirabo.

Q.   I'll go back to my question because it may not have been easily understood.  Before you saw Kayishema on the 14th of April, had you been told by anyone of any plan to attack those people who were at the Nyange church?

A.   Before Kayishema arrived, Télesphore Ndugutse came on the 13th of April.  There was a meeting at the commune office.  After that, he told us that the decision was made that we had to attack the people at Nyange church and kill the Inyenzi's there, in other words the Tutsis who were there.  This was on the 13th of April in the afternoon.  He told us that he had come from a meeting of communal authorities, and at that meeting they had decided that the only choice was to kill those Inyenzis who were there.
Q.   Did he tell you of any other decisions made at that meeting?

A.   Besides what I've just told you, in other words the decision was made to kill the Tutsis, he did not tell us about any other decisions made. However, he did say that it was said, if it was impossible to kill those enemies, the Astaldi company was going to assist in doing the job.
Q.   Did he indicate whether the authorities were concerned about the people at the parish who had taken refuge there being armed?

A.   He said that during that meeting a decision had been made to identify, amongst the authorities, some of them who would go to ensure or to find out whether the refugees were armed or not, and it was decided that Kananye, who – Kananye Ruhogogongage (phonetic), who was an assistant, should go, together with Father Seromba, in order to find out whether the refugees were armed or not.
Q.   All right, if I can now take you back to the 14th of April.  You've told us how Kayishema came and visited your area where you were living.  What happened after Kayishema had left?

A.   After Kayishema's departure, Ndugutse gathered together the inhabitants of our cellule and convinced them that we must all go to Nyange, and that's what we did, we went to Nyange.  When I refer to Nyange, what I mean is the church.
Q.   And did the people who went to Nyange carry anything with them?
A.   We were carrying traditional weapons, in other words machetes, clubs and spears.
Q.   And did you go with that group to Nyange parish on the 14th?
THE ENGLISH INTERPRETER: Can the Prosecutor please repeat the question for the benefit of the interpreter?
BY MR. MOSES: Q.   Did you go with the group of people to attack at Nyange on the 14th?
A.   Yes, I left together with the group.
Q.   When you arrived at Nyange church, were there any other people there to join in an attack?

A.   Yes.  Our cellule made up a small group, and we had to wait for other people who were coming from other secteurs, especially that of Kigali. I'm referring to Kigali secteur.  Please do not confuse that with the City of Kigali.
Q.   Thank you.  Approximately how many attackers were there at Nyange on the 14th of April?
A.   Actually, on the 14th we were relatively few because we had just arrived. I would suggest that there would be about 500 to 1,000 people, so in relation to the refugees we were relatively few.
Q.   And did you attack the people who had taken refuge at the church on that day?

A.   Yes, we did launch an attack, but the gendarmes stopped us because they said we were few in number.  So Ndugutse tried to convince them to let us go ahead, even if thereby it would be seen that we were few. I must say, however, that the attack did not succeed.  The gendarmes left the place where they were.  We threw stones at the refugees and the refugees also threw stones at us, and since they were more in number than we were, we fell back and we went home.
Q.   And on your way home did you see anyone that you recognised?

A.   Are you referring to those who I was with?  I don't quite understand to whom you are referring to.  Are you referring to the group in which I was or are you speaking about any other persons I may have seen who were in the location?  Can you be a bit clearer for me?
Q.   Certainly.  Did you see any officials on the way home?

A.   When we were going back home on the 14th I didn't see any persons of authority except those who were together with us.  However, a businessman who normally lived in Kigali, one Gaspard Kanyarukiga came across our path; he spoke to Ndugutse as we went by, and he told him that he had just come back home but that he had seen some Inyenzi at Mushubati who were coming toward us, so that they could release the Inyenzis, and he was referring obviously to the Tutsis in the parish. Consequently, he was saying that we need to look for reinforcements, so that we can come back and fight these people who had just repelled us.  After that conversation, Kanyarukiga continued on his way, and Ndugutse tried to explain to us what he had discussed with Kanyarukiga.  And that's how the day came to an end.
Q.   I now ask you to focus your attention on the following day, the 15th of April.  Did anything happen on the 15th of April; that you can recall?

A.   Yes, I remember something that happened on that date.  On the 15th of April 1994 Kayishema came back on the same vehicle I referred to earlier.  He went through our cellule, which has many roads, and he said, similarly that we needed to do something at Nyange church and get rid of the enemy; in other words the refugees who were there.  He continued on to other places, and the leader of our group, in other words Ndugutse, once again gathered the people together but, in fact, we weren't very far away.  We were well aware of the plan from the day before.  Vehicles belonging to the Astaldi Company came and we got onto them.  We were transported right up to the church, and I reached there at about nine in the morning.  I realised that there were already several people who had got there from all parts of the commune.
Q.   Thank you.  In terms of the number of people who were gathering there to attack, how did they compare to the previous day, which you've spoken about, the same number, less, more?

A.   The attackers on that day were more in number than those who had come the earlier day and even those who came on the first day.  The attackers on that day would have been five to six times more in number than those who had arrived the day before.  They had encircled the location.
Q.   Thank you.  Now, after you arrived there at the Nyange parish on the th, did you see any lead -- was there anyone who was taking a lead, leaders in the community?  Did you see anyone there?

A.   The officials were there, for instance Ndahimana, the bourgmestre; was present; Kayishema, the IPJ was also there; Habiyambere, the judge; Elias Sheba Rutese (phonetic) also was there; Vedaste Muragwabugabo, assistant bourgmestre also was there; as well as Kanyarukiga.  These individuals were there in a building. Subsequently, they left that building and they went to where the priests lived, then they came back to Codekoki, but I wouldn't be able to know what they talked, because I wasn't close by them.

Later on, when they left the Codekoki building they said, "We need to launch the attack."  And we did so.  We attacked the refugees.  That's how we started throwing stones at the refugees and they did likewise. At a given point in time, we withdrew and the refugees thought that they had the upper hand so they came out to the centre at a place known as Ishoshu.  There was one Rukara, who was a reservist.  He went onto the roof of the shops and threw grenades at the refugees.  Some refugees were killed and others turned back.  Rukara came down and continued to throw grenades at the mass of refugees; at the same time there were some of them who died.  We, ourselves, continued right up to the church.  Some of the refugees went into the church and had locked the doors.  Other refugees went into the presbytery courtyard; others still were killed on the courtyard, and others were able to flee into the woods which were nearby.

Later on, when there were no more refugees left outside in the courtyard, we attacked those who had managed to enter the presbytery courtyard, but since the door leading to that courtyard was locked. We had to break it down.  And that is when the priests and the gendarmes came and they stopped us from entering the presbytery courtyard.  During this time the authorities were asking us to stop the killings, and the priests asked that the killings be stopped, because there were many dead bodies and piles of stones which we had been throwing.  He asked us to remove the debris and the stones and the dead bodies.  Kayishema was there, together with others, and they asked us to stop the killings, Kayishema and Ndugutse, I mean they went to procure vehicles to help us to get rid of the dead bodies. They found one *****************************************************************.  It was, in fact, that individual who was sent to go and contact the Astaldi officials so that the vehicles could be brought.

Q.   Witness CBR, if I can just go back a little bit, you've described how the attack took place on the 15th and how, at one stage, you went towards the priests' compound and you say that there was a priest with gendarmes there. BY MR. MOSES: Q.   Witness CBR, prior to lunch we had been talking about the events at Nyange parish and, in particular, the events on Friday, the 15th of April.  You had told Their Honours how bodies of those who had been killed during an attack had been buried in a pit.  That's where we were up to prior to the lunch break. My first question for you is, were there any further attacks on the church and the refugees in the church on that day, namely the 15th of April 1994?

A.   On the 15th, after those bodies were buried, the attacks continued. The communal police officers began to fire their weapons.  There were also reservists who were shooting inside the church.  They were shooting through the windows of the church.  This is near the bell tower and near the door, which was right near the tower.  And so some of the refugees, who were inside the church, tried to move away from that part of the church and gathered in a different part of it.  And later on the assailants brought a pump and they started to spray that part of the church with gasoline.  I'm talking about the main facade of the church.  Someone went onto a ladder and attempted to spray gasoline inside the church as well, and then they started the fire. They used dried banana leaves to start the fire, and they tried to burn the main door, the front of the church, as well as the windows. Now, regarding the refugees inside the church, they were trying to protect themselves.

They used dust to try to put out the flames. There were also blankets that they used to try to put out those flames, but sometimes the blankets themselves caught on fire.  It was a confusing situation.  They shot again at the refugees and the fire had opened a hole in the door.  After that, they brought in dynamite to try to destroy the church.  But, in the end, they were unsuccessful.  They tried to blow up the church with dynamite and they put sticks of dynamite into the church, but they were unable to destroy it.  And so, after that, they decided to delay the attack until the next morning.  In fact, they had run out of ammunition.

Among the attackers, there were people who came from Kibilira commune. They had just arrived on site.  Regarding those persons who had just arrived, a decision was made that they should stay on-site to make sure that the refugees couldn't run away.  They said that the bourgmestre wasn't there, and he was in charge of the ammunition.  He had gone to a burial of an important person, a doctor who had died, and he was related to that doctor.  So he went to that burial ceremony for that person who it was said was killed by the Inyenzis. So we withdrew and the people from Kibilira remained on-site.  When I left I heard Ndugutse and Kayishema say that they were going to look for some kind of reward to give to those assailants who were going to stay on-site.
Q.   Thank you.  Can I now focus your attention on the following day, that is Saturday the 16th of April?  Did you return to Nyange church on that day?
A.   Yes, I returned on the 16th.
Q.   If I can just interrupt you there, please, approximately what time did you go to the church on that day?
A.   Do you mean on the 16th?
Q.   That's correct.

A.   I arrived very early in the morning between 6 and 7, but of course, I wasn't wearing a watch.  I'm only making an estimate.  Once again, other people were already there when I arrived, and those present on that day were larger in number than those found there on the 15th, the previous day.
Q.   Thank you.  Did you see any people in authority who were present there on that day, namely Saturday the 16th?

A.   Yes, authorities were there.  The bourgmestre was there, namely Ndahimana.  Kayishema was also there, he was the IPJ or the police inspector; Joseph Habiyambere was there, a businessman; Kanyarukiga was there; Telesphore Ndugutse, the teacher; and the head of the MRND was there.  Also the head of the Kivumu Popular Bank was present. Vedaste Murangwabugabo was also there and he was an assistant bourgmestre.  Once again, those people went into the presbytery courtyard and then they came out.  That is when the bourgmestre, Kayishema, went close to the church and opened fire on the church itself.  But in the meantime, the priest stayed in the presbytery.  I didn't see him.  So they tried to shoot at those people, but they were unsuccessful.  Then a decision was made to bring machines that had been used the previous day.  They had been brought back.  So Kayishema was in charge of getting the machines.  There was another vehicle belonging to the Astaldi company and then another vehicle, but I don't know where that came from.  They were transporting more attackers to launch more attacks on the church.

So the machinery arrived, and they began to destroy the church, but I should point out that I do not know who gave the order to begin to destroy the church.  I saw the machines at work.  They started to destroy the building at about ten o'clock in the morning.  The walls started to come down on top of the refugees who were inside the building.  At about 4 p.m. or perhaps 5 p.m., the tower came down.  It was the last thing to come down. When I left the area they were sorting through the bodies, sorting it from the debris that was there.  They had to bury a newly dug pit, and that pit was just behind the church.  So I was leaving, and at that point they were sorting out the bodies from the bricks and debris that had fallen onto the courtyard.  A vehicle loaded the bodies and went to dump them into the pit that had been dug.  This is what I know about that specific day.

BY MR. MOSES: Q.   Thank you, Witness.  If I can just go back a little bit and ask you a couple of details regarding the evidence you've just given.  On that day, namely, the 16th of April, did you see any priests?
A.   I haven't entirely understood your question.  Could you please repeat it for me, thank you?
Q.   On the day that the church was bulldozed, did you see any priest, any of the priests -- priest or priests from Nyange parish?

A.   On the 16th, I saw Seromba in the morning, and only in the morning. I didn't see him after that during that day.  Besides him, I didn't see any other priests.  However, on the 15th when there were the dead bodies lying on the ground, there were priests I saw, but I don't know where they came from or who they were and I saw them arrive to that site.  Their names were Father Nturiye, and Kayiranga.  I saw both of them arrive, but I did not see them after that.  I saw them when they arrived, not to ever see them again.  That is what I have to say about the priests.
Q.   You say that you saw Seromba on the morning and only on the morning of the 16th.  Where did you see him and what, if anything, was he doing?

A.   When I saw him, when the authorities were coming out of the courtyard from the presbytery, he was with them.  He was standing close to the door where he always stood and, in fact, I didn't see him do anything, nor did I hear anything about him.  I did hear something for the first time on that Friday, and only on that Friday.
Q.   All right.  Now, you have spoken about a bulldozer being used to destroy the church.  Did you know or recognise the driver or drivers of that bulldozer?

A. Those were the people operating those machines.  Now, regarding the truck drivers, I do not know who they were.
Q.   Were there many attackers near the bulldozers as they carried out their work?
A.   On that day, the 16th, there were many people, more than on the 15th. There were so many people.  The crowd was so dense that there was even a risk of suffocation.
Q.   Now, you spoke about the tower of the church being the last part of the church to be destroyed.  Were you able to see any people who were refugees in the tower?

A.   Yes, there were refugees in the tower.  I don't know how they got there, but the fact remains that they went into the tower, and from the tower they were even throwing stones.  I have no idea, however, how they got into the tower, how they gained access into it.  I recognised one person in fact; Charles Kagenza was his name.  However, I cannot tell you how he got in and how they were able to survive because I saw him after the war; he was alive.  I have no idea how he survived.
Q.   Thank you.  Now, had you lived in the commune for all your life, the same commune?
A.   Yes, that is correct.  I've always lived in my commune and I only left it after I was arrested and imprisoned.
Q.   In your opinion, who were the most important people in the commune?

A.   According to what I saw in the commune I lived in, the people who seemed the most influential and important, those who had the respect of the population included the bourgmestre; the judge was also an important person; the police inspector; the IPJ was an important person; the priest was also an important person within the community; and then some rich businessmen who were important.  These people had the respect of the commune.  Now, there are other categories of persons who were also influential; otherwise, the persons that I have just listed were respected by the population and the population listened to them.

Q.   Thank you.  Now, you have spoken about having seen a priest by the name of Seromba on the Friday the 15th, and also on Saturday, the 16th of April 1994.  Had you seen that person prior to the 15th of April ?

A.   Before the 15th of April I had never seen him.  Even though I was a Christian and a Catholic, I didn't normally go to mass.  This is because we had been unable to have children and, in truth, I did not attend mass.  I was not a practising Christian; I, rather, went to witch doctors because, as I have told you, we were unable as a couple to have children.

Q.   Thank you.  Now, you have told us, however, that you saw him, Seromba, on two separate occasions.  I know it has now been more than ten years, but do you think you could recognise Seromba if you saw him today in Court?
A.   As you rightly said, it was ten years ago, but I can try and see if I can recognise him if I were to be given the opportunity to meet him even if it was a long time ago since I last saw him.

Q.   Perhaps if you could stand up, and have a look around the courtroom and tell Their Honours if you recognise anyone that resembles the priest who you saw on the 15th and 16th.  Perhaps if you just stand up.
A.   Are you talking about this courtroom, Mr. Prosecutor?
Q.   Yes.  If you could stand up where you are in the witness box --

A.   I have a problem with my sight.  I shall try and look around.  I do think it's that person over there, the second person from the end, that is, the person to my left.  So maybe this man occupying the first position and -- I'm speaking about the one in the second place.
Q.   Well, do you see there are, in fact, three people sitting in that row?  Is the first one, the one in the middle, or the one on the end that you're pointing to?
A.   I'm speaking about the one who is in the middle; in other words, the second person.  Whatever side you begin from, it is the second person.
MR. MOSES: Your Honours, I ask that the record reflect that he did point to the Accused, Seromba.  Thank you.
BY MR. MOSES: Q.   Witness, finally, are you currently a prisoner in Rwanda?
A.   Yes, I am in prison.
Q.   And have you admitted any charges in Rwanda, and if so what have you admitted to doing?

A.   Yes, I have made a guilty plea.  I personally killed two people, but I also participated in other attacks during which other people killed others -- attacks during which I didn't kill anyone.  If someone was killed at a location where I had been, I admitted to being there. This was a period of war.  We would leave our homes with the intent to kill; that was the only objective.  We had been told that it was important, indispensable even, to look for the enemy and that the enemy was none other than the Tutsi, and that was the enemy who had to be killed; therefore, it had been necessary that I go along with the others with that objective in mind.  Consequently, I was obliged to kill.

Even when the attackers left before me, they would come and look for me because in my family there were Tutsis; we had had intermarriage with Tutsi families.  And so I was protecting them and, yet, I was supposed to accompany the killers.  I was ordered to kill and I did so.  I obeyed the orders.  At a given point in time, we were placed in detention so that we could kill the people we had been protecting.  I was told that a document was found in the home of my brother-in-law who had been hiding in my home.  In the beginning I was involved in the attack.  And since my younger brother was armed with a gun, I was afraid that maybe he could attack us.  And in order for us not to flee from our duties, we were placed under detention and we had to kill these people whom we had been trying to protect.

First of all, they had to place us in detention.  My younger brother who was a soldier and who had a gun was also placed under detention, he was placed in custody.  At the time when they came to arrest us, I was able to escape; however, the following day there was an attack on our home and those people were killed.  So, in brief, if I participated in those killings, including those at Nyange, it was in order for me to be able to protect people who were related to me by marriage.  Even at the church there were people whom I protected and to whom I tried to supply foodstuffs.  So the allegations made against me exist, and there are situations where I had wanted to kill, other people got there before me.  I therefore have to incline to any rulings made by the court.
Q.   Thank you.  Now, have you been sentenced in Rwanda for your -- the crimes that you have admitted?
A.   No.  No, I have not been tried; therefore, I have not come to any sentencing.
Q.   Yes, thank you.  Would you please answer any questions that my friends might have for you.
A.   Thank you.
