A.   The next morning, that morning, they didn't let us go to the toilet at all, because you could see that there were a lot of bodies in the compound in front of Room Number 3.  So that they didn't allow us to go out anywhere.  After that, a truck came.  First, a small truck came from the local utility company to pick up the dead and then, the guards really laughed because they had sent them this vehicle, and there was so many bodies.  It was a small truck that you couldn't even load ten people on to.  So then this small truck went back, and a trailer truck entered the Keraterm compound.  It was parked roughly near Rooms 1 and 2, and then the bodies began to be loaded.
Q.   Do you know who was loading the bodies on to the trailer truck?

A.   I know one man.  The people from Room Number 3 were supposed to do the loading.  I don't know why they couldn't do it.  Probably some of them were quite tortured.  Some of them were sick.  And they asked:  "Is anybody willing to volunteer to do this, people who are not horrified or afraid of such things?  So who is willing to come and help us with the loading?"  And they promised that those who helped would be returned to the cells.  And then one man from my room volunteered.
Q.   What happened then?

A.   After that, all the dead were loaded, all the wounded were also loaded, all those who were wounded that night.  And also, 15 fit, healthy men, were also put on the trucks allegedly for unloading of the bodies since the truck was covered with tarpaulin, the tarpaulin was closed, and the truck left the camp, going in the direction of Kozarac.
Q.   Did you talk to one of the people that had loaded the bodies on to the trailer truck?
A.   Yes, with the man who volunteered, and they really did return him to the cell.
Q.   Did he tell you how many bodies he had loaded?
A.   I think that there was talk about 128 dead bodies.  We, ourselves, could count about 45 wounded and 15 healthy men.
Q.   Did the truck leave the Keraterm camp that day?
A.   Yes, yes.
Q.   Were any of the people, the injured, or the 15 healthy, that you saw get on that truck, did you ever see or hear of them being alive again?
A.   No.
Q.   Do you recall an incident that happened a day or two after the Room 3 shooting involving the commander of the camp?

A.   Yes, I do.  That was a day or two later, after the massacre.  The men from Room Number 3 were driven out of their room and ordered to line up -- in fact, to lie down on the ground on their stomachs on the turf outside Room Number 3 with their hands behind their necks and sticking their heads as deep down into the grass as they could.  The then commander of the camp was there at the time, the warden, holding a rifle in his hand, and he was surrounded by a couple of guards.  Those men were told that whoever moved would be finished, gone.  The warden of the camp raised his rifle and seemed to be playing with it until he actually fired a shot in the direction of the people lying on the ground. Later on, one of the guards took out his pistol, walked among those people who were lying down, and fired a shot in the direction of somebody's head.
Q.   Were you able to see what happened to that person?  Did you actually see him being shot in the head?
A.   Well, from that distance, I can say that the guard was right next to the man, so the barrel of his gun must have been no more than 40 centimetres away from the person's head.

Q.   I want to go back to -- you were telling us about when the men from Brdo who were brought to the camp in late July were beaten before the massacre.  Was there anything else done to those men to humiliate them that you saw?
Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

A.   At one point, I mustered up all my courage to look outside, and I saw people naked from the waist down.  And half of them were standing, and half of them were kneeling.  And they were positioned in such a way as if engaged in intercourse.
Q.   These people that were naked that you saw were the prisoners from Brdo?
A.   Yes.  All of them were from Room -- from Cell Number 3.
Q.   I want to move on now to the day that the camp closed.  Can you tell us -- before I move on to that, what was the name of the camp commander that you referred to earlier?
A.   Commander Sikirica.
Q.   What happened on the day the camp closed?
Q.   Do you know who was living in that house in August of 1992, the ethnicity of that person?
A.   Until August 1992, it was the property of a Muslim man, that house that remained.
Q.   And then what happened?

A.   Not far from that house, there was another house, and I think that that was the only Serb who was living in Stari Grad.  And I heard -- I didn't see it myself -- that he wouldn't let them demolish that house because he demolished his own house because this other house was in a better condition.  So he moved into that other house.
Q.   You mentioned people being arrested and taken to Omarska and Keraterm.  When do you recall first hearing about the Omarska and Keraterm camps?
A.   Practically that same day.  We heard about it very quickly, that people were taken away.  We heard that on that same day.  And then shortly after we found out where they were, at which location.
Q.   Do you recall an incident that happened at Hambarine?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Hambarine.  What did you recall hearing on the radio about the incident at Hambarine?

A.   I heard that there was an incident at Hambarine at a checkpoint and that three or four Serb soldiers were killed there.  And after that, again, we heard an ultimatum over Radio Prijedor that the population of Hambarine had to hand over a certain person because of that incident, as the main culprit for that incident.
Q.   Now, at that time did you go to an area near Hambarine, another village in the area?
A.   Yes.  The next day, I went to Rizvanovici, which is more or less in the same position.  It's a village close to Hambarine.
Q.   Did Rizvanovici and Hambarine constitute two of about four Muslim villages that were known in this general area as the "Brdo" area?
A.   Yes, yes.
Q.   When you were in Rizvanovici, what did you hear after going there? What happened?
A.   I heard -- I'm sorry, you mean did I hear how the incident came about or...?
Q.   Well, let's go -- were you aware of an attack?  Tell us about the attack.

A.   When I went up there, I heard from the local population how this incident happened.  There was a checkpoint set up there by Muslims.  Since the Prijedor-Ljubija Road passed through Hambarine, so there were always unfamiliar armed people in vehicles passing through.  And since they simply felt that this wasn't all right, they began to check the vehicles that were passing through there.  And at one such check, they say that there were -- they said that there were five armed Serb soldiers in one vehicle.  And when they wanted to check their IDs, the Serbs wouldn't allow that, and they started firing from the vehicle.  They returned fire, and we heard information that four were killed and one person was captured there.
Q.   What was the response of the authorities after that incident?

A.   Well, they immediately demanded that a certain man be handed over, as I've already said.  And that the population of Hambarine -- in fact, the population of the entire Brdo -- surrender whatever weapons they had.
Q.   Just to be clear, the person that they demanded surrender is Mr. Aliskovic.  Is that correct?
A.   Aliskovic, yes.  The first name is Aziz.
Q.   Did the people in the Brdo region surrender their weapons, any or all of the people surrender their weapons?
A.   Not that day.
Q.   What happened?
A.   Then Serb forces started shelling Brdo.
Q.   How did you find out about the shelling?
A.   Well, I was up there myself.
Q.   What did you see or hear?
A.   There was not much you could see, but shells were falling all around us.  We were hiding in a basement, and we could hear the shells. We saw a couple of locations where they fell.
Q.   What did you do after the -- when the shelling slowed down?
A.   In the intervals between rounds of shelling, we found cases and empty shell cartridges scattered about the place.
Q.   Could you tell from -- did you have any idea what kind of weapons were being used?

A.   Well, from our earlier experience from the JNA, and there were several of us who had done our military duty, we concluded that those were tanks and mortars doing the shelling, although we couldn't see them.
Q.   The next day, did you go back to your neighbourhood near Prijedor town, through Biscani?
A.   Yes, I returned home.
Q.   Why did you go up to -- first of all, did you take part in any of the fighting or any fighting in the Brdo area?
A.   No, no, I didn't.
Q.   Were you ever a member of any militia or armed resistance group?
A.   No.  No.
Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
Q.   Why did you leave your neighbourhood and go to Rizvanovici?
A.   Simply because my house was surrounded by Serb homes, and my neighbours were Serbs.  And I thought I would feel more comfortable and safer up there.
Q.   Did you have family in Rizvanovici?
A.   Yes, because that's the place where we originally come from.
Q.   Were you arrested?
A.   Yes, in the month of June.

Q.   Would it be correct to say, then, that Hambarine was in the end of April -- excuse me, around the end of May, around the 25th of May, and you were in your neighbourhood in Prijedor town until the 18th of June?
A.   Yes, later when I returned from Rizvanovici, I was at home all the time.
Q.   Why did you stay at home all the time?
A.   Because I didn't know where to go.
Q.   Where you afraid to travel around Prijedor?
A.   It was impossible to travel anywhere.
Q.   You're saying that based upon the propaganda that was on the media at that time -- that was in the media?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Do you recall the 30th of May, 1992?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Were you home that morning, and if so, can you tell us what you remember?
A.   On the 30th of May, people used different names to describe it, but it was the Muslim attack on Prijedor, a group of armed Muslims and Croats on that day attacked Prijedor.
Q.   What was your experience?  What did you see, hear, and experience?

A.   I was woken up very early in the morning by blasts, explosions. We got up.  And I saw that the explosions were coming from the direction of the town.  And close to the hotel, I could see that after the explosion, I could see black smoke rising.
Q.   Did you hear shooting for some period of time that morning?
A.   Yes, you could hear shooting.
Q.   From where you lived, were you able to see Stari Grad?
A.   Yes.  It was right across the River Sana, and I could see it very well.
Q.   After the attack was over, did you hear any announcements on the radio regarding anyone marking their house?

A.   Yes.  That day, since the only sort of -- source of information, the only way we could find out approximately what was going on was to listen to Radio Prijedor, because we couldn't listen to anything else.  So that day, in the course of that day, there was an order that all non-Serbs had to put up white flags on their houses.  And this is what I also did.
Q.   Was it explained where you got a white flag?  What did people use for a white flag?
Q.   Can you describe what kind of orders were given to the population over the radio.

A.   First of all, that day, we heard an announcement.  It was a decree by the new authorities that they had taken over because the old authorities were not functioning.  It couldn't go on any more like that. And more or less, the proclamation was something to that effect, that they had taken over power in order to have a better life in our municipality.
Q.   When you say "they had taken over power", was it identified who was now the power in Prijedor?
A.   Yes.  Yes.  It was the Serb authorities.
Q.   Was it clear in these orders who among the -- when you say the Serb authorities, was there an institution or body that was named as the supreme authority?
A.   Yes, at that time there was already talk about a Crisis Staff.  I know that the Crisis Staff took power.  That's what they started to call themselves.
Q.   Was there a curfew ordered?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Did you hear any orders for the surrender of weapons?

A.   Yes, we did hear about that.  But I don't know when.  In any case, it was after the 30th of April when the proclamation started.  And one of those proclamations was to surrender the weapons.  But I don't know how long it was after this event.
Q.   Do you recall these orders for the surrender of weapons?  Were they directed to all the citizens of Prijedor or were they directed to particular citizens or particular areas?
Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
A.   It basically was for all citizens of Prijedor, non-Serb citizens, meaning Muslims, Croats, and others.
Q.   Were the orders for surrender directed to the entire municipality, or were they directed to particular neighbourhoods, over the course of various periods of time?
A.   In the beginning -- well, this applied to the territory of the entire municipality.  Later, the proclamations applied to certain parts or certain areas of the town and various units.
Q.   Did you hear anything on the media, the radio- or I don't know if you were able to watch TV or not- anything regarding that you considered propaganda?
A.   From that day on, everything was propaganda, both on the radio and on television.
Q.   Can you give the Judges some examples of things you recall hearing that you considered were inflammatory?

A.   Yes.  In any case, for example, they used terms such as "mujahedin," "Ustashas," and other derogative names.  They didn't call us any more by our proper names; they called us Green Berets and so on and so forth.
Q.   By the way, what did you do?  Did you have a weapon as a member of the reserve police?
A.   Yes.
Q.   What did you do with your weapon?
A.   I returned it to the police station.
Q.   If you were a Serb at that time living in Prijedor and listening to go the media that was going on at that time, how would you have felt about your non-Serb neighbours?

A.   Well, after all that I had seen on TV before and after the camp, at that time I wasn't able to watch television and listen to the radio. After all of my troubles, perhaps if I had been a Serb and had seen a Croat or a Muslim on the street, I would have shot him, too.  I don't know.
Q.   At that time, did you see Stari Grad, in August of 1992?

A.   I saw the area where Stari Grad was, because Stari Grad wasn't there any more.  It was the site of it, but now it was a green -- a grassy area, completely cleared, no buildings.  And in the middle, there was only one restaurant which was there before the war.  It was called Lovac, "the hunter," and it was the property of the hunters' association, hunting society, in Prijedor.  And then a little bit further away from the Lovac, there was one small house.  So these were the only two buildings standing in the Stari Grad.
A.   Anything white from the house, a sheet, any fabric, any object from the house.
Q.   Did life change after the Muslim attack?
A.   Yes, yes, drastically.
Q.   Can you describe what life was like living in Prijedor, after that day?

A.   That day, the concentration camps were opened.  Already on that day, certain parts of town had all the men -- all the male population from those parts of town transferred to the Omarska camp.  My wife's brother also was taken away.  So after that day, there were daily arrests and people were being taken to camps.
Q.   Did you see Stari Grad?  You mentioned you can see Stari Grad from your house.  Did you see any damage to Stari Grad after that day?
A.   That same day, I saw one of the first buildings to burn, the one that you could see most clearly.  And that was the old mosque in the Stari Grad, in the old part of town.
Q.   Now, we're going to come to some of your experiences in the camps. Did you return, though, to your house near Stari Grad before leaving Prijedor?
A.   Yes, I was released from the camp, and I went home.
Q.   Was that in August of 1992?
A.   Yes.

A.   On that morning, when I got up, the workers informed me, the workers going to work informed me, that there was a lot of soldiers in the town, more than usual.  And various points -- checkpoints were established in town.  A worker told me that she had been stopped ten times.  "The soldiers were there at the checkpoints, and I could hardly make it to work.  I don't know what is going on."  I said to her:  "Well, we will probably work anyway, open up the restaurant.  I suppose someone will come to have some coffee or fruit juice."  I didn't take the situation seriously. This was early.  This was around 7.00 in the morning.  Then I went down.  I went to my house in the main pedestrian area, and my restaurant was across from there.  And there, I saw many armed soldiers in town. They were carrying guns, weapons.  They were acting in a fairly -- there were posters throughout town.  They were not acting very respectful.

The radio stated that power had been taken over by the SDS, and this is what I saw happening.  At first, I was shocked.  In the proclamations which were put up throughout the town, posters were, in fact, put up, and the local radio station kept repeating this, that the SDS had taken over power because it could no longer watch the SDA lead the municipality to economic disaster, to further problems.  And the SDA could not resolve all those problems, and that is why the SDS took over power to make life better for the population, to improve the economic situation.  And this was repeated on the radio and on the various proclamations in town. Then a Crisis Staff was established.  This was rather a cynical thing.  The SDA itself did not hold power on its own in Prijedor.  The SDA had shared power with the SDS.  It also had a part in the power of Prijedor.  And to say that the SDA alone led the municipality to economic disaster was both ridiculous and cynical.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, in that last answer, you mentioned about proclamations and posters.  Could you very briefly say what you saw in them and what these proclamations were?

A.   Well, listen, there was a proclamation issued to the residents of Prijedor.  I have to say that ten years have passed since, and I can't remember what it said exactly in this proclamation.  But here is the gist of it:  That the SDS had taken over power because it was unable to simply watch how the SDA and the Muslims led the municipality into economic disaster, heavy economic losses, and et cetera, et cetera.  And it was signed underneath by the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality.  It was quite strange for me to see this Crisis Staff mentioned for the first time.  It was unusual for me.  I have to say that the situation in town was also quite unusual.  There were many checkpoints with troops on them, on all high-rise buildings, there were soldiers walking on rooftops.  So I saw that the situation was serious, and that this takeover of power, regardless how it was said on the radio constantly that the taken over without a single bullet, it still heralded bad times to me.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you spoke about a Crisis Staff.  Did you get to know or was it announced as to who the people who were involved in the Crisis Staff, or who held posts in the Crisis Staff?

A.   Never officially.  Never officially.  It was never announced who held positions in the Crisis Staff.  However, we knew after the municipality of Prijedor was created, the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, we knew and it was publicly announced that people who held leading positions were in the Crisis Staff.  Because this Serb municipality of Prijedor was in a dormant state until the takeover of power.  Once the power had been taken over, the president of the municipality or the president of the Crisis Staff was the post awarded to Milomir Stakic. This was not publicly spoken about, but we all knew it. And the names of other people who were involved in it were never publicly announced.
Q.   Did you -- are you aware as to what happened to the people who held posts in the legally elected government and the other members after the takeover?

A.   Well, these people remained in town.  I think the first day following the takeover was Saturday or Sunday.  So, a day or two after the takeover, these people, not knowing any better, went to their offices. And since in front of every institution, every enterprise, there were armed soldiers guarding the entrance, they turned back these people.  And Mr. Cehajic was turned back as well.  It was circulated for a long time afterwards that Mr. Nedzad Seric was turned back from the Court building. He was the president of the Court and a judge for a number of years.  He was a very respected man, because his father, his late father, used to work in the municipal administration as well.  He was a very popular man, a prominent man in town.  And when they turned him back from the Court building, when he was turned back from the reception of the Court building after he was not allowed to go into his office, people started whispering about Nedzad Seric being turned back.  Everybody condemned this, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats alike.

Nedzad Seric [Realtime transcript read in error "Ceric"], I see his name is spelled here.  It should be S-E-R-I-C. So this was a shock, a total surprise that these people were turned back.  And a majority of Croats and Muslims were turned back from their offices.  They were sent back home.  They were not allowed to enter their offices.

Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you said that you got to know about the Crisis Staff that was functioning after the takeover in 1992 in April.  Who were the people who were in the Crisis Staff according to your information and what is your source?

A.   I think as far as the main people are concerned, their names were publicly known.  The president of the Crisis Staff was Milomir Stakic. The president of the executive council was Dr. Kovacevic.  In that Crisis Staff, there was also a man who was the secretary of the secretariat of the interior, which was in fact the police, and that was Simo Drljaca.  So the people who were involved in the Serb municipality of Prijedor who had been established two months prior to that were involved in it.  So we knew it, as far as we could tell, Slobodan Kuruzovic was a member of the Crisis Staff.  He was a teacher before the war, and he spent a lot of time on the front in Croatia and later became the commander of the Territorial Defence.

So these were the main members of the Crisis Staff, and it was rumoured that there were some military representatives in the Crisis Staff as well, commander of the garrison, Radmilo Arsic, and somebody called Zeljaja. And these were the people who held the most prominent posts. We simply knew them to be people who were appointed by the Serb municipality of Prijedor to various offices within that municipality.
Q.   Did you have information as to when this Crisis Staff met or where they met?

A.   Based on our information, they met at the municipal building.  I don't know where else they could have.  Because Milomir Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff, and at the same time, he was president of the municipality.
Q.   Did you hear any announcements or any proclamations made by the Crisis Staff after the takeover?
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, under the multiparty system, what are the other parties which is prominent in Prijedor during that time?

A.   After these first multiparty elections, the greatest, the largest parties that had their deputies in the Municipal Assembly, in addition to my party which was a small party and had only one assemblyman, so these larger parties were the SDA.  That was the largest party.  It had 30 assemblyman.  Then we had Serbian democratic party known as SDS, which had 28 assemblymen.  And there was also, if I can call it that, former socialist party which had something around 13 assemblymen.  And then there was also the party called the Reformist Forces, that was the party of Ante Markovic.  It had some 10 assemblymen.  There was the HDZ there as well. It was a Croatian party, Croatian democratic party.  It had only 2 assemblymen. So there was another party.  It was called Democratic Socialist Alliance.  I think it had 5 assemblymen.  There was a total of 90 assemblymen in the party, and eight political parties represented there. I'm sorry, 90 assemblymen in the assembly.
Q.   Now, you described the composition of the Municipal Assembly. Could you very briefly say, the prominent members, specifically in the party of the SDA under the multiparty system?
A.   Do you mean the names, the individuals who represented that party?
Q.   Yes, please.

A.   Well, there was professor Muhamed Cehajic, who was later elected as the president of the Municipal Assembly.  He taught in the secondary school.  Then there was a man called Music, Ilijas.  He was a professor of physics.  He taught at another secondary school for economic education. Then, there was also Meho Tursic, who used to be the president of the Municipal Assembly, and later on he was a director of the public accounting office.  There was also a man called Talundzic, a man called Sarajlic.  And there were a lot of people who represented the top leadership of that party.  The chairman of the party was a physician, Mirza Mujadzic.  There was a lot of people involved actively in the SDA. There was a man called Nijaz Kapetanovic.  There were a lot of people.
Q.   Do you recall the name of one Mr. Becir Medunjanin?

A.   Yes, I apologise.  I cannot remember all of them.  There were so many of them.  Becir Medunjanin was a teacher at the elementary school, Rade Kondic in Kozarac.  He was married to a woman in Prijedor.  He lived in Kozarac.  I know his family personally.  He had two sons.  He and his wife both worked at the school in Kozarac up until those multiparty elections.  I knew him superficially as a teacher in that school.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, now that you have given the names with regard to the people in the SDA, could you also recall the names of the prominent people in the Serbian party, the SDS during that time.

A.   In the Serbian democratic party the prominent members were Simo Miskovic who was chairman of the party at that time.  Then Srdjo Srdic, then Milomir Stakic.  Then Dr. Kovacevic.  Slavko Budimir.  There was also a large number of people there who were active in that party.  There was a man called Timarac, who is deceased now from Omarska. He was also an assemblyman like Srdjo Srdic.  There were assemblymen in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, you described the composition and the amount of -- the number of members which are selected to the Municipal Assembly. Could you describe whether you knew or whether you were aware of any agreements between the two -- three main parties before the elections?

A.   Well, it was a public secret that those three parties as we used to call them, three national parties, that represented their own peoples. So by this, I mean the SDA, the SDS, and HDZ.  So it was rumoured that an agreement has been signed between them specifying that they will create a coalition, some kind of an informal alliance to divide power among them. This was an agreement before the elections.  I think that in the beginning it was honoured in Prijedor as well.  The people who held the positions were the people from the HDZ, the SDS, and SDA.  And even though the HDZ was a small party that had only two assemblymen, it was a coalition partner in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.  Together these three parties had 60 out of 90 assemblymen, and the rest of the political parties were the so-called opposition, and they had a total of 30 assemblymen among them, and I was one of them, representing a small political party.
Q.   What was the relationship that your party had with the other three main parties before the election and after the election?

A.   My political platform, the representatives of my political party, were all entrepreneurs, people representing those who were engaged in some kind of private business activity.  Although I have to say that entrepreneurs were represented in other political parties as well, but I, myself, and my political party, believed that we would best be able to protect our interests in a multi-party election.  This is why we decided to participate in the elections.  Their attitude towards us as a small marginal party in view of the number of our deputies was the same as the attitude towards all other political parties who were in the opposition. We didn't count much, so to speak, and we did not participate in the allocation of functions in the assembly.  This was done by these three main political parties.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, before we go to another area, could you also tell briefly the -- how the allocations were done after the elections?  Who held what post after the elections?

A.   Well, as I have already said, the SDS and the SDA, together with the HDZ, which had only two assemblymen but was participating in the division of power, because this was their previous agreement, they between themselves agreed to divide and allocate the functions among them.  So this allocation of functions in the assembly was agreed upon between them before.  They came out with this in the assembly, and that was adopted.  I don't know whether between themselves there were frictions regarding this allocation, but the most important position, the president of the municipality, was awarded to the SDA, because that party had the largest number of the assemblymen.  And it was logical for that party who had the largest body of voters and the largest number of assemblymen, it was logical for them to be given this position of the president of the municipality.  That was quite normal.

The position of the vice-president, which was second ranking position, was allocated to the SDS and Milomir Stakic, president of the executive council, as an office that had to coordinate contacts with enterprises, with various departments and divisions of the Municipal Assembly, was given to Dr. Kovacevic, also a member of the SDS.  Becir Medunjanin became the secretary of the municipal secretariat for people's defence.  This is what this body was called.  Therefore, Medunjanin became the secretary of the secretariat.  So these most important positions were allocated between these two most important political parties, with HDZ be given some smaller functions so that everybody was happy. And they had this proposal, or rather they came out with this proposal, and if I remember correctly, we voted on it and adopted it and this is how it became implemented.

Q.   Now, in that previous answer, you said the most important position, the president of the assembly, was given to the person from the SDA, Mr. Cehajic.  Could you explain what functions did the president of the Municipal Assembly perform under that multi-party system?

A.   Well, in that kind of system, I have to say that this was inherited from the previous regime, and unlike what we have today, the president of the municipality was a complete authority.  He not only chaired the assembly sessions, but was also superior to everybody else in the municipal administration.  Therefore, this person represented also the legislative and the executive power.  And this person had power over all secretariats, all departments of the municipality of municipal administration.  That person was in charge of hiring and firing employees, Was in charge of the budget, approving, adopting the budget.  Therefore, the president of the municipality had a dominant role, and he was assisted in his work as the vice-president of the municipality, who was the president's closest assistant.
Q.   Further, Mr. Murselovic, did the Municipal Assembly coordinate or cooperate with the police?

A.   Yes.  The then organisation of the police which at that time was known as the Secretariat of the Interior, or SUP, was directly subordinated to the municipality.  It was a municipal body just like all secretariats in the Municipal Assembly, but in terms of its professional competences, it was also subordinated to the ministries and had to coordinate its work with the ministry.  But at any rate, the secretary of the secretariat of the interior was an important position.  And after multi-party elections, Hasan Talundzic was appointed to that office as a prominent member of the SDA.  I remember that it was said that that was the first Bosniak who was appointed to that position after the Second World War.  He was the first Muslim and Bosniak to be appointed to that office.
Q.   Now, with the time passing, in approaching 1992, what was the working relationship within the coalition government that was functioning at the time?

A.   Well, it is generally believed that these three parties were able to find common ground only when it came to bringing down communists.  And this is what they did.  This is where they were in unison.  However, as the time passed, these so-called partners developed many antagonisms, and this was a heavy burden for the work of the municipality.  I think that these were simply two political options that were unable to work in harmony.  It is impossible to reconcile them. And as the time passed and as we got closer to 1992, these conflicts within the municipality and within the parties in power became more and more evident.  And we could say that by the time -- by 1992, nothing functioned properly any more.  The assembly sessions were scheduled.  However, they were frequently adjourned, and the sessions were interrupted and discontinued because we were unable to adopt decisions and do all the business that is normally within the sphere of Municipal Assembly's responsibilities.  It became obvious that there were many disagreements between the SDS and the SDA in many areas.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, during this time at the beginning of 1992, do you remember the establishment or proclamation of the Serbian municipality which was formed in Prijedor?

A.   Yes.  At the beginning of 1992, after several interruptions in the work of the Municipal Assembly, there were arguments and the demands in favour of the assembly taking a stance on an issue.  And we perhaps might say here that the most important point of friction was that the SDA wanted to pass a resolution about remaining in the federal state of Yugoslavia. But it was not a matter for the municipality to deal with, but there were interruptions and blockings of the work of the assembly.  And regular work of the Municipal Assembly simply could not evolve.  There were many blockades in the work of the assembly.  In early 1992, a Serbian municipality of Prijedor was set up.  There were Serbian deputies, deputies of the SDS there, and they proclaimed that part of the assembly which numbered 90 people, they proclaimed them the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor -- Serbian assembly of Prijedor.  And this, of course, was an abnormal situation, it was abnormal to ask that this be a Serbian municipality when the municipality counted a larger number of Bosniaks.

According to the 1991 census of the 12.000, there were 44 per cent Bosniaks, 42.5 were Serbs, and 5.6 Croats.  There were also Yugoslavs and others who pronounced themselves as national minorities, so that the Serb deputies wanted to proclaim the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, which was done officially.  And from my point of view, this was funny, ridiculous.  It was a mixed municipality.  There were not on one side Bosniaks and on the other side Serbs.  They were mixed.  They were intermingled.  There were Bosniak, Serb villages, Croat villages, and to proclaim it a Serb municipality, I think is ridiculous.  But this is, in fact, what happened, and at that assembly of the Serb municipality of Prijedor, they proclaimed all leaders in the Prijedor municipality who were in some way necessary, the vice-president, president, secretaries, heads of department, the presidents of the courts -- I apologise.  At the Serb municipality of Prijedor which was proclaimed in early 1992, I think it was in February of 1992, the Serb deputies proclaimed that municipality as a Serb municipality, and they appointed all the officials who, true enough, coincided with some of them who were in power at the time.

Q.   Mr. Murselovic, I would please request you to speak slowly, because the interpretation would be much easier then.  And also, do you know as to what post was held by Mr. Stakic in that Serbian municipality?
A.   Well, he was appointed president of the Serb municipality of Prijedor.
Q.   Who were the other people who held the prominent posts or positions in that formation?

A.   Well, the president of the courts, of the judiciary, there was Kreca Mico, president of the executive council remained Dr. Kovacevic who -- then Simo Drljaca was appointed head of the secretariat for internal affairs of the interior.  Budimir, Slavko was appointed secretary of the municipal secretariat for defence, and so on.  So they appointed parallel bodies.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, how did you get to know about this?  What was the source or how did you get to know the information about this Serbian -- all-Serbian municipality?
A.   Well, it was in the mass media, in the Kozarski Vjesnik, local

radio stations.  This was not concealed.  It was not a secret that this was proclaimed as Serb municipality, that people were appointed.  So it seemed ridiculous to us, funny.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, going to a different area, could you briefly and slowly explain to the Chamber the political situation or the atmosphere in Prijedor in 1991 with the war in Croatia?

A.   During the second half of 1991, the war in Croatia was in full progress.  From Prijedor, Serb soldiers would go to fight.  They were recruited -- mobilised by the municipality of Prijedor to go to Croatia and fight.  The representatives of the SDA opposed this mobilisation, and the soldiers from the reserve units of the JNA went to the battlefields of Slavonija, to Pakrac, to Lipik, to parts of Croatia.  From Prijedor, journalists would also go and accompany them.  The battle of the Serb people in Croatia was glorified.  And when the soldiers returned in periods of 20 days, there was much shooting.  It would seem that there were a lot of weapons.  There was shooting going on.  The people, citizens -- population was disturbed by this, the Muslims.  The Croats were condemned and publicly blamed for not taking part in that war which was considered by them -- the fact that they should not take part in that war. There was also an atmosphere of distrust that pervaded the area. There was fear.  There was shooting.  There were provocations going on. So it was an uncertain time for all citizens of Prijedor.
Q.   In brief, what you say is that the understanding or the trust was divide -- was getting lower, and also that there was fear between the major ethnicities in Prijedor?

A.   The citizens were very much disturbed.  Shooting went on throughout the night.  If the shooting went on from the trucks, and if weapons were used and carried in the streets, and if shooting went on throughout the night, even heavy weapons were being used, they were positioned in visible areas, and there were large quantities of weapons --
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, who were the people who were going in the trucks?

A.   They were Serbs, Serb soldiers, they were the only ones who had weapons.  They went to the front lines in Croatia.  I simply want to say that the Serb army, the Serbs were armed, the soldiers were armed.  There was a lot of shooting, as I said, was going on.  Much weapons were brought back from Croatia.  And it was rumoured that the greatest concentration of arms was in Bosnia.  There was a growing distrust among the peoples.
Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, if I take your mind to the period in 1992 before April, what was the political situation that prevailed in Prijedor during that time, if you could state very briefly?
A.   What do you mean when you say "political situation"?  I explained that the assembly had not been functioning.
Q.   Why do you say that?  Why didn't the assembly function?

A.   Well, the deputies of the SDS were leaving the assembly, and very often, the work of the assembly was blocked.  The sessions were convened. The meeting was opened, the quorum was established, and then a question was raised that could not be resolved by the assembly.  Given that situation, the deputies of the SDS would abandon the assembly of Prijedor. I remember very well that when the Serb deputies left the assembly, all the others left as well.  There were 60 deputies remained out of 90. There was also a situation where we had a quorum and we could work.  And Cehajic was chairing the meeting, and we said:  "We have to stop work because the SDS is leaving."  I got up and said:  "We can continue with the work.  We have a quorum."  But the work of the assembly was interrupted.  The SDA wanted to continue work, but the misunderstandings were so great that the result was that work was rendered impossible.
Q.   During this time before April, what was the function -- did you observe the propaganda which was in the media?

A.   Well, the propaganda was quite obvious in the sense that the Serbs had to be armed, that they should, at all costs -- that their fate of World War II be prevented, that they should be safeguarded.  That they cannot experience the disasters that they experienced in World War II again.  It was said that they were killed by the Ustasha, the camps were mentioned where they had suffered.  And the remnants of various saints were carried, and there was an atmosphere of preparation and -- in order to avoid the situation occurring, a situation of World War II, the Serbs thought that it was necessary to prepare for war.  They didn't want a repetition of the disaster of World War II, 50 years before. This, in fact, was in the Serb press.  Belgrade -- papers from Belgrade were read widely.  It was said that the Serbs were in danger, that they had to fight for their rights, and this is the way things went.
Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, you're aware that the takeover in Prijedor municipality was on the 30th of April, 1992?  Am I correct?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Before this, during the time that you spent as a member in the Municipal Assembly, did you see Mr. Stakic and know Mr. Stakic well?

A.   I met Stakic after the multiparty assembly was set up.  He was a young physician.  He comes from an area of Omarska, which is quite densely populated settlement in Prijedor.  But before 1992, I didn't -- that is to say, until 1990, I didn't know him.  Following the multiparty elections and the assembly, I got to know him because he became vice-president of the assembly of Prijedor.
Q.   Before the takeover on the 30th of April, have you spoken to Mr. Stakic when he held the post of vice-president in the Municipal Assembly, before the takeover?

A.   Quite sincerely, amongst the deputies, there is a normal communication.  I didn't have any specific contacts with Mr. Stakic, but we knew each other.  We would greet one another, and he would come to my snack bar for breakfast.  I'd see him around town, because he used to be, at the time, vice-president of the municipality in the street where I often went.  We knew each other, but we were not in particularly cordial relations.  But we knew each other.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, now, on the 30th of April, 1992, did you get to know that there had been a change in the power in the municipality of Prijedor?

Q.   Good afternoon, Witness.  Could you please state your full name for the record.
A.   My name is Muharem Murselovic.
Q.   Your date of birth?
A.   24th of November, 1947.
Q.   Where were you born?
A.   I was born in Prijedor.
Q.   Where were you raised?
A.   I completed my elementary and secondary schools in Prijedor.
Q.   What is your ethnicity?
A.   I'm a Bosniak of Islamic faith.
Q.   You said that you attended your elementary and secondary schools in Prijedor.  Did you specialise in any specific area?
A.   Yes, I did.  After completing my secondary school, I was trained in Opatija at the school for caterers and I completed my degree there. Opatija is currently located in the Republic of Croatia.
Q.   Did you teach at any school at any time?
A.   I used to work at the school for catering, because that was my trade, that was my specialty.  I was a lecturer there, and I thought subjects in the field of catering.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, are you married?
A.   I was married, and I have two adult children who are married now.
Q.   Where did you reside before the conflict in 1992?
A.   I have spent my entire life in Prijedor.  I have always worked there.  I used to work at a school for a time, and then after that, I was engaged in a private business.
Q.   What was your place of residence?
A.   I lived in the centre of Prijedor the entire time, in the main street.
Q.   Is it number 43, Marsal Tito?

A.   Yes.  Yes, the number was 43.  That's correct.  Before the war, I lived in Marsal Tito Street, number 43.  That's what it used to be called before the war.  Now it's called the Street of Peter 1st, the Liberator. The number is still 43.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, did you own any restaurants or were you in the business of running restaurants?

A.   Yes.  I have worked in catering my entire life.  At the end of 1978, I opened a private restaurant that was called Mursel.  That was my name, my nickname, in fact.  This was how I was known and that's how people normally call me.
Q.   Where was this restaurant located?
A.   The restaurant was located in the centre of the town.
Q.   Could you give a brief description of the restaurant that you had before the war.

A.   Well, it was a restaurant with some 50 seats.  It had one large room and a smaller parlour.  And it was mainly frequented by businessmen. It served European dishes in addition to some local specialties.  I tried to make it into a decent restaurant.  People of various nationalities and people from all over Bosnia and former Yugoslavia used to frequent my restaurant.  It was a restaurant that had many patrons, and I was quite busy.
Q.   Did you also have a snack bar other than the restaurant?

A.   Yes, I had another establishment.  It was a snack bar.  And it was quite a different establishment.  I served fast food there, hamburgers, pizza, sandwiches and so on, cakes, and well, other food items that are appropriate for a snack bar.  This snack bar was also located in downtown, in the pedestrian area in the street called Marsal Tito Street.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, before the conflict in Prijedor in 1992, could we say that you were a businessman of good standing, and well established?

A.   Well, as compared to the others, it was the time of socialist regime, and you could say that I had more than other people.  But you couldn't call it -- you can't say that I was particularly well off.  The establishments were owned by myself and my family.  My late father was involved in a similar business for over 50 years in Prijedor as was my late mother.  So I simply continued this family tradition, and perhaps you could say that by owning these two establishments and by owning my own apartment, that I was -- that I was well off as compared to the others. Of course, you couldn't say that I was well off as compared to the current times.  Yes, my family and I owned more than other people in the past, yes.
Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, before the conflict in 1992, did you sell the building and your -- the restaurant?

A.   Yes, I did.  I sold one building in which my restaurant Mursel was located, and an apartment -- rather two apartments above the restaurant. That was a move of mine that I can now analyse as a move expressing my desire to build something new, newer and better building.  I spent some 13, 14 years in that restaurant, and I thought it was better for me to sell it than renovate it.  It was quite logical for me to sell it and then perhaps invest in another one.  And my thoughts were along these lines, and therefore I sold the entire building together with the restaurant.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you were the owner of the house or the place that you resided before the war?  You owned the building?
A.   Yes.  Everything was owned by myself and by my family.  Some was owned by my mother, my late mother.  Something was owned by my wife.  But yes, everything was owned by my family.
Q.   Did you perform compulsory military service?

A.   Yes, of course.  In the former Yugoslavia I completed my military service in 1969 and 1970.  Part of my service I spent in Sisak, and the other in Crpia od Krki [phoen], that is near Zagreb, towards Ljubljana in Slovenia.  It is a small town, and I served there for some time.  I came back from the army in 1970 having spent there a bit less than one year.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you were a member of a political party under the multiparty system.  Am I correct?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Could you tell the name of the party and during what time, what period this was?

A.   I was a private entrepreneur, an independent private entrepreneur, as we used to call it in those days.  And after the multiparty system emerged, there were a number of political parties and we wanted to protect our own interests in that system in which the dominant force was the state capital.  We wanted to create a party which would regardless of everything be able to protect the interests of us private entrepreneurs.  And therefore, we established the party called the Party of Private Initiative.  I was a member of that party.  And during those first multiparty elections, I was elected for the first time to the Municipal

A.   Well, I think there might have been a misunderstanding.  I was an assemblyman of that party in the Municipal Assembly. A.   Yes, I did.  They didn't ask me anything then until I reached the police station, the secretariat of the interior.  It was a building about a hundred or 150 metres from my apartment. Q.   Did they detain after you?

Q.   And where did you spend the rest of the time in the police station?

A.   Well, when I left the office on the second floor, it was number 30 or 34.  I think the -- I saw that someone else was being brought to the police building.  Ilijaz Music, a professor who used to work with me at the school.  And we were taken down to a building in the yard.  We were closed, shut there.  This is a place where people were closed, shut, if they were caught drunk.  It had bars, iron bars, pretty high.  And there, I saw several people who had come there like me.  There was Music and there were several more people whom I knew.  I saw Mehmed Tursic, the head of the internal revenues department of Prijedor.  I said I saw Music, Dr. Sikora, a young physician, a Croat.  And someone called Juso Seric, a tradesman, who is employed in the Naftagas company.  And a young man who worked -- who was about 20, 25.  He worked at a restaurant where one of my colleagues worked.  We were talking.  We were wondering why we were there. We were all civilians.

After about half an hour, all of a sudden, the doors opened, and the president of the assembly, Muhamed Cehajic, entered.  I tried to joke with him, and I said:  "We are in good company, high-level company.  We have the president with us."  And while we were there in this building in the yard, the police were charging, unloading, loading their guns, and they were shooting, firing, and bullets were being fired.  And some of them were even fired in the direction of our building, and they kept saying:  "These are Ustasha, they should all be killed."  So we had to move away from the window.  And we spent the night there in that premise. We were standing or sitting.  We feared the shooting that took place from the yard.
Q.   You mentioned a person by the name of Music, Ilijaz Music.  Did he hold office in the SDA?  And what --

A.   Yes, he did.  He was a member of the top leadership of the SDA. And to tell you the truth, we knew each other.  We used to work together previously.  I also went to secondary school with one of his brothers.  We were the same age.  So he was in the top leadership of the SDA, and he was even one of the Bosniak candidates for the president of the municipality. However, within the party primary, Cehajic won more votes, and at least this is what I heard.  But at any rate, he was one of the prominent members of the SDA.
Q.   Do you know what happened to Ilijaz Music thereafter?

A.   When I was released the following day around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., I never saw Music after that.  So I was released, and I never saw Music afterwards.  And the following day, or on Monday, which was the first business day -- the first following business day, I got a call from his brother Dr. Music, who told me he had heard that I had been together with his brother, arrested.  So he inquired about his brother, because his brother went missing.  And I told him what I knew.  I told him that I had seen him, but that I didn't know what happened to him afterwards.  I didn't know whether he remained there or was released. And then Dr. Music, the older brother of Ilijaz Music, told me: "I'm going to look for him.  I will go to the police and the municipality tomorrow.  This is ridiculous.  What have they done to my brother?"  And later on, I learned that this doctor, in fact, did that, and went missing every since.  I never heard -- I never heard from him or saw him ever again.
Q.   He was a professor, Professor Ilijaz Music.  Am I correct?
A.   Yes, he was a professor of physics.
Q.   Now, you mentioned the name of Mehmed Tursic.  Have you seen him since?

A.   Well, frankly speaking, yes, I did see him.  Later on, when I came to Omarska, and after about some ten days, a bus came in, as usual.  It was bringing prisoners to Omarska.  And he came in the same group with the president of the Court, Mr. Nedzad Seric.  And I saw him leave the bus, and then kept seeing him for several days in the camp compound, because we would see each other when we ran to lunch.  However, three or four days later, I didn't see him any more.  But I did see him initially when he came to Omarska.
Q.   Do you know whether he survived the Omarska camp?

A.   He did not.  That's definite.  Because later, at the end of 1992, I met with his wife in Zagreb.  She left for Sweden in a convoy from Zagreb.  She left at the end of 1992 or later on.  And then I met her when she came to Prijedor in 1998 and 1999.  And at that time, she told me that Mehmed Tursic on the 23rd of May was arrested, and then released.  And then arrested again and taken to Omarska, and then she lost trace of him. So he wasn't seen from -- he wasn't seen later on, and it is certain that he had been killed in Omarska.
Q.   Very quickly, Mr. Mehmed Tursic, what position did he hold in the SDA, if you know?
A.   I don't know what was his position in the organisational structure of the SDA.  But the SDA appointed him as the director of the internal revenue agency.
Q.   The two people whom you mentioned Mehmed Tursic and Ilijaz Music, to what ethnicity did they belong to, if you know?
A.   They were Bosniaks.  Bosniaks and Muslims.
Q.   You mentioned about another person, Dr. Sikora.  A medical doctor. Do you know what happened to him?

A.   Well, let me tell you about him.  He was a young physician.  I knew him very well because he frequented my restaurant quite often.  He was very open and social and friendly.  I never saw him subsequent to that arrest, the one that took place on the 23rd of May.  And the following day, when I was released, his mother came to me, because the rumour had circulated that we both had been arrested.  So his mother came to me to inquire about her son.  I couldn't tell her anything because I didn't know anything.  I told her that I had been released and that he probably remained there.  And then I took her in my car to where she lived near the hospital in Urija.  I never saw his mother afterwards. I met his father, because he was in Omarska camp as well, and I used to speak to him there often.  He was an elderly man, some 75 or 76 years of age.  He went to Omarska and Manjaca, and later on he was released and I don't know what happened to him afterwards.  But their son, Zeljko Sikora, I never saw him again.
Q.   And you mentioned another person, Muhamed Cehajic.  This was on the 23rd of May, 1992, when you saw him in the cell in the SUP building. Did you see him thereafter?

A.   When I was arrested for the second time, I saw him in Omarska on the 30th of May.  So seven days later.  He was in Omarska in the same room where I was.  When we came to Omarska in the evening hours of the 30th, this is when I was arrested for the second time, I saw him sitting on the tile floor, and he had a beard.  He was unshaven, and I simply could not comprehend that he had been sleeping for seven days on a tile floor.
Q.   Do you know what happened to him thereafter?

A.   Since we were in the same room, I saw him there a lot.  I spoke to him a lot as well.  He stayed with us in that room for some time, and then he went to Banja Luka for some questioning.  He even showed me some kind of a draft indictment charging him for something.  He spent some 10 or 15 days in Banja Luka at the most.  And afterwards, he came back to our room. He said that it wasn't bad for him in Banja Luka.  They gave him enough food, cigarettes.  He was a passionate smoker.  And he was very pleased with the treatment he had received in Banja Luka.  So he stayed with us for some time in a situation where there were 700 of us in one large room. Later on, he was taken out and I never saw him again.
Q.   You spoke about Dr. Sikora.  Do you know to what -- what ethnicity he belonged to?
A.   Zeljko Sikora was a Croat.  He was a Catholic.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you said that you were released the next day. Could you explain very briefly as to how it happened.

A.   When they brought me back from that small cell where we had spent the night, back to that inspector who was called Krneta, on the 24th of May in the morning, he, who was a young man, told me that he was married to a Muslim woman and had a child with her.  I knew his father.  I had worked with him many years ago, 20 to 30 years ago in a national park. His father was a forester.  And I managed to establish rapport with him. And at one point, he told me:  "Listen, Murselovic, the Crisis Staff had denied the information that it was announced over -- there was announced on television regarding you."  And I was extremely pleased to hear that, and I asked him:  "Well, why don't you let me go, then?"  He said:  "Well, I can't do that, but we'll see what's going to happen to you."

And then I remained in that office until 4.00 or 5.00 p.m.  Some policemen came then, Mejakic came, Drago.  They even gave me some food. They treated me fairly decently.  And then they took me to see Ranko, Baja.  His last name was Mijic.  He was the head of the Criminal Investigation Department in the police.  I knew him.  He was a bit younger than me, maybe some ten years.  So I told him:  "Baja, what's going on? Why was I arrested?"  And he told me:  "You will be released."  And I said:  "Why am I here to begin with?"  And he said:  "It's fine.  You are going to leave this place."  And then he asked me if I had any intention of leaving town, and he -- he wanted to know whether I would remain in Prijedor, in case they needed something, and I told him even if I wanted to leave Prijedor I would be unable to because the town is completely blocked and a bird couldn't leave it unseen.  I told him that my family was in Belgrade, having left town some five or six days prior to that. And I told him that I perhaps might go to Belgrade myself.  And he said: "Okay, we'll let you go this time.  However, you may not leave Prijedor. You have to remain within our reach." And I was released at around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m.

Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you said that Krneta, the officer who had spoke to you before you spoke to Mijic, said that the Crisis Staff had denied the information.  Did he say from whom he had got the news?

A.   I have no idea.  He simply told me that this is what the Crisis Staff had said.  He said that that information regarding me had been denied, and that that was a positive move.  He didn't tell me anything else, and that was quite enough for me.
Q.   Then you spoke about a person by the name of Baja, or Baja is a nickname and his family name is Mijic.  He was a police officer attached to the Prijedor police station?
A.   Yes, that's right.  He was the head of the Criminal Investigation Department.  And he was in charge of all these investigators and inspectors.
Q.   Did you see him thereafter when you were detained in the Omarska camp?
A.   I saw him come to Omarska, and I even meet him now in Prijedor.  I saw him seven days ago in Prijedor.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, my question was the time you spent in Omarska during your detention, did you see Mr. Mijic come into the Omarska camp?
A.   I did.
Q.   Did you know for what purpose he was there?

A.   Well, all prisoners who had been brought to Omarska had to go through some interrogation, through some questioning.  And he was sort of in charge, and I suppose since he was the head of that department, all of
Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

these investigators, inspectors, were subordinated to him.  There were many investigators there who came daily on a bus in the morning.  And they used to investigate prisoners.  This is how we called it.  And I was interrogated as well.
Q.   Thank you. Were you again arrested on the 30th of May, 1992?

A.   That's right.  The police arrested me again on the 30th of May, in the morning around 11.00 or 12.00.  They banged on my door.  A neighbour of mine in a military uniform, Ranko Vujasinovic, a young man, banged on my door.  He was wearing a police uniform.  And he told me:  "Well, it's quite unsafe here.  There's some shooting going on, and why don't you go across the road to the Hotel Balkan."  There were several other policemen with him, and all of us, all of my neighbours, Serbs and Bosniaks, there were elderly people there, we all went across to the Balkan Hotel, and we sat in a cafe there, for at least three to four hours. Prior to that, they asked me whether I had any weapons, whether I had a pistol and so on.  I told them I had a pistol and a license to carry it.  They asked me to surrender it to them.  I went back to my apartment, took my pistol, my license, and turned it over to this neighbour of mine, Ranko Vujasinovic.
Q.   So you handed over the pistol and the license to the person who came and asked you to come out of the house?
A.   Yes.
Q.   And what uniform did he -- was he wearing?
A.   They were wearing police uniforms.
Q.   Did you know whether they were policemen?  Was he a policeman?
A.   He wasn't a professional policeman.  They were reserve policemen.
Q.   Now, you said that you and there were others taken to the Hotel Balkan.  Who were the others there at the hotel?

A.   There were lots of people from my neighbourhood there.  Many of my neighbours were there.  Many people I knew were there.  They were brought from all parts of the town.  And we sat there in the hotel not knowing why we were there.  We heard that there was much shooting going on, and we were told that we should stay there because it was a safer place.
Q.   Then what happened thereafter?  Were you taken anywhere?

A.   Then they said that the Serbs should remain, and that the Croats and Muslims should separate to another side, and males under 60, and that we should line up.  And when these groups separated, we were ordered to leave the hotel.  There were some buses waiting.  They were waiting before, even before.  And we were taken into those buses.  Of the people I knew, there were quite a number of them.  And I remember Sefik Terzic, Kiki, who was a barber.  Asef Kapetanovic, who was in the restaurant business.  There were not very many of us in the bus.  About 20, maximum 25 people in the bus.
Q.   [Previous translation continues]...  when they were ordered to get into the bus?

A.   The young policeman, the reserve policeman, by the name of Vujasinovic, Kiki Terzic, the barber tried to ask a question to find out where we were going because he used to know that person.  He was on friendly relations with his parents, with his father, Sveto, and the barber had a barber shop nearby.  This was all in the centre of the town. And this young man used to go to the barber shop frequently with his parents.  And the barber used to know him quite well. Well, this young policeman kicked this older man and told the driver: "Drive this shit."
Q.   Were you beaten at this instance?

A.   Well, no one beat me then.  But when we started moving, we actually started from the Balkan Hotel to the Mose Pijade Street, and the post office, and then we turned right to the post office and the police station.  On the Zebra Crossing [phoen] which separates the municipality and the police, the bus stopped.

And the policeman, who entered the bus with us and who was armed and whom I knew quite well, I forgot his name. It may have been Grahovac, I'm not sure.  I knew him nevertheless.  I asked him:  "Where are you taking us?  Why are we in the bus?  Where are you driving us?"  And he shrugged his shoulders and said:"I don't know". When the bus stopped, I asked him can I go out and go to the police station and see what is going on?  Why are you taking us? Why have you arrested us?  "Well, if you want, you can go out," he told me. Is there a commander there?  Is Drljaca there?  Is Jankovic there?  Who are these people?  Why are you argue us?  Where are you taking us?  I found this to be strange.  There were older people there, civilians, businessmen. It was quite unusual, abnormal.  Well, I left -- the policeman let me go off the bus.  I went in the direction of the police station to find out what was going on, to protest, simply.  And facing me was a soldier who was coming in my direction.

I think that he had some military insignia. And he asked me where I was going.  "Sir, I do not know you," I told him. I see that people are being arrested.  They are being taken somewhere, and I don't know what is going on.  I wanted to ask the commander what was going on and why we were being taken.  He didn't know me.  He was not from Prijedor.  Had he been from Prijedor, he would have known me.  He asked me what my name was.  When I said "Muharem Murselovic," the person was amazed.  "Well, you are those who are slaughtering Serb children.  Go back."  He kicked me in the behind, and I jumped into the bus.  And then he got on to the bus with me, and he said: "You are the ones who want to slaughter our Serb children.  Lie down," he told me.  And then we all laid down in the bus.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, did you observe as to the buses, the buses which were used?  From where did these buses come from?  Were they Autotransport buses?
A.   They were state-owned buses, owned by the state company Autotransport.  Some had names.  These were usually transport lines in the city.

A.   After the takeover, the Crisis Staff frequently made announcements under that name, "the Crisis Staff."  They asked the Bosniaks to surrender their weapons.  They also asked that the TO posts held by the Bosniak Muslims and villages be turned over as well.  They simply issued proclamations through mass media, through radio, and the local papers.
Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, did you meet Mr. Milomir Stakic after the takeover?  And if you did, where did you meet him?

A.   Well, at that time, I was one of the residents of the town.  All of these developments were quite unusual for me, and I went to inquire as to whether we were going to continue working, whether people would be going back to their offices, and how things are going to develop in general.  I was interested about our future.  So I call the municipality, and the secretary answered.  Her name was Mica.  That was her nickname.  I believe her last name was Radakovic.  And I asked her to get in touch with Dr. Stakic.  I simply wanted to hear from the first man of our municipality what was going on.  She told me to come the following day. And the following morning, I went there at about 9.30.  I went to the municipality.  I can't tell you exactly what day it was, but it was -- it might have been 3rd or 4th May, so several days after the takeover.
Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

I went there together with several prominent members of my association, Huso Hadzic was with me, Andrea Pavic.  I think there was also the secretary of our association there with us, Mr. Simatovic.  Mr. Stakic met with us at about 9.30.  I joked a little bit with the secretary, with Mica, and I told her:  "Listen, Mica, the presidents here keep changing, but you are constant.  You are also here.  She was the secretary for Mr. Cehajic before.  And during the socialist regime, the president of the municipality was Mirko Pavic, and she was his secretary as well.  So I told her:  "Well, listen, Mica, the presidents keep coming and going, but you are here always."

And so we went in Mr. Stakic's office, and Marko Palic came out of there, and we greeted each other because we knew each other.  We went to school together.  And when we were in Mr. Stakic's office, I asked him openly:  "What is this all about?  What is this all about?  Are we going to work?  Are we going to keep our cafes and catering establishments open? Are we going to have fuel?  What do you think is going to happen?  Nothing is going to change for the better" and so on.  And Mr. Stakic looked at me and said:  "Well, we'll see.  You seem to be not informed."  And then he mentioned Kupres.  And then he said he didn't really know how the situation was going to develop.  And then he told us he was about to go to Banja Luka at 10.00, and that he was going to find out what was going on. And then he told me to come back and see him upon his return.

So we stayed there for some 10 to 15 minutes.  I didn't learn anything new.  I didn't know what was going to happen.  Mr. Stakic told me he was going to go to Banja Luka.  He didn't tell me who he was going to see in Banja Luka.  He simply said he was going to gather information there.  And then he said:  "We'll see each other, we'll talk later on, and then I'll tell you about it."  However, he never called me.  Neither did I.  So this is where we left it off.  And then things started developing very quickly after that.

Q.   Mr. Murselovic, very briefly, when you went to Mr. Stakic on that day, where did you meet him?  Did you meet him in the president's office where Mr. Cehajic was occupying?

A.   Well, let me tell you:  The allocation of offices in the municipal building was always the same.  As you entered to the left was the office of the president of the municipality, because it was a large office and it also had a conference room.  And to the right was the office of the vice-president and it only had one room in it.  Mr. Stakic was already occupying the office to the left which was normally the president's office.  And this surprised me.  And I simply concluded that he had moved into Mr. Cehajic's office.  So a day or two later, after the takeover, he was already occupying that office.  And it was unusual to me, because I know that he used to have a different office, an office to the right from the entrance.
Q.   Thank you.
