MR. WAIDYARATNE: Q.   Mr. Murselovic, when you -- before the adjournment, you said that you met Mr. Stakic in his office.  When you went to the municipal building, were there any armed personnel or soldiers present?

A.   Well, in front of the building, there would usually be several soldiers, just like in front of all other buildings in town.  It wasn't the case just with the municipal building; there were armed soldiers in front of the Court building, the police building, banks, important institutions.
Q.   Now, with the takeover, what changes did you observe in the municipality of Prijedor?
A.   You mean in town?
Q.   Yes.

A.   Well, there were many soldiers walking around town.  They were armed.  In front of all buildings, or rather on top of all high-rise buildings in town, there were armed soldiers.  One could see them clearly on rooftops.  The situation was quite sad.  There was a curfew which lasted from 10.00 p.m. until 6.00 a.m.  And during the curfew, one could not walk about town.  The situation was tense, and I don't know myself, because I didn't walk around town myself.  But people were fearful, and it was not a normal situation for our town.
Q.   Did you know as to who imposed the curfew?
A.   The Crisis Staff imposed the curfew.  It was clearly announced that the Crisis Staff had decided what the hours of the curfew would be, from the evening until the morning hours.
Q.   Were the people able to get to their places of work?  Were they able to move freely?

A.   Well, during the day, people moved about town.  However, they did so fearfully.  A vast majority of Bosniaks and Croats were turned back from their work.  They were not allowed to enter the premises of their companies.  By this, I mean socially owned companies.  And the situation as I told you was quite tense.  The -- there was the curfew, there was a large number of soldiers around town, on rooftops.  A lot of troops were armed.  My employees complained that soldiers would come in drunk and leave their weapons on the bar or on tables.  So it was a situation where many people felt intimidated, were fearful.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, during this time, did you come to know of a situation where people had to take a loyalty oath to the Serb authorities?

A.   The policemen who were Bosniaks and Croats were required to sign a loyalty oath, confirming their loyalty to the Serb government, the Serb state, as they called it.  They had to undertake a written obligation to be loyal and participate in the work of the Serb government.  This especially applied to policemen.  A vast majority of policemen who were Bosniaks and Croats did not agree to sign this.  They were automatically fired from their jobs, and also disarmed. At that time, I have to add that various incidents or various events took place that increased the tension in town.

There were several murders that went unresolved.  Many instances of revenge took place. There were also cases where people were pulled off buses and killed.  A prominent businessman Kutkavic [phoen] was killed in the suburbs.  He was pulled off a tractor.  Some people were taken off the bus between Prijedor and Bosanska Dubica and killed.  And the Crisis Staff was the only contact -- Crisis Staff was the only source of information regarding this.  And they explained this as a case where this was a revenge for a soldier that had been killed in town.  So the times were very uncertain.  There were shootings going on.  One couldn't sleep at night from all the shooting that took place, and all of this contributed to the sense of fear among people.  So these were uncertain times.
Q.   Did you observe the soldiers and the police personnel in the Prijedor town acting in coordination or direction of the SDS or the Crisis Staff?

A.   It was absolutely synchronized and coordinated.  The Crisis Staff informed about everything as a Supreme Commander would be.  The Crisis Staff coordinated the work of the police, and in some ways the army was also involved.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, I would bring your attention to the 22nd of May, 1992.  Do you recall an incident at Hambarine at a checkpoint?

A.   Yes, that was on the 21st or 22nd of May.  I don't remember exactly.  There was an incident at the checkpoint held by Bosniaks, by Muslims.  Hambarine, where the incident took place, and six villages or six local communes, which prior to the war were inhabited by over 10.000 Bosniaks, organised their own Territorial Defence.  And in some ways, they tried to protect their own villages.  They did not leave their villages; they remained in Hambarine.  And at one checkpoint, which was on the road to Ljubija, another settlement, there was an incident where there was some shooting as a result of which one Serb soldier was killed. This incident, I think, took place on the 22nd of May, and the Crisis Staff addressed the population regarding this, requiring all of those who participated in that incident to surrender themselves.  They mentioned a name of some commander in Hambarine, some Aliskovic, yes Aliskovic.  Therefore, the Crisis Staff wanted him to surrender himself to the Serb authorities.  They believed him to be personally responsible for the death of this Serb soldier.

Naturally, the Bosniaks refused to surrender, and the Crisis Staff issued an ultimatum to surrender all weapons and to have those soldiers, as they called them, surrender to the Serb authorities.  So this was what the ultimatum was all about.  This ultimatum was broadcast throughout the entire day on the 22nd of May.  It was broadcast through the local radio. I have to say that for a long time prior to that, we were unable to listen to any other radio except for that local station.  We were unable to watch Belgrade television or Sarajevo or Zagreb television.  The only one available to us was the Banja Luka television and the one in Prijedor.
Q.   You said that there was an ultimatum which was broadcasted.  What happened after the ultimatum expired?

A.   Next day, there was a terrible shelling and bombarding of the village.  The shelling, the bombardment from all sorts of weapons, lasted almost the entire day.  There were even some tanks that crossed the bridge over the Sana River and moved in the direction of the Hambarine village. The regular forces of the army were also involved so this was terrible. And for the very first time, it was then that we were confronted with the artillery, the artillery was left in villages, in -- where the Serbs lived.  So the shelling lasted a long time, and there was much destruction in those villages and severe civilian casualties.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, what was clear from this sequence of events, after the Crisis Staff made an ultimatum and when it expired, the attack by the military?

A.   It was obviously that the Crisis Staff and the army and the police, that they worked in coordination because the ultimatum was issued by the Crisis Staff, and that the -- and the army, with its tanks and heavy artillery, attacked the village.  So we knew that all this was very much planned and coordinated.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, did you -- were you aware that subsequently, an area which is known as Kozarac was also attacked?

A.   Well, a few days following the attack on Hambarine, which, to be quite honest, did not meet with any special resistance.  There was vast destruction and people saw that their homes were being destroyed and that people were being killed and they were very much in a state of shock.  A few days later -- this was, in fact an unselective shelling of homes in the village. A few days later, an ultimatum was issued that Kozarac, too, that the TO of Kozarac, should also surrender its weapons.  I must say that Kozarac is in a different area of the town from Hambarine.  12 kilometres from Prijedor in the direction of Banja Luka.  And it is not a village. It is a small town.  It used to be a municipality.  It is composed of four local communities.  And before the war, about 19.000 Bosniaks lived.  A very small percentage of others, of Ukranians, and Croats and others lived there, too.  But 95 per cent of the population were Bosniaks.

And then an ultimatum was issued to Kozarac, according to which Kozarac was to surrender its arms, and that the TO should surrender.  The ultimatum was also issued by the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor.  And it was even demanded that the police should disarm.  And then terrible shelling ensued, and bombardment with heavy weapons, tanks, cannons of all calibres against Kozarac.  This was not done in a selective fashion.  From my own apartment, from Prijedor, I could see that from all directions, in the direction of Kozarac, shells were being fired.  Firing took place from different spots in the direction of Kozarac.  I'm not an expert in military matters, but we nevertheless could see how the rounds flew over us in the direction of Kozarac. In the case of Kozarac, I could also say that the ultimatum was issued both to the police and the TO.  The police in Kozarac was basically of Bosniak ethnicity.  Unfortunately, the police surrendered at that time, together with the commander, and none of them have been found nor have been exhumed.  They apparently were all killed.  The commander of the police station was Mahmuljanin.  I don't remember his name exactly.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, now I would take your attention to a different area.  When were you first arrested?  And briefly, how did that happen?

A.   Well, I was arrested the first time on May 23rd.  It was a Saturday.  I was at home alone.  I was watching television. Unfortunately, we could only see the programme -- the Serbian programme of Banja Luka from 7.00.  At one moment, the speaker -- the presenter said -- the announcer said, when reading out the news:  "A group of extremists from Kozarac admitted that the financing of Bosniaks, Muslims, that they were financed by a well-known caterer, someone from the restaurant business in Prijedor.  His name was Murselovic.  And there was also Dr. Kulenovic mentioned.  Someone who I did not know at all.  I was truly shocked when these names were mentioned on television.  At that very moment, I called the police, the policeman on duty answered.  And I said my name.  And I said that information was given on the news, on television.  "And what is this all about?  Can you give me an explanation? This is wrong information.  Can you explain it to me?"

A policeman by the name of Jankovic answered the phone.  I knew him personally.  He was a junior policeman.  He told me:  "I don't know anything about it.  Don't you worry."  I called him first on phone, and then I went to the premises, to the police building itself.  Because it is quite near from my home.  It was still daytime.  It was 7.00.  And I went there, and I said:  "What is going on?  Please deny the information, the truth of this information.  I have nothing to do with this.  Don't drag me into things that I have nothing to do with."  He told me:  "You go home. I know nothing about it.  If we need anything, you will find out soon enough".
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, were you a member of any resistance group at any
Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
time?
A.   No, I wasn't.
Q.   Did you ever finance the Kozarac TO or the SDA?

A.   Well, for five or six months I hadn't been to Kozarac.  I didn't even pass through it.  I had no special links at the time with Kozarac.  I had never financed -- well, I joked on that account.  I said that if someone asked some advice from me, I would give it willingly, but I was not in a position to offer money.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, after this announcement, you went to the police station and came back.  Thereafter, were you arrested immediately and taken to the police?

A.   Well, half an hour later, I was at home -- perhaps 20 minutes, 40 minutes.  I don't know exactly.  But about half an hour or so had elapsed, and then someone called from the pedestrian street, called my name from the pedestrian street, since my office there and everyone knew I was there at the time.  I sit there, watch television, read or write something. Someone called out my name.  I opened the window, and I saw two policemen who said that I should prepare, get ready, and come down.
Q.   Were the policemen in their police uniforms?
A.   Yes, two policemen.  There were two policemen.  One of them was Bato Kovacevic.  That was his surname.  I knew him well.  The other one, I didn't know.
Q.   Was the arrest to the Prijedor police station?
A.   Yes.  This whole area here, between the hangar, the entrance.  So this entire area here we called the "pista."  It was all covered in asphalt, and we called it the pista.
Q.   How would someone enter Mujo's room?
A.   Yes, you can see the entrance here on this side, right here.
Q.   What is the white building which is on the edge of the picture?
A.   This one here?
Q.   Yes.
A.   This was called "the white house."
Q.   Now, you also could see another small building away from the white house.  Do you know as to what it was called by the prisoners?

A.   This one here.  Well, this here was the white house, and the other one, I don't know what it was called.  Thank God, I never went either to the white house nor to the other one.  This other one was a red house or something like that.  But I never went there.  I never went to the rooms there in 1992.  I did not.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, what is the big building which is opposite the restaurant building?  Do you know as to what the prisoners called this big building?

A.   Well, this large building was called the hangar.  They had workshops there to repair heavy machinery, dampers, and the machinery that they used to load and unload the ore.  And they were quite large, so this entire area was called the hangar.
Q.   Were prisoners detained in the hangar building, too?
A.   Yes, they were.  The prisoners were in this entire area, this one here.

A.   Yes, it is.  This here is the restaurant, as I told you.  This is the entrance, and this is the staircase leading to the floor above.
Q.   Now, do you see the door on the side which also -- which enables someone, anyone to enter the -- anyone to enter the Mujo room?
A.   Yes, this is right here.
Q.   And also at the extreme end, could you find out the place where you called -- the place that you called the "garage"?
A.   Right here.
Q.   Thank you. Mr. Murselovic, also before we take the photograph away, would you be able to show in the picture where the interrogations were held?

A.   The interrogations took place up here following the staircase, there was a hallway, and offices on both sides.  So this up here were the offices where the interrogations took place.  So you would take the staircase, and then once you got up there, there was a hallway, and offices were to the left and to the right.
Q.   It was in the first floor?
A.   Yes.
Q.   A person who would enter the restaurant for meals, would you be able to show as to how one would enter the restaurant?

A.   During the day, in accordance with a predetermined schedule, we would go to have our meal.  And that lasted from 9.00 a.m. until 6.00 p.m. we would line up here in this area, and since we were close to the entrance of the Mujo's room, then 30 prisoners would line up and then run through this main entrance to enter the restaurant.  This was a self-service restaurant, a typical one.  And we had to get our food very quickly, as I told you, the food was bad indeed.  We would also take one-eighth or one-quarter of a loaf of bread.  We would eat it quickly, take the plates back to where we picked them up originally, and then usually take the same way back, running along it, and then get through the door back to the pista and line up there.  This whole process lasted not more than 3 minutes.  So lining up, running, getting the plates, getting the food, eating, putting the plates back, and running back.
Q.   Is it correct if I say that people who would go for the meals from the front door of the restaurant would be in the pista area for some time before they go for the meal?

A.   Well, yes.  We would line up here in groups of 30.  And only 30 people were allowed to go in for their meal.  And this is why this whole process took so long, because there were many of us.  So sometimes we would eat at 10.00 in the morning and sometimes at 5.00 p.m. Because only 30 people were allowed to line up in a group, and then enter the restaurant and back.
Q.   Is it correct if I say that you were only given one meal a day?
A.   Well, yes, there was just one meal a day given to us.  It was a bad meal at that.  You could hardly call it a meal.

Q.   Thank you. Now, Mr. Murselovic, when you were detained in the garage, the place that you call the garage, the latter part of your detention in Omarska, who were the people who were with you whom you could recall the names, whom you could recall?

A.   Well, I can recall a number of names.  People's names were called out in accordance with some preselection by the investigators -- or I don't know whom.  Dedo Crnalic was with me.  Nezir Krak.  Sefik, Kiki, Terzic, Dr. Sadikovic.  So there were a lot of people.  There was even one woman among us.  There was some hundred and 50 to 170 people in the garage with us. There was a woman called Hajra there as well.  She never left the camp. She must have been camp.
Q.   I'm sorry, please carry on.

A.   There were many prominent people.  Enes Kapetanovic.  It has been ten years, but still I was able to give you names of six, seven, eight people.  We were all crammed in that limited space, and this is how we spent our nights.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you mentioned the name of Kapetanovic.  Is it Enes or Asef?
A.   It was Enes Kapetanovic.  And he's a relative of Asef Kapetanovic. Asef Kapetanovic was taken out previously, and he was not in the same room with us.
Q.   You also mentioned about a woman being detained with you by the name of Hajra.  Do you recall the family name of this person?
A.   I think the last name was Hadzic or Hodzic, although I think it was Hadzic Hajra.
Q.   And you said that she never left the camp.  Why do you say that?

A.   Because immediately after that -- well, there was some 30 to 35 female prisoners in the camp.  I can't tell you the exact number.  But around that.  And all of those women, among whom I knew many, there was a lady judge there, Nusreta Sivac.  There was a lady called Besirevic Mugbila [Realtime transcript read in error "Basirovic"]. She was an economist.  She used to work in a bank.  There was an employee of mine there, Avdic Sadija.  Then there was Hajra.  Then there was Medunjanin. No, it was not Medunjanin.  There was a lady, Mahmuljin, Velida who was a teacher.  There was Jadranka Cigelj there as well.  There were many women that I knew from before there.  And a few days prior to that, a bus had arrived with investigators, and these women were taken back to Prijedor. I later learned that they were allegedly taken to Trnopolje or Prijedor. However, three or four women remained, and there was no trace of them thereafter.  Hajra was among them.
Q.   Now, you mentioned a person by the name of Velida Mahmuljin?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Have you seen her since the Omarska camp?
A.   Unfortunately, I never saw her again, but I knew her very well.
Q.   Did she hold any office or position in the assembly or the SDA?

A.   She was a deputy of the municipal assembly of Prijedor, and she was there on behalf of the SDA.  Otherwise, she was a teacher by profession, and she used to work for some time in Kozarac.  Her husband, his name was Suleja Mahmuljin, and he was a dentist by profession.  And her family name was Arnautovic, maiden name.  And she came from the part of the city called Tukovi.
Q.   You also mention the name Basirovic as in the transcript.  But is it Mugbila Besirovic?

A.   Yes, Mugbila Besirevic, she used to work in a bank.  She was an economist.  She came from Cejreci, a local community quite near the town. She was an elderly lady.  She was very active in her local community.  She was highly respected by the people, and she was one of those who never left the Omarska camp.
Q.   What you say is that she did not survive the camp, am I correct?

A.   Absolutely, she did not survive the camp.  She never left Omarska with the other colleagues when they were returned to Prijedor after having spent 50 or 60 days there.  And all traces of her were lost.  No one heard of her any more.  Her family never heard of her, her children.  And I saw her husband when I left Omarska after the war.  He lived in Bihac about eight months.  Following that, her husband unfortunately also died.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you mentioned about Hajra Hadzic or Hodzic --
A.   Hadzic.
Q.   -- Being detained in the garage with you in the latter part. Where were the other female detainees being kept?

A.   During the day, they used to sit in a corner of the restaurant. Some of them would help around when food was being served.  They would hand over the bread or food.  During the night, they were taken to the premises on the floor above, and we had no contact with them during the night.  So we didn't know what was going on during the night.  We don't know under what conditions they were living there.  But during the day, when we were having our meals, they would sit in the corner of the restaurant.  This was frequently the case. They would clean the area, the floors.  They handled the dishes. But in most cases, in 90 per cent of the cases, they would sit quietly in that corner and that is how they spent their day.
Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, taking your attention to another area, could you explain the times that you were beaten in the camp?
Q.   City of Prijedor?
A.   Yes, the city of Prijedor.
Q.   Did anybody accompany the people, the people who were in the bus? Were there armed guards?

A.   In that bus, in my bus, there was an armed policeman, not a soldier, an armed policeman who stood next to the bus driver, near the entrance to the bus.  And he kept us there.  We were lying face down in the bus, and when we had moved away from the town, then he felt sorry for us, I suppose, and he told us to sit down.
Q.   Now, where did the bus ultimately -- where did the buses go to?

A.   Well, all the buses headed for the Partizanska Street.  It's in the direction of the village of Gomjenica.  When we got up and sat down, we saw that we were heading towards Gomjenica.  And we drove for about half an hour.  And then we went to Sanicani -- Tomasica.  And then we reach the Omarska area, because Omarska is between Prijedor and Banja Luka.  But we entered the area from the other direction, the mine.  I had never been to that mine before.  I didn't know it.  I had no reason to go there before.  It was an iron ore, the Ljubija iron ore in the Omarska part, the Tomasica part.
Q.   Now, this was the 30th of May, 1992.  How long did you stay in Omarska?
A.   Well, from May 30th, I was in Omarska.  We saw that it was a camp, that there were guards there.  And that lots of things were happening there.  I stayed there until August 6th, 1992.

Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, coming to the Omarska camp and spending almost more than two months in the camp, could you briefly state the specific areas that you were detained in the camp?  The names of these places, as popularly known.

A.   Well, I spent about 70 days in the camp.  And the room where I was put, it was called Mujo's room.  It was behind the restaurant.  It is the place where the wardrobe used to be, the cupboards were pushed to one side.  And the room -- well, I was practically all the time in that room with the exception of a few days when I was taken to an area called pista.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, could you describe the Mujo's room to the Chamber, as to how the dimension of the room.
A.   That room, well, you entered it from the side.  Well, its dimensions were 15 by 12, more or less.  12 in width; 15 metres in length.
Q.   When you were first to the Mujo's room, on the 30th of May, 1992, how many people were there?
A.   At the time, in that room, well, there were not very many people there.  Ten, 15 people maximum.  Very few people.  And here, I met Mr. Cehajic, president of the assembly.
Q.   And approximately how many people would you estimate would have been there in that room?
A.   Well, it varied between 200, 300, up to 600 or 700.  We were in rows, like sardines.  Some people were being transferred there.  But on the average, there were about 500 people were there.
Q.   And were the -- did you know the ethnicity of these people who were detained in that room?
A.   Well, most of the people were familiar to me.  They were for the most part Bosniaks, Muslims.  But there was a fair number of Croats, too. But a lesser number than the Bosniaks.
Q.   Did you see a person by the name of Stipo Sosic in that room?

A.   Sosic, yes, he was there, too.  He was a Catholic priest from Ljubija.  I didn't know him before, but he greeted me and asked me how I was.  And the -- he said where his parish was.  And then we were frequently in contact.  He was detained there, too.  There was some other Croats, 5 to 10 per cent of us were Croats.  There weren't more.  There was a musician I knew, a music professor.  His name was Ivica Peretin. There was also a driver and his son.  They were also Croats.
Q.   Did you ask Stipo Sosic as to why he was detained there?
A.   I had no idea why he was detained.  He was detained because he was a Croat.  I didn't even know why I was detained, let alone I didn't know why the priest was there.
Q.   In time passing, what was the condition of the prisoners in Mujo's room?

A.   Well, the conditions in the camp, in the whole of the camp, were inhuman.  We slept on tiles.  Who had a piece of cardboard or some paper, well, he was considered to be privileged, not to have to sleep directly on the tiles.  Who had a coat would spread out his coat and lay on the coat. Simply, these were not normal conditions in all respects.  As regards food, well, we were fed once a day.  And 30 of us were crammed together. And in a very brief period of time, we had to run from pista to the kitchen to take the food, which was poured out there, to eat that food very quickly.  And even quicker than that, we had to run and return the plate.  It was usually spoiled food, beans or potatoes, swimming in something like water.  And we were usually beaten on the way out because sometimes, we would spill some water and oil, so that if we slipped, we were met by the people on guard and we were beaten.

We drank water from the Banjanica [phoen] River.  It was not drinking water.  It was industrial water.  And many of us suffered from dysentery, from stomach diseases.  And many people who refused to eat food were constipated, so they were unable to go to the toilet for as long as 30 or 60 days.  I didn't go for 30 -- over 30 days.  Simply, in our room, well, some of us were set aside, and the excrements were, in fact, all over the place.  So all this was swimming there and next to that, were the detainees, sitting crammed together.  It was very ugly, very sad.
Q.   Were you provided with medical assistance?

A.   No, we were not given any medical care.  There were many problems in that some people had chronic diseases like diabetes and so on, and they had to go without medication.  Allegedly, there was a doctor in the camp; however, he never saw detainees.  And after all the beating we'd received, the only medication we had available were cold compresses that we would put on our body to alleviate the results of all that beating.

A.   Yes, I was.  I spent two or three nights locked in there.  I slept, and I lived in something that we called a garage.  It was a room whose dimensions were 5 by 4 and a half metres, something like that.  And there was to the side of the other room where I spent most of my time, the so-called Mujo's room.

Q.   Witness, would you look at the exhibit which is on the ELMO, please.  You said that you were detained first in the room we just called the Mujo's room which is in the restaurant building.  On this photo could you kindly point out the building which you called "the restaurant building" please.

A.   This was the main entrance here, in this area here, the area that's protruding.  And it had -- it was covered by a roof.  And then this circular part is the staircase that leads to the first floor.  This here was the area that all of us called Mujo's room, this here.
Q.   Was this the building --
A.   And then there's an entrance here.
Q.   Was this the building which was called the, "restaurant building"?
A.   This is behind the restaurant.  The restaurant is right up here in front.  This is the restaurant.
Q.   Then to assist the Chamber, could you also show the place that you referred to as the "garage," the entrance to the garage.
A.   Right here.  This area here.
Q.   This was the room that you said that it was 4 by 5 metres in size?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Now, there was another place that you referred to in your evidence earlier as the pista.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, now, coming to the area of the people who were in charge of the camp, did you get to know or observe as to who was in command of the camp?

A.   Well, the man who introduced himself as the commander of the camp was Zeljko Meakic, and his assistant was allegedly Drago Prcac.  He was an elderly man, a retired policeman.  And there was Kvocka there, as well.  I can't remember his first name.  He was married to a Muslim lady, to a lady from Crnalic.  At least that was the rumour circulating.  There was a man called Kos.  We used to call him Krle.  In fact, he was a former student of mine.  I thought him during my first year of employment as a teacher. There was a man called Krkan.  I think his first name was Mladjo.  He was a chubby man.  And then there were some other people.  I can't remember their names.  Kos was the shift leader.  And shift leader was, so to speak, in charge from, say 7.00 a.m. To 7.00 p.m.  The shifts were usually 12 hours long.

And the shift leaders were in charge of policemen there. In addition to that, there were people who would come every day to investigate or to interrogate the prisoners.  There was a man that I had mentioned previously called Baja among them.  And these people were either professional policemen who had worked up to 1992 in the police like the man who interrogated me, Mijic and so on, but in addition to that, there were also people who subsequently became active and prior to that used to be reserve policemen, for example, Dragan Radakovic, who prior to the war was the director of the national park.  He was an art teacher before the war.  And I also mentioned Ratko Milosavljevic who was an agricultural engineer and used to work for the municipality and so on.  There were many people there, people of many professions who became active. It was also rumoured that some interrogators came from Banja Luka. They were looking for certain information and so on.  So these are the people who were in charge at the Omarska camp.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, now, you mentioned people coming for interrogation.  Did you see them coming to the camp for interrogations? How did they come?

A.   People would come by buses.  The buses would normally park on the pista.  People would be taken out.  And usually, while entering the camp, they would be fiercely beaten.  And they would beat them at that first entrance when they searched them, looking allegedly for weapons or I don't know what.  I just know that they severely beat these people.
Q.   May I interrupt you, if you didn't understand the question, I was asking about the people who came to conduct the interrogations.

A.   Oh, I'm sorry, I apologise.  Those who came to conduct interrogations would come daily on a small minibus.  It was a minibus that belonged to the iron ore company Ljubija.  It was driven by a chauffeur from either the Autotransport company or a chauffeur from the mine.  I knew him.  So this minibus would come at about 7.00 a.m., and the interrogators would normally stay there until 5.00, 5.30.  We would see them as they left the bus and as they boarded the bus to go back to Prijedor or wherever they lived.  So they came daily.
Q.   Now, Mr. Murselovic, you said that you used to see Mijic who worked in the police before coming to the camp.
A.   Yes.
Q.   When he came to the camp for interrogation, do you know as to what post or position he held in the Prijedor police?
A.   He was the head of Criminal Investigation Department.  So he was a boss to all of these civilian inspectors, if I can call them that.
Q.   Other than Mijic, did you recognise any other police officers who came for interrogation?

A.   Well, as I've told you, among those who interrogated me, there was -- there were two of them called very similarly, Nenad, Neso.  And I can't remember exactly their names, their last names, even though I still see them in Prijedor now.  One was short and the other one was tall.  But it has been ten years and I can't recall that now.  They were professional police workers prior to that.  And they would come regularly, daily, and conduct interrogations. There was another man there, Drago Mejakic.  I would see him as well.  So these were the people that were police employees before the war as well.  But there were those who would also come on that minibus to interrogate people.
Q.   The guards in the camp you mentioned in Omarska, what uniforms did they wear?
A.   They wore police uniforms.  They usually had blue police uniforms.
Q.   Did you see the commander whom you mentioned, Meakic, in the camp?

A.   Yes.  We saw him through the window when we ran.  He moved about the camp freely.  He was some 15, 20 years younger than me.  He was somewhat tall, blond, a handsome man.  And he acted as a commander.
Q.   How was he dressed?

A.   Well, he wore regular police blue uniform, the light one.  On one occasion, they took us out at night, and he was there.  Together with a policeman called Brk, and maybe some others.  So they took us out at, perhaps, 1.00 a.m.  I was taken out together with Dedo Crnalic, Kiki Sefik Terzic, and it was so pitiful, so ridiculous.  They told us the following: "See how poorly dressed the Serb policemen are, they don't have good uniforms.  So why don't you give them some money so they can buy some uniforms.  You are well-known entrepreneurs, we know you are successful businessmen.  Why don't you give them 10.000 deutschmarks so we can get them some good uniforms."  So you know, when somebody takes you out at 1.00 a.m., you can imagine what fear we felt.  And then how cynical it is to ask the prisoners to buy uniforms for their guards.  You didn't know whether they were joking or it was some kind of a provocation.  I kept quiet the whole time.  I didn't say anything.

And then Meakic addressed me, and then he said:  "Well, listen, Mursel" -- because this is how everybody called me -- "you're a smart man. You always come up with great ideas so how come you don't have a good idea to solve this right now?  And I told him:  "You take me out at some wee hour and then you want me to come up with good ideas.  Why don't you take us to Belgrade."  Because I knew what they were hinting on.  If we go there, we can send you money from there, and then they sent us back to our room to sleep and this is how it all ended.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, you said you were interrogated and they asked you questions.  Did they ever tell you why you were arrested and why you were detained?

A.   They never told me anything.  And right at this minute, I remembered what the last name of one of those interrogators was.  His last name was Tomcic; his first name, Nenad. So to go back to the other story, they kept me on a chair, a three-legged chair, for many hours.  And I was there with a slice of bread that I picked up during lunchtime.  I have to say that they treated me decently.  Nobody hit me at all.  They asked me where I spent that week between my first release until my second arrest, from the 23rd until 30th. I told them I was in my apartment, and I did nothing wrong.  And you should know this better than me.  And then they asked me something concerning the assembly, concerning Cehajic.  They asked me whether Cehajic asked money of me.  I told them:  "No, he didn't.  I don't have money anyway," along those lines.  So this lasted some 30, 40 minutes. Nobody hit me.  They simply asked me where I went, what I did, whether I'd financed the SDA.  I told them I had not been a member of the SDA, nor did I finance them.
They asked me about my contacts with Cehajic.  I told them he was the president of the municipality and I had a good rapport with him in the assembly, which was quite normal.  And...
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, after you left the camp or the time that you were in the camp, did they initiate any proceedings in a court of law?

A.   No.  They did not initiate any proceedings.  And during the interrogation, I did not sign anything.  They simply told me:  "Go back to where you were."  And I went back downstairs, because the interrogation offices were on the first floor and we stayed on the ground floor.  And I asked them to give me a policeman who could escort me downstairs because it was very typical for policemen to beat people who they were interrogating.  You could hear terrible screams during interrogations.  So these two interrogators who interrogated me gave me a policeman who escorted me downstairs to where my fellow prisoners were.

A.   I must say that during the interrogation which lasted about 30 or 40 minutes, I was, in fact, one of the last to be interrogated after having spent 30 days in Mujo's room.  Muja, the police, took me up the stairs, and during this questioning, I met Ratko Milosavljevic there.  He interrogated me.  He worked at the assembly as an agriculture engineer before.  He took me to a room which was on the left of the staircase.  On that occasion, I was not beaten.  I was interrogated by two persons.  I think one was called Nenad, and the other one Neso.  They used to be investigators, I think, in the police before.  On that occasion, I was not beaten.  They asked me some questions.  They didn't have much sense, where I was, where I had been, what I had been doing.  I told him that I had been arrested once.  Then one of them went to ask someone what to do with me.  I think one of them was tall and one of them was short.  He said I should be interrogated like all the others.

I wasn't beaten then.  I was beaten three or four times on later occasions. Once, I was beaten by the guards in pista where we used to sit after having our meals.  It was very risky to go and have the meal because then we would have to stay on pista, and then we were exposed to the guards.  Then Kevo Simo came on one occasion, and said:  "Look, here's Mursel, he used to persecute Serb children when he was employed at the school."  Well, I had not worked at the school for 14 years then.  But the person recalled that.  He used to work at the same time as me, when I used to work at the school.  And the guards then took hold of me.  They started beating me.  Well, with cable, with batons, longer than police batons.  I was beaten on the pista itself.

They said:  "You persecuted Serb children."  And a blond policeman called Marmat was the roughest amongst them.  Marmat was his surname, and it was familiar to me.  I had many students from the area, and these are strange surnames.  They don't end in "ic" which is mostly the case.  Their names were Marmat, Vuceta [phoen] And so forth. And people who worked in the school remember those names of the other teachers. Two policemen beat me fiercely indeed.  I tried to defend myself. I was in a crouching position.  And I think Marmat was the worst of all. At one moment, I saw red, and I told Marmat:  "Ask Borka whether I persecuted Serb children."  When I mentioned the name Borka, he just

stopped.  He recalled the name.  It may have been his relative, his sister.  And at that moment, they stopped beating me, and they said: "We'll see about that."  Then Kiki Terzic was the target of the beatings, and they let me go.  But before that, I was severely beaten on the head and on the shoulders.  This was one occasion. Then on another occasion, I met Marmat again in the restaurant. He was standing behind the counter.  And he shouted to me:  "Mursel, where are you?"  And I turned around because on those occasions, you just looked straight ahead of you.  You don't turn right or left.  Then I saw Marmat, and I just couldn't help asking him:  "Did you check up on what I told you?"  I was referring to Borka and the fact that he said I had persecuted Serb children.  He said:  "Well, sorry," he said, "that is something I experienced."  This is one occasion when I was beaten.
Q.   Mr. Murselovic, in your detailed description of that beating, you mentioned the name Kevo Simo.  Is it Simo Kevic?
A.   Yes.
Q.   Was he a guard at the camp?
A.   No, he wasn't.  I don't know what his business was there in Omarska.  And unlike the others, he was wearing an army uniform, an SMB, olive-green uniform.
Q.   Now, you were beaten again severely once when you went to get your meal.

A.   Yes.  There was some unwritten rule in the case of the guards that they would -- they simply spilled a bit of oil and water, and since we were running we frequently slipped and fell.  Once on my way back, I was running, and there were some young fellows behind me.  One of the guards was standing alone.  And he hit every prisoner on the head or on the shoulders with his baton.  Sometimes, there were five or six of them who beat the prisoners.  But on that occasion, there was one guard who beat absolutely everyone who passed by.  He hit me on the ear.  And then the boys behind me pushed me, and I fell because I had slipped.  And I slipped on my knees, and I hit the door.  And the pain was very intense, because I was hit.  Then the boys got up.  I had felt a pain in my foot, and the guard I hadn't met before, he collected his wits about him.  He hit me while I was lying down, ten times with the baton -- with the thick cable.

I was standing alone.  There was no one behind me, so he was able to beat me very hard indeed.  I was able to run the 5 or 6 metres and join the other prisoners.  Well, about 15 minutes, I was trying to get up, and he kept beating me, so I can barely muster the strength to cross over to the other prisoners.  This was a fortunate thing for me because someone came and helped me up.  And when he saw in what condition I was, he said: "Well, he is useless." MR. TRALDI:  Yes, Your Honour. I will now read a brief oral summary of the witness's evidence for the public record. Mevludin Sejmenovic was one of the founders of the Party of Democratic Action, or SDA, and served as a representative from Prijedor. Sejmenovic observed the development of the Serbian Democratic Party, or SDS, and its pursuit of ethnic separation.  In Prijedor he saw the SDS demand the large majority of the land for Serbs.  On 29 and , Prijedor town was taken over by Serb soldiers and policemen.  In May 1992, Sejmenovic and other SDA leaders met with military officers and the Prijedor SDS president at the Prijedor SDS building.  The officers did almost all the talking.  They demanded that the Muslims surrender several thousand weapons, and when the Muslim representatives said they did not have that many weapons one officer said, "That's your problem.  If you do not do that, I will raze Kozarac to the ground."

Sejmenovic observed an organised campaign of expulsion in Prijedor, including the attack on Kozarac foreshadowed by this meeting and charged at Schedule A6.1 of the indictment.  Throughout Prijedor he saw the same pattern:  Serb forces would surround an area, open fire from all directions, and send the survives to Omarska and Trnopolje.  Numerous Muslim villages were destroyed. Eventually Sejmenovic entered Trnopolje.  He heard about killings and rapes.  Then six people who had helped him were killed, relevant to Scheduled Incident B13.5 and he escaped.  He later snuck back into the camp but soon surrendered to save the lives of other detainees.  He was then sent to Omarska.  Mr. Sejmenovic's evidence about these camps is relevant to the counts of torture and cruel treatment charged at Schedules C15.2 and C15.4 of the indictment. While at Omarska, Sejmenovic was interviewed by two Serb journalists.  One of them brought him a script to read and told him if he did so it would save his life.  He was forced to give a false statement implicating Muslim leaders in the conflict in Prijedor. And, Your Honours, that concludes the public summary of the witness's evidence.

TRALDI: Q.   Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to turn to a meeting between SDA leaders and leaders of the Serb community held in Prijedor which you discuss in your statement, now P283, beginning in paragraph 4. And, sir, I'm going to ask you a series of focused questions about this meeting.  You say here the meeting was held at the SDS headquarters.  When you arrived outside headquarters, who did you first meet?

A.   First we ran into several policemen, and although we had been announced and the SDS has approved our arrival and ordered the check-points to let us through because we were coming from Kozarac surrounded by police and military forces, the police still intercepted us before the premises of the SDS, asked to see our IDs and check us.  They were facing people whom they knew very well, officials, but they were just intimidating us.  At that point Simo Miskovic came out and invited us in.  He told the policemen to stop checking our IDs.
Q.   And then, I take it, you went inside.  Can you describe for the Chamber the room where you and Miskovic and the others went?

A.   It was a large room with two smaller rooms on the side, including a kitchenette, Dusan Kurnoga was sitting there and SDS officials, Slobodan Kuruzovic also an SDS official, one person I didn't know.
Q.   Let's skip with the room for a moment.  Were you all at one long table or were there a group of chairs distributed around the room?

A.   There was a long conference table.  The people I enumerated were already sitting on one side.  And an acquaintance of mine, Dusan Kurnoga, was in a smaller room off to the side and a girl who worked there as a secretary.  We started talking but --
Q.   Before we get into the conversation, where at the table was Mr. Miskovic sitting?

A.   Mr. Miskovic was sitting facing the rest of us.  He occasionally stood up and walked to the smaller room, sometimes of his own accord, sometimes summoned by Mr. Kurnoga.  They were expecting a fax.
Q.   And about how far away from you was he at the time?
A.   Very close.
Q.   And you describe in your statement that then some military officers arrived and joined the meeting.  Where did Major Zeljaja sit at the meeting?

A.   Major Zeljaja was sitting in the second chair behind the table. Colonel Arsic was sitting in the first chair, next to him Major Zeljaja. And next to Zeljaja the third person they brought in sat down and he was introduced as their military security officer.  Then there was Miskovic, next to Miskovic a person whose name I didn't know from the police, and next to Miskovic Slobodan Kuruzovic was sitting.  On the other side of the table we were sitting in this order.

Q.   Now, you say in paragraph 24 of your statement, on page 6 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S, that the Serb military and political figures at the meeting took identical positions.  Did one of them, one or the other - the military or the politicians - seem to be more in charge during the meeting, seem to be taking the lead?

A.   Miskovic as the president of the SDS spoke very little and he did not want to begin the meeting before Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja arrived.  We wanted to begin but he said he couldn't begin the meeting without them.  When the meeting began Colonel Arsic was taking the floor most of the time in the first part of the meeting and then Major Zeljaja took over and he ended the meeting.

Q.   And, sir, you discuss many of the details of what was said in your statement.  So I just want to ask you one more question about this meeting.  Based on your observations and the conversation during the meeting, did you develop an impression of what the Serb authorities in Prijedor intended to do next relative to Kozarac?

A.   Not only did we get an impression, we were told so in so many words.  At the beginning of the meeting they were playing cat and mouse with us and they made some jokes in very bad taste, at our expense; and we were very anxious, fearful, and we were hoping to -- we were looking for some hope at that meeting.  However, they gave us an ultimatum.  They told us how many troops they had under arms and what kind of weapons. But obviously they had not agreed beforehand so they gave us different figures.  One said that there were 5.000 armed men, Zeljaja said that Kozarac had 7.000 weapons, and this security officer said he had the best information and he said in fact we have 10.000 pieces of weapons --
Q.   I'm going to interrupt you just for a second.  When you say "they had not agreed beforehand," are you referring to agreement on how many weapons the Muslim community had?
A.   Correct, correct --
Q.   Thank you --
A.   -- the military security officer said.
Q.   Then I want to return to the question I'd asked you a moment ago: Did you develop an impression of what they intended to do next relative to Kozarac?

A.   Major Zeljaja said in so many words, I quote, "Unless you surrender 7.000 weapons, I will raze Kozarac to the ground."  He repeated that several times, and that was the last thing he said.  And he also added, Unless you surrender 7.000 weapons and unless the Serbian flag is flying over Kozarac and the Serb police have control, I'll raze Kozarac to the ground.  And he said at the end, When you return those weapons then we can go on talking.  Becir Medunjanin answered, How can we return them if we don't have them?  And to that he only said, That is your problem, gentlemen, this meeting is over.
Q.   When he said, "That is you problem gentlemen," did you get an impression of what was going to happen next?
A.   He repeated he would raze Kozarac to the ground unless we handed over the required --
Q.   [Previous translation continues]...
Q.   [Previous translation continues]...
A.   -- number of weapons.  He said we shouldn't play with him, the Banja Luka Corps.

Q.   Next, sir, I'm going to ask you three focused questions about the attempts to expand the Kozarac TO after the meeting which you describe in P283.  First, as best you can tell at its highest, about how many men were in the Kozarac TO?
A.   Do you mean the number before the expansion of the TO or after?
Q.   The most at any point.

A.   In peacetime it could have numbered several hundred at most, 1- to 200, that's my rough estimate, although I'm not really qualified to make it.  But in the attempt to enlarge the Territorial Defence we were still not able to boost it over a couple of hundred and this process of expansion was never finished because we neither had time nor the capability.

Q.   And in paragraph 28 of P283, on page 6 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S you talk about Serb leaders making reference to the Green Berets.  As far as you knew, were there any Green Berets in Prijedor in May and June of 1992?
A.   No, there were no Green Berets or any other formation.  The term "Green Berets" was used by Serb officers as propaganda without any substance to it.
Q.   Now, sir, have you heard of a village named Radmilovo in the Prijedor?

A.   Radmilovo village does not exist in the Prijedor municipality and it never did.  I heard that the Serb army had renamed Kozarac into Radmilovo village after their successful operation offensive and the razing of Kozarac.  It was done by Zeljaja.  I heard that Zeljaja's name was Radmilo and that they renamed Kozarac after him.  I was not there to see it, but I was informed that there was even a [indiscernible] at the entry into Kozarac with that name.

Q.   And, sir, at paragraph 40 of your statement, on page 9 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S, you describe the destruction of non-Serb villages and say Serb-populated villages experienced little or no damage.  I have only one question:  Is what you say about this the distinction that I just repeated, is that based on your personal observations?
A.   Yes, I was able to see that myself as I was being taken out of Trnopolje to be taken to the prison in Prijedor, and when I was taken from the prison in Prijedor to Omarska.
Q.   And, sir, was your own property damaged in Prijedor during this period?
A.   I did not have any property in Prijedor.  At the time I had -- I lived in an old house and it was partly damaged.
Q.   And, I'm sorry, when I said "Prijedor" I meant to refer to the municipality rather than the town.  That old house you referred to, that ; right?
A.   Correct.
Q.   And do you know during this period what happened to the mosques in Prijedor municipality?
A.   The mosques were destroyed, usually by tanks or they were blown up.
Q.   And when did you hear about the mosques being destroyed?

A.   We heard about that often from people who were deported to Trnopolje camp from various parts of Prijedor, and we heard it practically first-hand because some of those people were witnesses to that destruction.  And I was able to see it myself as I was being deported from the prison in Prijedor towards Omarska.  There had been a lot of mosques along that road, but not anymore.
Q.   And do you know the name of any of the specific mosques that had previously been along that road?
A.   Along that road was the mosque in Mujkanovici, Kozarusa, Kamicani, Jakupovici, and I've listed only some of them.
Q.   And, sir, I'd now like to turn to your time in Trnopolje.
MR. TRALDI:  And I'd ask the court officer to please call up 65 ter 11338.
Q.   And, sir, in your statement you described entering Trnopolje. Can you describe the physical condition of the people you saw who were held there?

A.   In the camp I first heard only hearsay information, but when I came closer, like 700 metres from the camp, I could see people inside. They looked exhausted.  They moved slowly, gazing with dull eyes.  Some of them were lying on the grass because they had no accommodation, not even improvised.  Later I went in and had contact with some of the people and I got more specific information.
Q.   And does this picture of the detainee in the front of this picture, does this accurately reflect the state of health of the people you saw in Trnopolje?

Q.   Mr. Sejmenovic, in paragraph 56 of P283, it's page 12 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S, you mention that Islam Bahonjic, Becir Medunjanin, and Mr. Medunjanin's wife were killed in Omarska.  I only have one question about this paragraph.  Do you know the first name of Mr. Medunjanin's wife?

A.   Your Honour, it is difficult to express this feeling.  You are in a pot where everything is death and death alone.  And then a person appears from top political echelons and it's as if nothing had happened, tries to talk to you only about politics.  Of course I was in fear, I was tense, and I thought that this was another thing I had to face before my death.  I kept silent for the most part and Vojo Kupresanin spoke and this was not really a conversation it was more of a monologue.
